Scope and evidence standard

“Doosan” here means Doosan Enerbility, formerly Doosan Heavy Industries & Construction. Evidence is primarily from South Korean supplier programmes, with historical Doosan Vina examples identified separately. Doosan Corporation, Bobcat, Infracore and construction affiliates have their own systems and are not interchangeable. Doosan’s customer-facing turbine supply contracts and internal factory investments are not treated as upstream supplier development.

The live reference document was accessible and its Research–Auto methodology, Auto evidence decisions and criteria, Samsung distinction and existing Doosan material were reviewed. Layer 1 retains qualification, monitoring, corrective-action and support practices. Layer 2 asks what changed at suppliers because of identifiable buyer, supplier and expert contributions, how that was checked, and what learning remained. A KEEP decision does not imply Level 5.
2 Supplier selection and support
Five distinct decisions

Supplier entry begins with a registration review. The 2026 report identifies creditworthiness and business suitability, followed by evaluation of price, quality, delivery and technical capability. Electronic ESG and ethical-management commitments are part of the entry and bidding process. This is a qualification mechanism; passing it does not establish readiness for every future product or entitlement to technical assistance. [1, p.59]

Ongoing assessment is a separate activity. The 2023 report distinguishes a biennial comprehensive assessment of Tier 1 suppliers on quality, price and delivery from annual ESG assessment; 695 suppliers underwent the former in 2022. Current reporting continues to describe regular capability assessment, but does not confirm that this historical cadence still applies to every business group. [6, p.53; 2, pp.59–60]

Support selection is clearest in ESG. The current website describes annual self-diagnosis, review of evidence and selected on-site due diligence with specialist organizations. Poor results lead to corrective-action requirements; high-risk suppliers can receive visits and help with improvement plans. This establishes a response beyond collecting declarations, while leaving the exact risk cutoffs and allocation of consulting hours undisclosed. [2]

Technical support follows a different pathway. The K-Nuclear programme concerns suppliers involved in nuclear manufacturing and offers specialist knowledge transfer. Historical consulting matched supplier needs with external consultants or retired executives. The published material does not establish one common decision formula covering strategic importance, quality problems, technical complexity, financing need and willingness to implement change. [5, 8]
Ownership and escalation

Current governance places Shared Growth/Procurement under the Management Division, with the Shared Growth Team responsible for support programmes and supply-chain ESG work. Business-group procurement organizations perform operating procurement; assessment issues reach top management and the ESG Committee. The 2024 report shows a different procurement-office structure. These are dated organizational descriptions, not simultaneous layers in a reconstructed global hierarchy. [1, p.59; 10, p.51]

The Supplier Call Center gives suppliers a route to raise problems with the Win-Win Growth Team, which refers matters to the relevant function and provides feedback. This is useful problem intake. It does not publish a service-level commitment, engineering-resource approval rule or capability-project exit standard. [10]

The linked ESG indicators make the assessment expectations more explicit: training investment, safety systems, product inspection procedures and test records, plus suppliers’ own upstream ESG management. These are published expectations and diagnostic prompts. They do not prove that the supplier has implemented them effectively. [23, PDF pp.11–14]
How support is scaled—and what is not disclosed

The published model uses several delivery channels: broad education, small-group instruction, tailored visits, technical specialists, government-linked support and financial institutions. It can therefore reach different needs without relying entirely on a single central engineering team. That is an analytical reading of the programme mix, not a disclosed resource-optimization model. [2–5, 8]

Important allocation details remain missing: who approves intensive technical projects, minimum supplier commitments, specialist caseloads, visit cadence, duration, co-investment rules, stop/go criteria, handover and deterioration-triggered re-entry. The 2026 report does disclose a KRW 240 million, equally company/government-funded SME ESG programme serving 72 suppliers in 2025. This is a specific ESG programme budget; it cannot stand in for the overall supplier-development budget. [1, p.61]
3 Findings by domain
A Future business readiness
Layer 1 Technical preparation and regional entry

The 2022 report connects portfolio change with supplier technology exchanges and joint preparation for new businesses. It reports item-level supply-chain establishment for the Gimpo CHP project and the 8 MW wind-turbine model, while SMR, cask and waste-to-energy supply-chain work was still in progress. These are different completion states. They support a defined technical-preparation route, but not validated supplier capacity or a completed ramp-up intervention. [12, printed pp.70–71; PDF p.38]

A5 is rated 3 because the preparation route is reinforced by an operating technical-support mechanism for nuclear suppliers. The July 2024 account describes knowledge exchange with welding, machining and nondestructive-testing specialists, quality consulting and learning from failures. It identifies participating supplier employees and managers. This is more informative than a generic commitment to innovation, although it does not show one supplier acquiring and qualifying a new production process. [8]

Localization support has a different scope. The current strategy lists overseas client prequalification assistance and joint entry into overseas sites. The historical 2017 report describes a Vietnam arrangement offering land access through Doosan Vina and advice on administration, finance, management and HR, alongside provincial assistance. This addresses the organizational burden of establishing overseas operations; it is not simply switching orders to a local source. A4 is rated 3 within this dated regional-development scope. [3, 5, printed pp.78–79; PDF p.42]
Layer 2 Vietnam establishment: promising, incompletely verified

The evidence chain begins with a need for suppliers to enter overseas markets and a gap in local establishment know-how. The historical buyer contribution was an enabling location and advisory support; suppliers would establish offices and factories; the province would assist with administration and incentives. A 22 August 2018 Vietnam News Agency report names six Korean firms receiving licences and starting factory construction near Doosan Vina, including Samshin Valve Vina and Nasan Vietnam. This is implementation progress, not evidence that all transferred processes had reached qualified production. [5, 14]

Decision: INVESTIGATE. The 2017 corporate account and 2018 regional report are consistent with an establishment pathway, but do not prove that the same six-company cohort completed qualified production because of the stated support. A separate December 2018 article describes an association with 11 Vietnamese suppliers; it is a distinct population and cannot be combined with the Korean entrants. Later supplier accounts or factory acceptance records would be the best next evidence. [14–15]

The historical status matters. Doosan’s governance page records approval of a Doosan Vina share-sale agreement in 2025. This is sufficient reason to avoid treating the old Vietnam arrangement as a current Doosan Enerbility operating model; approval alone is not used here to assert a completed sale date. [16]
Demand, capacity and ramp-up boundaries

A1, A2 and A3 remain NE. Business-outlook presentations, a new supply base and a buyer’s own expansion plan do not establish supplier-level future volume/mix planning, demonstrated available capacity or controlled rate increase. The missing evidence is a recurring supplier readiness review connecting future load to machines, skilled labour, qualified processes, sub-tier constraints and validated milestones.

Digital projects are relevant leads. EMRO’s original project announcement describes an integrated procurement platform using quotation and order history for supplier evaluation and development, with completion planned for the second half of 2026. Its webpage carries a January 2026 posting timestamp but the release body is dated 5 June 2025. No completion is inferred from the target date. A May 2026 industrial-district article describes AI supply-chain demonstration work and output-growth targets; targets are not achieved supplier readiness gains. [17–18]
B Supplier production-system capability
Layer 1 Qualification, preventive quality and corrective action

A detailed historical nuclear presentation helps explain what sits behind supplier evaluation. In November 2018, Doosan’s QA manager described submission of a Vendor Information Report to procurement, technical and quality evaluation, audits by qualified lead auditors and registration on an approved vendor list. For safety-related complete items, the presentation specifies an audit before the initial order, triennial renewal audit and annual evaluation. Those controls are historical nuclear evidence, not a current global supplier manual. [11, slides 9, 11]

The same presentation separates initial qualification, procurement control and periodic management. It includes source inspection, surveillance, corrective-action follow-up and a staged restriction process for serious quality problems. This is an established oversight mechanism and remains valuable in Layer 1. Its statement that vendors are monitored or coached does not disclose an implemented coaching project or demonstrate transferred competence. Recommendations on reducing duplicate audits are expressly recommendations, not evidence that those reforms were adopted. [11, slides 12–15]

Current quality reporting is consistent with preventive control rather than reliance on certification alone. The 2024 report’s DQMS architecture includes vendor quality plans, inspection management, nonconformance records, root-cause/corrective-action records and recurrence-prevention tasks. These records can connect a defect with an accountable action and later review. They do not establish that all suppliers operate the same daily production system or that corrective-action closure means employees have learned to solve future problems independently. [9, p.43]

The 2025 report gives a more specific knowledge-sharing routine: external Quality Alerts ask partner companies to check for similar critical or recurring problems and undertake preventive activities. Quality Information covers systems, procedures and code requirements; other communications share improvement cases. This supports a defined cross-supplier learning and escalation route, while leaving response compliance and sustained application unclear. B1, B3 and B6 are therefore 3 in the quality-management scope, not assessments of an entire lean production system. [13, p.49]
Layer 1 Improvement support and employee learning

The quality-training figures show activity over multiple periods. The 2024 report records 503 people from 205 suppliers receiving quality guidance/improvement training in 2023; the 2025 report records 180 companies in 2024. These are reach measures with different units, not a trend in acquired skill. The current programme menu also includes a national HR-development consortium and benefit sharing. B7 requires more than programme availability: it asks whether employees apply and retain production problem-solving capability. [9, p.53; 14, p.58; 4]

Historical implementation is more concrete than the current menu alone. In 2017, external consultants visited suppliers to identify and execute improvement assignments. The report attributes an average 10.4% cost reduction to the 26 suppliers supported since 2014, spanning purchasing, productivity and design. It also records need-matched consulting from retired executives and quality-system assistance from experienced Master Hands. These facts support B2 at 3; the result does not establish today’s coverage, a repeatable factory-wide improvement cycle or Level 5. [5, printed pp.78–79; PDF p.42]
Layer 2 K-Nuclear technical support: deployed mechanism

The business need is nuclear manufacturing competence. The support mechanism places experienced buyer specialists in direct contact with supplier technicians rather than limiting engagement to senior executives or compliance staff. The July 2024 event included 18 technicians and three managers from major nuclear suppliers, shared quality-improvement examples and a technical exchange at Changwon. Supplier Yungjin Techwin is named; an employee described the value of the exchange and seeing installed products. This is participant testimony about learning opportunity, not proof of improved production performance. [8]

Decision: KEEP—supporting mechanism. The publication states that tailored quality consulting, failure-case education and safety/quality discussions are continuously available. It establishes delivery beyond an announcement. The missing links are supplier-specific diagnosis, what process or skill changed, the acceptance check and subsequent independent use. A discussion with Yungjin Techwin could test whether expert advice was incorporated into work standards or qualification records. Until then, B7 remains 3 for defined production learning support. [8]
Layer 2 Historical consulting: outcome lead with incomplete mechanism

Decision: INVESTIGATE the 26-supplier consulting cohort as completed capability-building proof; KEEP its deployed support route in Layer 1. On-site diagnosis, assignment execution and an aggregate cost outcome are reported. However, the source does not identify a supplier, define the cost baseline, separate procurement savings from production improvements, or explain which equipment, methods or routines changed. It also does not provide post-project retention. Those omissions prevent reconstruction of the full evidence chain, despite the attractive numerical result. [5]
Layer 2 Safety-management case: completed within its scope

A January 2018 account of the 2017 programme addresses a specific SME gap: limited safety expertise and resources. Buyer experts supported risk assessment, practical training and certification preparation. Supplier employees periodically filmed real high-risk work, identified unsafe behaviour and discussed how to remove the hazards; supervisors and senior managers attended an intensive three-day workshop. Thus the intervention includes an implemented worker routine and management involvement, not just a requirement to obtain a certificate. [7]

The account reports risk-assessment recognition for 43 of 51 participating suppliers and safety-management certification for 25; 23 obtained both. Sungjin Technology’s representative reports that employees became more active in prevention. Decision: KEEP—completed intervention, historical South Korean safety scope. Certification provides an external check of a management capability, but the buyer reports the counts and supplier ownership is testimonial. No longitudinal incident result or independent future problem-solving is demonstrated. The case informs operating routines and learning; it does not establish yield, throughput or tested supply recovery. [7]

A June 2024 safety programme launch with 53 suppliers shows continuing attention to similar needs and planned external consulting. It is not follow-up evidence for the same 2017 cohort, nor proof of completed 2024 results. This distinction prevents a historical intervention and a later announcement being presented as one sustained case. [19]
Flow and sustainable output remain unproven

B4 and B5 remain NE after searches for bottleneck, throughput, lead-time and productivity interventions. DESM provides equipment/material schedule and site-handling visibility, while the latest report describes a partner-equipment progress-management solution. Those are useful buyer-side coordination practices. They do not establish supplier factory queue reduction, constraint management or sustainable end-to-end output improvement. Nor can internal robotic-welding or AI gains at Doosan’s own plant be assigned to upstream suppliers. [13, p.49; 2, p.51]
C Resilience and continuity
Layer 1 Recurring exposure-based prioritization

C2 is the clearest routine practice. The 2024 report describes annual updating of significant Tier 1 suppliers using strategic item importance, transaction scale and continuity, together with country and procurement risk. Current reporting links classification to ESG management intensity. This supports 4 for recurring prioritization within the disclosed strategic/ESG scope. It does not establish a complete multi-tier dependency map, site-level single points of failure or quantified time-to-recover. [9, p.51; 2, p.60]

Financial and payment support can help suppliers absorb constraints. The current strategy lists interest-free direct support, preferential lending arrangements, order/performance-linked loans, safety-management costs and payment systems. These are enabling mechanisms. The reviewed evidence does not trace financing into a specific supplier’s capacity investment or show restoration of interrupted critical supply. [3]
Layer 2 ESG improvement: assessment linked to verified change

The July 2024 Korean account distinguishes two groups: suppliers receiving their first ESG evaluation attended small-group education, while suppliers with weaknesses in the preceding assessment received tailored visits. Consultants selected weak indicators, showed other companies’ examples and supplied practical material. This establishes need-specific support rather than a uniform lecture. [4]

For 2025, the latest report identifies a cohort of 31 suppliers targeted for rating improvement: all received guidance visits and 24 achieved improved ratings. Decision: KEEP—completed intervention for assessed ESG management improvement. Supplier action plans, buyer/expert assistance and a reported follow-up result are linked at cohort level. The record lacks named-supplier operating changes and long-term autonomous learning. Better ratings do not prove higher yield, shorter recovery time or uninterrupted supply. [1, pp.60–62]
Layer 2 Carbon-data capability: implemented support infrastructure

HanaLoop’s supplier publication describes a concrete regulatory-data gap: Doosan’s existing platform did not provide supplier-inclusive product carbon data needed for CBAM response. The provider reports implementing supplier data input, evidence management, product mapping and automated reporting, with supplier onboarding and training. Decision: KEEP—supporting mechanism. The evidence concerns a deployed data-and-support infrastructure; the commercial provider gives no named supplier competence test, adoption denominator or later independent operation. [20]

This is useful adaptation preparation and remains in Layer 1 for C4. It is insufficient for a score on continuity through structural change. Similarly, published corporate BCM and cybersecurity exercises concern Doosan’s own operations, not demonstrated supplier recovery exercises. C1, C3 and C4 remain NE because supplier-owned disruption response, recurring demand/supply adjustment and maintained supply through structural changes are not sufficiently established. [13, information-security section; 21]

Anchor calibration: 1 Ad hoc—reactive or individual-dependent; 2 Emerging—limited practice/pilot with uneven ownership or follow-through; 3 Defined—documented processes/roles are used but integration or follow-through is uneven; 4 Routine—regular use, ownership and recurring follow-up within scope; 5 Leading and sustained—improvement over time with learning embedded in operations. Qualitative evidence can support 5. No criterion reaches 5 here.
5 Case decisions

Each decision applies to a candidate evidence claim, not to the value of the programme as a whole. Completed interventions can have unresolved sustainment; supporting mechanisms remain useful even when supplier results are not public.
KEEP — completed intervention | 2017 supplier safety management

South Korean Doosan Heavy Industries programme: practical risk-assessment support, worker video reviews, management workshops and achieved certification/recognition. This is the clearest chain from expertise gap through changed routines to an external capability check. Supplier ownership is reported in testimony; long-term retention is not established. Next: obtain Sungjin Technology’s later risk-assessment records, supervisor handover and worker-led hazard examples. [7]
KEEP — completed intervention | 2025 ESG rating improvement

The targeted cohort, guidance visits and improved ratings are reported together. Useful evidence of implemented assessed-management improvement, with the cohort result in Section 3. Missing: named suppliers, changed controls, rating-verification method and later sustainment. Next: ask Shared Growth for one anonymized before/after action file and a subsequent assessment. This case does not upgrade production or recovery scores. [1, pp.60–62]
KEEP — supporting mechanism | K-Nuclear Technology Supporters

The July 2024 account documents operating technical exchange and available tailored services. Buyer specialists and supplier employees are identified. Missing: case-level diagnosis, implementation and acceptance. Next: interview Yungjin Techwin on a specific welding, machining or NDE issue and request changed work instructions, qualification evidence and a later supplier-led solution. [8]
KEEP — supporting mechanism | Supplier carbon-data system

HanaLoop reports implementation and supplier training/onboarding. Missing: supplier adoption, data-quality checks, competence and independent maintenance. Next: obtain one supplier’s completed data flow and the record of corrections made without provider help. Commercial-provider testimony requires corroboration. [20]
INVESTIGATE | Historical external-consulting cohort

Executed assignments and an aggregate cost result are promising. Missing supplier identity, exact production change, outcome baseline and post-support record. Next: request one original project-closure file or a supplier case from the 2014–2017 cohort. Keep the consulting mechanism in Layer 1 even if no further record becomes available. [5]
INVESTIGATE | Vietnam supplier establishment

Advisory/site support and subsequent licences/construction are documented in different accounts. Missing matched cohort, operating factories, qualified output and current ownership boundary. Next: Samshin Valve Vina or Nasan Vietnam’s commissioning and customer-approval history. Do not equate a factory licence with production capability. [5, 14–16]
INVESTIGATE | AI supply-chain and procurement projects

Specific project scope exists, but implementation completion and supplier-level gains are unresolved. Next: EMRO system acceptance, Gyeongnam Technopark demonstration results and a participating supplier’s planning changes. The press article’s output and revenue figures are targets. [17–18]
REJECT as standalone proof | Qualification and three-out controls

Audits, approval lists and restrictions establish qualification and oversight. Without a delivered support intervention, they do not establish transferred capability. Keep the operating details under B1/B3/B6. Next question: which quality finding led to coaching and what could the supplier do afterward? [11]
REJECT as standalone proof | Attendance, awards and approvals

Partner’s Day attendance, training reach, shared-growth awards and benefit-sharing approval counts establish activity or recognition. They do not demonstrate applied supplier learning. Keep them as programme context; request completed work and follow-up evidence before making effectiveness claims. [1, 9, 13, 21]
REJECT as standalone proof | 2024 safety launch and buyer-only gains

A launch commits resources but does not prove completed supplier change. Internal factory AI/robotics, customer turbine contracts and company BCM do not establish upstream supplier capability transfer. Keep relevant context with its boundary. Next: supplier-specific implementation or recovery evidence. [1, 19]
6 Potential relevance to Siemens Energy

The following are analytical hypotheses for programme design and peer discussion. They are not assertions about Doosan’s operating practices beyond the cited evidence, and they do not affect maturity scores.
Match technical support to the process that constrains delivery

The specialist-to-technician model is worth investigating for low-volume, high-complexity components. Siemens Energy could select a small number of exposed suppliers where a specific welding procedure, machining setup, inspection method or engineering-document gap threatens a project milestone. The intervention should begin with the supplier’s actual job, not a generic maturity presentation. Adaptation would require the applicable turbine, grid or nuclear codes, customer approval obligations and controlled handling of technical information. The K-Nuclear mechanism is the observed starting point; this proposed selection design is a hypothesis. [8]
Use assessment to choose the help, then verify a different thing

Doosan’s ESG pathway suggests a useful design principle: an assessment identifies the weakness, and support is tailored to that weakness. For production capability, Siemens Energy would need a different verification measure. A supplier with repeated weld repairs might need coached parameter control and operator qualification; closure should check accepted weld quality and the supplier’s ability to diagnose a later variation. Repeating the assessment alone would risk measuring documentation rather than learning. [2, 4]
Separate working capital from manufacturing investment

Finance can enable development when a capable supplier cannot fund the next step. The funding decision should specify whether it covers working capital, a qualified machine, tooling, skilled labour or process approval. For long-lead equipment, milestones should reflect design release, material availability, first accepted operation and a repeatable production cycle. The existence of Doosan’s finance channels supports investigating this combination; no causal supplier-capacity result is assumed. [3]
Turn quality alerts into supplier-owned learning

External alerts can scale lessons across suppliers, but distribution is only the first step. A Siemens Energy adaptation could ask suppliers to identify exposure, demonstrate the preventive change and teach the lesson to relevant employees. A later review should sample whether the practice is still used and whether the supplier can address a similar issue without another buyer intervention. This would strengthen the learning chain beyond the documented communication mechanism. [13]
Use regional partners without confusing establishment with readiness

The Vietnam example suggests combining technical qualification with local administrative and management assistance. For Siemens Energy, a localization project would need explicit transfer acceptance: equipment capability, trained personnel, approved sub-tier sources, inspection capacity and logistics. Local authorities or industry bodies could reduce establishment friction, while the buyer and supplier retain responsibility for production readiness. The historical example is a hypothesis source, not evidence that the same model remains available today. [5, 14–16]
Add continuity development to risk classification

A criticality list should lead to action on the underlying dependency. For a scarce forging or specialized heat-treatment source, the useful development output may be a tested alternate route, a recovery work package or a qualified backup team. Siemens Energy should investigate whether Doosan has examples beyond its published classification. This chapter found no supplier recovery case strong enough to validate the proposed extension. [9]
Define completion and handover before support begins

A practical pilot could use five review points: an agreed business exposure; a jointly diagnosed supplier gap; an implemented change with named supplier ownership; an accepted result over a relevant production cycle; and a later supplier-led problem or repeated application. In long-cycle production, sustainment may require reviewing the next comparable order rather than waiting for an arbitrary monthly output target. This is a proposed application of the evidence chain, not a claimed Doosan project methodology.

Korean supplier-development research supports examining training, evaluation, information sharing, finance and partnership together. Lee’s 2020 study reports a relationship between supplier-development programmes and technological competence, with strategic partnership mediating that relationship. The accessible abstract informs interview design; it neither evaluates Doosan nor establishes causality for Siemens Energy’s supply base. [22]
7 Research limitations and references
Evidence limits and unresolved contradictions

The public record is materially stronger on programme architecture, activity and ESG follow-up than on supplier factory outcomes. It does not disclose a complete development allocation model or a current public Enerbility supplier quality manual covering all business groups. The 2018 nuclear presentation is unusually detailed but remains historical. The separate Bobcat quality manual was excluded from Enerbility claims.

The 2026 report gives conflicting Shared Growth Fund figures for end-2025: approximately KRW 81.7 billion disbursed in the narrative on p.60, versus KRW 77.6 billion supported in the table on p.62, against a KRW 89 billion fund. The reviewed text does not explain the basis difference. Neither figure is used to estimate programme effectiveness. The report also identifies 20 currently at-risk suppliers and a 31-supplier improvement cohort; these are different measures/populations and are not combined. [1]

Historical Vietnam accounts differ on the number of Korean partners associated with 2017 arrangements: the corporate report describes six, while the December 2018 VNA article refers to five. This may reflect scope or timing, but cannot be resolved publicly here. The 2018 six-factory construction report is retained as a lead without claiming exact cohort continuity. Its reported land area also appears implausible and is not used. [5, 14–15]

The reports’ external assurance does not make every programme outcome an independently verified intervention result. Aggregate ESG rating improvement may reflect documentation, operational change, cohort composition or several factors; these effects cannot be separated. Supplier testimony and provider case studies are attributed. No claim of universal supplier effectiveness follows from them.

Doosan Enerbility Supplier Capability Development
Extended deep research for Siemens Energy and the Kearney Student Lab

Research cut off 16 October 2026. This chapter examines Doosan Enerbility's supplier support, including historical Doosan Heavy Industries and Construction practices where explicitly identified. Doosan Corporation, Bobcat and Infracore evidence is not attributed to Enerbility. The sixteen Siemens Energy criteria are a discovery guide only. No maturity scores are assigned.
1 Executive assessment

Doosan Enerbility offers a substantial set of supplier support mechanisms relevant to power equipment: specialist technical assistance, expert-led quality support, worker-led safety improvement, tailored ESG consulting, financing and help entering overseas markets. The strongest contemporary evidence identifies owners and follow-up for ESG improvement. The strongest historical operational evidence reports external consulting and supplier cost improvement. Technical mentoring is credible, but supplier-level production results and independent learning remain less visible. [1][5][7]

The sources support several different delivery systems rather than a single seamless development funnel. Nuclear qualification protects safety and product conformity. Shared Growth programs supply technical, organizational and financial help. ESG evaluation selects a separate improvement cohort. Historical safety work embeds practical risk routines. These systems should be connected analytically only where a source establishes the link.

For Siemens Energy, the most promising mechanisms are access to scarce manufacturing experts and the combination of diagnosis with practical assistance. Public reporting also exposes a recurring evidence problem: certification, consulting reach, improved assessment ratings and process performance are different outcomes. The report preserves all four without treating any one as a substitute for the others.
1.1 Scope and evidence boundaries

The 2026 Integrated Report primarily covers calendar 2025 with selected 2026 updates. Historical reports concern Doosan Heavy Industries and Construction before its renaming. Korean releases are translated or paraphrased here, with their event dates retained. A Vietnam establishment initiative is a historical regional example, not evidence of current global deployment. The evidence chain ends only when the supplier can retain and reuse what changed.
2 Supplier selection and support delivery
2.1 Owners and entry channels

The 2026 report places oversight with the executive responsible for Shared Growth and Procurement under the Management Division. The Shared Growth Team operates support programs and supplier ESG evaluation; procurement organizations in each Business Group handle sourcing. ESG results and material issues reach senior management and the ESG Committee. This identifies governance and delivery ownership, without proving that the same committee approves every technical intervention. [1, pp.59–62]

The Supplier Call Center provides another intake route. Matters are assigned to an appropriate representative; the public page identifies the Win-Win Growth Team and allows suppliers to receive feedback on actions. It is a channel for difficulties and concerns, not a published entitlement to engineering support or a disclosed technical-project prioritization process. [9]
2.2 Assessment translated into tailored support

The current Supplier ESG page describes annual specialist evaluation, supplier self-diagnosis and document review, with selected onsite due diligence and improvement guidance. High-risk suppliers can receive visits and help preparing improvement plans. This is more specific than merely requesting a questionnaire: evidence is reviewed, risks are differentiated, and selected suppliers receive practical support. The source does not publish universal selection weights or the amount of support per supplier. [2]

A July 2024 Korean implementation account differentiates first-time assessed suppliers from suppliers with weak prior ratings. The former receive explanatory education; the latter receive tailored visits focused on deficient indicators. Consultants use examples and practical materials to help suppliers improve. This establishes that support content can follow a diagnosis. It does not identify a resulting change in a particular supplier's manufacturing process. [4]

In its calendar-2025 performance table, the 2026 report states that all 31 suppliers targeted for ESG rating improvement received onsite guidance and 24 improved their ratings. These are visit coverage and assessment outcomes, not evidence that defects, capacity or lead time improved. The same report identifies a separate ESG support budget shared with public funding; that amount should not be described as the budget for all supplier development. [1, p.62]

3 Future business readiness
3.1 Nuclear qualification and technical competence

Jeong Sun Kim's 2018 presentation at the OECD Nuclear Energy Agency explains a nuclear supplier evaluation sequence involving procurement, technical review and quality assurance. It covers vendor information, assessment or audit, approval, surveillance and renewal. Initial audit and periodic renewal protect the approved supply base; annual evaluation is a separate monitoring layer. This is a historical practitioner account of assurance, not a completed coaching project. [10, slides 9–15]

The relevant readiness distinction is between approval for safety-related work and development of a missing manufacturing skill. A supplier can comply with an approved quality system yet still need assistance with a difficult weld, machining sequence or inspection technique. Conversely, a useful expert visit does not automatically qualify a new nuclear process. The public sources do not provide a linked case demonstrating both steps for the same supplier.
3.2 Specialist assistance and overseas preparation

The K-Nuclear Technology Supporters program was launched in 2023. A July 2024 release describes access to experts in welding, machining and nondestructive testing, tailored technical help, failure-case sharing and discussion of supplier difficulties. At the July 3 event, 18 supplier technicians and three managers joined company leaders and three technical masters. A named Youngjin Techwin employee described the value of technical exchange and seeing installed equipment. This establishes deployed support and reach, not a measured supplier quality gain. [7]

The current Shared Growth strategy page also lists support for overseas client prequalification, joint entry to overseas construction sites, technical and human-resource development, benefit sharing and finance. These are documented support options. They should not be represented as a completed readiness pathway for every gas-turbine, wind or nuclear supplier. [3]
3.3 Historical Vietnam establishment case

The 2017 report describes an arrangement under which six suppliers could use part of Doosan Vina's site and obtain administrative, finance, management and human-resource advice, with provincial administrative support. Vietnam News Agency's August 2018 account identifies six Korean investments and construction commencement, including Samshin Valve Vina and Nasan Vietnam. This advances the evidence beyond a training announcement to physical establishment activity. It does not verify production acceptance, local workforce competence or repeat delivery. 4 Production system interventions and learning
4.1 Consulting tied to improvement assignments

The 2017 report states that external professional consultants visited suppliers to identify and execute improvement assignments. Twenty-six suppliers had received help since 2014, with reported effects in purchasing, productivity and design and an average cost reduction of 10.4%. This is an aggregate company claim; the report does not publish the denominator calculation, supplier-level countermeasures or persistence of the savings. [5, pp.78–79]

Decision: KEEP as a completed intervention at the disclosed aggregate level. The consultants helped execute work, rather than merely assessing suppliers. Nevertheless, the average should not be read as a universal productivity improvement: purchasing savings and design changes can reduce cost without increasing output. A useful next source would separate the improvement categories and show a completed supplier work package.
4.2 Quality Master Hands and management advice

The same historical report describes matching supplier needs with retired executive advisers and using experienced quality Master Hands to help establish supplier quality systems. These are specific sources of expertise beyond procurement enforcement. The report does not describe the individual work instructions, control plans or later supplier-led projects. [5]

For Siemens Energy, the distinction between technical knowledge and advisory time matters. An expert may know the process but still need the supplier's production data, operators and management authority to implement a change. The source establishes access to expertise; it does not quantify how those complementary resources were secured or maintained.
4.3 Safety routines with supplier employee participation

A January 2018 release describes the 2017 safety and health program: company experts helped suppliers identify hazards, assess risks and prepare for recognition or certification. Supplier workers filmed high-risk work, discussed unsafe behaviors and developed improvements. Supervisors and senior managers attended an intensive three-day risk workshop. Of 51 participating suppliers, 43 obtained risk-assessment recognition and 25 safety-management certification, with 23 obtaining both. Sungjin Technology's leader attributed stronger worker participation to the support. [6]

Decision: KEEP as a completed intervention in safety-management capability. The routine requires employees to examine their own work and contribute to controls; it goes beyond an attendance-only course. Recognition supports verification of management arrangements. It does not demonstrate a lower incident rate, faster restart or independent problem-solving after Doosan's involvement reduced. The supplier statement is evidence of perceived ownership, not independent longitudinal validation.
4.4 Quality information and recurring prevention

The 2024 report describes Doosan's quality-management information arrangements, including supplier quality plans, inspection, nonconformity handling and prevention of recurrence. The 2025 report describes external quality alerts intended to prevent serious issues recurring elsewhere in the supply base, alongside supplier guidance and training. These are information and prevention mechanisms, with reporting-period scope retained. They do not establish that every recipient adopted the lesson or changed a control. [8][12]

The important learning question is whether an alert becomes an implemented supplier routine. A supplier could read a failure notice without reviewing its own process, updating an inspection point or teaching an operator. Public training reach therefore remains separate from completed preventive action and retained capability.

6.1 Analytical hypotheses for Siemens Energy

A manufacturing expert pool is worth testing where supplier problems are highly technical and occur infrequently. Welding, NDT and difficult machining skills may be too scarce for every category team to hold. An adapted model would combine a central specialist with the supplier's process owner and a local buyer engineer, with the scope set around one difficult operation.

A second hypothesis is to connect practical diagnosis with funding approval. If a constraint requires fixtures, training or inspection equipment, financing should be tied to a validated process need and acceptance test. The reviewed Doosan sources show both support types but do not establish that this integrated decision rule already exists.

Finally, the safety-video example offers a concrete approach to supplier ownership. Siemens Energy could adapt the principle to a controlled technical problem: supplier staff document the work, identify the failure mechanism and propose a countermeasure, while the expert coaches rather than writes the answer. Confidentiality, nuclear quality rules and safe observation would need to be addressed. Verification should include a later problem solved by supplier staff.
7 Research limitations and references

Confidence is high in identified governance and the reported delivery of guidance. Confidence is moderate in aggregate operational effects and supplier testimony; the underlying project records are not public. Confidence is low in sustained autonomous production improvement across the broader supplier population.

Sources were reviewed through 16 October 2026. Current program pages and Korean implementation releases were read alongside the reporting series. No capability claim is borrowed from other Doosan businesses.

Follow-up searches covered nuclear technical support, quality experts, ESG guidance, overseas establishment, safety, finance and carbon reporting. They did not produce a named supplier production case with both sustained operating data and evidence of independent problem-solving. General Korean supplier-development research provides context but does not establish Doosan-specific causality. [15]

The priority evidence request is one technical assistance record covering initial gap, assigned experts, supplier contribution, changed process, acceptance data and later supplier ownership. The absence of that public record is an evidence limitation, not a conclusion that the capability is absent. References retain publication and case dates; access or recheck date is 16 October 2026.

GE Vernova | Supplier Capability Benchmark

Evidence reviewed: 17 October 2026. Ratings describe maturity visible in public evidence; segment-level, role-based, historical and single-site observations retain their stated scope. GE Vernova became an independent company in April 2024, so most public evidence covers a short post-spin period and inherits programmes designed inside GE.
1. Summary and scope

GE Vernova's benchmark combines a disclosed corporate lean system with measured results inside its own factories, dedicated supplier-facing capacity and lean roles, a qualification-and-audit architecture inherited from GE, and a nuclear supplier group created to build qualified capacity for a new product. The clearest production-system evidence sits in GE Vernova's own plants; supplier-site application is evidenced by role design and sourcing routines rather than by a published supplier case with before-and-after results. Segments and periods are distinguished throughout.

Overall maturity: 3.39 / 5. Evidence coverage: 15/16 criteria. A Future business readiness: 3.60 (5/5); B Supplier production-system capability: 3.57 (7/7); C Resilience and continuity: 3.00 (3/4). Domains have equal weight; NE is excluded. These are evidence-bounded maturity ratings, not enterprise performance. Audit completed 17 October 2026.
2. Supplier selection and support delivery

Supplier qualification, current performance status and selection for intensive capability-building are separate decisions. The evidence below distinguishes the signal for attention, the people involved, the intervention and its verification.
Pillar
Q1 — Which suppliers to target?
Q2 — How to structure and scale support?
Future business readiness

Prioritize strategic commodities on the critical path of capacity growth — investment castings and cores, forgings, airfoils and structures, high-voltage components — plus suppliers entering a new product's supply chain. For the BWRX-300, membership requires pre-defined criteria, customer requirements and demonstrated willingness to invest in supply-chain capability. Spend or supplier size are not published selection rules. [GV5, GV6, GV10]

Gas Power maintains Supplier Capacity Leader roles that build a capacity roadmap with strategic suppliers from the current year to three-plus years out, remove bottlenecks across the supplier value stream, set Safety / Quality / Delivery / Cost action plans, report progress weekly and work onsite during ramp actions. Budgets, headcount and exit rules are not public. [GV10]
Supplier production-system capability

Best fit for suppliers whose lead time, on-time delivery, inventory or quality performance constrains the segment. Supplier scorecards and risk-based audits provide the signal; a published rule for selecting suppliers for intensive lean support was not found. [GV3, GV9]

A regional supplier lean role is defined to deploy lean at supplier sites using value-stream maps, gemba walks, Action Work Outs and pull systems, with improvement plans tracked through supplier scorecards and up to 50% travel. The published improvement cases with figures are GE Vernova's own plants. [GV7, GV8, GV9]
Resilience and continuity

Risk-based tiering across roughly 17,000 suppliers in about 109 countries drives standard or heightened due diligence by location, type, volume of work and product. Audit refresh runs on a one-, three- or five-year cycle by risk profile. This tiering is built for compliance risk, not for supply-continuity criticality. [GV2, GV3]

Company-level business continuity planning, crisis management and cross-business supply chain and procurement councils that share resiliency best practices, with risk-management tools being enhanced for lead times, availability, commodity prices and tariffs. Supplier exercises and recovery measures are not public. [GV1]

GE Vernova reports purchasing approximately $20 billion in materials and components sourced from over 100 countries, and a supplier base of about 17,000 suppliers in roughly 109 countries. It describes a risk-based supplier onboarding process with due diligence covering performance, labor standards, ethical sourcing and human rights, backed by an audit programme, and states that it is “building new capabilities to scale our supply chain aligned to our business growth.” [GV1, GV2]

The audit architecture is the most quantified part of the public record. The Supplier Responsibility Guidelines (SRG) programme, established inside GE in 2002 and carried over, assesses new suppliers before onboarding and re-audits existing suppliers on a one-, three- or five-year cycle based on risk profile. GE Vernova states its goal is “to work with and coach the suppliers to bring their practices into compliance” and that findings must be closed “promptly and permanently,” with suspension or termination otherwise. Reported volumes: 576 global audits in 2024 (559 suppliers approved, 17 rejected) with 3,013 findings, against 604 audits and 3,651 findings in 2023; 24% of 2024 findings concerned human rights and labor. [GV2, GV3]

Boundary: this is a social-compliance assessment and remediation system. It shows that GE Vernova can run audits at scale, coach suppliers and track findings to closure, but it should not be presented as GE Vernova's production-capability assessment or as its supplier-development selection system. The auditor-development figures point the same way: a 2024 campaign trained 81 new and existing SRG auditors over three days, with refresher training at least every three years. Auditor capability is not supplier capability. [GV2, GV3]

The supplier-facing technical functions are visible mainly through role design. A Gas Power Supplier Capacity Leader for investment castings and cores is accountable for a capacity roadmap built with strategic suppliers, for understanding “capacity and constraints on the full investment casting value stream,” for projects that “remove bottlenecks,” for part qualification, process revision, asset establishment and part industrialization, for weekly progress reporting, and for working regularly onsite with key suppliers during capacity ramp actions. A Supplier Performance Regional Lean Expert is accountable to “drive lean initiatives across the suppliers,” “deploy the Lean implementation at supplier sites,” manage supplier value stream maps, run Action Work Outs, introduce pull systems where continuous flow is not possible, and own supplier audits and improvement plans. [GV9, GV10]

Boundary on role evidence: job descriptions establish intended design, ownership and method vocabulary. They do not establish deployment volume, supplier coverage or outcomes, and one of the two listings was removed in November 2025. They are treated here as moderate evidence for architecture and weak evidence for use.

The programme GE Vernova publicly brands as supplier development is a different thing. Supplier Empowerment supports small-business, veteran and minority supplier capacity, governed by a Supplier Empowerment Council with Standard Work, Data/Reporting/Outreach & Development, and Awards & Recognition committees, with annual recognition for employees and suppliers. No production-capability curriculum, supplier counts or performance metrics are published there. It is retained as Layer 1 context and rejected as production-capability evidence. [GV11]

The clearest forward-looking construct is the BWRX-300 supplier group, announced on 30 April 2024 by the nuclear business then operating as GE Hitachi Nuclear Energy. Its stated purpose is “a reliable, cost effective and innovative process” for manufacturing and commercialising the reactor; eligibility requires meeting pre-defined criteria and customer requirements and showing willingness to invest in BWRX-300 supply-chain capabilities. GE Hitachi's then president and CEO said “supplier collaboration is expected to help build capacity and support cost reduction.” BWXT Canada was named the first member; it had announced a C$80 million expansion of its Cambridge, Ontario plant intended to raise large-component manufacturing capacity by 50% and add more than 200 long-term jobs. The supplier funded that capacity; what GE Hitachi contributes to members — design information, qualification support, engineering help — is not disclosed. [GV5, GV6]
Resources, scale and measurement

Lean is disclosed as a company-level operating method with budget consequences rather than as a supplier programme. GE Vernova states that it will “employ and evolve lean practices across our operations,” that it seeks “continued cost savings through lean operations and supply chain management,” that Electrification is “deploying lean initiatives to reduce lead-times” where demand outstrips supply, and that it invests only once waste has been eliminated from existing processes. Gas Power is described as having “collaborated closely with suppliers” alongside its lean initiatives, without further detail. [GV1]

Where lean is measured, it is measured inside GE Vernova. The Wind business certified 25 manufacturing lines in 2024 with ten more pursuing certification in 2025. The Charleroi, Pennsylvania grid factory ran a kaizen week in February that cut assembly time for its largest circuit breaker by about 67% and operator walking distance by about 37%, identified 15 implementable safety improvements, and had 60 further kaizen events planned for 2025. One diagnosis in that event was a supplier problem — current transformers arriving stacked out of order, forcing repeated unpacking — but the published account does not say the supplier took part. [GV7, GV8]

Capacity money is disclosed in detail and supplier money is not. GE Vernova published site-level US investment of nearly $600 million over two years with about 1,800 new factory and research jobs, including over $90 million at Schenectady, over $160 million at Greenville, up to $90 million at Charleroi and over $50 million at Wilmington for nuclear fuel, stating the aim of strengthening “our domestic supply chain.” Electrification adds a $200 million transformer plant at Hai Phong, Vietnam, staged to full operations in 2028 with about 450 jobs by 2030 and planned training and knowledge-sharing programmes to build local skills, alongside the $5.3 billion Prolec GE acquisition with about $1 billion planned for 2026–2028, inside roughly $11 billion of capex and R&D from 2025 to 2028. None of these disclosures separate supplier capability spend from GE Vernova plant spend. [GV4, GV12]

Research implication: the defensible description is a strong internal lean system plus a compliance-grade supplier assessment system, with a thin published layer between them. The supplier-facing capacity and lean roles are the bridge, and they are the part of the architecture with the least public outcome evidence.

3. Future business readiness
Domain A: 3.60 / 5; 5/5 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

GE Vernova's readiness evidence is organised around capacity rather than around a readiness score. The Gas Power Supplier Capacity Leader role carries a named forward horizon — a capacity roadmap built with strategic suppliers from the current year to three-plus years out — with weekly reporting, milestone tracking and onsite presence during ramp actions. The same role coordinates part qualification, process revision, asset establishment and part industrialization, which is the readiness work for a new or changed part. [GV10]

For a genuinely new product, the BWRX-300 supplier group converts readiness into an entry condition: members must meet pre-defined criteria and customer requirements and show willingness to invest in supply-chain capability. The reactor itself is designed to reduce what suppliers must absorb, using a design-to-cost approach built on existing fuel, plant simplifications and proven components, on a design certified in 2014. BWXT Canada's C$80 million Cambridge expansion, targeting 50% more large-component capacity, is a realized capacity increase in a named supplier, funded by that supplier. Separately, GE Hitachi holds a memorandum of understanding with Sheffield Forgemasters for UK-sourced steel forgings. [GV5, GV6]

Localization and capacity disclosures are site-level and specific: nearly $600 million across US sites with about 1,800 jobs, a staged $200 million Vietnam transformer plant with planned training and knowledge-sharing to build local skills, and the Prolec GE acquisition for North American transformer capacity. These establish where capacity is being added; they do not describe how a supplier's capability is transferred or verified. [GV4, GV12]

Evidence limit: GE Vernova publicly documents forward capacity roadmaps, qualification and industrialization coordination and new-product supplier entry criteria, but it does not disclose supplier capacity-confidence thresholds, a common ramp-up stress test, a readiness scorecard, or a standardized localization-transfer method.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Business need and capability: a gas-turbine capacity ramp and a first-of-a-kind reactor both require suppliers to add qualified capacity, not merely to pass a first article. The published evidence identifies the need and the owner, and in one case the realized capacity increase, but it does not document the gap-closing work between them: the supplier's starting constraint, the engineering contributed by each side, the investment or training added, and the verification that the changed capability holds.

Two specific gaps follow. First, the capacity roadmap is described as a role accountability, so its cadence is credible but its results are unpublished. Second, the nuclear supplier group's value to members is asserted (“expected to help build capacity”) rather than described; the single named investment was the supplier's own. Industry context raises the stakes: the OECD Nuclear Energy Agency notes a declining number of nuclear-grade suppliers and skill loss in some regions, which makes supplier qualification capacity a real constraint on the programme. [GV5, GV6, GV10]
Future readiness and the limits of inference

Capacity investment, backlog growth and localization announcements answer a different question from supplier readiness. A new GE Vernova factory, a staged plant in Vietnam and an acquired transformer manufacturer each add capacity that GE Vernova owns or controls; they do not demonstrate that an independent supplier became better able to perform work it previously could not. Likewise, planned training programmes at a new site build GE Vernova's own local workforce. These are retained as Layer 1 context and are not scored as supplier capability building. [GV4, GV12]
4. Supplier production-system capability
Domain B: 3.57 / 5; 7/7 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

GE Vernova discloses a repeatable improvement method, a certification mechanism for production lines, and a supplier-facing role designed to carry that method outward. The method vocabulary is consistent across sources: value-stream mapping, gemba walks, Action Work Outs, pull systems, standard work and kaizen events. The Wind business certified 25 manufacturing lines in 2024, with ten more in progress in 2025, and the Salzbergen plant is described as having used comprehensive standardization for more than 20 years. [GV1, GV8, GV9]

The supplier-facing application is defined but not evidenced in use: the regional supplier lean role is accountable to deploy lean at supplier sites, manage supplier value-stream maps, run Action Work Outs to remove constraints and train staff, install pull systems, and own supplier audits and improvement plans, with reduced product lead time, inventory and waste as stated objectives. [GV9]
Evidence limit: GE Vernova publishes measured improvement cases in its own plants and a defined supplier lean role, but no supplier case with a baseline, an intervention record and a verified result.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Situation: the Charleroi grid factory faced demand growth it could not meet by adding floorspace, with hand-assembled, customized high-voltage products and a testing bottleneck, against a target of quintupling output of its largest breaker. Capability built: observing work, quantifying motion and waiting, and changing the assembly sequence rather than the building. Intervention: a kaizen week diagnosed over a kilometre of walking per shift, 30 minutes of average waiting for a shared overhead crane and 44 minutes spent removing bolts; the team added a fixture on a lift table to insert the central conductor without the crane, moved bracket attachment earlier in the sequence, sorted slings by length and relocated a tool kit. Reported result: assembly time down about 67% and walking distance down about 37% in one week, with 15 implementable safety improvements and 60 further events planned for 2025. [GV7]

Roles and transfer: the work was done by cross-disciplinary plant teams, with the plant manager owning the cadence and the group CEO attending the event. Boundary and domain fit: Charleroi is a GE Vernova factory. The case is strong evidence that the method produces measured operating gains and that leadership attention is real; it is not evidence that a supplier's production system improved. [GV7]

The nearest published supplier-involved intervention is smaller. At the Pensacola wind plant, a weeklong kaizen event organised around safety, quality, delivery and cost took up a wirer's suggestion to remove unnecessary wiring, and the plant “worked with a supplier to create quick connects on panels”; reported outcomes are improved safety and quality and reduced standard work time, with no figures. This is co-development with a supplier on a product interface rather than development of the supplier's own production system, and it carries no sustainment evidence. [GV8]
Where GE Vernova's production evidence sits, and why the distinction matters

Three published cases — Charleroi's kaizen week, the Baodi bushing line where human handling of each bushing fell from twelve encounters to two through robotic support, lasers, cameras and machine lifting, and Pensacola's certified line — all sit inside GE Vernova's own manufacturing network. For this benchmark the core test is what a supplier became better able to perform and what the buying company did to help build it. On that test, GE Vernova's internal cases establish method credibility and transferable technique, and the supplier lean role establishes intent and ownership, but the supplier-side outcome record is empty in public sources. The honest reading is a company with a proven improvement engine whose supplier-facing deployment is not yet publicly documented — which is a different weakness from not having the engine. [GV7, GV8, GV9]
Gaspé: quality failure and remediation inside a wholly owned manufacturer

On 13 July 2024 a blade failed at Vineyard Wind; GE Vernova attributed it to a manufacturing deviation, described as insufficient bonding, at the LM Wind Power plant in Gaspé, Quebec. The company re-inspected 150 blades produced at that factory, its chief executive described a low single-digit proportion of manufactured blades as carrying a similar deviation, and GE Vernova said it had “taken corrective actions at our blade facility in Gaspé” following an internal review of its blade manufacturing and quality assurance programme. Reported accompanying changes include management departures and suspensions and the creation of an employee committee to prevent recurrence; the regulator suspended power production and blade installation pending investigation. In its 2024 annual report GE Vernova also describes progressing an AI-enabled digital blade inspection certification so blades leave the factory “right the first time.” [GV1, GV13]

Interpretation: LM Wind Power is a GE Vernova subsidiary, so this is internal manufacturing remediation, not supplier capability building. It is retained for two reasons. It shows what detection and corrective capability look like when they fail at a manufacturing site that behaves like a critical single-source supplier, and it shows the company's own stated remedy running toward inspection technology and quality assurance rather than production-system coaching. One local media allegation about quality-data falsification was anonymously sourced and not confirmed by the company; it is recorded here and not used in scoring. [GV13]
5. Resilience and continuity
Domain C: 3.00 / 5; 3/4 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

GE Vernova describes internal risk management including cyber mitigation, business continuity planning and crisis management, cross-business councils for supply chain and procurement that share resiliency best practices, monitoring of ferrous, non-ferrous, precious metals and energy commodity prices, and an intention to maintain a globally diverse supply chain for operational resiliency while localizing where possible. It states that it is “enhancing our risk management tools” for market trends, commodity pricing, availability, lead times, tariffs and ESG compliance — language that places the tooling in development rather than in established use. [GV1]

On dependency visibility the company documents its own limit. GE Vernova asks first-tier suppliers to disclose sub-tier suppliers, particularly where parts are made solely for its products, and reports that suppliers are often “unwilling to disclose information” that could affect their competitive advantage. It also states that its highest modern-slavery risk sits in the sub-tier supply chain, “where visibility is most limited.” That is a credible, self-reported account of incomplete multi-tier visibility. [GV2]

Evidence limit: public materials describe company-level continuity governance and risk tooling, but give no supplier-level criticality model, no supplier continuity exercises or drills, no recovery-time targets and no tested supplier recovery outcomes.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Situation: a long-lead-time equipment portfolio with concentrated sources for forgings, castings and high-voltage components, and sub-tier visibility the company itself describes as limited. Capability that would need developing: a supplier's ability to anticipate, withstand and recover from disruption while continuing to supply. What the public record shows instead is buyer-side control — councils, monitoring, diversification, localization and acquisition of capacity. Under the benchmarking standard, risk visibility and buyer-side mitigation without supplier capability-building are flagged rather than counted. [GV1, GV2]

The one realized response in the record is the 2024 blade event, and it ran inside a wholly owned manufacturer: re-inspection of 150 blades, corrective actions at the plant, management changes and a worker committee, under a regulatory suspension. 9. Extended Deep Research - GE Vernova: Supplier Capability-Building Benchmark

This section re-examines GE Vernova against the same sixteen criteria at greater depth, with a wider source base than sections 1–8. Three sources located during the deeper pass change the picture materially and are flagged wherever they bear on a judgement: the 2025 Annual Report, which discloses sole-source and concentrated-source exposure and a mitigation ladder that sections 1–8 did not have; a supplier-side account of GE Vernova's 2025 APAC Supplier Partnership Summit, which names a Gas Power Sourcing Lean Engagement Model built on five gates; and a second measured internal lean case at Stafford with an external Japanese sensei leading the work.

The net effect is that GE Vernova's supplier architecture is more complete than the first pass showed, and its outcome record is no better. The company now demonstrably has a named supplier engagement model, a global supplier convening mechanism, a capacity function with a multi-year horizon, and a capital governance rule that rewards demonstrated lean. What it still does not publish is a single supplier whose capability changed.

Scoring note: the deeper evidence raises confidence in several rows of the criterion table in section 6 without changing the scores themselves, because the new material establishes more architecture and no new outcomes. Where it would change a score, this section says so explicitly and the change is carried into section 6 rather than left here.
1. Executive Summary
Strongest evidence of actual supplier capability building

GE Vernova's strongest supplier-facing evidence is architectural rather than demonstrated. The Gas Power Sourcing Lean Engagement Model, described by a participating supplier as a five-gate approach covering supplier capacity, transformation and sustainability, is the first named supplier development construct located for this company. A Supplier Capacity Leader function carries a three-plus-year capacity roadmap with weekly reporting and onsite presence during ramps. A Supplier Performance Regional Lean Expert role is defined to deploy lean at supplier sites with value-stream maps, gemba walks, Action Work Outs and pull systems. Together these describe a complete intervention chain. None of the three is accompanied by a published supplier result. [GV9, GV10, GV15]
A proven improvement engine, pointed inward

Where GE Vernova does publish outcomes, they are inside its own factories, and they are good. Charleroi cut assembly time on its largest circuit breaker by about 67% and operator walking distance by about 37% in a single kaizen week, with 60 further events planned for 2025. Stafford's Redhill facility raised valve module production capacity by 40% through eight simultaneous kaizen events run in the week of 15 September 2025 under Sensei Junichi Nakazawa of the Shingijutsu Institute, with packaging cycle time down 56%, testing down 23%, 37 safety improvements and 46% more space released in the pick-face storage area. More than 100 employees took part, after eight weeks of value-stream pre-work. [GV7, GV17]

The Shingijutsu lineage is worth naming in a benchmark whose reference chapter is Toyota: GE Vernova is buying its sensei capability from the consultancy founded by Taiichi Ohno's direct disciples. The method GE Vernova is deploying internally is, by descent, the method Toyota deployed at Umemura. The difference is where it is pointed. [GV17]
Future-business readiness

The 2025 Annual Report adds a mechanism the first pass missed: GE Vernova states that it maintains “strong supplier relationships and connected forecasting” to identify capacity risks early. That is joint forward planning with suppliers, and it sits alongside slot reservation agreements, long-term supply agreements and the Supplier Capacity Leader's three-plus-year roadmap. Forward readiness is therefore better evidenced than sections 1–8 indicated, and still without a single published instance of a supplier capacity gap being closed. [GV10, GV14]
Resilience and continuity

The 2025 filing is markedly more candid than the 2024 one. GE Vernova states that it operates in a supply-constrained environment, that some inputs are “limited or sole-sourced, concentrated with a small number of suppliers” or mainly sourced from one country — naming semiconductor chips and critical materials including specialty metals and rare earths — and that supply chain pressures are expected to persist. It lists its mitigation levers explicitly. Every lever is buyer-side except one: cost-sharing with suppliers. No supplier continuity requirement, exercise or tested recovery appears anywhere. [GV14]
Overall assessment

GE Vernova presents as a company that has rebuilt a credible lean capability since separating from GE in April 2024, has tied factory capital to demonstrated lean use, convenes its supply base globally, and has designed — but not evidenced — the supplier-facing half of that system. Its overall maturity of 3.39 reflects a consistent pattern across all three domains: the mechanism exists and the outcome is unpublished. For a benchmark whose core test is what the supplier became better able to do, GE Vernova is the clearest case in this cohort of an engine built and not yet shown running outside the fence.
