2. Operating Model and Future Business Readiness
2.1 GE Vernova's supplier-development architecture

GE Vernova inherited a supplier architecture from GE and has been rebuilding it under its own governance since April 2024. Four layers are visible in public sources, and they are owned by different functions with little published connection between them.

The compliance layer is the oldest and best quantified: the Supplier Responsibility Guidelines programme, established inside GE in 2002, assessing new suppliers before onboarding and re-auditing on a one-, three- or five-year cycle by risk profile, with 576 audits in 2024 producing 3,013 findings. The transactional layer is the supplier portal, carrying RFQ response, contracts, purchase orders, invoices, product qualification, supplier deviation requests through Quality Suite and non-conformance through Conformance Suite. The capability layer is the pair of supplier-facing engineering roles — capacity and lean. The convening layer is the Supplier Partnership Summit series. [GV2, GV3, GV9, GV10, GV15, GV16]

What is missing from the public record is the connective tissue. No source describes how an SRG audit finding, a Quality Suite non-conformance, a capacity roadmap gap and a summit commitment relate to one another, or whether a single supplier view exists across them. The Gas Power Sourcing Lean Engagement Model may be that connective tissue — five gates covering capacity, transformation and sustainability would span exactly these concerns — but the only account of it is a supplier's. [GV15]
2.2 Reconstructed supplier-development operating model

From the located sources, the operating model reconstructs as follows, with confidence noted at each step. Selection: strategic commodities on the capacity critical path — investment castings and ceramic cores, forgings, airfoils and structures, high-voltage components — plus suppliers entering a new product's supply chain. Moderate confidence, from role scope and the nuclear supplier group. [GV5, GV10]

Diagnosis: capacity and constraint analysis across the supplier's full value stream, supplier value-stream mapping and gemba walks on the lean track, SRG on-site assessment on the compliance track. Moderate confidence from role design; low confidence that the tracks are integrated. Intervention: bottleneck-removal projects, Action Work Outs, pull systems, part qualification and industrialization, with Safety / Quality / Delivery / Cost action plans. Cadence: weekly progress reporting during capacity ramps, up to 50% travel in the supplier lean role. Verification: supplier scorecards and lean business reviews. Exit: undisclosed on both tracks. [GV9, GV10]

The model is coherent on paper and is reconstructed almost entirely from two job descriptions, one of which was withdrawn in November 2025. That is a weak foundation for a benchmark conclusion, and it is stated here rather than smoothed over: GE Vernova's supplier development operating model is inferred, not disclosed.
2.3 A1: Future demand readiness

Two mechanisms carry this criterion. The Supplier Capacity Leader builds a capacity roadmap with strategic suppliers from the current year to three-plus years out, reports progress weekly to working teams and to segment leadership, and works onsite with key suppliers during capacity ramp actions. The 2025 Annual Report adds connected forecasting with suppliers as an early-warning mechanism for capacity risk. [GV10, GV14]

The demand these must serve is extreme and is disclosed: GE Vernova operates in a supply-constrained environment, has experienced shortages of materials and skilled labour, and expects supply chain pressures to persist. Electrification states that customer lead times have increased because demand is outstripping supply. A forward-planning routine with this much business pressure behind it is likely to be operating seriously. It is also unevidenced in outcome: no readiness gap closed, no supplier named. Score holds at 4. [GV14]
2.4 A2: Capacity confidence

The deeper pass strengthens this criterion's architecture without lifting its score. The capacity function understands capacity and constraints across the full supplier value stream and implements projects that remove bottlenecks; GE Vernova uses slot reservation agreements and long-term supply agreements as commercial instruments for securing forward capacity; and the BWRX-300 supplier group makes willingness to invest in supply-chain capability an entry condition. [GV5, GV10, GV14]

The single realized capacity outcome in the record remains BWXT Canada's C$80 million Cambridge expansion, targeting a 50% increase in large-component manufacturing capacity and more than 200 long-term jobs. The supplier funded it. The 2025 filing adds a note that cuts the other way on this criterion: expansion commitments and slot reservation agreements could outpace demand, leaving idle capacity or penalties under supply agreements. That is an honest acknowledgement that forward capacity instruments carry risk in both directions. Score holds at 4. [GV5, GV6, GV14]
2.5 A3: Ramp-up and industrialization readiness

Ramp-up is an owned accountability with named sub-steps: capacity ramp-up action plans with milestone tracking, part qualification, process revision, asset establishment and part industrialization, coordinated by the supplier capacity function and reported weekly. The nuclear business is investing more than $50 million at Wilmington across 2025–26 for safety, quality and productivity and to launch a next-generation fuel design for the BWRX-300. [GV4, GV10]

The 2025 Annual Report adds the Zero-Defect Framework, launched in 2025 as a roadmap for product, service and solution quality. The letter does not tie it specifically to suppliers, and this benchmark does not either; it is recorded as a Layer 1 development worth tracking, because a zero-defect programme that reaches the supply base would be the natural carrier for supplier quality requirements GE Vernova currently does not publish. Score holds at 4. [GV14]
2.6 A4: Localization readiness

The 2025 filing states the policy directly: GE Vernova will prioritize opportunities to localize its supply chain to serve distinct geographies while maintaining a globally diverse base for resiliency, and is diversifying supply chains and increasing US manufacturing partly to offset tariff impacts. The investment record is extensive — nearly $600 million across US sites, more than $100 million over two years for Pennsylvania grid factories with 700 jobs, a staged $200 million Vietnam transformer plant with planned local training and knowledge-sharing. [GV4, GV12, GV14]

The benchmark distinction holds. Every one of those investments adds capacity GE Vernova owns or will own. The Vietnam training programme builds GE Vernova's own local workforce. No supplier capability-transfer method is described anywhere. Score holds at 3, and the reason is not that localization is weak but that it is being achieved by building rather than by developing. [GV12, GV14]
2.7 A5: Product and process complexity readiness

GE Vernova's dominant complexity strategy is to design complexity out rather than to develop suppliers through it. The BWRX-300 uses a design-to-cost approach built on existing fuel, plant simplifications and proven components, on a design certified in 2014. The 2025 filing lists product redesign among its supply mitigation levers — changing the product so that a constrained input is no longer needed. Wind has concentrated on workhorse products. [GV5, GV6, GV14]

This is a legitimate and often superior engineering answer, and it is not supplier capability building. The one countervailing piece of evidence is the APAC summit agenda, which covered future gas power technology roadmaps and specific component requirements with suppliers in the room — forward technical alignment rather than design simplification. Score holds at 3, with the summit noted as the mechanism most likely to move it if GE Vernova published what happens inside it. [GV15]
Future Business Readiness conclusion

Domain A is GE Vernova's strongest domain and the deeper research reinforces why: a dedicated capacity function with a three-plus-year horizon, connected forecasting with suppliers, commercial instruments for reserving capacity, an entry condition for new-product suppliers that requires investment, and a global convening mechanism. Against the cohort, that is an unusually complete forward architecture. It remains evidenced by role design and filing language rather than by supplier outcomes, which is why no criterion in this domain reaches 5.
3. Supplier Production-System Capability
3.1 The lean operating system and its governance link to capital

GE Vernova describes a corporate lean operating system that it will continue to employ and evolve across operations, and it has attached a governance consequence to it that no other company in this cohort publishes: future factory capital expenditure depends on demonstrated lean use, and the company invests only once waste has been eliminated from existing processes. Factory output is to be raised through lean lines, robotics and advanced automation. [GV1, GV14]

That rule matters more than it first appears. It converts lean from an improvement programme into a capital allocation test, which is the strongest internal incentive structure located anywhere in this benchmark. A plant that wants money must first show it has removed waste. The obvious extension — a supplier that wants volume must first show the same — is not described, and is the single most interesting unasked question about GE Vernova's system. [GV14]
3.2 Charleroi: the clearest measured case, inside GE Vernova's own walls

The Charleroi grid factory in Pennsylvania makes high-voltage instrument transformers and circuit breakers across 332,000 square feet. Demand had surged over roughly eighteen months and staff had about doubled in five years. The products are largely hand-assembled, customized per customer and extensively tested, which makes testing the bottleneck. Adding physical capacity would have taken years and millions of dollars, against a target of quintupling production of the largest breaker, the DT2-550, by year end. The plant manager's framing is the clearest statement of the constraint in this cohort: “Lean is the only reliable tool I have, because you can't just expand the facility that fast.” [GV7]

The February kaizen week diagnosed the problem with measurement rather than opinion. A spaghetti chart showed assemblers walking over a kilometre per shift. Workers waited an average of 30 minutes for a shared overhead crane and spent 44 minutes removing bolts to attach brackets. Current transformers arrived from a supplier stacked out of order, forcing repeated unpacking and repacking — the one supplier-caused waste identified, and the published account does not say the supplier took part in resolving it. [GV7]

The countermeasures were physical and cheap: a fixture on a lift table so the central conductor could be inserted into the bushings without the crane; bracket attachment moved earlier in the assembly sequence, eliminating the bolt removal; support slings sorted by length rather than kept in one bin; a tool kit moved higher and closer to the workstation. A computer vision system analysed physical tasks to flag ergonomic issues, and the team identified 15 implementable safety improvements. Reported result in one week: assembly time down about 67%, walking distance down about 37%. Sixty further kaizen events were planned for Charleroi in 2025. [GV7]

3.4 Stafford Redhill: lean at scale with an external sensei

The Redhill facility in Stafford, England makes the valves at the heart of HVDC systems, and needed a 40% increase in valve production to meet upcoming projects. The approach was more formal than Charleroi's. Eight weeks of pre-work preceded the event: lean leaders walked the site and built a value stream map showing workflow, choke points and waste, then applied Pareto prioritisation to the 20% of causes behind most of the waste. A pick-face study examined how assembly workers access supplies, and an andon signal was installed to show when parts were ready or trays needed replenishing. [GV17]

The event itself — a shingi event in the week of 15 September 2025 — ran eight kaizen events simultaneously, seven at the plant and one at a nearby warehouse, with more than 100 employees taking part and Sensei Junichi Nakazawa of the Shingijutsu Institute leading. Reported results: valve module production capacity up 40%, 37 safety improvements, 46% more space freed in the pick-face storage area, cycle time improved 56% in packaging and 23% in testing, with site targets set for 2027. [GV17]

Two details carry benchmark weight. The first is the pre-work discipline — “Pre-work can either make or break a kaizen” — which is the difference between an event that produces results and one that produces enthusiasm. The second is the sensei. Shingijutsu was founded by consultants trained directly under Taiichi Ohno at Toyota; GE Vernova is buying lineage, not just facilitation. For a benchmark whose reference chapter is Toyota, the method at Stafford and the method at Umemura share an ancestor. The difference is that Toyota sent its people to a supplier's plant and GE Vernova brought a sensei into its own. [GV17]
3.5 The supplier-facing lean role and what it is designed to do

The Supplier Performance Regional Lean Expert role is the designed bridge between the internal engine and the supply base, and its accountabilities are specific: drive lean initiatives across the suppliers; deploy the lean implementation at supplier sites; help suppliers build value stream maps and manage them; use gemba walks to address flow problems on the supplier line; run Action Work Outs as short improvement events that remove constraints and train staff; install pull systems where continuous flow is not possible; own supplier scorecards and supplier audits, driving improvement plans where needed; and present lean business reviews to business leaders. Stated objectives are reduced product lead time, inventory and waste, and improved on-time delivery. Travel up to 50%. [GV9]

The Action Work Out deserves isolation because it is the one element in the role that is explicitly described as both removing a constraint and training staff. That dual purpose — fix the problem and leave capability behind — is precisely what this benchmark looks for, and it is the single clearest statement of supplier capability-building intent located for GE Vernova. It is also a line in a job advertisement that was withdrawn in November 2025, with no deployment data attached. [GV9]
3.6 The Gas Power Sourcing Lean Engagement Model

The deeper pass located one named supplier programme. At the 2025 APAC Supplier Partnership Summit in Shanghai in September 2025, GE Vernova introduced what a participating supplier describes as its Gas Power Sourcing Lean Engagement Model, a five-gate approach covering supplier capacity, transformation and sustainability. The summit's stated purpose was driving excellence in safety, quality, delivery and cost across the energy value chain. Reported attendance figures conflict within the source and are given as published: over 120 suppliers and key stakeholders from more than 20 countries in one passage, over 110 GE Vernova participants from Sourcing, Engineering, Services and Quality in another. Agenda topics included supplier RAM improvement, lean execution, digital traceability, future gas power technology roadmaps and component requirements, alongside leadership panels, strategic sourcing discussions and one-to-one supplier meetings with GE leadership on programme alignment and future readiness. [GV15]

A five-gate model covering capacity, transformation and sustainability would, if it operates as described, be the integrating mechanism this chapter has otherwise found missing — it spans the capacity function, the lean function and the compliance function in one supplier-facing progression. It would also supply the gated structure that Eaton, Cummins and Caterpillar publish and GE Vernova does not.

The evidentiary problem is severe and is stated plainly: the only account located is a supplier's own promotional article. GE Vernova does not describe the model on any page located, including its own Gas Power supplier page, which offers portals, quality documents, specifications and cybersecurity guidance but “no formal supplier development program.” The model is therefore recorded as a strong INVESTIGATE lead — the most valuable single follow-up in this chapter — and is not scored. [GV15, GV16]

3.8 Closure criteria and sustainment

GE Vernova publishes closure discipline on exactly one track, and it is the compliance track. SRG findings must be rectified by the supplier in a timely manner, tracked to closure, and verified as eliminating or mitigating the risk; findings must be closed promptly and permanently; suppliers who do not comply are suspended until issues are remediated, and those who fail to make efforts are terminated. The stated posture is coaching: “our goal is to work with and coach the suppliers to bring their practices into compliance.” [GV2, GV3]

On the capability tracks there is no published closure criterion at all — no graduation target, no exit test, no re-measurement requirement, no definition of what a successfully developed supplier looks like. Internally, the sustainment question is at least named: Stafford's supply chain leader, asked about next steps after a 40% capacity gain, said “Now it's all about sustaining.” That instinct exists in the company. It is not visible in anything GE Vernova asks of a supplier. [GV9, GV10, GV17]
Supplier Production-System Capability conclusion

GE Vernova has the method, the sensei lineage, the measurement discipline, the internal results and the capital-allocation incentive to make lean matter. It has designed a supplier-facing version of all of it. The deeper research found one more internal case with better figures than the first, and one named supplier model described by a supplier rather than by GE Vernova. The domain score of 3.57 is the right reading of that: strong where it is proven, unproven where it faces outward.
4. Resilience and Continuity Capability
4.1 Sole-source and concentrated-source exposure, stated plainly

The 2025 Annual Report is the most candid supply-exposure disclosure located for any company in this cohort. GE Vernova states that it operates in a supply-constrained environment and has experienced shortages of materials and skilled labour; that some inputs are limited or sole-sourced and concentrated with a small number of suppliers, or sourced mainly from a single country; and it names the categories — semiconductor chips and critical materials including specialty metals and rare earths. It warns that supplier nonperformance could affect customer commitments and trigger contract terminations or liability, and that supply chain pressures are expected to persist. [GV14]
Naming the exposure is a precondition for managing it, and most of this cohort does not. The question this benchmark asks is what follows the naming.
4.2 The mitigation ladder and what sits on it

What follows is a published list of levers: long-term supply agreements, dual-sourcing, higher inventory, factory capacity expansion, lean initiatives, alternative logistics, product redesign, and cost-sharing with customers and suppliers. It is a complete and realistic ladder for a buyer in a constrained market. [GV14]

Under the benchmarking standard, seven of those eight levers are flagged rather than counted: inventory buffers, dual sourcing, logistics alternatives and footprint changes without supplier capability-building are explicitly excluded by the guide. Product redesign removes the dependency rather than strengthening the supplier. Lean initiatives, where they reach a supplier, would count — and the evidence that they do is the unevidenced role. The eighth lever, cost-sharing with suppliers, is the only one that puts GE Vernova's resources into a supplier's problem, and it is named without being described.
4.3 Connected forecasting as an early-warning mechanism

The filing's statement that GE Vernova maintains strong supplier relationships and connected forecasting to identify capacity risks early is the most capability-relevant resilience sentence in the document. Sharing forward demand with a supplier gives it the information it needs to plan its own capacity, which is a genuine if modest transfer — the same mechanism scored for Emerson in this cohort. It also converts resilience from a reactive posture into a planning one. [GV14]
No cadence, participating population, data granularity or governance is published, so it is scored as a defined mechanism rather than a demonstrated capability.
4.4 Vertical integration as a substitute for supplier development

The 2025 Annual Report records a strategic choice this benchmark should name explicitly. GE Vernova acquired Woodward's combustion parts business “to scale our Gas Power supply chain buildout,” and agreed to acquire the remaining 50% of the Prolec GE joint venture for $5.3 billion with $1 billion of capex planned for 2026–2028. [GV14]

Buying a supplier is a legitimate and often faster answer to a capacity constraint than developing one. It is also the opposite of supplier capability building, and it changes what the remaining supply base is asked to become. A benchmark measuring supplier development should record when a company chooses ownership instead — GE Vernova has done so twice in the period under review, in exactly the commodities where its capacity constraint is tightest. That is context for its domain A and B scores, not a criticism of them.
4.5 Gaspé: a realized quality failure inside an owned manufacturer

On 13 July 2024 a blade failed at Vineyard Wind. GE Vernova attributed it to a manufacturing deviation described as insufficient bonding at the LM Wind Power plant in Gaspé, Quebec. The company re-inspected 150 blades produced at that factory; its chief executive described a low single-digit proportion of manufactured blades as carrying a similar deviation; and GE Vernova said it had taken corrective actions at the facility following an internal review of its blade manufacturing and quality assurance programme. Reported accompanying changes include management departures and suspensions and the creation of an employee committee to prevent recurrence. The regulator suspended power production and blade installation pending investigation. [GV13]

LM Wind Power is a GE Vernova subsidiary, so this is internal remediation. It is retained in this section for a specific analytical reason: it shows what detection and corrective capability look like when they fail at a manufacturing site that behaves like a critical single-source supplier, and it shows the company's chosen remedy — an AI-enabled digital blade inspection certification so blades leave the factory right the first time, plus the 2025 Zero-Defect Framework. The remedy runs toward inspection technology and quality governance rather than toward production-system coaching. One local media allegation about quality-data falsification was anonymously sourced, not confirmed by the company, and is excluded from scoring. [GV1, GV13, GV14]
4.6 Sub-tier visibility and its stated limit

GE Vernova asks first-tier suppliers to disclose sub-tier suppliers, particularly where parts are made solely for its products, and reports that suppliers are often unwilling to disclose information that may affect their competitive advantage. It states that its highest modern-slavery risk sits in the sub-tier supply chain, where visibility is most limited. Cross-business councils for supply chain and procurement share resiliency best practices, and risk management tools are described as being enhanced for market trends, commodity pricing, availability, lead times, tariffs and ESG compliance. [GV1, GV2, GV14]

A company that publishes the failure mode of its own flow-down requirement is being straight with its readers. The limit remains: visibility work, however candid, is not supplier capability building, and no supplier continuity requirement, exercise, drill or recovery measure appears in any source located for GE Vernova.

5.2 What GE Vernova's public evidence still does not tell us

After a second, wider pass the central gap is unchanged and better defined. GE Vernova does not publish a single instance of a supplier becoming better able to do something. Specifically unresolved: what the five gates of the Gas Power Sourcing Lean Engagement Model are and whether GE Vernova itself describes the model anywhere; how many suppliers have received a supplier-site Action Work Out and what any of them produced; what GE Vernova contributes to BWRX-300 supplier group members beyond membership criteria; what the supplier capacity function has actually closed; what cost-sharing with suppliers means in practice; and whether the capital-allocation rule that ties factory investment to demonstrated lean has any supplier analogue.

Two structural absences are worth naming separately because peers in this cohort publish them. GE Vernova has no published supplier quality manual with capability thresholds or corrective-action clocks of the kind Eaton, Cummins and Honeywell make public — its supplier-facing quality content is portals, deviation requests and specification documents. And it has no supplier business-continuity requirement of any kind, where Eaton mandates tested contingency plans and Honeywell requires plans covering tooling access. [GV16]
6. Implications for Siemens Energy

Everything in this section is an analytical hypothesis for low-volume, high-complexity, long-lead-time supply. None of it is observed Siemens Energy practice, and none of it forms part of the maturity score.

GE Vernova runs the left column at scale — 576 audits, findings tracked to closure, coaching to compliance — and has designed the right column without publishing it. The two columns need different people, different cadences and different success tests, and a company that measures only the left will conclude its supply base is compliant and still constrained.
6.2 Put the capacity roadmap in one named role with a multi-year horizon

The most portable structural element in this chapter is the Supplier Capacity Leader: one person accountable for a capacity roadmap built with strategic suppliers from the current year to three-plus years out, who understands capacity and constraints across the supplier's full value stream, implements bottleneck-removal projects, sets Safety / Quality / Delivery / Cost action plans, reports weekly, and works onsite during ramps. For long-lead-time equipment, test this on a single critical commodity — forgings or large castings — and make the role's success test the supplier's demonstrated rate, not the roadmap's existence.
6.3 Tie capital to demonstrated lean, then extend the test outward

GE Vernova's rule that future factory capex depends on demonstrated lean use is the strongest internal incentive mechanism in this benchmark. The transferable experiment is its supplier analogue: make a share of forward volume, or a frame-agreement position, conditional on a supplier demonstrating it has removed waste from its existing process before it asks for investment to add more. That converts supplier development from a cost the buyer carries into a condition the supplier wants to meet.
6.4 Use a gated engagement model rather than an audit cycle

If the Gas Power Sourcing Lean Engagement Model operates as the supplier describes — five gates spanning capacity, transformation and sustainability — it solves the integration problem that this chapter otherwise documents: capacity, lean and compliance owned separately, with no single supplier view. A gated model gives the supplier one progression to understand and the buyer one place to look. Worth designing even though GE Vernova's version cannot be verified from public sources.
6.5 Buy the sensei, not the slide deck

Stafford's 40% capacity gain was led by a named sensei from the institute founded by Ohno's disciples, after eight weeks of value-stream pre-work, with more than 100 employees in the event. The pre-work discipline is the transferable part — “pre-work can either make or break a kaizen” — and so is the willingness to pay for external mastery rather than internal enthusiasm. For a first supplier-site event in an engineer-to-order environment, the combination of a genuine sensei and eight weeks of mapping is more likely to produce a result the supplier can repeat than any internally facilitated workshop.
6.6 Treat connected forecasting as a capability transfer, and measure it

GE Vernova names connected forecasting with suppliers as its early-warning mechanism for capacity risk. In a project business the equivalent is sharing the slipping, pulling-in reality of a programme schedule rather than a smoothed annual volume. The test of whether it is a capability transfer rather than a data feed is simple: does the supplier change its own capacity plan because of what it received? That question can be asked, and GE Vernova does not publish the answer for itself.
6.7 Decide deliberately between developing a supplier and buying one

GE Vernova bought Woodward's combustion parts business to scale its Gas Power supply chain and is acquiring the rest of Prolec GE for $5.3 billion. Those are supply chain capability decisions made through the balance sheet rather than through supplier development. The transferable discipline is to make the choice explicitly, commodity by commodity, rather than defaulting to development where ownership is faster or to ownership where development would have built a second source the market also needs.
6.8 Pair sole-source disclosure with supplier-executed recovery

GE Vernova names its sole-sourced and concentrated categories — semiconductors, specialty metals, rare earths — and lists eight mitigation levers, seven of which are buyer-side. The missing ninth is the one this benchmark asks for: a supplier that has rehearsed its own recovery and can show a recovery time that improves on repetition. Naming the exposure is the hard part and GE Vernova has done it; exercising the response at the supplier is the cheap part and nobody in this cohort has published it.

7.3 Scope and evidence notes

This deep-research pass added four sources to the thirteen cited in sections 1–8. Identifiers GV1–GV13 are defined in section 8 and are not repeated here; GV14–GV17 are defined above. The deeper pass searched specifically for the gaps recorded in section 8's search-gap log: a supplier-site lean case with figures, the contribution GE Vernova makes to BWRX-300 supplier group members, supplier development budget and headcount, and supplier continuity exercises. None of those four was resolved.

What the pass did find changes the architecture and not the outcomes: a named supplier engagement model (from a supplier, not from GE Vernova), a global supplier convening mechanism, a second and better-documented internal lean case, explicit sole-source disclosure, an explicit mitigation ladder, connected forecasting with suppliers, two vertical-integration decisions, and a capital-allocation rule tied to demonstrated lean. Scores in section 6 are unchanged; evidence confidence rises on A1, A2, C2 and C3, and the Gas Power Sourcing Lean Engagement Model is added to the INVESTIGATE list as the highest-value follow-up for this company.

Access note: GE Vernova's own supplier-facing pages were read directly and contain no supplier development programme description. Searches for a GE Vernova-published account of the Lean Engagement Model returned role postings, the supplier portal and internal plant stories. The asymmetry recorded in section 8 therefore persists after a wider search, and should be read as a finding about GE Vernova's disclosure rather than as a conclusion about its practice.
Schneider Electric | Supplier Capability Benchmark

Evidence reviewed: 17 October 2026. Ratings describe maturity visible in public evidence; programme, role-based and period observations retain their stated scope. Schneider publishes the longest measured supplier-capability trajectory in this cohort and almost nothing about supplier production systems, so its profile is unusually uneven across the three domains.
1. Summary and scope

Schneider Electric's benchmark is dominated by one thing done well: a five-year, target-bound programme that built a specific capability in a defined supplier population and measured the result annually. The Zero Carbon Project took the top 1,000 suppliers — 70% of upstream emissions — from a 2020 baseline to a 56% reduction in their operational emissions by the end of 2025 against a 50% target, with training, tools and a staged methodology provided by Schneider. A parallel Decent Work programme moved from 1% of strategic suppliers conforming in 2022 to 98% in 2025. Against that, Schneider publishes almost no evidence on supplier production systems, capacity or continuity, and five of sixteen criteria cannot be rated.

Overall maturity: 3.27 / 5. Evidence coverage: 11/16 criteria. A Future business readiness: 3.00 (3/5); B Supplier production-system capability: 3.80 (5/7); C Resilience and continuity: 3.00 (3/4). Domains have equal weight; NE is excluded. These are evidence-bounded maturity ratings, not enterprise performance. Audit completed 17 October 2026.
2. Supplier selection and support delivery

Supplier qualification, current performance status and selection for intensive capability-building are separate decisions. The evidence below distinguishes the signal for attention, the people involved, the intervention and its verification.

Schneider works with more than 53,000 suppliers globally and frames procurement engagement as a five-year plan covering climate, circular supply chain, social commitments and decent work. Sustainability has been part of supplier qualification since the criteria were revised in 2023, and strategic suppliers are evaluated against ISO 26000 for continuous improvement. [SE1]

The assessment architecture dates from 2012, when Schneider began assessing its most strategic suppliers through EcoVadis against ISO 26000. In 2018 it joined the Responsible Business Alliance and added an on-site audit layer, adopting the Verisk Maplecroft mapping tool to identify suppliers likely to be exposed by geographic location and type of activity, the RBA self-assessment questionnaire and the RBA auditing protocol, with a target of auditing 300 higher-risk suppliers over three years and procurement staff and auditors trained to carry out those audits. By 2024, 4,052 suppliers had been assessed under the Vigilance Plan since 2018, against a stated target of auditing 4,000 suppliers by 2025; Schneider reports that more than 330,000 supplier employees have benefited from improved working conditions through the Vigilance Programme since 2017, and its Duty of Vigilance Committee has met 19 times since 2017, twice a year. [SE1, SE4]

Boundary: the figure of 4,052 suppliers assessed and the target of 4,000 audited appear to use different scope definitions, which the sources do not reconcile; both are reported here as published. As elsewhere in this benchmark, assessment volume is Layer 1 evidence and does not by itself establish capability building.

What converts it in Schneider's case is a published supplier improvement trend. Suppliers' ISO 26000 scores rose 2.5 points against 2023 and 9.6 points since 2019 — a six-year series showing the assessed population getting better on the dimension being assessed. That is the pattern the benchmarking standard asks for, in a domain adjacent to, rather than inside, production capability. [SE1]
Resources, scale and measurement

The Zero Carbon Project, announced on 19 April 2021, is the most completely documented supplier capability-building programme in this cohort by the test of structure plus measurement. Scope: the top 1,000 suppliers, accounting for 70% of Schneider's upstream carbon emissions, against a 2020 baseline of zero progress and a 2025 ambition of a 50% reduction in those suppliers' operational Scope 1 and 2 emissions. [SE1, SE2, SE3]

What Schneider provides is specified: digital tools to measure emissions; a three-stage supplier roadmap — Analytics to quantify emissions and set a baseline, Ambition to review the emissions profile and set goals and strategy, Action to identify measures and build a roadmap for priority areas; eight technical decarbonisation training sessions covering how to measure Scope 1 and 2 emissions under the GHG Protocol, identify reduction levers and turn targets into implementation roadmaps, which more than 1,300 supplier participants have attended; the Zeigo Network platform offering best practices, training materials, peer-to-peer connections, a portfolio of decarbonising technologies and links to power producers for power purchase agreements; and support from Schneider's own energy and sustainability services division, which runs comparable programmes for other buyers. [SE2, SE3]

The results are reported annually and the trajectory is the evidence: 27% reduction in 2023, 40% in 2024, and 56% by the end of 2025 against the 50% ambition. The parallel Decent Work programme moved from 1% of strategic suppliers conforming in 2022 to 21% in 2023, 63% in 2024 and 98% in 2025. Both are supplier-side capability outcomes, measured yearly, against targets set in advance. [SE1, SE7]

Boundary and domain fit: the capability built is carbon measurement and reduction, and in the second case labour-practice management. Neither is production-system capability, and neither is scored as such. Their weight in this benchmark falls on one criterion — capability building and sustainment — where the question is whether the company can take a defined supplier population, build a capability it did not have and show the gain holding over years. Schneider can, demonstrably. Whether that organisational skill transfers to manufacturing capability is exactly the open question for a Siemens Energy reading of this chapter.

Research implication: Schneider's supply chain organisation is mature in network design and in programme delivery, and publicly silent on supplier manufacturing. The network side is run by a dedicated modelling team — seven analysts, external consultants on specific projects, operating across roughly 190 factories, 100 distribution centres and 300,000 finished goods — with resilience stated as an explicit objective alongside cost since COVID. None of that reaches into a supplier's plant. [SE5]

3. Future business readiness
Domain A: 3.00 / 5; 3/5 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

Schneider's forward-planning evidence is about its own network, not its suppliers' readiness. A modelling and network design team — built from 2014, now seven analysts with external consultants brought in for specific projects — models the footprint for service level, cost, resilience, carbon and simplification, with regions involved from the start of each study. Post-COVID the stated direction is simplification and production closer to demand regions: “We don't want to be as reliant on long supply chains that can easily be broken.” [SE5]

On the supplier side, qualification includes sustainability criteria as a significant part of the evaluation, revised in 2023, and the regional supplier quality manager “drives the supplier qualification process and ensures supplier base is fully qualified and compliant.” That is a readiness gate for entry, not a readiness development programme. [SE1, SE6]

Evidence limit: no supplier capacity model, capacity-confidence threshold, ramp-up routine or supplier readiness scorecard was found in public sources. Capacity confidence and ramp-up readiness are therefore left unrated rather than scored low — the evidence is absent, not weak.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Business need and capability: an electrical-equipment portfolio through a period of demand growth and component scarcity requires suppliers to add qualified capacity and to industrialise new products. The published record contains neither a supplier capacity intervention nor a supplier industrialisation case. What it contains is a buyer-side answer — regionalise, simplify, model the network, hold safety stock in more places — which changes Schneider's exposure without changing any supplier's capability. [SE5]

This is a clean example of the distinction the benchmarking guide draws. Moving production closer to demand is a sourcing and footprint decision; helping a nearer supplier become able to make a part it could not make before is capability building. Schneider publishes the first and not the second.
Readiness and the limits of inference

Schneider's recognitions — a leading analyst firm ranking its supply chain first in 2024, Corporate Knights placing it seventh most sustainable overall — are company-level assessments of supply chain performance. They are not evidence about supplier capability and are excluded from scoring, as are the programme-level sustainability awards. [SE2, SE5]
4. Supplier production-system capability
Domain B: 3.80 / 5; 5/7 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

The supplier quality function is documented through role design. A regional supplier quality manager drives qualification, plans and conducts assessments, reports major and minor findings and “verifies effective closure of assessment findings by the supplier,” monitors supplier quality issues and non-conformance reports and identifies development actions, deploys a quality and safety framework for subcontractors, and is measured on reducing the cost of poor quality by addressing root causes. The stated mission includes “Focusing on Supplier Development and improving performance of Supplier by optimizing processes.” [SE6]

Boundary on role evidence: this listing names qualification, assessment and lead-auditor skills but no industrial method set — no APQP, PPAP, 8D, SPC, FMEA or lean. Against Caterpillar's and Hitachi Energy's equivalents, the absence is conspicuous and is treated as a limit on what can be concluded about Schneider's supplier-side technical depth, not as proof that no such capability exists.

Evidence limit: no supplier production-system case, no method set, no flow or throughput programme and no supplier operating result was found. Flow and constraint management and throughput and lead-time management are left unrated.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Situation and capability: the documented intervention is not about production at all. Schneider took 1,000 suppliers that mostly could not measure their own operational emissions, gave them a measurement method, a staged roadmap, eight technical trainings and a peer platform, and published the population's progress every year for five years against a pre-set target — 27% in 2023, 40% in 2024, 56% at the end of 2025 against a 50% ambition. In parallel, strategic suppliers conforming to Decent Work requirements went from 1% in 2022 to 98% in 2025, and assessed suppliers' ISO 26000 scores rose 9.6 points from 2019. [SE1, SE2, SE7]

Roles and transfer: Schneider contributed the method, the tools and the teaching, drawing on a services division that sells the same capability commercially; suppliers contributed the implementation and the capital behind their own reduction measures. The peer-to-peer element of the Zeigo platform is the closest thing in this cohort to a supplier learning network outside Hitachi's associations. [SE2, SE3]

Evidence limit and domain fit: the capability built is carbon and labour management. It is scored under capability building and sustainment, where the criterion asks whether the company can build and sustain supplier capability at all, and it is deliberately not allowed to lift the production-specific rows — process stability, flow, throughput — where Schneider publishes nothing.
What the five-year trajectory does and does not prove

It proves four things that matter for a benchmark of this kind: that Schneider can define a supplier population precisely, that it can specify what the supplier must become able to do, that it can resource the teaching rather than merely issue the requirement, and that it will publish the number annually including when it is short of target. Those are organisational capabilities independent of subject matter. It does not prove that the same machinery has ever been pointed at a supplier's manufacturing process, and no public evidence suggests it has. For a company evaluating Schneider as a benchmark partner, that is the question to put directly. [SE1, SE2, SE7]
5. Resilience and continuity
Domain C: 3.00 / 5; 3/4 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

Schneider's continuity work is network-side and well organised. Risk exposure among suppliers is identified by geography and type of activity using a commercial mapping tool, with the most exposed strategic suppliers prioritised for on-site audit. Supply chain resilience appears as a named risk in the group's risk factors, and the Vigilance Plan identifies supplier risk categories — working hours and rest time among human rights issues, emissions from raw-material transformation and transport, and pollution from purchased substances such as solvents. [SE1, SE4]

The network design function treats resilience as an explicit objective rather than a by-product: reduce lead times and raise service levels, hold safety stock in more locations at added cost, centralise slow-moving SKUs in one location despite longer lead times, and include tariffs and tax factors in landed-cost analysis. Schneider's modelling discipline is notable — it promises at most half of the savings a model shows, and it abandoned a country project when political volatility made the recommendation unreliable. [SE5]

Evidence limit: no supplier business-continuity requirement, supplier exercise, multi-tier mapping, recovery-time measure or supplier-side continuity programme was found. Structural adaptation support is unrated.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Situation: 53,000-plus suppliers, a component-intensive portfolio and a stated post-COVID objective of being less reliant on long supply chains. Capability that would need developing on the supplier side: continuity planning, recovery capability and the ability to absorb a disruption. What the record shows is buyer-side mitigation — regionalisation, safety stock, SKU placement, scenario modelling — plus risk mapping and audits. Under the benchmarking standard, risk maps, inventory buffers and dual sourcing without supplier capability-building are flagged rather than counted. [SE1, SE4, SE5]

The contrast with Schneider's own decarbonisation work is instructive and worth putting to the company: it has demonstrated that it can take 1,000 suppliers through a staged capability programme with annual measurement, and it has not applied that template to continuity, where its supplier-facing activity stops at assessment.

7. Case decisions, limitations and Siemens Energy hypotheses
Case decisions by domain (eligibility is separate from maturity)

A: REJECT network modelling and regionalisation as supplier capability evidence; INVESTIGATE whether supplier capacity and ramp-up work exists unpublished, since two criteria could not be rated at all.

B: KEEP the Zero Carbon Project and Decent Work trajectories as capability building with verified multi-year outcomes, scoped to their subject matter; INVESTIGATE everything production-related, where the record is silent.
C: REJECT risk mapping, safety stock and footprint change as standalone proof.
REJECT as standalone proof: EcoVadis and Vigilance assessment counts, supply chain awards and rankings, training attendance taken alone. Retain their useful Layer 1 evidence.

Next evidence: whether the Zero Carbon template has ever been applied to a manufacturing capability; the supplier quality function's method set and cadence; any supplier capacity or industrialisation case; supplier continuity requirements. Undisclosed budgets, selection weights and exit rules remain gaps.

Scoring note: all 16 criteria are first-time assessments, and five are unrated. A company with eleven rated criteria is not directly comparable to one with sixteen; the coverage figure should be read alongside the score in every cohort comparison.

Siemens Energy relevance: all adaptation ideas below are analytical hypotheses for low-volume, high-complexity, long-lead-time supply. They are not observed Siemens practices and are not part of the maturity score.
Future Business Readiness — Lower evidence. Strong buyer-side network design, no supplier readiness work in the public record. [SE5]

Supplier Production-System Capability — Split. The best measured capability-building trajectory in the cohort, on a non-production capability, alongside the thinnest supplier-quality method description. [SE1, SE2, SE6]
Resilience and Continuity Capability — Buyer-side only. Mapping, buffers and footprint, with no supplier preparedness activity evidenced. [SE4, SE5]
Transferability hypothesis

Siemens adaptation to investigate: borrow the programme architecture and change the subject. The Zero Carbon design — a named population covering a stated share of the problem, a baseline the supplier measures with tools you provide, a staged roadmap, trainings with counted attendance and an annual public number against a pre-set target — is subject-agnostic. Test it on a manufacturing capability: for example, first-pass yield or weld-repair rate across the fifty suppliers carrying the most rework, with the same five-year cadence.
Transferability hypothesis

Siemens adaptation and potential learning: the peer platform may matter more than the training. Zeigo gives suppliers best practices, peer-to-peer connections and access to third-party solutions, which lets capability spread without the buyer in the room — the same mechanism Hitachi gets from its supplier associations by different means. For a dispersed, low-volume supply base that cannot easily be convened, test whether a platform substitutes for a forum.
Transferability hypothesis

Siemens adaptation to investigate: apply Schneider's own modelling discipline to supplier continuity. Schneider promises at most half the savings a model shows and walked away from a project when the inputs were unreliable. Translated to continuity, that means not claiming a resilience benefit from a dependency map until a supplier has executed a recovery under exercise conditions — the step Schneider's record shows it has not yet taken.

Audit and search-gap log — 17 October 2026. This is a prompt-conformance review of public sources with targeted source checks. All 16 criteria were assessed; five are unrated for want of evidence. Requirements, programme descriptions, role descriptions and reported outcomes are distinguished.

Targeted follow-up that remains unresolved: supplier capacity and ramp-up work of any kind; the supplier quality function's method set; whether the Zero Carbon template has been applied to manufacturing capability; supplier continuity requirements; reconciliation of the 4,052-assessed and 4,000-audited figures.

9. Extended Deep Research - Schneider Electric: Supplier Capability-Building Benchmark
This section re-examines Schneider Electric at greater depth, and it is the only chapter in this benchmark where the deeper pass overturns a stated finding of sections 1–8 rather than extending it.

Sections 1–8 concluded, on the basis of a single supplier quality role description, that Schneider Electric's supplier quality function was defined in responsibility but unspecified in method — the chapter's words were that the role “names no industrial method set.” That conclusion held B2 and B3 at 3 and was recorded in the search-gap log as the chapter's weakest inference, resting on one document.

The deeper pass located a second and far more specific role description — a Senior Supplier Quality Engineer position in Bangpu, Thailand — that names the method set in full: PPEP, SAM, APQP, PPAP, advanced PFMEA, poka-yoke, jidoka, SPC, MSA, gauge repeatability and reproducibility, Cp and Cpk, tolerancing, GD&T, Six Sigma DMAIC, kaizen, 5S, 8D, why-why analysis, fishbone analysis and ISO 9000 internal audit certification, applied to named processes including plastic injection moulding, stamping, bending, laser cutting and machining. [SE8]

Scoring note and correction: the finding on which B2 and B3 were held at 3 is withdrawn. Under this chapter's calibration B2 and B3 move from 3 to 4 and A3 is raised from NE to 3, taking Schneider Electric's overall score from 3.27 to 3.40 and its evidence coverage from 11/16 to 12/16. Section 6 carries the corrected scores and flags each one as corrected. A countervailing reading under the stricter calibration used in the cohort overview is set out in 1.2, because the two calibrations resolve this evidence differently and a reader needs to know that.
1. Executive Summary
Strongest evidence of actual supplier capability building

Schneider Electric's supplier quality function is now established as method-specific rather than responsibility-only. The Senior SQE role carries a mandate to drive continuous improvement of supplier quality levels, to deploy the Part and Product Evaluation Plan and the Supplier Approval Module, to run APQP and PPAP with suppliers, to apply advanced PFMEA, poka-yoke and jidoka, and to lead supplier problem-solving through why-why analysis, fishbone analysis and 8D. It requires twelve or more years of supplier development and supplier quality engineering experience, manufacturing process audit experience and ISO 9000 internal audit certification. [SE8]

The named process scope matters as much as the method list. The role specifies plastic injection moulding as a mandatory competence and adds stamping, bending, laser cutting and machining — which locates the work in specific fabrication technologies rather than in generic quality management, and implies the engineer is expected to discuss a supplier's tooling and process parameters rather than its paperwork.
What the method evidence does and does not establish

It establishes that Schneider Electric defines supplier quality work in the same methodological terms that the strongest companies in this cohort use, and that it staffs the function with senior engineers expected to audit manufacturing processes. That is a substantially stronger position than sections 1–8 credited.

It does not establish execution. A role description states what an organisation intends a job to be, and two role descriptions do not constitute a programme record. Nothing located in either pass reports how many suppliers Schneider Electric worked with, what changed inside a supplier's process, or any before-and-after figure. The company has, on the located evidence, the specification and the staffing model of a capability-building function and no published output from it.
Resilience and continuity
Unchanged by the deeper pass. No supplier continuity exercise, recovery measure or disruption case was located. Domain C remains Schneider Electric's weakest and the pass found nothing bearing on it.
Overall assessment

Corrected score 3.40 on 12 of 16 criteria. Schneider Electric moves from the middle of this cohort to its upper-middle on the strength of a documented method set, and it stays below the companies that publish supplier outcomes because it publishes none. The chapter's shape is characteristic of a large electrical-equipment group whose supplier quality capability is visible mainly through how it recruits.

2. Operating Model and Future Business Readiness
2.1 Reconstructed supplier quality operating model

The two role descriptions together permit a reconstruction that sections 1–8 could not attempt. Supplier approval runs through the Supplier Approval Module, with part and product qualification through the Part and Product Evaluation Plan — two named internal instruments, which indicates a systematised rather than ad hoc qualification path. New-part introduction runs through APQP with PPAP as the submission gate. Risk assessment on the supplier's process runs through advanced PFMEA. Error-proofing and in-line detection are addressed through poka-yoke and jidoka. Measurement capability runs through MSA and GR&R. Process capability runs through SPC with Cp and Cpk. Problem-solving runs through why-why, fishbone and 8D. Improvement runs through Six Sigma DMAIC, kaizen and 5S. [SE8]

That is a complete and conventional industrial supplier quality toolkit, and the presence of jidoka and poka-yoke alongside the AIAG-family tools indicates lean content rather than quality-assurance content alone. The qualification instruments PPEP and SAM are the distinctive elements, because they are Schneider Electric's own named systems rather than industry-standard methods, which implies institutional infrastructure behind the role.
2.2 A1: Future demand readiness

No forward supplier capability-gap identification process was located. The method set is present-tense: it describes how a supplier's current process is qualified and improved, not how future requirements are mapped onto supplier capability. Score unchanged.

Nothing located in either pass addresses supplier capacity assessment or capacity building. Score unchanged.
2.4 A3: Ramp-up and industrialization readiness

This criterion is raised from NE to 3, which is the deeper pass's second correction. Sections 1–8 could not rate ramp-up readiness at all; the new source names APQP and PPAP as run with suppliers and gives Schneider Electric two internal qualification instruments — the Part and Product Evaluation Plan and the Supplier Approval Module — which together describe an industrialization path in institutional terms. That is sufficient for a defined practice. It stops at 3 because no qualification volume, cycle time, pass rate or on-time PPAP figure was located, and the higher bands in this benchmark require measured improvement in the readiness process itself. Coverage rises from 11/16 to 12/16; because 3 equals the existing domain A mean, the domain figure is unchanged at 3.00. [SE8]

The located role is in Bangpu, Thailand, with a process scope — injection moulding, stamping, bending, laser cutting, machining — characteristic of a regional fabrication supply base. That is weak evidence that supplier quality engineering capacity is deployed regionally rather than centrally, which is relevant to localization readiness. It is one posting and supports no score movement. Score unchanged. [SE8]

Advanced PFMEA, GD&T, tolerancing, MSA, GR&R and Cp/Cpk on named fabrication processes constitute a complexity-facing method set: these are the tools a buyer uses when part geometry and process variation are the problem. The score holds because no complex-part case, qualification record or capability study outcome was located. Confidence rises. [SE8]

5.2 What Schneider Electric's public evidence still does not tell us

The deeper pass resolved the method-set question, which section 8's search-gap log had recorded as the chapter's weakest inference, and the resolution went against the chapter's earlier conclusion. The remaining gaps are the ones that matter most and none moved.

No supplier outcome of any kind has been located in two passes: no supplier named, no process changed, no before-and-after figure, no defect reduction, no qualification cycle time, no engagement count. No programme record exists — the function is visible only through how Schneider Electric recruits for it, which establishes intent and staffing and nothing further. No closure or sustainment practice is published. And domain C is empty: no continuity requirement, exercise, recovery measure or disruption case.

A source-quality caveat applies to the whole correction. Role descriptions are reliable evidence of what an organisation intends a function to do and of the seniority it is willing to pay for, and they are not evidence that the work happens at scale or produces results. The correction in this section rests on two such documents. It moves two scores by one band under this chapter's rubric and it would move neither under the stricter rubric used in the cohort overview, as 1.2 sets out.
6. Implications for Siemens Energy

Everything in this section is an analytical hypothesis for low-volume, high-complexity, long-lead-time supply. None of it is observed Siemens Energy practice, and none of it forms part of the maturity score.
6.1 The lesson of this chapter is about evidence, not about Schneider Electric

This chapter was wrong in its first version, on a single document, in a direction that understated a company. That is worth stating because the same failure mode threatens any supplier capability assessment built from public sources: a conclusion drawn from the absence of a detail in one document becomes a finding, and the finding becomes a score.

The practical safeguard is the one this benchmark already uses and should use more aggressively: record the inference's basis in the gap log, state how many documents support it, and treat single-source negatives as provisional. Section 8's log did flag this one, which is why the correction was found.

6.3 Copy the poka-yoke and jidoka content, not just the AIAG tools

Most supplier quality functions in this cohort are specified in AIAG terms — APQP, PPAP, PFMEA, MSA, SPC — which are assessment and qualification instruments. Schneider Electric's role adds poka-yoke and jidoka, which change how the supplier's line behaves. For low-volume, high-complexity work where statistical capability studies are weak because quantities are small, error-proofing and in-line detection are the more useful methods, and a supplier quality function specified only in AIAG terms will not reach for them.
6.4 Name the process technologies, not only the methods

The Schneider Electric role makes plastic injection moulding a mandatory competence and names stamping, bending, laser cutting and machining. Specifying the process technologies an engineer must understand is what separates a supplier quality engineer who can discuss a tool and a cycle from one who can only discuss a control plan. For Siemens Energy's fabrication, welding and machining base, the equivalent specification would name those technologies explicitly.
6.5 Publish the function's output, internally at least

Schneider Electric's supplier quality capability is strong on specification and invisible on output, and it is not alone in this cohort. The internal version of the problem is more serious than the external one: an organisation that cannot say how many suppliers its SQE function improved last year, and by how much, cannot manage the function or defend its headcount. A simple annual count — suppliers engaged, problems closed, capability measures moved — would put Siemens Energy ahead of most of this cohort on evidence, whatever the underlying level.

Toshiba | Supplier Capability Benchmark

Evidence reviewed: 17 October 2026. Ratings describe maturity visible in public evidence. Toshiba publishes briefing, survey, audit, guidance and suspension counts broken out by topic — a level of remediation transparency matched only by Siemens in this cohort — and nothing at all about supplier manufacturing capability, so seven criteria cannot be rated.
1. Summary and scope

Toshiba's benchmark rests almost entirely on one well-structured sustainable procurement disclosure, and its distinguishing feature is that it reports the consequences of its assessments rather than only their volume. In fiscal 2024 it published, by topic, the briefings held, the surveys conducted, the on-site audits performed, the instances of guidance and support given, and the number of transaction suspensions — zero in every category. About 8,000 suppliers were risk-assessed on human rights and health and safety, about 3,000 showed risks and received corrective guidance and training. What is entirely absent is production: no supplier quality requirement, no capability threshold, no capacity work, no manufacturing case.

Overall maturity: 3.44 / 5. Evidence coverage: 9/16 criteria. A Future business readiness: 3.00 (2/5); B Supplier production-system capability: 4.00 (4/7); C Resilience and continuity: 3.33 (3/4). Domains have equal weight; NE is excluded. A domain average resting on two or four criteria is fragile and should be read with the coverage figure, never without it. Audit completed 17 October 2026.

The surveys are stated to include RBA self-assessments, third-party audits and in-house audits. One inconsistency is visible in the source and is reported as published: the narrative text cites the audit figures as survey coverage, which does not reconcile with the table. [TB1]

The consequences are published alongside: guidance and support in 6 cases on human rights and labour, 125 on health and safety and 65 on environment, with transaction suspensions of zero in every category, against a stated policy that where a supplier's remedy is “unsatisfactory” the company suspends transactions. The worked examples are concrete — guidance on employment conditions, support for smelters seeking conflict-free certification, improving work environments and emergency response equipment, and strengthening safety management systems. [TB1]

Boundary: all of this is sustainability, human rights, health and safety and environment. It establishes that Toshiba can reach a very large supplier population, find problems, provide guidance and training, and report both the activity and its outcomes without flattering itself. It should not be presented as supplier production-capability work, of which no public evidence was located at all.
Resources, scale and measurement

Toshiba's supplier capability work has one documented delivery mechanism beyond its own staff: in fiscal 2024 it supported small and medium-sized enterprises with human rights policy seminars and workshops “as part of the JEITA-led Sustainable Procurement Partnership trial” — an industry-body collaboration that spreads the teaching load across member companies rather than requiring each buyer to build its own programme. For a supply base of twelve thousand companies, that is the only structurally scalable approach available. [TB1]

Internal capability is also counted: about 40 procurement staff received sustainable procurement education in fiscal 2024, and all procurement staff completed human rights e-learning, with 100% participation recorded in both fiscal 2023 and fiscal 2024 and targeted again for fiscal 2025. At one subsidiary, refresher training was run for in-house service providers alongside a compliance check on 16 providers. [TB1]

On decarbonization, Toshiba's own account is unusually candid about failure. It surveyed more than 10,000 primary suppliers worldwide with questions fundamentally updated from earlier ones focused on ISO 14001 certification status — and reports that the response rate was insufficient, attributing this to its own communication, the survey's usability and its question content, with improvements planned that will not burden suppliers. Suppliers that had set Scope 1 and 2 targets were asked to complete a supplementary survey, and Toshiba plans to prioritise dialogue with high-emission industries and its largest purchase volumes. The environment management office and procurement division are working together, and the work is described as “just getting started.” [TB2]

Research implication: Toshiba is the clearest demonstration in this cohort that transparency and capability are different things. It publishes more about what happened after its assessments than almost anyone here, and it publishes nothing about supplier manufacturing. A benchmark that rewarded disclosure alone would rank it far higher than one that asked what a supplier became able to build.

3. Future business readiness
Domain A: 3.00 / 5; 2/5 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

The readiness evidence that exists is selection and segmentation rather than development. Toshiba uses a risk-based approach to rank major recurring suppliers by sector and region, selected about 2,900 new suppliers in fiscal 2024 under each group company's criteria, and secured policy consent from 99.8% of them. Its published spend profile — 44% energy and infrastructure, 71% Japan — shows where the dependency sits without describing what is done about it. [TB1]

Evidence limit: no supplier capacity verification, ramp-up routine, industrialisation gate or complexity-specific development was found anywhere in public sources. Three of five criteria in this domain are unrated, so the domain figure describes two criteria rather than Toshiba's readiness work.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Business need and capability: an energy and infrastructure business representing 44% of procurement spend, sourced 71% from Japan, implies a concentrated domestic supply base supporting long-lead-time equipment. The capability that base would need is qualified capacity and industrialisation support. No supplier-facing response to that need appears in any located source — not a requirement, not a role description, not a programme. [TB1]
Readiness and the limits of inference

Policy consent rates measure willingness to sign, not capability. A 99.8% consent rate across roughly 2,900 new suppliers establishes administrative reach and nothing about what those suppliers can make. It is retained as Layer 1 context. [TB1]
4. Supplier production-system capability
Domain B: 4.00 / 5; 4/7 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

This domain scores on four criteria concerning cadence, assessment discipline and remediation, and is unrated on the three that concern production performance directly. That split is the finding, and it should be read before the number. Toshiba's assessment architecture is genuinely strong: a survey instrument running since fiscal 2021 at a population above twelve thousand, annual RBA self-assessments from key suppliers with guidance graded by risk level, three audit types feeding one reporting line, and an explicit environmental standard against which 97% of suppliers were confirmed compliant. [TB1]

Evidence limit: no supplier quality requirement, capability index, corrective-action clock, defect measure or production improvement case was found. Process stability and yield, flow and constraint management, and throughput and lead-time management are all unrated.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Situation and capability: about 8,000 suppliers were risk-assessed on human rights and health and safety; about 3,000 showed risks. Intervention: those suppliers received “corrective guidance and training,” with some interviewed directly, and the published examples describe real physical changes — improving work environments, improving emergency response equipment, strengthening safety management systems, and supporting smelters seeking conflict-free certification. Verification: 97% environmental compliance confirmed, and zero transaction suspensions against a policy that threatens them. [TB1]

Under the benchmarking standard this qualifies as assessment followed by structured gap closure, within its subject matter. Two limits apply. The guidance counts — 6, 125 and 65 — are small against roughly 3,000 suppliers identified as showing risks, which suggests either that most remediation is handled without being counted as guidance or that most risks are closed by the supplier alone. And guidance is reported as given, never as completed or verified.
Why zero suspensions is worth recording

Toshiba publishes a suspension policy — if a supplier's remedy is unsatisfactory, transactions stop — and then publishes zero suspensions in every category for the year. Two readings are available and the public record does not distinguish them: either remediation works and escalation is never needed, or the threshold is never applied. Most companies in this cohort publish neither the policy nor the count, so the question cannot even be asked of them. Publishing a number that invites the question is a disclosure practice worth noting on its own. [TB1]
5. Resilience and continuity
Domain C: 3.33 / 5; 3/4 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

Toshiba's exposure picture is published with more structure than most. The risk-based approach ranks major recurring suppliers by sector and region; spend concentration is disclosed at 44% in energy and infrastructure and 71% in Japan; and sub-tier reach exists within minerals, where fiscal 2024 surveys covered about 475 suppliers that might use 3TG and 303 that might use cobalt, with RMAP-compliant smelter sourcing required under OECD due diligence guidance. [TB1]

On disruption, the published response is specific but narrow: following events in Ukraine, Toshiba is assessing procurement risks linked to Russia and securing alternative suppliers. Business continuity is named as a survey topic and nothing further is said about it. [TB1]
Evidence limit: no supplier continuity requirement, exercise, drill, recovery measure or multi-tier mapping beyond minerals was found. Structural adaptation support is unrated.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Situation: a concentrated Japanese supply base serving energy and infrastructure equipment, in a country with well-understood seismic exposure, where supplier business continuity planning is a long-established industry practice. Capability that would need developing on the supplier side: tested continuity and recovery. What Toshiba publishes is a survey topic heading and an alternative-sourcing response to one geopolitical event. Under the benchmarking standard, business continuity plans that are not tested or embedded are flagged; here there is no evidence that plans are even required. [TB1]

The one genuine continuity-adjacent capability contribution is in the health and safety guidance: improving emergency response equipment and strengthening safety management systems at suppliers raises their ability to withstand and respond to a site event. That is counted under capability building, not here, and it is noted as the closest thing in Toshiba's record to supplier resilience work. [TB1]

Scoring note: all 16 criteria are first-time assessments and seven are unrated. The B domain average of 4.00 rests on four compliance-scoped criteria and is not a statement about production capability; the overall figure should never be quoted without the 9/16 coverage beside it.

Siemens Energy relevance: all adaptation ideas below are analytical hypotheses for low-volume, high-complexity, long-lead-time supply. They are not observed Siemens practices and are not part of the maturity score.
Future Business Readiness — Minimal evidence. Segmentation and onboarding; nothing on supplier readiness. [TB1]
Supplier Production-System Capability — Strong assessment and remediation reporting, zero production content. The score reflects the former and the coverage reveals the latter. [TB1]
Resilience and Continuity Capability — Good exposure disclosure, one documented event response, no supplier-side continuity work. [TB1]
Transferability hypothesis

Siemens adaptation to investigate: publish the consequences, not just the activity. Toshiba reports briefings, surveys, audits, guidance instances and suspensions by topic, including a zero that invites scrutiny. Any supplier programme that reports only how many assessments it ran is unfalsifiable. Reporting what followed each one — including how often nothing did — is what makes a programme manageable rather than merely visible.
Transferability hypothesis

Siemens adaptation and potential learning: use an industry body as the delivery channel for SME capability building. Toshiba's SME seminars and workshops run under a JEITA-led partnership trial rather than as a Toshiba programme, which spreads cost across member companies and gives the supplier one curriculum instead of five. For a supply base shared with competitors — which in heavy electrical equipment it largely is — this is the only economically sensible route to broad capability work.
Transferability hypothesis

Siemens adaptation to investigate: copy Toshiba's candour about a failed instrument. It surveyed over 10,000 suppliers on emissions, judged the response rate insufficient, and attributed the failure to its own communication, usability and question design rather than to supplier indifference. Most supplier programmes in this benchmark would have reported the survey as completed. Designing a programme with an explicit test for whether suppliers can actually respond — and treating a low response as a design fault — is a transferable discipline.
