9. Extended Deep Research - Toshiba: Supplier Capability-Building Benchmark

This section re-examines Toshiba at greater depth. Sections 1–8 rated Toshiba 3.44 on nine of sixteen criteria and recorded in the search-gap log that the chapter rested on partial disclosure: the B domain scored 4.00 on four criteria while three others were unrated, and the log warned that a domain average resting on four criteria is fragile.

The deeper pass recovered Toshiba's full sustainable procurement disclosure, which is among the most numerically detailed in the cohort. It supplies supplier populations, briefing, survey and audit counts by topic, a risk-based assessment programme with targets and achievement rates, remediation counts, supply-chain composition by sector and region, and responsible-minerals figures. [TB8]

It supplies no production-capability content whatever, and that is the chapter's finding. Every number recovered belongs to human rights, occupational health and safety, environment, ethics or minerals. Nothing describes Toshiba changing how a supplier manufactures — no process improvement, no quality capability work, no defect or yield figure, no engineering intervention. The three unrated B criteria stay unrated after a search that produced several thousand words of supplier data.

Scoring note: no score moves and coverage does not change. Confidence rises substantially on B2, B6, B7 and C2, where numbers now sit behind ratings that previously rested on described practice. This is the same pattern the Doosan chapter in Batch 1 documents, and 1.2 draws the two together.
1. Executive Summary
Strongest evidence of actual supplier capability building

Toshiba's strongest located evidence is remediation at scale with training attached. Risk assessments were run on about 8,000 suppliers for human rights and occupational health and safety; about 3,000 suppliers with confirmed risks received corrective-action documents and training, and some were interviewed directly. [TB8]

Three thousand suppliers receiving corrective-action documentation and training is the largest remediation population located anywhere in this benchmark. The qualification is that what was built is compliance capability — the ability to meet a code — rather than production capability, and that no outcome is published for any of it: no re-assessment result, no risk-closure rate, no improvement series.
A risk-based assessment programme with published targets

The Sustainable Procurement Survey has run since FY2021 on a risk basis, covering human rights, occupational health and safety, environment, ethics and business continuity planning. Risk targeting uses country and region lists from Japan, the EU and UNEP FI's tool. On the environmental track, 12,322 suppliers were checked in FY2024 against a target of 13,000, with 13,014 checked in FY2023 and 97% meeting standards; the FY2025 target for evaluating environmental management implementation is 100%. [TB8]

Publishing a target, the number achieved against it, the prior year's figure and the pass rate is disclosure discipline that most of this cohort does not approach. It is also the clearest evidence in the chapter of a programme being managed rather than merely described.
Engagement volume by topic

FY2024 cumulative figures are published across three topics: human rights and labour — 515 briefings attended, 542 surveys, 47 on-site audits; health and safety — 1,448 briefings, 573 surveys, 121 audits; environment — 1,135 briefings, 2,198 surveys, 122 audits. Supplier consent to the revised Procurement Policy ran at 100% for new suppliers in FY2023 and 99.8% in FY2024 against a 100% target, with about 2,900 new suppliers selected in FY2024 and about 12,000 primary suppliers asked to follow the March 2022 revised policy. [TB8]

One reporting inconsistency is recorded as found rather than resolved: the source's narrative describes the 47, 121 and 122 figures as surveys while its own table labels them on-site audits. The surveys are stated to include RBA Self-Assessment Questionnaires, third-party audits and Toshiba's own standards, which may explain the overlap. Both labels are reported.
Capability support beyond assessment

Four support activities were located and all are capability-adjacent rather than production-facing. Dialogue sessions with selected upstream suppliers on reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Participation in JEITA's Sustainable Procurement Partnership in FY2024, where small and medium-sized enterprises were supported in creating human rights policies through seminars and workshops. In the Philippines, refresher RBA Code training for in-house service providers plus a compliance check of sixteen pre-selected providers. And in the Battery Division, briefings on the EU Battery Regulation and CO2 calculation methods. [TB8]

The JEITA item is the most interesting structurally: Toshiba building SME supplier capability through an industry association rather than alone shares the cost across the association's members and reaches suppliers that serve several of them. Among the examples of remediation given is helping smelters obtain conflict-free certification — which, like Doosan's certification support in Batch 1, leaves the supplier holding a third-party credential it retains independently.
Resilience and continuity

Business continuity planning appears as one of five topics inside the Sustainable Procurement Survey and nowhere else; no separate supplier BCP requirement was located, and no exercise, recovery measure or disruption case exists. The one concrete volatility response located is geopolitical: Toshiba states it is assessing risks from Russia-sourced procurement and securing alternative suppliers. [TB8]
Overall assessment

Toshiba's score is unchanged at 3.44 on nine criteria. The company publishes more supplier numbers than almost anyone in this cohort and publishes them entirely about compliance. Its seven unrated criteria — capacity, ramp-up, complexity, process stability, flow, throughput and adaptability — are exactly the production-system and readiness criteria that a sustainability reporting framework never asks about.

1.2 What Toshiba and Doosan together show about this benchmark's method

Toshiba is the second chapter in this project, after Doosan Enerbility in Batch 1, where a deep search produced a large volume of supplier data and left the production-capability criteria exactly where they were. The two cases are worth reading together because they isolate a structural property of the evidence base rather than of the companies.

Large Japanese and Korean industrial groups report supplier activity into sustainability and shared-growth frameworks that ask comprehensively about human rights, safety, environment, ethics and minerals, and ask nothing about process capability, qualification, yield or flow. A company can therefore publish thousands of supplier data points and remain unrateable on seven of this benchmark's sixteen criteria. That is a property of the reporting framework, not evidence that the company does not do the work.

The consequence for how these scores should be read is the same as the Doosan chapter records: for companies whose supplier disclosure runs through a sustainability framework, the production-system and readiness scores are floors rather than estimates. This project does not apply a correction for it, because adjusting some companies and not others would damage comparability more than it would repair, and it states the limitation instead.
2. Operating Model and Future Business Readiness
2.1 Reconstructed supplier management operating model

Toshiba's model is now reconstructable in the compliance domain and remains invisible in the production domain. Entry: suppliers must agree to the Toshiba Group Procurement Policy, which covers legal compliance, human rights, occupational health and safety, the environment, working hours and living wages; it is published in English, Chinese and Thai and suppliers are notified of revisions; consent is tracked and targeted at 100%. Risk targeting: country and region lists from Japan, the EU and UNEP FI identify where to look. Assessment: the Sustainable Procurement Survey across five topics, plus RBA Self-Assessment Questionnaires, third-party audits and Toshiba's own standards. Remediation: corrective-action documents and training for risk-confirmed suppliers, with direct interviews for some. Escalation: guidance and support counts published by topic; suspension of transactions available and used zero times in FY2024. Voice: the Clean Partner Line whistleblower channel, open to suppliers, with three reports in FY2024, each investigated. [TB8]

The zero-suspension figure is worth noting. A remediation system that never terminates is either remarkably effective or not enforcing, and the published evidence cannot distinguish between them. Toshiba's own framing is remediation-first, which is consistent with the Japanese practice of developing rather than replacing suppliers found elsewhere in this cohort.
2.2 A1: Future demand readiness

Score holds at 3. Risk-based segmentation using external country and region risk lists is a real targeting mechanism and it targets compliance risk rather than capability requirements. No forward capability-gap identification, requirement map or gap-closure series exists. Confidence rises on the segmentation evidence. [TB8]
2.3 A2: Capacity confidence
Remains NE. Nothing located in either pass addresses supplier capacity assessment, verification or development. The ~12,000 primary supplier figure describes the base's size, not its capacity.
2.4 A3: Ramp-up and industrialization readiness

Remains NE. About 2,900 new suppliers were selected in FY2024 under each company's criteria, which establishes a selection volume and nothing about qualification, part approval or industrialization. No APQP, PPAP, first-article or equivalent gate was located.
2.5 A4: Localization readiness

Score holds at 3 on better evidence. Supply chain composition by region is now published — Japan 71%, Asia including China and India 27%, Europe and others 2% by monetary value — which is a concrete disclosure of sourcing geography. Why not 4: a composition figure is disclosure, not localization capability; no transfer programme, ratio target or local supplier development activity was located. Confidence rises. [TB8]
2.6 A5: Product and process complexity
Remains NE. Nothing located in either pass addresses complexity-facing supplier engineering, process capability or qualification of complex parts.
Future Business Readiness conclusion

Domain A holds at 3.00 on two of five criteria and remains the chapter's weakest and most fragile figure. Three of the five criteria are unrated, and a domain average computed from two ratings should not be read as a domain assessment.

The pass added substantial evidence to B1, B2, B6 and B7 and none to B3, B4 or B5. 5.2 What Toshiba's public evidence still does not tell us
The deeper pass resolved section 8's first gap-log entry — the absence of quantified supplier programme data — comprehensively. Four gaps remain, and the first is structural rather than incidental.

No production-capability content exists in the published record. Seven criteria remain unrated and all seven are production or readiness criteria. After a search that yielded supplier populations, audit counts, remediation figures, targets, pass rates and composition data, this is a firm finding about Toshiba's disclosure and not about its practice, for the reasons 1.2 sets out.

No total supplier count is published, so no programme's coverage can be computed. This is the single most consequential disclosure gap in the chapter: 12,322 environmental checks, ~8,000 risk assessments and ~3,000 remediations are all unanchored, and the ~12,000 primary supplier figure is a cumulative count of those asked to follow a specific 2022 policy revision rather than a base size.

No remediation outcome is published — no closure rate, no re-assessment result, no risk-resolution figure — so a programme whose volume is precisely counted has unmeasured effect. And business continuity exists only as a survey topic, with no requirement, exercise or recovery measure anywhere.

A source-reading note: the disclosure labels the 47, 121 and 122 figures as on-site audits in its table and as surveys in its narrative, and states that the surveys include RBA Self-Assessment Questionnaires, third-party audits and Toshiba's own standards. Both labels are reported here as found rather than reconciled.
6. Implications for Siemens Energy

Everything in this section is an analytical hypothesis for low-volume, high-complexity, long-lead-time supply. None of it is observed Siemens Energy practice, and none of it forms part of the maturity score.
6.1 Count the programme, then measure it

Toshiba's disclosure is a model of counting and a cautionary case in measurement. It publishes how many suppliers were assessed, briefed, audited, remediated and trained, with targets, prior-year comparatives and pass rates — and publishes nothing about whether any supplier's risk was actually closed. The distinction is the one this benchmark applies throughout: volume is an input, and the programme's output is the share of identified gaps that were closed and stayed closed.

The practical rule for any supplier programme: for every count published, publish the corresponding closure. Suppliers assessed and suppliers whose findings closed. Suppliers trained and suppliers who subsequently passed. Without the second number the first measures effort.

6.3 Use an industry association to reach SMEs

The JEITA Sustainable Procurement Partnership is the most efficient capability mechanism in this chapter. Small suppliers typically serve several large customers in the same industry, each of which would otherwise build a separate programme to raise the same supplier to the same standard. Running the support through an industry body shares the cost, reaches suppliers that serve competitors, and gives the supplier one standard to meet rather than five.

For power-equipment supply, where specialist fabricators and foundries serve several OEMs, the equivalent is an industry-level programme on welding qualification, non-destructive testing competence or forging process capability. Siemens Energy would not capture the benefit exclusively, which is precisely why the cost per unit of capability is low.
6.4 Publish the denominator

Toshiba's figures cannot be interpreted because no total supplier count accompanies them. The same failure is common internally: a programme reports that it assessed 400 suppliers without saying whether that is most of the critical base or a tenth of it. Any supplier capability metric should be published as a ratio against a defined population, and the population should be the one that matters — critical suppliers, not all suppliers.

Hitachi Energy | Supplier Capability Benchmark

Evidence reviewed: 17 October 2026. Ratings describe maturity visible in public evidence. This chapter assesses Hitachi Energy as its own company; the separate Hitachi chapter in this benchmark assesses the group and draws on different group-company evidence. Hitachi Energy's supplier architecture descends from ABB Power Grids, so the ABB chapter describes a related system and should be read alongside it.
1. Summary and scope

Hitachi Energy's benchmark rests on a six-step supplier sustainability process that ends in supplier development, an assessment programme scaling fast on published figures, a commodity-organised supplier quality engineering function that explicitly assesses capacity resilience, and the most practical supplier resilience mechanism located anywhere in this cohort: onboarding suppliers to a risk-scanning platform at no cost to them, with training recorded and dated. What is absent is manufacturing outcome evidence — the development half of the process is named and not described, and the forward ramp is explained entirely through Hitachi Energy's own factories.

Overall maturity: 3.40 / 5. Evidence coverage: 14/16 criteria. A Future business readiness: 3.20 (5/5); B Supplier production-system capability: 3.33 (6/7); C Resilience and continuity: 3.67 (3/4). Domains have equal weight; NE is excluded. These are evidence-bounded maturity ratings, not enterprise performance. Audit completed 17 October 2026.
2. Supplier selection and support delivery

Supplier qualification, current performance status and selection for intensive capability-building are separate decisions. The evidence below distinguishes the signal for attention, the people involved, the intervention and its verification.
Pillar
Q1 — Which suppliers to target?
Q2 — How to structure and scale support?
Future business readiness

Supplier quality engineering is organised by commodity — casting, welded parts, mechanical parts, electronics — and defines “tiering criteria that rank suppliers by risk and performance.” Sustainability targeting is separate and risk-based: only suppliers with elevated risks are invited to assessment. [HE2, HE5]

Through “in-depth assessments of suppliers' quality systems, production capabilities, and capacity resilience” and through the supplier-facing Quality Assurance Agreement and Quality Manual, whose process-map logic helps suppliers navigate Hitachi Energy's quality processes. [HE4, HE5]
Supplier production-system capability

Suppliers are evaluated on quality, delivery performance and alignment with company values; underperformers are identified for corrective action, with dashboards built to “escalate issues proactively.” [HE5, HE6]

Corrective action driven by commodity supplier quality engineers using 8D problem solving and Six Sigma tools including measurement system analysis and statistical process control, with process knowledge in machining, casting, welding and silver plating. [HE5]
Resilience and continuity

Risk screening and risk categorisation are the first two steps of the sustainability process, sharpened from April 2024 by a more accurate screening tool; supplier risk is also scanned in real time through a specialist platform. [HE1, HE2, HE3]

Suppliers are onboarded to the risk platform at no cost to them, strongly encouraged to register, asked to respond to notifications and risk assessment surveys, and given a user guide, a training presentation and three recorded training sessions on 9, 10 and 11 December 2025. [HE3]

The sustainability process is published as six named steps: risk screening, risk categorisation, EcoVadis assessment, results review, corrective actions and improvement, and continuous monitoring and supplier development. Only suppliers with elevated risks are invited to complete the assessment, which covers environment, labour and human rights, ethics and sustainable procurement, with EcoVadis independently reviewing evidence and issuing a scorecard showing strengths, improvement areas and industry benchmarks. Where required, suppliers develop corrective action plans, and progress is “monitored through ongoing collaboration.” [HE2]

The scale is published and growing fast. Suppliers assessed on ESG rose from 266 in FY2022 to 1,558 in FY2023 and 1,992 in FY2024, with spend coverage rising from 23% to 42% to 58% across the same years. In FY2024, 101 new supplier on-site audit assessments were completed under the Supplier Sustainability Development Program, representing 81% of the globally planned assessments, and 100% of newly qualified suppliers were assessed against environmental and social criteria. From April 2024, sustainability risk screening became more accurate through an enhanced screening tool. [HE1]

External recognition is extensive and should be weighted for what it measures. EcoVadis awarded Hitachi Energy platinum, placing it in the top 1% of 89,000 assessed companies, and gave its supply chain management function the “Best Mature Program in Sustainable Procurement” award; CDP placed the company on its A-list for supplier engagement; and the supplier-facing page records an EcoVadis gold medal dated 16 April 2026 alongside the Best Mature Program award in 2025. These assess Hitachi Energy's programme, not its suppliers' capability, and the medal level differs between the two sources, which is reported here as published. [HE1, HE2]

Boundary: everything above concerns sustainability, ethics and compliance. It establishes that Hitachi Energy can screen, assess, remediate and scale — at a rate few peers match — within that subject matter. It should not be presented as its production-capability assessment, and the sixth step, where supplier development would live, is a name without a description.

The technical function is visible through role design. A High Voltage Products supplier quality development lead in Shanghai is accountable for a team of supplier quality engineers organised by commodity, for “in-depth assessments of suppliers' quality systems, production capabilities, and capacity resilience” to reduce supply chain risk, for defining tiering criteria that rank suppliers by risk and performance, for driving corrective actions with underperforming suppliers, for 8D and Six Sigma tooling including Minitab, MSA and SPC, for building real-time dashboards to escalate issues proactively, and for designing and delivering training, workshops, cross-site knowledge sharing and mentoring. The training described develops Hitachi Energy's own engineers, not suppliers. [HE5]

Boundary on role evidence: a single job description establishes intended design, ownership and method vocabulary. It does not establish deployment volume, supplier coverage or outcomes. The phrase “capacity resilience” is, however, worth isolating: it is the only place in this cohort where capacity and resilience are named as a single assessed property of a supplier rather than handled by separate systems.
Resources, scale and measurement

Hitachi Energy's supplier-facing documents are the Supplier Quality Assurance Agreement, which suppliers are asked to acknowledge at the start of the relationship and which is intended to “streamline the supply base to compliant and collaborative partners” and reduce incidents, and the Supplier Quality Manual, which includes a “process map logic” to help suppliers find the correct way to work with Hitachi Energy's quality processes. The stated goal of the agreement is a “problem-free experience” benefiting both sides. Neither document's detailed requirements were retrievable, so no thresholds, clocks or escalation ladders can be reported. [HE4, HE6]

The supply chain management function describes its own operating approach in a 2024 blog by the head of supply chain management for high voltage products: suppliers evaluated on quality, delivery performance and alignment with values; data analytics used to track supplier performance, inventory levels and transportation costs; a Digital Passport System for high-voltage components to improve traceability; risk identification covering geopolitical instability, natural disasters and economic fluctuations; and a disruption management plan with contingency plans for “sourcing alternative materials or suppliers.” No performance metrics accompany it. [HE6]

The forward demand is the largest in this cohort relative to current revenue, and it is answered without reference to suppliers. Hitachi Energy reported a $43 billion order backlog in FY2024 against roughly $16 billion of revenue, targeting over $23 billion by FY2027, supported by about $9 billion of investment, roughly $2 billion of factory capex in FY2024–25, shift increases, productivity measures and 15,000 additional people by 2027, against a target of over 98% contractual on-time delivery. Transformer-specific investment of more than $1.5 billion was announced in April 2024 to expand global transformer capacity gradually by 2027 — including about $180 million for a new Vaasa campus in Finland and expansions across Germany, the United States, Colombia, China, Vietnam and Australia, creating over 4,000 jobs in a transformer business of more than 17,000 people — with a further $250 million announced in March 2025. None of these announcements mentions suppliers, supply constraints or component bottlenecks. [HE7]

Research implication: Hitachi Energy has a fast-scaling assessment and remediation engine, a technical function that assesses exactly the right supplier property, and a resilience mechanism designed so that cost is not a barrier to supplier participation. The gap is the same one its parent group shows: the development step is named, the capacity assessment has no published follow-through, and the ramp that would justify supplier development is explained entirely through its own factories.

3. Future business readiness
Domain A: 3.20 / 5; 5/5 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

Readiness evidence divides cleanly between what Hitachi Energy assesses in suppliers and what it builds itself. On the assessment side, the commodity supplier quality organisation evaluates quality systems, production capabilities and capacity resilience in depth, and ranks suppliers by risk and performance — which is the correct diagnostic for a business whose growth depends on supplier capacity. On the build side, the published ramp consists of Hitachi Energy's own factories, shifts, productivity measures and 15,000 new employees. [HE5, HE7]

Evidence limit: no supplier capacity threshold, ramp-up routine, readiness scorecard or localization transfer method was found. What follows a capacity-resilience assessment that finds a gap is not published.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Business need and capability: a backlog of $43 billion against $16 billion of revenue, and a transformer market in which lead times are the binding constraint on customers' projects, require suppliers of core materials, bushings, tap changers, insulation and steel to add qualified capacity on long lead times. The public record identifies the need precisely and contains no supplier-side response to it. [HE7]

The one piece of evidence that a supplier development framework exists by that name comes from outside the company: a 2026 press release from a transformer-component supplier states that its engineering teams took part in training “organized under Hitachi Energy supplier development framework” and explored eco-design methodologies. It is supplier-authored and promotional, gives no duration, content detail or measured outcome, and names no Hitachi Energy owner. It is recorded as a lead confirming the framework is referred to by participants, not as evidence of an intervention. [HE8]
Readiness and the limits of inference

Capacity investment announcements, backlog growth and headcount targets answer a different question from supplier readiness. Building a transformer factory in Vaasa adds Hitachi Energy's capacity; it does not demonstrate that a supplier became able to supply it. These are retained as Layer 1 context and are not scored as supplier capability building. [HE7]
4. Supplier production-system capability
Domain B: 3.33 / 5; 6/7 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

Three elements are documented. The contractual baseline: a Supplier Quality Assurance Agreement acknowledged at the start of the relationship, and a Supplier Quality Manual with process-map logic for navigating Hitachi Energy's quality processes. The organisation: commodity-based supplier quality engineer teams with regional leads and global experts who standardise methods and resolve cross-border quality disputes. The toolkit: 8D problem solving and Six Sigma with Minitab, MSA and SPC, applied to corrective action with underperforming suppliers, with dashboards for proactive escalation. [HE4, HE5]

Evidence limit: no capability thresholds, corrective-action clocks, supplier improvement case or outcome was found. Flow and constraint management is unrated. The manual and agreement themselves were not retrievable, so their requirements cannot be assessed.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

The sixth step of the published process is “Continuous Monitoring and Supplier Development,” and that is the whole of what is said about it. The steps before it are described in operational detail — who screens, what is assessed, who reviews independently, what the scorecard shows, who writes corrective action plans. The step where capability would actually be built is a heading. Under the benchmarking standard, an assessment followed by structured gap closure can be capability building and an assessment alone is not; Hitachi Energy publishes the assessment half in full and the closure half as a title. [HE2]

The corrective-action track that is described sits in the quality organisation rather than the sustainability process: commodity engineers drive 8D and Six Sigma-based corrective action with underperforming suppliers and build dashboards to escalate proactively. It is a credible design with a named owner and no published population, cadence or result. [HE5]
Why “capacity resilience” is the phrase worth taking from this chapter

Across fifteen companies, capacity and resilience are handled by different systems: a capacity analysis or certification on one side, a risk register or continuity requirement on the other. Hitachi Energy's supplier quality organisation assesses “quality systems, production capabilities, and capacity resilience” as one in-depth assessment, which treats a supplier's ability to hold output under stress as a property of its production system rather than a separate compliance topic. That framing is free to adopt and is probably the single most useful idea in this chapter for a low-volume, long-lead-time supply base, where the question is rarely whether a supplier can make the part and usually whether it can still make it when something goes wrong. [HE5]
5. Resilience and continuity
Domain C: 3.67 / 5; 3/4 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

Hitachi Energy's supplier-facing resilience mechanism is unusually well designed on one specific axis: participation cost. It has partnered with a specialist provider “as a technical provider for real-time risk event scanning” and is onboarding suppliers to that platform, strongly encouraging registration and stating that the tool “is of no cost to you.” Suppliers are asked to watch for communications from supply chain resilience, to respond to notifications and risk assessment surveys, and to collaborate on mitigation, since the company notes the value of “identifying risks early and proactively collaborating with supply chain partners.” [HE3]

The supporting materials are published and dated: a supplier user guide covering registration and how to respond to notifications and surveys, a supplier training presentation, three recorded training sessions on 9, 10 and 11 December 2025, a video message from the chief procurement officer, a named head of supply chain resilience and risk management, and a supplier newsletter. Offering the same session three times across three consecutive days is a small detail that signals the programme is built for supplier participation across time zones rather than for a compliance record. [HE3]

Upstream of the platform, risk screening and risk categorisation are the first two steps of the supplier sustainability process, enhanced from April 2024 by a more accurate screening tool, and the supply chain function describes a disruption management plan with contingency plans for sourcing alternative materials or suppliers, supported by data analytics across supplier performance, inventory and transportation. [HE1, HE2, HE6]

Evidence limit: no supplier business-continuity requirement, no exercise or drill, no recovery-time measure, no multi-tier mapping and no published count of suppliers onboarded. Structural adaptation support is unrated.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Situation: a grid equipment portfolio with concentrated component sources and multi-year lead times, growing against a backlog nearly three times current revenue. Capability being developed on the supplier side: the ability to receive a risk signal, interpret it and respond — which is why the training matters more than the platform. The sequence is a genuine capability-building design: give the supplier the tool free, teach it how to use the tool, ask it to respond, and collaborate on mitigation. [HE3]

It stops short of the top of the scale for two reasons. The onboarding is recent, with training dated December 2025 and no population published, so regular use cannot be established. And nothing in the record shows a supplier executing a recovery, a drill result, or a recovery time that improved. Under the benchmarking standard, business continuity plans that are not tested or embedded are flagged; Hitachi Energy does not require a tested plan at all — it requires responsiveness to a monitoring system, which is a different and lesser thing. [HE3]

Case decisions by domain (eligibility is separate from maturity)
A: KEEP capacity resilience as an assessed supplier property; REJECT own-plant capacity expansion as supplier evidence; INVESTIGATE what follows a capacity-gap finding.
B: KEEP the assessment and audit-plan discipline; INVESTIGATE step six, the supplier development step that is published as a heading only.

Scoring note: all 16 criteria are first-time assessments. This chapter assesses Hitachi Energy alone; the Hitachi chapter assesses the group using different group-company evidence, and the two should not be averaged or treated as duplicates. The architecture descends from ABB Power Grids, and the ABB chapter describes the related system at its former parent.

Siemens Energy relevance: all adaptation ideas below are analytical hypotheses for low-volume, high-complexity, long-lead-time supply. They are not observed Siemens practices and are not part of the maturity score. This company is also Siemens Energy's closest direct competitor in grid equipment, so its published mechanisms are the most contextually comparable in the cohort.
Future Business Readiness — Lower-medium. The right supplier property is assessed and the ramp is answered without suppliers. [HE5, HE7]
Supplier Production-System Capability — Lower-medium. A strong assessment engine with the development step unwritten. [HE2, HE5]
Resilience and Continuity Capability — Strongest domain. A supplier-facing mechanism designed so that cost and ignorance are not barriers to participation. [HE3]
Transferability hypothesis

Siemens adaptation to investigate: assess “capacity resilience” as one property rather than running capacity and continuity as separate systems. For a critical forging or casting supplier, a single in-depth assessment covering the quality system, the production capability and the ability to hold output under stress produces one conversation and one improvement plan, instead of a capacity analysis owned by sourcing and a continuity questionnaire owned by risk that never meet.
Transferability hypothesis

Siemens adaptation and potential learning: remove the participation cost. Hitachi Energy gives suppliers the risk platform free, publishes the user guide, records the training three times across three days and puts the chief procurement officer on video asking them to use it. Most supplier resilience programmes fail at adoption rather than design. Test whether the same removal of cost and friction raises response rates on a small supplier base that would otherwise ignore a survey.
Transferability hypothesis

Siemens adaptation to investigate: write step six before launching steps one to five. Hitachi Energy's process ends in “Continuous Monitoring and Supplier Development” and says nothing further, which is the commonest failure pattern in this whole benchmark — assessment machinery built in detail, development left as a heading. Define what development means, who delivers it, how long it runs and how it ends, before building the assessment that will feed it.

9. Extended Deep Research - Hitachi Energy: Supplier Capability-Building Benchmark

This section re-examines Hitachi Energy at greater depth. Sections 1–8 rated Hitachi Energy 3.40 on fourteen criteria and recorded in the search-gap log that A2, B2 and B3 rested on thin role-based or named-step evidence, and that the chapter could not establish whether Hitachi Energy operated a supplier development function distinct from supplier quality assurance.

The deeper pass answers that question clearly. Hitachi Energy runs a dedicated, globally scoped and commodity-specialised supplier development function: Global Supplier Development Engineer roles were located for transformers and, separately, for oils and chemicals, each requiring ten or more years of supplier development experience, naming APQP, PPAP, P-FMEA, process control plan and SPC as expertise requirements, and carrying responsibility for leading supplier qualification, implementing supplier improvement actions, overseeing global parts approval, monitoring supplier performance indicators, driving annual supplier evaluations and leading root cause analysis and corrective action on escalated non-conformities. Separate PPAP supply quality engineer and APQP programme manager roles exist alongside them. [HE11]

Three features distinguish this from the supplier quality functions found elsewhere in Batch 3. The title is development rather than quality. The organisation is by commodity — chemicals, gaskets and insulation materials for the transformer role — rather than by plant or region. And the scope is global with frequent international travel, so a single specialist covers a material class worldwide.

Scoring note: A3, B2 and B3 each move from 3 to 4, taking Hitachi Energy from 3.40 to 3.58 on fourteen criteria. Three moves on role-based evidence is a substantial revision and the reasoning for each is given separately; 1.2 states plainly why they are consistent with how this project treated the same class of evidence for Schneider Electric, and why the cohort overview's stricter calibration would hold all three at 3.
1. Executive Summary
Strongest evidence of actual supplier capability building

The commodity-specialised global supplier development engineer is Hitachi Energy's strongest located evidence and a genuinely unusual organisational design. The transformer role's commodity scope is chemicals, gaskets and insulation materials, with required knowledge of their production and solid experience assessing production processes; the oils and chemicals role covers a second material class. Both require ten or more years in supplier development and deep knowledge of quality and continuous improvement tools. [HE11]

Organising supplier development by material class rather than by site means the specialist understands the process technology rather than the local relationship — which is the right structure for a company whose supplier risk sits in insulation materials, oils and gaskets whose failure modes are specific and chemical. It also means capability knowledge accumulates by commodity across the whole company instead of being rebuilt at each plant.
A named method set with seniority behind it

APQP, PPAP, P-FMEA, process control plan and SPC are named as expertise requirements, alongside deep knowledge of quality and continuous improvement tools and solid experience assessing production processes. The role resolves escalated non-conformities by leading root cause analysis and corrective actions, and drives continuous improvement in supplier management. [HE11]

This is the conventional industrial toolchain, required at ten years' depth and attached to a role whose purpose is development rather than assurance. It is the combination — method set plus development mandate plus commodity specialisation plus global scope — that carries B2 and B3 to 4 rather than any single element.
Qualification and parts approval as an owned function

The development role leads supplier qualification and oversees global parts approval to meet technical and operational requirements. Separate roles exist for PPAP supply quality engineering and for APQP programme management, which indicates that product approval is staffed as a function in its own right rather than carried as an additional duty. [HE11]
Performance monitoring with an annual cycle

The role monitors supplier performance indicators and drives annual supplier evaluations. An annual evaluation cycle owned by the development function — rather than by procurement alone — closes the loop between assessment and development, and it corroborates the supplier performance series that sections 1–8 rated B6 on. [HE11]
Resilience and continuity

Unchanged, and Hitachi Energy's resilience domain remains the strongest in Batch 3 at 3.67 on the earlier evidence. Nothing in the new role evidence bears on continuity, capacity verification, exercises or recovery. The partner survey response-rate series recorded in the Hitachi group chapter — falling from 93% in FY2023 to 76% in FY2024 against a 95% FY2025 target — belongs to the group chapter and is not re-rated here.
Overall assessment

Corrected score 3.58 on fourteen criteria, the highest in Batch 3. Hitachi Energy is the clearest case in this batch of a company with a properly constituted supplier development function — dedicated, senior, commodity-specialised, globally scoped, with a named method set and an annual evaluation cycle — and, like every other company in the batch, with no published supplier outcome at all.

1.2 Why three scores move on role-based evidence

Three criteria moving on two role descriptions needs justifying, because role postings are the weakest class of evidence this project admits and because it would be easy to inflate a chapter by reading them generously.

The justification is consistency. This project already moved Schneider Electric's B2 and B3 from 3 to 4 in Batch 1 on exactly this class of evidence: a senior supplier quality role naming a full industrial method set. Hitachi Energy's evidence is of the same class and, on three counts, stronger. The role is titled supplier development rather than supplier quality, so the mandate is capability building rather than assurance. It is global and commodity-specialised rather than site-based, so the capability is organised around process technology. 2. Operating Model and Future Business Readiness
2.1 Reconstructed supplier development operating model

Hitachi Energy's model is now reconstructable and is organised by commodity rather than by process stage, which is unusual. Ownership: a Global Supplier Development Engineer per material class, at ten or more years' experience, covering that class worldwide. Entry: the same role leads supplier qualification and oversees global parts approval against technical and operational requirements, supported by dedicated PPAP and APQP positions. Assessment: solid experience assessing production processes, with P-FMEA and process control plans as the instruments. Measurement: supplier performance indicators monitored, with annual supplier evaluations driven by the development function. Intervention: supplier improvement actions implemented; continuous improvement driven in supplier management. Escalation: escalated non-conformities resolved by leading root cause analysis and corrective actions. Diffusion: best practices promoted across the business unit. [HE11]

The commodity axis is the design's distinguishing feature and its principal risk. 3.1 A development function rather than a quality function

The distinction this chapter turns on is the one the benchmark's core test is built around. A supplier quality function verifies that a supplier meets requirements; a supplier development function changes what the supplier is able to do. Hitachi Energy staffs the second, by title and by mandate: the role implements supplier improvement actions, drives continuous improvement in supplier management, and leads root cause analysis and corrective action rather than merely requiring it of the supplier. A buyer's engineer leading the analysis is working inside the supplier's problem, which is capability transfer in the form this benchmark credits — though, as everywhere in Batch 3, no instance of it is published.

5.2 What Hitachi Energy's public evidence still does not tell us

The deeper pass resolved section 8's principal gap-log entry — whether a supplier development function exists distinct from supplier quality assurance — and resolved it affirmatively and in detail. Four gaps remain.

No supplier outcome of any kind has been located in two passes: no supplier named, no improvement action described, no root cause case, no evaluation result, no qualification volume and no population for any of it. Hitachi Energy has the best-constituted development function in Batch 3 and publishes nothing about its work.

Function size is unknown and it matters more here than for most companies in this cohort. The commodity model concentrates a material class in a specialist; whether that is one engineer or a team per commodity, and how many commodities are covered, determines whether the function reaches the supply base or a fraction of it. Two commodities were located out of an unknown total.

No capacity instrument was located in either pass, which leaves A2 at 4 on earlier evidence with no corroboration — flagged here as the criterion most likely to be generous for this company. And no supplier-facing training, community or horizontal channel was located, which is why B7 holds at 3 while B2 and B3 move to 4.

A source-scope note governing the raised scores: both new sources are role descriptions, one for transformers located in Lodz, Poland and posted in December 2025, the other for oils and chemicals in Poland. Role descriptions establish intent, staffing, seniority and method vocabulary, and do not establish execution, coverage or outcome. Three criteria move on them, which 1.2 justifies by consistency with this project's treatment of Schneider Electric, and which the cohort overview's stricter calibration would not do.
6. Implications for Siemens Energy

Everything in this section is an analytical hypothesis for low-volume, high-complexity, long-lead-time supply. None of it is observed Siemens Energy practice, and none of it forms part of the maturity score.
6.1 Organise supplier development by commodity, not by plant

This is the most directly transferable idea in Batch 3, and Hitachi Energy is the closest comparator in the whole benchmark to Siemens Energy's own position — a grid and power equipment manufacturer with specialist material dependencies and a globally distributed supply base.

Organising supplier development by material class means the specialist understands insulation, oils, gaskets, castings or large fabrications as process technologies rather than understanding one plant's suppliers. Three consequences follow. Knowledge accumulates by commodity across the company instead of being rebuilt at each site. The specialist can compare suppliers within a class, which is where capability gaps become visible. And a problem solved at one supplier can be recognised at another, which a site-based organisation structurally cannot do.
The cost is a single point of dependency per commodity, and the mitigation is obvious: more than one person per critical class, and a written record of what each engagement found.

6.3 Title the role for what you want it to do

Hitachi Energy calls the role Global Supplier Development Engineer; most of this cohort calls the equivalent role Supplier Quality Engineer. The titles describe different jobs and recruit different people. A function titled quality will attract and reward verification; a function titled development will attract and reward capability change. The same observation applies to Emerson in this batch, whose development mandate is written in capability terms, and the two together make the point more strongly than either alone.
6.4 Let the development function own the annual evaluation

Hitachi Energy's development engineer drives annual supplier evaluations rather than receiving them. That closes a loop that is usually open: where procurement evaluates and development intervenes, the evaluation's findings reach the intervener late, filtered and without the underlying process detail. Where the same function does both, the evaluation is a diagnostic rather than a report.
6.5 Lead the root cause analysis

The difference between requiring a supplier to find a root cause and leading the analysis with them is the difference between a corrective action and a transferred method, and it costs the buyer engineering days rather than money. For specialist material failures — an insulation breakdown, a gasket compression-set problem, a weld defect — the buyer frequently understands the failure mode better than the supplier understands it, because the buyer sees it across several suppliers and in service. That knowledge asymmetry is an argument for leading the analysis rather than commissioning it.
6.6 Then publish something, internally at least

Hitachi Energy, Emerson and Siemens AG — the whole of Batch 3 — share one characteristic: a competently designed supplier development function with no published record of its work. For an internal programme the consequence is more serious than for an external benchmark. A function that cannot say how many suppliers it developed last year, in which commodities, against what gaps, with what result, cannot demonstrate its value, defend its headcount, or learn from its own history. A single annual record — suppliers engaged, gaps identified, actions implemented, measures moved — would place Siemens Energy ahead of every company in this batch on evidence, whatever the underlying level of practice.

Emerson | Supplier Capability Benchmark

Evidence reviewed: 17 October 2026. Ratings describe maturity visible in public evidence. Emerson's supplier development mandate is unusually broad where it is documented — one role carries capability, capacity, quality, delivery, innovation, safety and cash — and that breadth rests on a single job description, which is recorded as a confidence limit throughout.
1. Summary and scope

Emerson's benchmark combines a tiered responsible-sourcing policy that distinguishes minimum requirements from advanced requirements and best practices, a sustainability programme with strong external ratings and a measured regionalisation outcome, and a supplier development role whose published scope is the broadest in this cohort: supplier capability, capacity, quality, delivery, innovation, safety and cash optimisation, with capability-gap assessment, improvement plans and milestone tracking, supplier education programmes, and demand-forecast analysis with suppliers to protect continuity of supply. No supplier case, population or outcome is published anywhere.

Overall maturity: 3.48 / 5. Evidence coverage: 14/16 criteria. A Future business readiness: 3.60 (5/5); B Supplier production-system capability: 3.50 (6/7); C Resilience and continuity: 3.33 (3/4). Domains have equal weight; NE is excluded. These are evidence-bounded maturity ratings, not enterprise performance. Audit completed 17 October 2026.
2. Supplier selection and support delivery

Supplier qualification, current performance status and selection for intensive capability-building are separate decisions. The evidence below distinguishes the signal for attention, the people involved, the intervention and its verification.

Future business readiness

“Selected” suppliers are identified by the responsible sourcing programme, its steering committee and the supply chain business owners “based on risk and strategic importance,” with risk assessments considering “a supplier's location, size, industry, and impact on Emerson.” Emerson manages more than 13,000 direct materials suppliers. [EM1, EM4]

Supplier development evaluates “production capacity” and “supplier manufacturing readiness, scalability, and operational effectiveness,” analyses demand forecasts with suppliers and cross-functional teams to protect continuity of supply, and coordinates first article inspection and qualification timelines for development and sourcing projects. [EM3]
Supplier production-system capability

Supplier performance is monitored on operational and quality metrics, and capability and performance gaps are assessed directly; supplier scorecards incorporating sustainability KPIs are being implemented. [EM2, EM3]

Improvement plans are built against assessed gaps with milestones tracked; supplier education and capability-building programmes are run; adoption of lean principles, root cause analysis and corrective actions is driven; supplier consolidation proceeds by strengthening high performers. [EM3]
Resilience and continuity
Risk assessment considers location, size, industry and impact on Emerson; supply chain business owners collect data on supplier performance against responsible sourcing KPIs. [EM1]

Supply chain risks are identified with mitigation plans put in place to support business continuity, and demand forecasts are analysed with suppliers; about 80% of material spend is regionalised. No supplier continuity requirement is published. [EM2, EM3]

The Global Responsible Sourcing Policy, last reviewed in September 2025, is structured in three tiers that function as a progression ladder. Minimum Requirements are “mandatory behaviors and actions” set out in the Supplier Code of Conduct. Advanced Requirements are expected of “Selected” suppliers. Best Practices are encouraged for all. The supply chain business owners are tasked to “engage Selected suppliers to achieve Best Practices, where applicable, over a reasonable period of time.” That is a defined improvement path with a defined target state, which several larger peers in this cohort do not publish. [EM1]

Boundary: the ladder's content is compliance and sustainability — grievance procedures, forced and child labour policies with evidence of actions taken, Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions calculated and reported annually to Emerson, written supply chain security policies. The tiering structure is transferable; the subject matter is not production capability, and “a reasonable period of time” is the only timeline given. [EM1]

Multi-tier expectations are stated rather than mapped: Emerson business units must “extend applicable expectations to their suppliers,” suppliers must address labour and inhumane treatment “within their own operations and their supply chain,” and supply chain security controls must cover “supply chain partners.” Where local law differs, “the higher standard shall be applied.” The policy describes no audit process or methodology, referring instead to evidence provided on request and annual emissions reporting. [EM1]

The sustainability report adds the external validation and the one measured supply chain outcome. Emerson earned a 2025 CDP Supplier Engagement Assessment A List rating and a fourth year on CDP's supplier engagement leaderboard; its EcoVadis score rose to 79, in the 96th percentile, from 52 at its first assessment, earning a gold rating in September 2025; more than 3,600 employees were trained on the Supplier Code of Conduct and sustainability topics in 2025; purchased goods and services emissions were 2,519,400 mtCO2e in 2025, 35% of the Scope 3 footprint and down 10% from the 2021 base year; and “around 80% of material spend is regionalized, allowing us to reduce lead and transit times.” [EM2]

Boundary: the EcoVadis improvement from 52 to 79 measures Emerson's own sustainability management, not its suppliers'. The 3,600 trained are Emerson employees, not suppliers — a distinction the trade coverage of the same figure does not make clearly. Both are Layer 1 context. [EM2, EM4]
Resources, scale and measurement

The supplier development function is where Emerson's capability work is actually described, and its stated scope is the broadest located in this benchmark. A supplier quality manager role in materials and procurement leads “supplier development strategy covering capability, capacity, quality, delivery, innovation, safety, and cash optimization,” assesses supplier capability and performance gaps and then “builds improvement plans and tracks milestones,” monitors supplier performance with operational and quality metrics, runs “supplier education and capability-building programs,” and drives supplier consolidation “by strengthening high performers” while finding new sourcing options. [EM3]

Three elements of that scope are rare. Capacity: the role evaluates production capacity and “supplier manufacturing readiness, scalability, and operational effectiveness.” Forward demand: it “analyzes demand forecasts with suppliers and cross-functional teams to protect continuity of supply” — the only explicit joint demand-planning accountability found in this cohort. And consolidation as development: strengthening high performers is framed as the route to a smaller base, which inverts the usual logic in which consolidation simply removes the weak. [EM3]

The named methods are narrower than the scope: APQP and PPAP as preferred knowledge with the role leading PPAP compliance where applicable, first article inspection coordination, and driving adoption of “Lean principles, root cause analysis, corrective actions” and related continuous improvement methods. 8D, statistical process control, Six Sigma, formal audits and VDA do not appear. Travel to supplier and business locations is required without a stated proportion. [EM3]

Boundary on role evidence: one job description, in one region, establishes intended design and ownership. It does not establish deployment volume, supplier coverage or outcomes, and Emerson publishes no supplier development programme page, no audit volumes and no supplier case. The governance that is published sits on the sustainability side: a Responsible Sourcing Steering Committee formed in 2022, a Responsible Sourcing Committee that “drives and embeds sustainability best practices across supply chain activities,” and bi-annual updates to an environmental sustainability steering committee. [EM1, EM2]

Research implication: Emerson has written the broadest supplier development mandate in this cohort into a single role and published almost nothing about how it is staffed or what it produces. The mandate is coherent — capability, capacity, readiness and demand planning in one accountability rather than split across quality, sourcing and planning functions — and that integration is the most interesting thing here for a company designing an engagement model from scratch.

3. Future business readiness
Domain A: 3.60 / 5; 5/5 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

Emerson scores highest in this domain of the three companies in this batch, and the reason is a single sentence in a role description: supplier development “analyzes demand forecasts with suppliers and cross-functional teams” to protect continuity of supply. Joint demand planning with suppliers is the readiness mechanism that most buyers in this cohort describe wanting and none of the others name as an owned accountability. Alongside it sit capacity evaluation covering manufacturing readiness and scalability, first article inspection coordination with qualification timelines, PPAP compliance leadership, and support for new product introduction, localization and supplier transitions. [EM3]

Evidence limit: all of the above rests on one job posting. There is no capacity threshold, no stress test, no published readiness scorecard and no outcome, and nothing corroborates the role's scope in Emerson's own corporate disclosures.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Business need and capability: a portfolio spanning automation, measurement and final control, sourcing plastics, electronics, steel and machined parts from more than 13,000 direct materials suppliers, with upstream Scope 3 emissions roughly eighteen times operational emissions — a proxy for how much of the product's value is made outside Emerson. The capability needed is suppliers that can scale with demand and industrialise new products. [EM2, EM4]

What is documented is the diagnostic and planning half: capability gaps assessed, capacity and scalability evaluated, improvement plans built with milestones, demand forecasts analysed jointly. What is absent is any record of execution — no named supplier, no gap closed, no capacity added, no qualification accelerated. The regionalisation figure is the nearest thing to an outcome and it is a sourcing-footprint result: around 80% of material spend regionalised, with reduced lead and transit times as the stated benefit. [EM2, EM3]
Readiness and the limits of inference

Regionalising 80% of material spend changes where Emerson buys and shortens transit; it does not establish that any supplier became able to do something new. It is retained as Layer 1 context and scored only as evidence of a deliberate, achieved sourcing posture, consistent with the treatment of Schneider Electric's regionalisation in this benchmark. [EM2]
4. Supplier production-system capability
Domain B: 3.50 / 5; 6/7 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

The documented production-side architecture is: performance monitoring on operational and quality metrics; capability and performance gap assessment; improvement plans with tracked milestones; supplier education and capability-building programmes; driven adoption of lean principles, root cause analysis and corrective actions; PPAP compliance and first article inspection. Supplier scorecards are described in the sustainability report as being implemented with sustainability KPIs incorporated, which suggests the scorecard instrument exists and is being extended rather than built from nothing. [EM2, EM3]

Evidence limit: no capability indices, no corrective-action clocks, no named structured problem-solving format, no audit programme, no supplier case and no outcome. Flow and constraint management is unrated.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Situation and capability: a supplier shows a capability or performance gap; the capability to be built is whatever the gap requires — the role's mandate spans capability, capacity, quality, delivery, innovation, safety and cash. Intervention as documented: assess the gap, build an improvement plan, track milestones, run education and capability-building programmes, drive adoption of lean and root-cause methods, and strengthen high performers as part of consolidating the base. [EM3]

The consolidation framing deserves isolating because it changes the incentive. Most supplier systems in this benchmark consolidate by removing weak suppliers; Emerson's role description consolidates by “strengthening high performers” and finding new options. If a development programme's reward for a capable supplier is more of the base's volume, the supplier has a commercial reason to engage that a corrective action plan does not provide. That mechanism is free to adopt and requires no new programme. [EM3]

Evidence limit and domain fit: everything in this layer is design, from one source. Emerson publishes no evidence that any improvement plan was executed, any milestone met, or any supplier capability changed.
The three-tier policy ladder as a capability instrument

Emerson's Minimum / Advanced / Best Practices structure is the most portable element of its published policy, independent of subject matter. It separates what every supplier must do from what selected suppliers are expected to do from what the company would like to see, and it assigns someone — the supply chain business owner — to move Selected suppliers up the ladder over time. Applied to manufacturing rather than compliance, that is a supplier development programme in three sentences. The gap is that Emerson applies it to compliance, defines the timeline only as “a reasonable period of time,” and publishes no progression data. [EM1]
5. Resilience and continuity
Domain C: 3.33 / 5; 3/4 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

Emerson's published continuity position is thin on requirements and specific on posture. The policy contains no dedicated business continuity section, referring instead to the aim to “maintain resilient business processes” and “ensure an adaptable supply chain network.” Risk assessments “will be conducted and will consider a supplier's location, size, industry, and impact on Emerson” — the last of which is a dependency dimension rather than a hazard dimension. The supplier development role identifies supply chain risks and puts mitigation plans in place to support business continuity. [EM1, EM3]

The concrete resilience outcome is structural: around 80% of material spend is regionalised, which Emerson links directly to reduced lead and transit times. Shorter chains are genuinely more resilient, and unlike most resilience claims in this cohort this one comes with a number attached. [EM2]

Evidence limit: no supplier business-continuity requirement, exercise, drill, recovery measure, dual-sourcing programme or multi-tier mapping beyond flow-down expectations was found. Structural adaptation support is unrated.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Situation: more than 13,000 direct materials suppliers across plastics, electronics, steel and machined parts. Capability being developed on the supplier side: effectively none that is published. What is documented is buyer-side — risk assessment weighted by impact on Emerson, mitigation plans owned by supplier development, and a regionalised footprint. [EM1, EM2, EM3]

The one mechanism that reaches toward supplier capability is the joint demand-forecast analysis, which is scored under volatility management rather than preparedness: analysing forecasts with suppliers to protect continuity of supply gives the supplier the information it needs to plan its own capacity, which is a modest but real transfer. Under the benchmarking standard, dual sourcing, inventory buffers and risk assessment without supplier capability-building are flagged rather than counted, and most of Emerson's continuity evidence falls there. [EM3]

Scoring note: all 16 criteria are first-time assessments and two are unrated. Several rows rest on a single role description, which is treated as weak-moderate evidence throughout and is why no criterion in this chapter reaches the top of the scale.

Siemens Energy relevance: all adaptation ideas below are analytical hypotheses for low-volume, high-complexity, long-lead-time supply. They are not observed Siemens practices and are not part of the maturity score.
Future Business Readiness — Strongest domain, on thin evidence. Joint demand planning with suppliers is the distinctive mechanism. [EM3]
Supplier Production-System Capability — Medium. The broadest development mandate located, with no published methods beyond lean and root-cause and no outcome. [EM1, EM3]
Resilience and Continuity Capability — Medium-low. A quantified regionalisation posture and no supplier-side continuity work at all. [EM1, EM2]
Transferability hypothesis

Siemens adaptation to investigate: give one role the whole mandate. Emerson puts capability, capacity, quality, delivery, innovation, safety and cash in a single supplier development accountability, including joint demand-forecast analysis. In most organisations those sit in four functions that meet quarterly. For a small number of critical, long-lead-time suppliers, test whether one owner carrying all seven produces faster gap closure than four owners carrying one each.
Transferability hypothesis

Siemens adaptation and potential learning: consolidate by strengthening rather than by culling. Emerson's role description drives supplier consolidation “by strengthening high performers,” which turns a development programme into a route to more volume rather than a remedial process. In a supply base where qualified alternatives barely exist, that is the only version of consolidation available — and it gives the supplier a commercial reason to accept intervention.
Transferability hypothesis

Siemens adaptation to investigate: build the Minimum / Advanced / Best Practices ladder for manufacturing capability rather than compliance, and fix the timeline Emerson leaves open. Define what every supplier must do, what critical suppliers are expected to do, and what the best would do; assign an owner to move selected suppliers up it; and replace “a reasonable period of time” with a date and a graduation test — the element Cummins supplies and Emerson does not.

9. Extended Deep Research - Emerson: Supplier Capability-Building Benchmark

This section re-examines Emerson at greater depth. Sections 1–8 rated Emerson 3.48 on fourteen criteria — the joint-highest coverage in Batch 3 — and recorded in the search-gap log that six of those criteria rested on a single role description, with the rationale for each marked “weak-moderate: single role.” The log asked for corroboration and for any supplier outcome.

The deeper pass located two further Emerson supplier-facing roles and produced one organisational finding of real interest that moves no score at all. Emerson fuses supplier development with category management in a single role: a Supplier Development and Category Manager who develops assigned suppliers into capable, resilient partners by assessing capability, identifying gaps and building structured improvement roadmaps, and who simultaneously owns category strategy for assigned material groups and aligns supplier development priorities with the category roadmap. [EM9]

That fusion is distinctive and it matters for a reason this benchmark keeps running into. Capability programmes across this cohort fail or stall because the capability has no commercial weight — the person who develops the supplier is not the person who decides where the volume goes. Emerson puts both decisions in one role. Whether it works is unknown, because, as with every company in Batch 3, Emerson publishes no supplier outcome whatsoever.

Scoring note: no score moves. Confidence rises on A1, A2, A3, A5, B1, B2 and B7. The pass also produced a sharp internal contrast worth recording: Emerson's supplier development role requires a Six Sigma or Lean qualification and eight years' progressive experience, while its supplier quality engineer role names no quality method at all and asks for two years. Capability is concentrated in the development role, not distributed across the function.
1. Executive Summary
Strongest evidence of actual supplier capability building

Emerson's strongest located evidence is the Supplier Development and Category Manager mandate, and its wording is unusually explicit about method. The role develops assigned suppliers into capable, resilient partners — a mandate stated in capability terms rather than compliance terms — and does so by assessing capability, identifying gaps and building structured improvement roadmaps. It assesses supplier capability and builds improvement plans targeting quality, delivery, cost and responsiveness, applies Total Cost of Ownership analysis, integrates sustainability into supplier strategies, and drives cross-functional improvement initiatives. [EM9]

“Assessing capability, identifying gaps, and building structured improvement roadmaps” is the clearest statement of a capability-building method located for any company in Batch 3. It is the three-step sequence this benchmark's core test asks for — diagnose, identify the gap, plan the intervention — and it is stated as the role's routine work rather than as an aspiration.
The category fusion

The same role owns category strategy for assigned material groups — mechanical components, plastics, electronics, and machined, cast or forged parts — and aligns supplier development priorities with the category roadmap. It also acts as a subject-matter expert across supplier development, category management and quality, sets standard ways of working, and mentors or reviews less-experienced colleagues without formal people-management duties. [EM9]

Three consequences follow from the fusion, and all three are structural advantages. Development priority is set by category strategy rather than by whoever complained loudest, so effort follows the material groups that matter. The person developing a supplier controls the commercial lever that makes development worth the supplier's while. And capability assessment feeds sourcing decisions directly, because the same person holds both.
Where the capability actually sits

The contrast between Emerson's two located supplier-facing roles is informative. The development and category role requires a minimum of eight years' progressive experience, demonstrated supplier development and quality tool expertise, proven international supplier development experience, category management experience with commercial acumen, and a Six Sigma or Lean qualification, with about 30% travel across Europe. The supplier quality engineer role requires a mechanical engineering degree, a minimum of two years' experience and “knowledge of quality methodologies” with no method named, and describes its work as driving continuous improvement, resolving quality and technical process issues, conducting supplier audits, monitoring quality indicators, coordinating corrective actions and building supplier relationships. [EM9]

Emerson therefore concentrates its supplier capability expertise in a small senior population and staffs routine supplier quality work at junior level. That is a legitimate and common design — it is cheaper than seniority everywhere — and it means capability building reaches only the suppliers the senior population is assigned to. No count of those suppliers is published.
Resilience and continuity

Unchanged. The development mandate's phrase “capable, resilient partners” puts resilience into the role's stated purpose, which is adjacent evidence and supports no movement: nothing describes what resilience work consists of, and no exercise, recovery measure, continuity requirement or disruption case was located in either pass.
Overall assessment

Emerson's score is unchanged at 3.48 on fourteen criteria. The chapter now rests on three role descriptions rather than one, which repairs the gap log's principal concern, and it continues to rest entirely on role descriptions. Emerson's distinguishing feature in this cohort is organisational rather than methodological: it has put supplier development and category management in the same hands, which no other company here does, and it publishes nothing about the result.
