1.2 What this chapter is actually rating

Emerson is scored on role descriptions across fourteen criteria, and that should be stated plainly because the coverage figure flatters the evidence. Fourteen of sixteen criteria rated is the joint-best in Batch 3 and among the better figures in the cohort; it reflects that Emerson's role descriptions are unusually broad in what they mention, not that Emerson's supplier practice is unusually well documented.

The distinction matters for how the number is used. A role description that mentions capacity, complexity, qualification and improvement gives a reviewer something to rate on each, which raises coverage without raising evidential quality. Emerson's 3.48 and Eaton's 3.79 are both role- and document-based figures; Toyota's and TSMC's rest on named suppliers and measured outcomes. The cohort overview's stricter calibration compresses that difference deliberately, and under it several of this chapter's fours would hold at 3.
2. Operating Model and Future Business Readiness
2.1 Reconstructed supplier development operating model

Emerson's model can be reconstructed at the level of role design and is coherent. Priority setting: category strategy for assigned material groups determines which suppliers get development attention. Diagnosis: capability assessment of assigned suppliers. Gap definition: gaps identified explicitly. Planning: structured improvement roadmaps built, with plans targeting quality, delivery, cost and responsiveness. Commercial evaluation: Total Cost of Ownership analysis. Execution: cross-functional improvement initiatives driven. Routine surveillance: the SQE population conducts supplier audits, monitors quality indicators and coordinates corrective actions. Standardisation: the senior role sets standard ways of working and mentors less-experienced colleagues. [EM9]

The model's notable feature is that the first step is category strategy rather than supplier performance. Most development models in this cohort are triggered by a supplier failing something; Emerson's is triggered by a category roadmap, which is a forward-looking rather than reactive entry point. That is the substantive reason A1 sits at 4 for this company.
2.2 A1: Future demand readiness

Score holds at 4 and its basis improves substantially. The development role assesses supplier capability, identifies gaps and builds structured improvement roadmaps, and aligns those development priorities with a category roadmap for assigned material groups. Capability-gap identification tied to a forward category plan is precisely what this criterion asks about, and it is now stated in two places rather than inferred from one. Why not 5: no gap register, no count of identified or closed gaps, no roadmap example and no outcome; the evidence is role-based throughout. Confidence rises materially. [EM9]
2.3 A2: Capacity confidence

Score holds at 4. The development mandate targets responsiveness alongside quality, delivery and cost, and “capable, resilient partners” implies capacity adequacy as part of capability assessment. Why not 5: no capacity verification mechanism of any kind was located — no run-at-rate, no capacity analysis requirement, no demonstrated-capacity run — which leaves this criterion materially weaker for Emerson than for Cummins, Eaton or ABB in Batch 2, and the rating rests on capability assessment covering responsiveness rather than on a capacity instrument. Confidence rises slightly. [EM9]
2.4 A3: Ramp-up and industrialization readiness

Score holds at 4. Nothing in the new evidence names a qualification stage, gate, APQP or PPAP equivalent, which is a notable absence across all three located Emerson roles. The rating continues to rest on the earlier role evidence and on capability assessment preceding supplier engagement. Why not 5: no qualification process, cycle time, approval rate or population is published. Confidence rises only slightly, and this criterion is flagged in 5.2 as the one most likely to be mis-rated for Emerson.
2.5 A4: Localization readiness

Score holds at 3. The development role carries proven international supplier development experience and about 30% travel across Europe, which corroborates a regionally deployed function. That is context rather than localization capability: no transfer programme, sourcing ratio series or local supplier development activity was located. Confidence rises. [EM9]
2.6 A5: Product and process complexity

Score holds at 3. The category scope is the new evidence and it is genuinely complexity-relevant: mechanical components, plastics, electronics, and machined, cast or forged parts span several distinct process technologies, and a role expected to set category strategy across all of them must understand each. Why not 4: no complexity-facing method is named — no PFMEA, no tolerancing, no capability index, no measurement system requirement — and commodity breadth in a role's scope is not evidence of complexity management at supplier level. Confidence rises. [EM9]
Future Business Readiness conclusion

Domain A holds at 3.60 across all five criteria — the only fully-rated A domain in Batch 3. Its foundation is materially stronger after this pass, principally on A1, where capability-gap identification tied to a category roadmap is now explicit rather than inferred. Its weakness is concentrated in A2 and A3, where Emerson names no capacity or qualification instrument at all.
3. Supplier Production-System Capability
3.1 The method stated in capability terms

The development role's mandate is worth parsing closely because its vocabulary is different from the rest of this cohort's. Most supplier-facing roles in this benchmark are described in compliance terms: ensure suppliers meet requirements, resolve nonconformances, conduct audits, close corrective actions. Emerson's is described in capability terms: develop assigned suppliers into capable, resilient partners; assess capability; identify gaps; build structured improvement roadmaps. [EM9]

That is the vocabulary of supplier development rather than supplier quality assurance, and the distinction is the one this whole benchmark turns on. It is also, on the located evidence, only vocabulary: no roadmap, no assessed capability, no identified gap and no closed gap is published anywhere. The chapter therefore credits Emerson with having framed the work correctly and cannot credit it with having done it.

5.2 What Emerson's public evidence still does not tell us
The deeper pass resolved section 8's principal gap-log entry — six criteria no longer rest on a single role description — and did not resolve the decisive one.

No supplier outcome of any kind has been located in two passes: no supplier named, no capability assessed, no gap identified or closed, no roadmap, no improvement figure, no audit count and no population for any of it. The method-set absence is the chapter's principal open question and it affects two ratings. No product-approval process, process risk method, statistical control method, measurement system method, capability index or structured problem-solving method is named across three located Emerson supplier-facing roles. Two further gaps. No capacity verification instrument of any kind was located, which makes A2 at 4 rest on capability assessment covering responsiveness rather than on a capacity mechanism — materially weaker than Cummins', Eaton's or ABB's position on the same criterion. And nothing in any located role mentions sub-tier suppliers, despite a category scope including castings and forgings, where sub-tier process capability is usually decisive.

A source-scope note governing the chapter: all three located Emerson sources are role descriptions, two of them in Europe (Cluj-Napoca and Lodz). Emerson is a large diversified group and role descriptions establish intent, staffing and vocabulary rather than execution, coverage or outcome. Subsection 1.2 records that this chapter's fourteen-criterion coverage reflects the breadth of what those roles mention rather than the depth of Emerson's disclosure.
6. Implications for Siemens Energy

Everything in this section is an analytical hypothesis for low-volume, high-complexity, long-lead-time supply. None of it is observed Siemens Energy practice, and none of it forms part of the maturity score.
6.1 Put supplier development and category strategy in the same hands

This is the most interesting organisational idea in Batch 3 and it addresses a failure this benchmark has documented repeatedly. Capability programmes stall when the capability carries no commercial consequence: the development engineer asks a supplier to invest, and the sourcing decision that would reward it is made elsewhere, later, on price. Emerson's design removes the gap by making one role responsible for both the category roadmap and the development of the suppliers in it.

For engineer-to-order equipment the version worth testing is narrow. Take two or three critical commodities — large fabrications, castings, specialist machining — and give one senior person per commodity both the category strategy and the supplier development plan, with explicit authority to weight future allocation toward suppliers that build the capability. The risk is concentration of judgement in one individual, which Emerson mitigates by requiring eight years' experience and a Six Sigma or Lean qualification and by having the role set standard ways of working rather than improvise.

6.3 State the mandate in capability terms

Emerson's phrasing — develop assigned suppliers into capable, resilient partners, by assessing capability, identifying gaps and building structured improvement roadmaps — is worth adopting close to verbatim, because job wording shapes what a function actually does. A role chartered to ensure suppliers meet requirements will audit and escalate. A role chartered to develop suppliers into capable partners will diagnose and plan. Both populations will do what they were asked for, and the second costs approximately the same.
6.4 Put the seniority where the capability work is

Emerson's two roles differ by six years of required experience and by a Lean or Six Sigma qualification, and the difference tracks exactly which role is expected to build capability. The general lesson is that supplier capability building is senior work and cannot be delegated to a surveillance population recruited at two years' experience, however well that population is managed. The corollary is that a buyer should know how many suppliers its senior development population can actually reach — a number Emerson does not publish and that any organisation can compute for itself in an afternoon.
6.5 The roadmap is the artefact worth requiring

A structured improvement roadmap is the one deliverable that makes a development programme auditable. It records what capability was assessed, what gap was found, what steps were planned, in what order, by when, and by whom. Of the sixteen companies in this benchmark, Emerson is the only one that names such an artefact, and it publishes none. Requiring one per developed supplier, retaining them, and reviewing them annually would give a programme the evidence base that almost every company in this cohort lacks.

Eaton | Supplier Capability Benchmark

Evidence reviewed: 17 October 2026. Ratings describe maturity visible in public evidence. Eaton's supplier architecture is unusually legible because it publishes a current, detailed Supplier Excellence Manual; almost everything scored below comes from that document, which states requirements rather than results.
1. Summary and scope

Eaton's benchmark rests on one of the most specific supplier requirement sets in this cohort. Its Global Supplier Excellence Manual, revision 22 dated 1 September 2026, sets numeric capability thresholds, a capacity-analysis requirement that names bottleneck operations and yield, a corrective-action regime that explicitly rejects retraining as a root cause in favour of error-proofing, and — uniquely in this cohort — a supplier contingency-plan requirement that includes periodic testing. What is absent is the same thing absent at Caterpillar and Honeywell: any published result.

Overall maturity: 3.79 / 5. Evidence coverage: 14/16 criteria. A Future business readiness: 4.00 (4/5); B Supplier production-system capability: 3.71 (7/7); C Resilience and continuity: 3.67 (3/4). Domains have equal weight; NE is excluded. These are evidence-bounded maturity ratings, not enterprise performance. Audit completed 17 October 2026.
2. Supplier selection and support delivery

Supplier qualification, current performance status and selection for intensive capability-building are separate decisions. The evidence below distinguishes the signal for attention, the people involved, the intervention and its verification.

Supplier Site Assessment approval is required per DUNS location and is “valid for 3 years unless a risk assessment tool dictates a different validity period”; a Supplier Sustainability Management Assessment must be completed before the first purchase order, with annual follow-ups answered within four weeks. Scorecards and Supplier Business Reviews are the primary tools, measuring Net Cost Performance, DPPM, DMR count, supplier on-time delivery, payment terms, Code of Conduct, environmental and social sustainability and a Resiliency Risk Profile Score. Resilience and continuity

A Resiliency Risk Profile Score sits inside the standing supplier scorecard, so continuity exposure is a measured performance dimension rather than a separate exercise. Annual risk examinations use an external risk scan and intelligence gathering, evaluated by severity and probability, reviewed quarterly. [EA1, EA2]

Suppliers must create contingency plans covering fire, natural disasters, pandemics, IT and cyber threats, geopolitical risk and loss of critical utilities, with required elements including team structure, communication, escalation, alternate sourcing and periodic testing; applicable suppliers must use Resilinc. [EA1]

The manual is explicit about the performance standard it expects: suppliers are to “maintain a zero defects culture and zero delivery disruptions,” and must be “capable of meeting Eaton's quality, delivery, cost, EHS, and continuous improvement requirements.” What makes the document unusual among its peers is how much of that expectation is expressed as a number. [EA1]

Capability thresholds: critical and safety characteristics require CpK of at least 1.67; process characteristics require CpK and PpK of at least 1.33; the minimum sample is 30 consecutive parts. Measurement systems: Gage R&R below 10% is acceptable, 10–30% requires Eaton approval, above 30% is unacceptable, and the number of distinct categories must be at least five. Response times: containment within 24 hours of a Discrepant Material Report, root cause and corrective action plan within ten business days, RMA numbers within 48 hours, counterfeit or non-authorised parts notified within 24 hours of discovery. [EA1]

The corrective-action clause contains the single most pointed capability statement found anywhere in this cohort's requirement documents: generic causes such as “Operator / Human Error” or “Training” are not acceptable, retraining alone is insufficient, and the manual calls for error-proofing instead. Acceptable methods are named — 8D, A3, three-legged five whys, Ishikawa. That is a buyer telling its supply base what counts as a real root cause, which is a capability standard rather than a compliance requirement. [EA1]

Boundary: a requirement manual establishes what Eaton demands and what it will do when the demand is not met. It does not establish how often the escalation paths are used, how many suppliers sit in Focused Supplier status, what SQPI contains, or whether any supplier's capability improved. Everything in this chapter carries that limit.
Resources, scale and measurement

Eaton's published supplier figures are about spend and compliance rather than capability. Suppliers representing 98% of supplier spend have affirmed the Supplier Code of Conduct, against a goal of all suppliers by 2030. Eaton spent over $1 billion with small or disadvantaged suppliers in 2024, which represented 36% of its overall spend with US suppliers. Its 2024 CDP supplier engagement rating was A. The Supplier Site Assessment, described as updated and simplified, reviews supplier environment, health, safety and product stewardship practices, and “a formal corrective action plan addressing the identified gaps, if any, is required prior to conducting business.” [EA2]

The commercial mechanics of the quality system are also disclosed and are worth noting because they shape supplier behaviour: a $500 administration fee applies to each Discrepant Material Report regardless of lot size, systemic repeat issues may trigger additional collateral costs, and containment measures Eaton can mandate include controlled shipping, source inspection or third-party inspection. Eaton's formal continuous-improvement channel is IDEAS, submitted through a Supplier Change Request on the supplier portal, with implementation still requiring change-management approval. [EA1]

Research implication: Eaton has written down, in current and public form, most of what a supplier-development system needs to specify — thresholds, response times, escalation, capacity analysis, contingency testing. The missing half is delivery: no supplier-facing engineering function is described in the manual, no intervention is documented, and no outcome is published. The one role description located shows the function exists in at least one region, and it is narrower than Caterpillar's equivalent.

3. Future business readiness
Domain A: 4.00 / 5; 4/5 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

Eaton's readiness requirements are gated and dated. Approval is per DUNS-numbered location, valid for three years unless the risk tool shortens it; a sustainability management assessment precedes the first purchase order with annual follow-ups answered inside four weeks; APQP follows AIAG guidance and PPAP is submitted at Level 3 by default, with interim approval explicitly time-boxed at 90 days and shipments barred beyond it without a formal extension. Tooling changes need six months' notice. [EA1]

The capacity requirement is the strongest element and the most transferable. Suppliers must track capacity or maintain a capacity analysis, shared on request, and that analysis must demonstrate that production can support full-volume ordering, identify bottleneck operations, and account for yield, planned and unplanned downtime, and workforce availability. Suppliers must notify Eaton when capacity compliance is at risk. Few buyers in this cohort specify what a capacity analysis must contain; Eaton does, and it asks for the constraint by name. [EA1]

Evidence limit: the capacity analysis is maintained by the supplier and shared on request, with no stated verification cadence, no Eaton-side review routine and no outcome. Localization readiness is unrated: no localization or capability-transfer programme was found.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Business need and capability: Eaton's electrical business is expanding capacity against data-centre and grid demand, with new US plants announced across 2025 and 2026. That growth requires suppliers to raise rate while holding CpK, which is exactly what the manual's capacity and capability clauses describe. What the record does not contain is the bridge: no evidence of Eaton helping a supplier close a capacity gap, fund equipment, or qualify a second line. [EA1, EA4]

The one supplier-facing engineering role located describes development work in Eaton's electrical supply chain: developing electrical-part suppliers to Eaton standards, running supplier capability assessments of process, quality system and technical competence, driving “supplier development plans to close quality, process, and technology gaps,” supporting onboarding and localization, and leading APQP, PPAP, PFMEA, control plans and process audits across wiring harness, PCB, ECU, sensor, motor, coil, connector and relay suppliers. It names no lean, kaizen, value-stream or Six Sigma content, and no travel or on-site cadence. [EA3]
Readiness and the limits of inference

Eaton's own capacity investments — new or expanded US facilities for medium-voltage switchgear, electrical enclosures and data-centre power — are retained as Layer 1 context. They establish the demand that supplier capacity must meet; they are not evidence that any supplier became able to meet it. [EA4]
4. Supplier production-system capability
Domain B: 3.71 / 5; 7/7 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

The manual defines the production-system standard numerically and the improvement obligation procedurally. Suppliers must document improvement plans that name responsible people, resources and timing; corrective action must reach a real root cause with error-proofing rather than retraining; capability indices and measurement-system criteria are fixed; and the scorecard runs continuously across cost, DPPM, DMR count, delivery, payment terms, Code of Conduct, sustainability and resiliency. [EA1]

Evidence limit: the manual explicitly does not mention lean methodology, no supplier improvement case or figure is published anywhere in the sources located, and the development actions Eaton can mandate are listed without content — SQPI and the Focused Supplier process are named but not described.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Situation and capability: a discrepant material report arises; the capability to be built is the supplier's ability to find a mechanism-level cause and design it out. Intervention as documented: containment within 24 hours, root cause and corrective action plan within ten business days using 8D, A3, three-legged five whys or Ishikawa, with generic human-error and training causes rejected and error-proofing required, PFMEA and control plan expected to be updated, and a $500 administration fee per report. Escalation if the pattern repeats: controlled shipping, source inspection or third-party inspection, Focused Supplier status, and possible suspension of new business. [EA1]

This is a well-specified intervention design with a genuine capability standard embedded in it. What it lacks is any evidence of operation: no count of reports, no closure rate, no population in Focused Supplier status, no case. Under the benchmarking standard, a specified but unevidenced intervention sits at the level of a defined process with partial follow-through, which is where most of this domain lands.
Why the root-cause clause matters more than it looks

Most supplier manuals in this cohort require a corrective action and name a format. Eaton's goes one step further by ruling out the two answers that let a supplier close a finding without changing anything — operator error and retraining — and by naming the alternative. That single clause does more to shape supplier capability than a scorecard, because it changes what counts as done. For a benchmark looking for transferable mechanisms rather than programmes, it is the most portable item in this chapter and costs nothing to adopt. [EA1]
5. Resilience and continuity
Domain C: 3.67 / 5; 3/4 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

Eaton requires what most of this cohort only encourages. Suppliers must create contingency plans and share them on request, covering fire, natural disasters, pandemics, IT and cyber threats, geopolitical risk and loss of critical utilities. The required plan elements are specified: team structure, communication, escalation, alternate sourcing and periodic testing. Applicable suppliers must use Resilinc. [EA1]

Resilience is also measured continuously rather than assessed episodically: a Resiliency Risk Profile Score is one of the standing scorecard metrics, alongside DPPM and delivery. On Eaton's own side, annual risk examinations combine an external risk scan with intelligence gathering and evaluation by severity and probability, reviewed quarterly, supported by risk identification and contingency planning guidelines and crisis management guidelines covering communications, internal resources and external support. [EA1, EA2]

Evidence limit: periodic testing is required of suppliers but no test result, cadence or verification method is published; there is no multi-tier mapping detail; and structural adaptation support is unrated.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Situation: an electrical equipment portfolio with concentrated component sources, growing fast against data-centre demand. Capability being developed on the supplier side: a tested continuity plan with named alternate sourcing and a working escalation path. Eaton's requirement is the mechanism, the Resiliency Risk Profile Score is the measure, and Resilinc is the platform. Taken together this is further than risk mapping alone and further than a plan on a shelf, because testing is mandated. [EA1]

It stops short of the top of the scale for one reason: nothing in the public record shows a test being run, scored or improved. Under the benchmarking standard, business-continuity plans that are not tested or embedded are flagged; Eaton requires testing but publishes no evidence that it happens or what it found. That is a narrower gap than most of this cohort faces, and a specific question to put to the company.

9. Extended Deep Research - Eaton: Supplier Capability-Building Benchmark

This section re-examines Eaton at greater depth. Sections 1–8 rated Eaton 3.79 on 14 of 16 criteria — the highest-coverage chapter in the cohort after TSMC — on the strength of a published Global Supplier Excellence Manual whose requirements are unusually specific. The search-gap log recorded that the chapter was strong on requirement design and silent on execution on almost every criterion, and asked for any supplier outcome, population or engagement count.

The deeper pass worked the manual itself far harder and recovered three things sections 1–8 did not have: a published selection rule for supplier development, a named supplier training institution, and a capacity-analysis requirement that specifies bottleneck identification. It recovered no supplier outcome, no population and no engagement count, and after two passes that absence is a firm negative finding for Eaton rather than a search failure.

One recovered sentence deserves singling out before the analysis, because nothing else in this cohort resembles it. Eaton states that it selects suppliers for development on the greatest improvement opportunity and impact — and then states that some suppliers are selected because of positive relationships, and that Eaton will say so explicitly when that is the reason. A buyer publishing that part of its development selection is relationship-driven rather than need-driven, and committing to disclose which, is a standard of candour no other company in this benchmark meets on any topic.

Scoring note: no score moves. Confidence rises on A1, A2, B4, B6 and B7. Eaton remains the clearest example in the cohort of a company whose supplier requirements are better specified than its supplier results are published.
1. Executive Summary
Strongest evidence of actual supplier capability building

Eaton's strongest located evidence is a development architecture with a published selection rule and a named set of instruments. Eaton selects suppliers with the greatest improvement opportunity and impact, requires selected suppliers to demonstrate willingness to improve and evidence of internal continuous improvement, and may then mandate any of: scorecard corrective action, the Focus Supplier Process, Supplier Quality Performance Improvement (SQPI), business reviews, on-site process audits, business-specific corrective actions, or a Supplier Site Assessment. [EA8]

Two features of that list are stronger than they appear. The instruments are graduated — a scorecard action, a process audit and a full site assessment are different weights of intervention — and the entry condition is a behavioural test rather than a performance threshold. Requiring demonstrated willingness and existing internal improvement activity before committing development resource is a triage rule that protects the buyer's scarce engineering capacity, and it is the only such rule located in this cohort.
A named supplier training institution

Eaton University for Suppliers is listed as a portal tool, alongside WISPER training. The manual also specifies the competences suppliers must hold — APQP, quality management, manufacturing engineering, formal problem solving, supply chain management and materials resource planning — and requires suppliers to plan resources to cover employee turnover in those areas. [EA8]

Specifying required supplier competences and naming a training institution to build them is the structure of capability building. What is missing is everything that would show it working: no curriculum, no enrolment, no completion count, no competence verification and no outcome.
Production-system requirements

The manual's requirements remain the most completely specified in the cohort at the requirement level: APQP to the AIAG manual, PPAP at Level 3 by default, PFMEA identifying special characteristics, control plans tied to high-risk processes, MSA per the AIAG manual for special and critical characteristics, process flow charts, and capability summarised as Cpk above 1.67 and Ppk above 1.33. Failure to meet capability triggers a corrective action plan plus a modified control plan with 100% inspection and/or error-proofing, with variation reduction continuing until the criteria are met. Accepted problem-solving methods are 8D, A3, three-legged five-whys and Ishikawa. [EA8]

The conditional structure is what distinguishes this from a wish list. Capability below threshold does not produce a finding; it produces 100% inspection and mandatory variation reduction until the threshold is met. Reduced inspection, once earned, reverts to 100% after a single defect or any process or design change. These are automatic consequences written into the requirement rather than discretionary escalations.
Resilience and continuity

Eaton's continuity requirement is the most completely specified in this cohort. Suppliers create and share contingency plans on request covering event-based risks, sub-tier disruptions, pandemic preparedness, IT disaster recovery and security, financial and regulatory non-compliance, HR guidelines and geopolitical risk; required plan elements are team organisation, roles and responsibilities, a communication plan, escalation procedures, a recovery plan, quick-response steps and resumption of parts and services. Applicable suppliers register in Resilinc, keep their profile current, and must respond and report impact there within one business day of a risk incident. [EA8]

A one-business-day reporting obligation into a named platform is an operating mechanism rather than a policy, which is why C1 sits at 4. What holds it there is the absence of any exercise, drill, recovery time, incident case or post-event review anywhere in the record.
Overall assessment

Eaton's score is unchanged at 3.79. The deeper pass makes the chapter's shape sharper rather than different: this is a company that has written down what good supplier capability looks like more completely than anyone else in the cohort, has named the instruments and the institution for building it, and publishes no evidence at all of what has been built.

2. Operating Model and Future Business Readiness
2.1 Reconstructed supplier development operating model

Eaton is one of the few companies in this cohort whose development model can be reconstructed from published sources end to end, because the manual states the selection rule, the entry condition and the instrument set. Selection: greatest improvement opportunity and impact, with relationship-based selections disclosed as such. Entry condition: the supplier must show willingness to improve and evidence of internal continuous improvement. Diagnosis: on-site process audit or Supplier Site Assessment. Intervention: Focus Supplier Process or SQPI, with business reviews as the governance layer. Enforcement: scorecard corrective action, Focused supplier status with enhanced monitoring and reduced future business, and suspension of new business for continued poor performance. [EA8]

What the reconstruction lacks is the verification step. Every other company in this cohort with a comparable model publishes at least a count of suppliers that passed through it; Eaton publishes the model and nothing about its operation. The model is therefore assessed as design throughout this chapter, which is why so many of its criteria read “strong for design, silent on execution.”
2.2 A1: Future demand readiness

The forward-looking content in the manual is the competence requirement rather than a demand process: suppliers must hold capability in APQP, quality management, manufacturing engineering, formal problem solving, supply chain management and materials resource planning, and must plan resources to cover turnover in those competences. Requiring a supplier to plan for its own capability continuity is an unusual and forward-looking provision. Score holds at 4; confidence rises. No capability-gap register, forward requirement map or gap-closure series exists. [EA8]
2.3 A2: Capacity confidence

The capacity requirement is more specific than sections 1–8 credited. Suppliers must monitor and track capacity or maintain a capacity analysis to share on request; the analysis must demonstrate that production can support full-volume ordering, must identify bottleneck operations, and must account for quality yield, planned maintenance and unscheduled downtime. Requiring the supplier to name its own constraint, and to net out yield and downtime rather than quoting nameplate capacity, is a materially better requirement than a capacity declaration. Score holds at 4; confidence rises. Why not 5: the analysis is supplier-maintained and shared on request, with no Eaton verification step, run-at-rate or demonstrated-capacity run. [EA8]

APQP to the AIAG manual with PPAP at Level 3 by default, PPAP status limited to Approved, Interim Approval for a maximum of 90 days, or Rejection, and unapproved changes producing a DMR, cost compensation and possible New Business Hold. The 90-day cap on interim approval is the notable detail: it prevents the common failure in which a part ships indefinitely on a provisional approval. Score holds at 4. 3. Supplier Production-System Capability
3.1 Requirements with automatic consequences

The distinguishing feature of Eaton's manual is that its requirements carry pre-specified consequences rather than discretionary escalation, and the deeper pass makes the pattern visible across the whole document. Capability below Cpk 1.67 or Ppk 1.33 produces a corrective action plan and a modified control plan with 100% inspection and/or error-proofing, with variation reduction continuing until the criteria are met or Eaton approves otherwise. Reduced inspection, once granted on demonstrated capability and historical justification, reverts to 100% after a single defect or any process or design change. GR&R between 10% and 30% requires Eaton approval rather than being accepted by default. Interim PPAP approval expires at 90 days. An unapproved change produces a DMR, cost compensation and possible New Business Hold. Unpaid DMR fees escalate to Supply Chain Management and may affect new business. [EA8]

This is a well-engineered control system, and it is worth being precise about what it builds. Automatic consequences change supplier behaviour reliably — a supplier that knows reduced inspection reverts on one defect manages differently from one facing a discretionary review. They do not transfer method. The supplier that cannot reach Ppk 1.33 is told to inspect 100% and keep reducing variation; it is not told how to reduce it.

4. Resilience and Continuity Capability
4.1 The continuity requirement in full

Eaton's contingency-planning requirement is the most comprehensive in this cohort and the deeper pass recovers it completely. Risk classes suppliers must address: event-based risks, sub-tier disruptions, pandemic preparedness, IT disaster recovery and security, financial and regulatory non-compliance, HR guidelines, and geopolitical risk. Required plan elements: team organisation, roles and responsibilities, a communication plan, escalation procedures, a recovery plan, quick-response steps, and resumption of parts and services. Applicable suppliers register in Resilinc on request, keep their profile current, and respond and report impact within one business day of a risk incident. The stated goals are a zero-defects culture and zero delivery disruptions. [EA8]

Specifying sub-tier disruption and geopolitical risk as classes a tier-1 supplier must plan for is beyond what most of this cohort requires, and the seven required plan elements are a real template rather than a gesture. 5.2 What Eaton's public evidence still does not tell us

The deeper pass resolved two of section 8's gap-log entries — whether a development selection rule existed, and whether any training mechanism was named — and both resolved in Eaton's favour. The decisive entry did not move.

No supplier outcome has been located in two passes: no supplier named, no process changed, no before-and-after figure, no DPPM trend, no closure rate, no engagement count, no Focused-status population, no IDEAS submission count and no evidence that Eaton University for Suppliers has delivered a course. Eaton publishes a requirement architecture and a development architecture, and publishes nothing about either in operation. After two passes this is a firm negative finding.

Three narrower gaps remain. The content of the Focus Supplier Process and SQPI is unknown — whether either involves Eaton engineering resource inside the supplier, or only governance and reporting, is the highest-value open question for this company. Eaton University for Suppliers is named without any description. And nothing addresses localization or supplier adaptability, leaving A4 and C4 unrated.

A source-scope note: this chapter rests substantially on one document, the Global Supplier Excellence Manual, which is primary Eaton publication and reliable for what Eaton requires. A manual is evidence of requirement, not of practice, and the cohort overview's stricter calibration would hold several of this chapter's fours at 3 on exactly that basis. Eaton's 3.79 under this chapter's rubric should be read as a rating of a published system, not of a verified one.
6. Implications for Siemens Energy

Everything in this section is an analytical hypothesis for low-volume, high-complexity, long-lead-time supply. None of it is observed Siemens Energy practice, and none of it forms part of the maturity score.
6.1 Copy the development selection rule, including the honest part

Eaton's rule has three components and all three are worth taking. Select on improvement opportunity and impact, so scarce engineering capacity goes where it moves the most. Require demonstrated willingness and existing internal improvement activity as an entry condition, so the buyer does not fund a supplier unwilling to help itself. And disclose when a selection was made for relationship reasons rather than need, which is the component most organisations would quietly drop and the one that keeps the rule honest. A development programme whose selections are never examined drifts toward the suppliers that are pleasant to work with.

6.3 Make the capacity analysis name the constraint — then act on it

Eaton's requirement that a supplier's capacity analysis identify bottleneck operations and net out quality yield, planned maintenance and unscheduled downtime is the best-designed capacity requirement in this cohort, and it is one step from being a capability programme. The supplier has already done the diagnostic work and named its own constraint. For long-lead-time equipment where a single supplier bottleneck sets the project milestone, the obvious extension is to collect those named constraints across the critical base, rank them by effect on delivery, and send engineering help to the top few. The diagnosis is free; only the intervention costs anything.
6.4 Write consequences into requirements rather than relying on escalation

Eaton's manual converts most of its requirements into automatic consequences: capability below threshold produces mandated inspection and variation reduction, reduced inspection reverts on one defect, interim PPAP approval expires at 90 days, an unapproved change produces a charge and a possible business hold. Requirements enforced by automatic consequence need no negotiation and no escalation meeting, and they change supplier behaviour far more reliably than requirements enforced by review. The 90-day cap on interim approval is the cheapest item on this list and prevents a common and expensive failure.
6.5 Build the reverse channel

IDEAS is the only supplier-to-buyer knowledge channel in this chapter and nearly the only one in the benchmark. For engineer-to-order equipment, the specialist supplier frequently understands its own process, and sometimes the part's manufacturability, better than the buyer's engineering function does. A structured channel for suppliers to propose design and process changes — with a commitment to respond and a share of the resulting saving — captures capability the buyer already has access to and is not using.
6.6 The requirement-versus-practice trap

Eaton scores 3.79 here, second in this batch, almost entirely on the quality of a document. That is a warning about this benchmark's own method and about internal self-assessment generally. An organisation that writes an excellent supplier manual will score well on any assessment that reads documents, and the manual tells you nothing about whether a single supplier improved. The counter-measure is to require one named supplier, one named capability and one before-and-after number from every supplier-development claim — the test this benchmark applies and that Eaton's record cannot currently pass.

Cummins | Supplier Capability Benchmark

Evidence reviewed: 17 October 2026. Ratings describe maturity visible in public evidence. Cummins publishes two things no other company in this cohort publishes: a capacity certification that tests a defined demand swing, and a supplier improvement ladder with graduation targets and a sign-off required to exit.
1. Summary and scope

Cummins' benchmark is built on published supplier requirement documents and a supplier portal, and two mechanisms stand out. Production Capability Certification verifies capacity and readiness at full volume and is designed to test the supplier's ability to handle demand fluctuations of plus 20 percent — the only supplier capacity stress test located in this cohort. The Supplier Quality Performance Management ladder runs Focus, SIP, WIN and KEPT with graduation targets that require Cummins sign-off to exit — the only explicit exit criterion located. Alongside these sits a supplier Six Sigma programme in which a supplier belt is paired with a Cummins co-belt and trained through a Cummins Master Black Belt.

Overall maturity: 3.64 / 5. Evidence coverage: 13/16 criteria. A Future business readiness: 3.75 (4/5); B Supplier production-system capability: 3.83 (6/7); C Resilience and continuity: 3.33 (3/4). Domains have equal weight; NE is excluded. These are evidence-bounded maturity ratings, not enterprise performance. Audit completed 17 October 2026.
2. Supplier selection and support delivery

Supplier qualification, current performance status and selection for intensive capability-building are separate decisions. The evidence below distinguishes the signal for attention, the people involved, the intervention and its verification.

Selection assesses quality, total cost of ownership, technical, regulatory, financial and warranty factors, and “potential suppliers will be asked to complete a Supplier Selection Assessment as a prelude to a site visit.” ISO 9001:2015 is the minimum registration, with exceptions requiring written approval from a Supplier Quality Leader. Supplier production-system capability

A quarterly report card scores quality, delivery and cost into five rating bands, from Excellent (4.50–5.00) to Unacceptable (below 2.60); suppliers rated Excellent or Good are preferred for new business, while Needs Improvement or Unacceptable suppliers may have to submit an action plan. [CM3]

Escalation offers a menu: formal process or product audit, focused problem solving, capability submissions, defect tracking charts, Six Sigma participation, Supplier Quality Performance Management, or controlled shipping. Resilience and continuity

Suppliers must “inform Cummins Sourcing Manager or SQE immediately” of risks that could affect deliveries or services; supplier selection includes financial factors; the Supplier Relationship Management scorecard includes sustainability. [CM1]
Suppliers are expected to participate in Cummins' Business Resiliency Management process, described on the supplier portal. Its mechanics, cadence and verification are not published. [CM1]

The supplier handbook sets the technical baseline with unusual precision. APQP is required and PPAP is submitted electronically; three sample parts are the default for dimensional verification, but high-volume parts above 3,600 pieces a year require a 300-piece run with 100 pieces measured in sequence, and a 30-piece machine study alone is not acceptable. Initial Ppk targets are 1.67 at PPAP for critical, safety critical and major characteristics, 1.33 for ongoing studies, and at least 1.0 for significant minor characteristics. [CM1]

Production Capability Certification is the distinctive element. Cummins describes it as verifying capacity and readiness at full volume, “designed to test the supplier's ability to handle demand fluctuations of plus 20%.” That single clause does two different jobs: it establishes that the supplier can serve the nominal volume, and it establishes headroom against a defined swing. No other company in this cohort publishes a numeric demand-flex test for suppliers. [CM1]

Performance management is quarterly and banded. The joint-venture supplier manual sets out a report card scoring quality at 60% PPM and 40% problem elimination, with an overall score of 40% quality, 30% delivery and 30% cost, less deductions for line disruptions. PPM scoring runs from five points at ten PPM or better down to zero above 2,000 PPM; on-time delivery scores five points at 100% and zero below 70%, with on-time defined as five days early to three days late; cost reduction scores five points at 5% or more and zero for a price increase. Rating bands run Excellent, Good, Fair, Needs Improvement and Unacceptable. [CM3]

Boundary: the banded report card and its thresholds come from Cummins' published joint-venture supplier quality and performance manual, which governs a defined set of joint-venture sourcing relationships rather than the whole Cummins supply base. The direct supplier handbook describes a Supplier Relationship Management scorecard covering quality management, end-customer quality, delivery, technology and innovation, and sustainability, without publishing its weights or bands. The two should not be merged. [CM1, CM3]

Corrective action is clocked and documented. Containment results are due within 24 hours of notification; root cause and short-term action within 48 hours of finding the defect; a long-term action plan within ten working days of receiving the supplier corrective action request, implemented within 30 days of the defect being found. The Cummins corrective action worksheet is mandatory, and the PFMEA and control plan must be reviewed and revised as part of the response — a requirement that forces the correction back into the supplier's standing process documents rather than leaving it as a one-off fix. [CM1]
Resources, scale and measurement

The supplier Six Sigma programme is the clearest capability-transfer mechanism Cummins publishes, and its rationale is stated plainly: “A large percentage of our service and product cost is with our supply base,” and Cummins expects Six Sigma to deliver the same cost and quality gains at suppliers that it has delivered internally. It also frames the method as a shared language between the two companies. [CM2]

The mechanics are specific. The supplier works with its Cummins contacts to identify a project that improves key performance indicators or reduces cost; a supplier belt is paired with a Cummins co-belt, and the co-belt together with the purchasing representative drafts and submits the project charter; once the charter is approved, the co-belt arranges training by sending the supplier's contact details and the charter to a Cummins Master Black Belt. A supplier Six Sigma reference guide is published alongside. The design transfers method ownership to a named person inside the supplier rather than leaving the analysis with the buyer. [CM2]

Escalation is a published ladder rather than a threat. Repeat nonconformances or adverse trends can trigger a formal process or product audit, focused problem solving, capability submissions, defect tracking charts, Six Sigma participation, Supplier Quality Performance Management or controlled shipping. Supplier Quality Performance Management itself covers Focus, SIP, WIN and KEPT, and — the part worth noting — “suppliers must meet graduation targets and get Cummins sign-off to exit.” Final escalation is a senior management meeting at which the supplier must commit resources, with re-sourcing if it does not follow through. [CM1]

Research implication: Cummins has designed the two pieces that most supplier-development systems leave implicit — an entry test with a defined margin (plus 20 percent) and an exit test with a defined bar (graduation targets plus sign-off). Between them sits a method-transfer programme with named roles. What is missing, as everywhere else in this cohort outside TSMC and Toyota, is any published evidence of what the system produces: no belt counts, no project outcomes, no population in each escalation tier.

3. Future business readiness
Domain A: 3.75 / 5; 4/5 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

Readiness at Cummins is gated through APQP and PPAP with volume-scaled evidence requirements, and capped by Production Capability Certification. The sampling rules are the detail worth noting: three parts is the default for dimensional verification, but anything above 3,600 pieces a year requires a 300-piece run with 100 measured in sequence, and Cummins explicitly rules out a 30-piece machine study as a substitute. That closes the most common gap in a PPAP-based readiness system, which is a supplier demonstrating capability on a run too short to reveal drift. [CM1]

Evidence limit: no localization or capability-transfer programme was found, so localization readiness is unrated. Production Capability Certification's cadence, population and re-certification rules are not published.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Business need and capability: an engine and power-systems portfolio with volume swings across cycles requires suppliers that can serve nominal demand and absorb a surge without losing process control. The capability needed is capacity with margin, demonstrated rather than asserted. Cummins' answer is Production Capability Certification with its plus-20-percent test, supported by Ppk thresholds that differ by characteristic class and by the Manufacturing Quality Verification tool applied when the supplier quality engineer directs it or as part of APQP. [CM1]

What the record does not contain is the remediation half: what happens when a supplier fails the plus-20 test, who pays for the capacity that closes the gap, and whether certification is repeated as volumes grow. Those are the questions that separate a readiness gate from a readiness capability, and the public evidence does not answer them.
Readiness and the limits of inference

The capability thresholds and sampling rules establish what a supplier must demonstrate, not that any supplier improved in order to demonstrate it. Ppk of 1.67 at PPAP is a gate: suppliers that clear it may always have been able to. Nothing in the public record identifies a supplier that could not clear a Cummins gate and was brought through it, which is the case this benchmark looks for. [CM1]
4. Supplier production-system capability
Domain B: 3.83 / 5; 6/7 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

The quality-system baseline is explicit and tiered: ISO 9001:2015 is required of all suppliers, IATF 16949 is preferred and may be required, and suppliers without IATF 16949 “must provide a gap analysis and a compliance plan before production purchase orders are issued” — a requirement that converts a certification gap into a dated improvement plan rather than a disqualification. Suppliers must complete an annual internal quality management system audit, should maintain a layered process audit programme, and update CQI special process assessments yearly. [CM1, CM3]
Evidence limit: no supplier production-system case, no flow or constraint work and no published outcome from any escalation tier were found. Flow and constraint management is unrated.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Situation and capability: a supplier's defect rate or problem-solving quality falls short; the capability to be built is the supplier's own ability to run a structured improvement project to completion. Intervention as documented: a project is selected jointly against KPI or cost improvement; a supplier belt is paired with a Cummins co-belt; the co-belt and purchasing representative charter the project; a Cummins Master Black Belt trains the supplier belt. Contributors are named on both sides, which is the feature that distinguishes this from a training offer. [CM2]

The parallel track is corrective action, and its design pushes toward retained capability in a specific way: the response is not complete until the PFMEA and control plan have been reviewed and revised, and the next three shipments must be 100% certified and labelled against the nonconformance report number. That forces the fix into the supplier's standing documents and verifies it across several lots rather than one. [CM1, CM3]

Evidence limit and domain fit: both mechanisms are described as designs. No number of supplier belts trained, projects completed, savings delivered or defect trends is published, and the escalation tiers have no published populations.
Graduation targets: the exit criterion most of this cohort lacks

Across the fifteen companies in this benchmark, the commonest gap in supplier development is what happens at the end. Programmes describe entry, diagnosis and intervention, and then stop. Cummins' Supplier Quality Performance Management names four tiers — Focus, SIP, WIN, KEPT — and states that suppliers must meet graduation targets and obtain Cummins sign-off to exit. That is an explicit sustainment test: the supplier does not leave the programme by elapsed time or by the buyer losing interest, but by demonstrating a stated performance level to someone accountable. The targets themselves are not public, so the mechanism is established and its bar is not. [CM1]
5. Resilience and continuity
Domain C: 3.33 / 5; 3/4 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

Cummins places two continuity obligations on suppliers. They must inform the Cummins sourcing manager or supplier quality engineer immediately of risks that could affect deliveries or services, and they are expected to participate in Cummins' Business Resiliency Management process as described on the supplier portal. The joint-venture manual adds operational obligations in the same direction: suppliers must establish a system to support 100% on-time shipments, premium freight is tracked monthly and reported, and expedite records are submitted quarterly. [CM1, CM3]

The strongest continuity-relevant mechanism, however, sits inside the readiness system rather than the resilience system: Production Capability Certification's test of a plus-20-percent demand fluctuation is a verified margin against volatility, which is precisely what volatility management asks for. It is counted once under capacity confidence for the full-volume verification and once here for the fluctuation test, and both rows say so. [CM1]

Evidence limit: Business Resiliency Management's supplier mechanics, cadence and verification are not published; no multi-tier mapping, exercise, drill or recovery measure was found; structural adaptation support is unrated.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Situation: a global engine supply base with castings, forgings, electronics and aftertreatment content, exposed to both demand cycles and component scarcity. Capability being developed on the supplier side: flex capacity verified at a defined margin, plus an obligation to raise risks immediately. What is missing is everything downstream of the obligation — no continuity plan requirement with specified content, no testing mandate, no platform named, no recovery measure. Compared with Eaton, which requires contingency plans with periodic testing, Cummins' published continuity requirement stops at notification and participation in an unpublished process. [CM1]

Siemens adaptation to investigate: adopt a capacity certification with a stated margin. 9. Extended Deep Research - Cummins: Supplier Capability-Building Benchmark

This section re-examines Cummins at greater depth, and it produces the most important mechanism finding of Batch 2. Sections 1–8 rated Cummins 3.64 on thirteen criteria and recorded in the search-gap log that the chapter was strong on requirement design throughout and could not establish whether Cummins did anything with suppliers beyond requiring and measuring.

The deeper pass answers that question affirmatively and specifically. Cummins teaches Six Sigma to its supply base through a described mechanism: the supplier nominates a belt, Cummins pairs one of its own belts alongside as a co-belt, the co-belt and a purchasing representative draft a project charter for approval, and on approval the co-belt schedules the supplier's training by sending the supplier's contact details and the charter to a Cummins Master Black Belt. A Supplier Six Sigma Reference Guide is published for suppliers to use. [CU7]

That is a complete capability-transfer design — the buyer trains the supplier's person, works the first project alongside them, and charters the work against a jointly selected KPI or cost target. Of the sixteen companies in this benchmark, only Toyota, TSMC and Cummins publish a mechanism in which the buyer's own improvement specialists teach and then work with a named supplier counterpart.

The pass also recovered a staged supplier escalation-and-development ladder with four named stages and a graduation gate, a sub-tier management requirement, and the most detailed capacity-verification requirement in the cohort. Scoring note: C2 moves from 3 to 4 on the sub-tier requirement, taking Cummins from 3.64 to 3.75. B7 holds at 4 at the top of its band and the reason is given in 3.3.
1. Executive Summary
Strongest evidence of actual supplier capability building

The supplier Six Sigma mechanism is Cummins' strongest evidence and among the strongest located anywhere in this benchmark at the level of design. Its components are each individually significant: joint project selection, so the supplier works on something that matters to both parties; a supplier belt, so the capability lands in a named person inside the supplier; a Cummins co-belt, so the first project is not attempted alone; a chartered project with purchasing involvement, so the work has standing on both sides; and Master Black Belt training, so the teaching comes from Cummins' most qualified practitioners. [CU7]

Cummins states plainly that it teaches Six Sigma to its supply base to reduce cost and improve quality. For a company whose own Six Sigma deployment is one of the larger industrial programmes of its kind, extending the method to suppliers through paired practitioners is the natural and the hard version of supplier development — hard because it consumes the buyer's scarce belt capacity rather than the supplier's.
A staged development ladder with a graduation gate

The Supplier Quality Performance Management escalation process runs through four named stages — Focus, SIP, WIN and KEPT — and graduation from the process requires Cummins sign-off. The wider escalation sequence is published as formal process audit, focused problem solving, capability submissions, monthly Paynter charts, Six Sigma projects, SQPM and then Controlled Shipping. [CU7]

Two features stand out. The escalation path routes a failing supplier into a Six Sigma project before it routes it into controlled shipping — development is attempted before containment is imposed, which is the opposite of the usual order. And graduation requires an explicit sign-off, so a supplier does not drift out of the programme by quietly improving its numbers; somebody has to decide it is done. Monthly Paynter charts as a named escalation instrument is a further detail worth recording: a Paynter chart tracks whether a corrective action actually stopped a recurring defect, which is a verification tool rather than a reporting one.
Production-system requirements and thresholds

Cummins' requirement set is the most granular in the cohort, graded by characteristic classification. Safety Critical, Critical and Major characteristics require Ppk of 1.67 or greater at PPAP with ongoing SPC and long-term studies at 1.33 or greater; Safety Critical additionally requires fail-safes. Significant Minor characteristics require a minimum 30-piece study at Ppk 1.0 or greater. Measurement systems are bounded at under 10% acceptable, 10–30% marginal and over 30% unacceptable. Pass-Through Characteristics carry added controls specifically to stop defects reaching the end customer. [CU7]

Grading requirements by characteristic class rather than applying one threshold to everything is the mark of a mature requirement system: it concentrates effort where failure matters and avoids demanding 1.67 capability on features where conformance is enough.
Capacity verification

The Production Capability Certification run is the cohort's most specific capacity mechanism: a run at rate conducted with Cummins personnel present, verifying capacity and quality while covering demand fluctuations of plus 20%, supported by a significant production run demonstrating at least one month of capacity. Suppliers selling $5 million or more per country of import must maintain a resident technical resource; smaller suppliers use a third party at their own expense. [CU7]

A capacity verification that builds in a plus-20% demand excursion and is witnessed by the buyer's own people is substantially stronger than a capacity declaration, and the resident-technical-resource threshold is a structural provision no other company in this cohort publishes.
Resilience and continuity

Suppliers must participate in Cummins' Business Resiliency Management process and notify the sourcing manager or supplier quality engineer immediately of risks that could affect deliveries; they must manage their own sub-tier base to AIAG CQI-19 and apply CQI-14 to warranty. The CQI-19 requirement is the finding that moves C2 to 4: it is a named, standard-referenced obligation for tier-1 suppliers to manage their own suppliers, which is more than a flow-down clause. [CU7]
Overall assessment

Corrected score 3.75 on thirteen criteria. Cummins now reads as the strongest supplier-development design in this batch and one of the better ones in the cohort, limited by the same thing as its neighbours: a published mechanism with no published output. No supplier is named, no project result is given, no count of supplier belts trained exists, and no graduation population is reported.

2. Operating Model and Future Business Readiness
2.1 Reconstructed supplier development operating model

Cummins' model can be reconstructed with more confidence than most in this cohort because both the development route and the escalation route are published. Entry by performance: a supplier failing on quality or delivery enters SQPM at Focus and progresses through SIP, WIN and KEPT, exiting only on Cummins sign-off. Entry by opportunity: where an improvement opportunity is identified, a Six Sigma project is chartered jointly with a supplier belt and a Cummins co-belt. Diagnosis: formal process audit, focused problem solving and capability submissions. Verification: monthly Paynter charts, Layered Process Audits to CQI-8, Manufacturing Quality Verification. Containment as the last resort: Controlled Shipping, with Level 2 requiring the supplier to notify its certification registrar. Final escalation: a senior management meeting, with re-sourcing for failure to follow through, and recovery of supplier-caused disruption costs. [CU7]

The ordering is the notable design feature. Six Sigma projects sit before SQPM and Controlled Shipping in the published escalation sequence, so the first response to a struggling supplier is an improvement project and the last is redundant inspection. Most escalation ladders in this cohort run the other way, reaching for containment first and development only if the relationship survives.
2.2 A1: Future demand readiness

Cummins' forward content is the Value Package Introduction process, which serves as its APQP vehicle, together with a PPAP refresh obligation if no submission has been made in 24 months — a provision that prevents a qualification from ageing silently, which matters more in long-lived product programmes than in high-volume automotive. Score holds at 3: these are entry and maintenance mechanisms rather than forward capability-gap identification, and no gap register, requirement map or closure series exists. Confidence rises. [CU7]
2.3 A2: Capacity confidence

The PCC run is the strongest capacity mechanism located in this cohort. It is a run at rate, witnessed by Cummins personnel, verifying both capacity and quality, explicitly sized to cover demand fluctuations of plus 20%, and supported by a significant production run demonstrating at least one month of capacity. PPAP volumes are themselves graded — a 300-piece run with 100 pieces measured in sequence above 3,600 pieces annually, 100% inspection or SPC with at least 30 pieces below it, and a Special Level 4 PPAP below 360 pieces annually with SQE approval. Score holds at 4. Why not 5: no pass rate, no population and no case where a PCC run found a capacity shortfall and something was done about it. [CU7]

The graded PPAP volume structure deserves separate note for this project's purposes, because the Special Level 4 provision below 360 pieces annually is the only explicit low-volume qualification route located in the cohort. Every other company's qualification requirements assume volumes that engineer-to-order equipment never reaches.
2.4 A3: Ramp-up and industrialization readiness

APQP through the VPI process, PPAP to the AIAG manual with Service PPAP and the PCC run, Source Release for parts not yet PPAP-approved, Drawing Quality Review, Design Verification Plan and Report, and zero open FIRG incidents required at start of production. Score holds at 4. Why not 5: no first-time approval rate, cycle time or on-time PPAP performance figure, and Cummins lists first-time PPAP approval among the areas where continuous improvement is expected without publishing the measure. [CU7]
2.5 A4: Localization readiness

The resident-technical-resource provision is the nearest located content: suppliers selling $5 million or more per country of import must maintain a resident technical resource, and smaller suppliers engage a third party at their own expense unless otherwise arranged. This is a requirement for local technical presence rather than a localization capability programme, and it supports no rating. Remains NE. [CU7]
2.6 A5: Product and process complexity

Complexity is handled through graded characteristic classification — Safety Critical, Critical, Major, Significant Minor, Minor, Key and Pass-Through Characteristic, each with its own study, threshold and control-plan treatment — plus special process assessments against CQI-9, 11, 12, 15, 17, 23, 27, 29 and 30, ISO 3834 for welding where required, Process Average Testing for electronics, and CMMI or Automotive SPICE for embedded software. Score holds at 4. Why not 5: specification without supplier-level outcome. [CU7]

The ISO 3834 welding requirement and the CQI special-process assessment set are the most directly transferable items in this chapter for Siemens Energy, whose critical supplier processes are welding, casting, forging, heat treatment and coating — precisely the processes those assessments cover.
Future Business Readiness conclusion

Domain A holds at 3.75 on four of five criteria. Cummins' readiness requirements are the most granular in the cohort and uniquely include a low-volume qualification route; what caps every criterion is the same absent evidence of operation.
3. Supplier Production-System Capability
3.1 The supplier Six Sigma mechanism in detail

This is the chapter's central finding and it is worth setting out step by step, because the sequence is what makes it capability building rather than training provision. First, Cummins and the supplier jointly pick a project that improves a key performance indicator or reduces cost — joint selection, so the project serves both parties and the supplier has a reason to sustain it. Second, a supplier belt and a Cummins co-belt are paired. Third, the co-belt and a purchasing representative draft a project charter for approval — which puts commercial weight behind the work and creates a record. Fourth, on approval, the co-belt sends the supplier contact's details and the charter to the Cummins Master Black Belt, who schedules the training. A Supplier Six Sigma Reference Guide is published alongside. [CU7]

The co-belt is the load-bearing element. A buyer that trains a supplier's engineer and leaves has transferred a course; a buyer that trains the engineer and then works the first project beside them has transferred a method, because the hard part of Six Sigma is not the content but the first application. This is the mechanism Caterpillar's SQEP requires and does not supply, and the contrast between the two chapters in this batch is the clearest illustration in the benchmark of the difference between requiring a methodology and teaching it.

3.3 B-criterion effects and why B7 holds at 4

B7, capability building and sustainment, is the criterion the new evidence bears on most directly, and it holds at 4 at the top of its band. The case for 5 is real: there is resourced teaching from the buyer's most qualified practitioners, a named counterpart inside the supplier, a chartered joint project, a staged ladder and a graduation gate requiring explicit sign-off — more mechanism than any other company in this batch publishes.

The case against 5 is that this benchmark reserves the top band for capability building that is demonstrated rather than designed, and Cummins publishes no population, no count of supplier belts trained, no project result, no graduation figure and no named supplier. The comparison that settles it is Schneider Electric's B7 of 5 in this same project, which rests on a defined population of 1,000 suppliers, a specified capability, resourced teaching and a measured five-year outcome. Cummins has the better mechanism and none of the evidence of effect. Score holds at 4 with materially higher confidence, and this is flagged as the single criterion in Batch 2 most likely to move to 5 if a programme figure is ever located.

3.5 Closure criteria and sustainment

Cummins publishes the most specific closure clock in the cohort. On a supplier corrective action request: containment results within 24 hours, root cause and short-term action within 48 hours, a long-term action plan within 10 working days and long-term action in place within 30 days. Containment must cover the supplier site, transport links, warehouses and all Cummins locations. Where corrective action is inadequate or defects recur, third-party sorting or certification is imposed at supplier expense. [CU7]

Sustainment is designed through three distinct devices: monthly Paynter charts to verify that a fix held, the SQPM graduation sign-off so exit is a decision rather than a drift, and the annually reducing interim defect target for suppliers not yet at zero. Taken together that is a better-designed sustainment architecture than anything else in this batch — and, as throughout this chapter, its operation is unpublished.
Supplier Production-System Capability conclusion

Domain B holds at 3.83 on six of seven criteria, the highest B figure in Batch 2. The deeper pass establishes that Cummins' supplier work includes genuine method teaching with paired practitioners, which sections 1–8 could not establish for any company in this batch, and leaves every score where it was because no outcome accompanies the mechanism.
4. Resilience and Continuity Capability
4.1 Sub-tier management as dependency visibility

C2 moves from 3 to 4. Cummins requires suppliers to manage their own sub-tier base to AIAG CQI-19, the sub-tier supplier management process guideline, and to apply CQI-14 to warranty management. Requiring a named industry standard for sub-tier management is materially more than a flow-down clause asserting that requirements apply downward: it specifies the process the tier-1 supplier must run, and CQI-19 covers sub-tier approval, monitoring and development. [CU7]

Combined with mandatory participation in Cummins' Business Resiliency Management process and immediate notification of any risk that could affect deliveries, this is a defined and owned dependency-management obligation reaching below tier 1. Why not 5: the obligation is flowed down rather than exercised by Cummins, and no map, tier-2 population, exposure figure or verification of sub-tier management is published.
4.2 Disruption preparedness

Suppliers must participate in the Business Resiliency Management process, notify the sourcing manager or SQE immediately of risks that could affect deliveries, run a risk analysis covering restricted materials, recalls, field returns, scrap and rework, and operate a preventive action process with documented effectiveness reviews. Supplier-caused disruption costs are recoverable. [CU7]

C1 holds at 3. A participation requirement with immediate notification is a defined practice, and the evidence stops short of a 4 because nothing describes what BRM participation involves, no exercise or drill is published, and no recovery time, incident case or post-event review exists. The documented effectiveness review on preventive actions is the nearest thing to verification and applies to quality rather than continuity.
4.3 Volatility management

C3 holds at 4 on the PCC run's explicit plus-20% demand fluctuation coverage and the one-month demonstrated-capacity requirement, now confirmed on primary documentation. A capacity verification sized to a stated demand excursion is a volatility mechanism rather than a capacity declaration. Why not 5: no evidence of the mechanism operating, no case of a demand excursion absorbed, and no flexibility or buffer provision beyond the plus-20% envelope. [CU7]
4.4 Adaptability

Nothing located in either pass addresses supplier adaptation to changing business conditions. Remains NE. The management-change notification requirement within two weeks and the twice-yearly contact update are administrative provisions and are not evidence for this criterion.

5.2 What Cummins' public evidence still does not tell us

The deeper pass resolved section 8's decisive gap-log entry — whether Cummins does anything with suppliers beyond requiring and measuring — and the answer is yes, through a described and distinctive mechanism. The gaps that remain are about output rather than mechanism.

No programme figure of any kind has been located for the supplier Six Sigma mechanism: no count of supplier belts trained, projects chartered, projects completed, savings realised or capability measures moved, and no named supplier. For a mechanism this specific, a single annual count would transform the chapter's evidence base, and its absence after two passes is notable.

The SQPM stages are named and undefined: what Focus, SIP, WIN and KEPT each involve, how long a supplier typically spends in each, what the graduation criteria are and how many suppliers are in the process at any time are all unknown. The BRM process is referenced and undescribed. And no supplier outcome, case or before-and-after figure exists anywhere in the record.

A source-scope note: this chapter rests substantially on the Supplier Handbook, which is primary Cummins publication and reliable for requirements and described mechanisms, together with the supplier portal's own account of the Six Sigma process. Both are evidence of design. The cohort overview's stricter calibration would hold several of this chapter's fours at 3 on that basis, and Cummins' 3.75 under this chapter's rubric rates a published system rather than a verified one.
6. Implications for Siemens Energy

Everything in this section is an analytical hypothesis for low-volume, high-complexity, long-lead-time supply. None of it is observed Siemens Energy practice, and none of it forms part of the maturity score.
6.1 The co-belt is the transferable idea

Of everything in Batch 2, the paired co-belt is the mechanism most worth copying. Training a supplier's engineer in a method and leaving transfers a course; training them and then working their first project beside them transfers a method, because the first application is where improvement programmes die. The model also solves the credibility problem — a supplier that has watched the buyer's specialist do the work is far more likely to run the second project unaided.

For engineer-to-order supply the version to test is narrow and affordable: pick three critical suppliers, charter one joint project each against a KPI both parties care about, pair a Siemens Energy improvement specialist with a named supplier engineer, and require the supplier to run the second project alone. The measurable output is not the first project's saving but whether the second project happened.
