6.3 Put development before containment in the escalation ladder

Cummins' published escalation sequence runs formal process audit, focused problem solving, capability submissions, monthly Paynter charts, Six Sigma projects, SQPM and only then Controlled Shipping. Most escalation ladders reach for 100% inspection early because it protects the buyer immediately, and in doing so they consume the supplier's cash and goodwill at precisely the moment development would be cheapest. Sequencing development ahead of containment is a policy choice available to any buyer at no cost.
6.4 Grade requirements by characteristic class and by volume

Two of Cummins' grading schemes matter directly for low-volume equipment. Characteristic classification concentrates capability work where failure has consequences instead of demanding 1.67 capability everywhere, which is unachievable and therefore ignored. And the volume-graded PPAP — a Special Level 4 route below 360 pieces annually — is the only acknowledgement in this entire cohort that standard qualification requirements are built for volumes engineer-to-order work never sees. A buyer whose parts are made in tens rather than thousands needs a published low-volume route, or its own requirements will be waived informally and inconsistently.
6.5 Verify that fixes held, not that they were made

The monthly Paynter chart is a small, cheap discipline with a large effect. It tracks whether a defect recurred after the corrective action, which converts closure from an administrative event into an evidenced outcome. Most supplier quality systems in this cohort close an 8D and move on; a buyer that requires recurrence tracking for a defined period afterwards finds out which of its closures were real.
6.6 Require a graduation decision

SQPM graduation requires Cummins sign-off. Without that, improvement programmes end by attrition — the numbers drift back into range, attention moves on, and nobody records whether the capability was built or the problem simply receded. An explicit exit decision costs one meeting and produces the only population data such a programme will ever have.
6.7 Use the special-process assessment standards already written

Cummins requires CQI-9, 11, 12, 15, 17, 23, 27, 29 and 30 by process type and ISO 3834 for welding. These cover heat treatment, plating, coating, welding, soldering and casting — the processes that actually determine quality in heavy electrical and rotating equipment. They are published, audited industry standards that a buyer can require without writing anything, and requiring them is substantially cheaper than developing an in-house process-assessment framework.

1 Executive assessment

Siemens Energy is assessed here on the same sixteen criteria, the same anchors and the same evidence standard as the fifteen companies already in this benchmark. It is the only chapter in the project whose subject is also its reader, and that creates one methodological problem worth stating before any finding: the people reading this can see what the reviewer cannot. A low rating here describes what an outside researcher could establish from public sources in a structured pass. It does not describe practice.

The evidence is strongest for a defined and staged sustainability qualification architecture, a risk-based audit route with binding corrective action, and multi-tier minerals due diligence reaching smelter level. It is weakest — in the sense of being almost entirely absent — on supplier production capability. No named supplier case, no process intervention, no before-and-after figure and no production-method requirement was located in either research pass.

The proposed public-evidence maturity is 3.19 out of 5, with 9 of 16 criteria rated. No criterion receives 5 and none receives 1 or 2. Seven criteria are NE, and all seven are readiness or production-system criteria: A2 capacity, A4 localization, A5 complexity, B3 stability, B4 flow, B5 throughput and C4 adaptability. B7 is rated 3 on sustainability training rather than NE, and section 4 explains why that differs from the ABB treatment.

2 Supplier selection and support
Qualification is staged, volume-triggered and sustainability-scoped

Siemens Energy's published qualification architecture is more structured than the first research pass established. All new suppliers must commit to declaring products containing REACH and RoHS substances. Suppliers with an expected annual procurement volume of €10,000 or more must complete a Sustainability Self-Assessment, valid for three years, covering legal compliance, employee health and safety, responsible raw material sourcing, human rights and labour, environmental protection and the supply chain. Where answers fall short, suppliers must take corrective measures. Additional modules apply where relevant: contractor safety for on-site services, and cyber security for suppliers accessing systems, storing data or delivering software or firmware. Suppliers above the volume threshold may need additional modules to reach R4B status. [1]

This is a real gate with a threshold, a validity period, named modules and a named end state. What it is not is a technical qualification. It establishes nothing about whether a particular supplier operation can hold a welding procedure, run a capable measuring system or deliver a qualified forging. For a benchmark that scores production capability, the distinction is the whole question: a supplier can be R4B and still be unable to make the part.
Different triggers lead to different routes

Four separate populations are generated by four separate mechanisms, and they are not interchangeable. An annual sustainability risk analysis categorises risk by commodity and country, using indicators such as collective bargaining, worker safety and human rights, and incorporating the German Supply Chain Due Diligence Act risk categories; high-risk suppliers are prioritised for external audits and large-volume suppliers are flagged. A self-assessment indicating potential risk can itself trigger an audit. Incident-driven inspections occur where there is strong suspicion of a Code violation, such as a media report. And a separate decarbonization programme engaged more than 3,400 suppliers covering over 75% of the supply chain carbon footprint in fiscal 2024. [1, 2]

A commercially critical supplier, a high-risk-country supplier, a large-footprint emitter and a supplier that cannot hold a tolerance can be four different companies. Only the first three generate a published route.

Exit and sustainment

Suppliers that fail to fix persistent problems, or are unwilling to, are removed from the approved supplier list; local blocks escalate to central procurement, which decides whether to impose a global block. [1]
Administrative removal is an enforcement outcome, not a capability outcome. No positive exit — graduation on demonstrated competence — is described anywhere.
Supplier support delivery in practice

The published support route is remediation-led and sustainability-scoped. A self-assessment answer that falls short obliges corrective measures; an external audit or incident inspection produces corrective actions that are binding; serious findings lead to repeat or follow-up audits; and a central warning system exists so that procurement can agree remedial steps quickly. Siemens Energy states that it aims to help suppliers improve. [1]

That is a complete enforcement loop with a stated improvement intent, and it is the strongest process evidence in this chapter. What it does not contain is any description of what the help consists of. Whether a supplier receives documentation, a training module, an auditor's advice, an engineer's time or a funded change is not established by any source located. The distinction matters because a binding corrective action compels a result without transferring a method, which is the pattern this benchmark finds in ten of its sixteen chapters.

Two support mechanisms are described in more positive terms. Web-based supplier training on sustainability in the supply chain is offered to all suppliers, with specific training for third-party intermediaries. And supplier days and workshops are named as engagement channels alongside the Responsible Minerals Initiative. Neither has a published population, curriculum, completion figure or competence check. [1, 3]
Priority questions for an internal interview

Because the subject of this chapter is the reader, the usual framing — questions to ask the company — inverts. These are the records that would settle the chapter's open ratings, and they exist internally or they do not exist at all. Ask who may authorise engineering effort at a supplier and how that decision differs from issuing a corrective action. Request one completed supplier improvement project: the original need, the resource committed, the supplier manager and operator responsibilities, the verification standard and the handover. Then request a later case in which the same supplier applied the method with less assistance. If the first record cannot be produced, the chapter's B-domain ratings are correct as published evidence and the gap is real rather than a disclosure artefact.
3 Findings by domain
A Future business readiness
Layer 1 Qualification, risk and forward planning

The qualification architecture described in section 2 supports A3 at 3. It is staged, volume-triggered, time-bounded at three years, modular and terminates in a named status. Its boundary is that it qualifies a company on sustainability rather than qualifying a part or a process. No enhanced launch control plan, run-at-rate, production part approval, first-article requirement or equivalent gate was located in any Siemens Energy source. [1]

A1 sits at 3 on forward risk management rather than forward capability planning. Annual risk assessments cover the entire supplier base; Global Functions manage supply chain expertise to secure critical components and minerals and monitor risk exposure; critical supply chain is named among fiscal 2024 sustainability-related risks; and supplier networks are being diversified and regionalized while long-term contracts secure material availability and price stability. These are real forward mechanisms. None of them identifies a capability a supplier will need and does not yet have. [2, 3]

A2 remains NE and is the most consequential unrated criterion in the chapter. No supplier capacity assessment, verification, run-at-rate, capacity analysis obligation or demonstrated-capacity requirement was located. Four companies in this cohort publish a named capacity instrument; Siemens Energy's order book makes supplier capacity a first-order constraint; and the public record contains nothing.

A4 remains NE. Diversification and regionalization of the supplier network, and requirements that vary by country, region or location, are buyer-side exposure management and administrative variation. This is the same treatment the ABB chapter applied to local-for-local sourcing, and consistency requires it here: no supplier whose production was transferred, workforce trained and output qualified with Siemens Energy assistance was identified. [1, 3]

A5 remains NE. Circular economy due diligence tracks recycled content for steel, copper, aluminium, plastics and critical raw materials, and the business areas describe supplier categories including specialised turbine parts, high-voltage components, electronics and castings. That establishes technical scope, not complexity-management capability. No PFMEA, capability index, tolerancing, measurement system or complex-part qualification requirement was located. [1, 3]
Layer 2 No elevated readiness case located

This chapter has no Layer 2 readiness case. The ABB chapter at the equivalent point carries the SKF joint bearing development, a year-long project with a supplier-owned design output, which lifts its A5 to 4. Nothing comparable was located for Siemens Energy in either pass: no joint development project, no co-engineering case, no named supplier and no technical collaboration record.

This is recorded as an absence of located evidence rather than an absence of activity. A company building gas turbines, transformers and electrolysers certainly co-develops with suppliers. The benchmark scores what is published, and nothing is.
B Supplier production system capability
Layer 1 Controls, remediation and routines

B1 sits at 3 on an assessment architecture that is now clearly documented: self-assessment across six areas with corrective measures where answers fall short; External Sustainability Audits conducted on site by appointed third-party auditors on a risk basis; incident-driven inspections; supplier quality audits that carry sustainability questions; continuous monitoring through the Third Party Risk Management Tool with dashboards; and an escalation path ending in local and global blocks. This defines how conformity is maintained. It is not evidence that any supplier operates a complete production system or could solve a future problem unaided. [1, 3]

The reference to supplier quality audits including sustainability questions is the single most important sentence located for domain B, because it establishes that a supplier quality audit programme exists. Everything about that programme other than its existence — standard, scope, criteria, frequency, population, findings — is unpublished. [1]

B2 sits at 3. Corrective measures are obligatory where self-assessment answers fall short; corrective actions agreed after inspections are binding; serious findings produce repeat or follow-up audits; a central warning system allows procurement to agree remedial steps quickly; and the Gas Services role leads supplier improvement programmes and carries out corrective and preventive actions with suppliers. The mandate language is development-oriented, and the record contains no implemented case. The ABB chapter reaches 4 on this criterion on the strength of two named implemented interventions; Siemens Energy has none. [1, 5]

B6 sits at 4 and is the chapter's strongest B rating. The cadence is genuine and multi-layered: annual risk assessment across the entire supplier base, a three-year self-assessment renewal cycle, risk-based audit selection, continuous monitoring with dashboards, supplier days and workshops, more than 3,400 suppliers engaged in a decarbonization assessment in a single year, annual public reporting against dated targets with prior-year comparatives, and Executive Board-level human rights reporting. Why not 5: the entire cadence is sustainability-domain, and no production or quality operating routine is published. [1, 2, 3]

B3, B4 and B5 are NE. No supplier process variable, control plan, reaction plan, capability study, defect or yield trend, flow mechanism, bottleneck analysis, throughput measure or end-to-end lead-time method was located in any source. For a company whose deliveries are constrained by forging, heat treatment, large machining and specialist inspection, these three absences are the most striking feature of the published record.
Layer 2 Case S1 The decarbonization due diligence programme

The Carbon Reduction@Suppliers programme runs with an external provider using an input-output economic model that estimates supplier CO2e from procurement volume and material-country combinations. In fiscal 2024, more than 3,400 suppliers, covering over 75% of the supply chain carbon footprint, were encouraged to join a decarbonization due diligence assessment and report their measures, with those assessments intended to inform future target tracking. Reported performance: upstream Scope 3 at 9,238 kt CO2e against 9,230 kt the prior year, an increase of 0.1% in absolute terms; intensity at 0.408 kg CO2e per euro against 0.414, a reduction of 1.3%; and 19.6% against a partially extrapolated fiscal 2018 base, against a 30% target for 2030. [2]

KEEP — supporting mechanism, not a completed capability intervention. The programme establishes a measurement model, a large engaged population and a published performance series, which is more than most companies in this cohort can show on any topic. It does not establish that any supplier gained a capability: suppliers are encouraged to join and report, the model is spend-based rather than measured, and the absolute footprint rose. B7 is supported at 3 by this plus the training route; it is not lifted to 4, because engagement volume is not enablement.
Layer 2 Case S2 The TenneT supply chain partnership

Announced in July 2024, Siemens Energy and TenneT aim to cut emissions from their shared supply chain activities by 30% by 2030, with ten actions identified over five years including the use of recycled or greener copper, steel and aluminium. Starting with transformers made from 100% recycled copper is expected to save about 6,500 tons of emissions. [2]

KEEP — supporting mechanism, bounded to buyer-side material specification. Two customers coordinating demand for lower-carbon materials is a real and relatively unusual lever, and the expected saving is quantified. The capability change it implies sits in the material supply chain rather than in a named supplier's process, no supplier is identified, and the 6,500 tons is an expectation rather than a realised result. It does not support any B-domain rating above its current level.
Layer 2 Case S3 Contractor EHS capability

Contractors and temporary workers are expected to meet the same standards as Siemens Energy employees, and contractor incidents are shared with Business Areas and Global Functions for lessons learned. Fiscal 2024 additions comprise a Zero Harm engagement app for onboarding temporary labour, a new Zero Harm building block for temporary labour, and new general EHS requirements for contractors covering all Business Areas. [2]

KEEP — supporting mechanism in safety competence, with an explicit horizontal learning element. The incident lessons-learned loop across Business Areas and Global Functions is a structured knowledge transfer mechanism, and the onboarding instruments are deployed rather than planned. Its scope is contractor and temporary-labour safety, not supplier manufacturing capability, so it supports B1 and C1 as context without lifting either.
C Resilience and continuity capability
Layer 1 Exposure management

C2 sits at 4 and is the chapter's highest-rated criterion. The supporting evidence is unusually layered. Annual risk assessments cover the entire supplier base. Risk is categorised by commodity and by country, incorporating the German Supply Chain Due Diligence Act categories, using indicators such as collective bargaining, worker safety and human rights. Physical climate risk is assessed at country level using NOAA or KNMI meteorological data, with suppliers ranked by risk level to guide supplier selection and mitigation for high-risk segments. Business partner due diligence runs risk-based screening and onboarding with continuous monitoring through the Third Party Risk Management Tool and dashboards. Conflict minerals due diligence covers the entire supply chain rather than tier 1 alone, reaching the raw minerals and including smelter assessments under the Responsible Minerals Initiative. Circular economy due diligence tracks resource inflows and recycled content for steel, copper, aluminium, plastics and critical raw materials. Supplier sustainability risk coverage reached 44.5% in fiscal 2024 against a goal of covering 80% of the total sustainability risk score within five years. [1, 2, 3]

Why not 5: coverage stands at 44.5% with no prior-year comparative published, so no improvement trend exists; the exposure models are built for sustainability and carbon rather than for supply continuity; and no manufacturing dependency map — shared furnaces, constrained inspection capacity, common sub-tier sources behind apparently separate suppliers — was located. The ranking by physical climate risk is the closest the record comes to a continuity-facing dependency instrument.

C1 sits at 3. Critical supply chain is named among sustainability-related risks; Global Functions secure critical components and minerals and monitor exposure; physical climate risk ranking guides mitigation for high-risk segments; and the contractor EHS programme builds prevention capability. Why not 4: no supplier business continuity requirement, contingency plan template, required-element list, risk platform obligation, exercise, drill, recovery time, incident case or post-event review was located. Four companies in this cohort publish specific continuity instruments; Siemens Energy publishes risk identification. [1, 2, 3]

C3 sits at 3. Supplier networks are being diversified and regionalized to reduce dependence on specific regions or raw materials; long-term contracts are used to secure material availability and price stability; a multi-bank supply chain finance programme offered to selected suppliers converts receivables into non-recourse cash; and supply chain disruptions and raw material shortages are named as key industry challenges. These are deliberate, named volatility levers. Why not 4: no demonstrated recurring adjustment decision, no supplier-side flexibility outcome, no second-source qualification count and no population for the finance programme. [3, 4]

C4 remains NE. Diversification and regionalization are buyer-side structural responses. No supplier was traced through a transition — a site move, a technology change, an ownership change or a tariff response — with a documented Siemens Energy work package and verified continuity afterwards. This mirrors the ABB treatment and is applied for the same reason.
Layer 2 No elevated resilience case located

The ABB chapter carries Unique Punch System at this point: an assessed gap, intensive engagement, a year of implementation and a changed supplier routine. No comparable Siemens Energy case was located. The nearest equivalent is the contractor EHS programme, which is retained as a supporting mechanism in section 3 rather than as a supplier prevention case, because its subject is contractors and temporary labour rather than supplying firms.

4.1 Calibration notes

No live Siemens Energy chapter exists in the benchmark, so there is no prior rating to calibrate against. Two calibration decisions are nevertheless worth recording, because both could reasonably have gone the other way and both affect the headline figure.

Rated 3 on a documented web-based training route offered to the whole base plus supplier days and workshops.

The ABB chapter rates B7 as NE on the grounds that production-skills transfer is unproven. Applying that here would give NE and raise domain B to 3.33 on 3 criteria. Rejected for cohort consistency: Toshiba and Mitsubishi Electric are both rated 4 on compliance-domain capability building in this project, so rating Siemens Energy NE for the same class of evidence would be inconsistent. A4 and C4
Both NE. Diversification and regionalization treated as buyer-side exposure management.

Rating them 3 on the strategic levers would raise the overall figure to about 3.25. Rejected because the ABB chapter rejects local-for-local sourcing as standalone capability proof, and the same evidence class must be treated the same way.

Rating NE is defensible, since the gate is sustainability-scoped and says nothing about industrialization. The chapter is therefore sensitive to three judgement calls, and the plausible range on the published evidence runs from roughly 3.1 to 3.3. None of the available readings changes the chapter's substantive finding, which is that seven criteria cannot be rated and that all seven concern production capability and readiness.

6 Internal verification priorities

The other fifteen chapters in this benchmark close with potential relevance to Siemens Energy. That section is omitted here, because recommendations addressed to Siemens Energy inside an assessment of Siemens Energy would be circular. What follows instead is the list of internal records that would settle this chapter's open ratings. Each either exists internally — in which case the gap is disclosure — or does not, in which case the gap is real.
6.1 One completed supplier improvement project

The single most valuable record. Reconstruct it from original need through handover: the business consequence, the diagnosed gap, who authorised the effort, what Siemens Energy contributed, what the supplier changed, how it was verified, and what happened afterwards. Then ask the supplier to describe the same sequence. Differences between the two accounts reveal whether the work transferred a method or enforced a requirement. One such record would move B2 and B7 and would be the first elevated capability case in this chapter.
6.2 The supplier quality audit programme

The public record establishes that supplier quality audits exist, because they are described as carrying sustainability questions. Everything else is unknown. Establish the audit standard, the scope, the criteria, the population, the frequency, the findings profile and the closure rate. If a process audit standard comparable with VDA 6.3 is in use, B1 is understated here.
6.3 Whether supplier capacity is assessed at all

A2 is NE and it is the most consequential unrated criterion in this chapter given the current order book. Establish whether any run-at-rate, capacity analysis obligation, demonstrated-capacity requirement or capacity roadmap exists for critical suppliers, and whether any supplier's capacity constraint has been diagnosed and relieved. Four companies in this cohort publish an instrument here.
6.4 Whether a method set is required of suppliers

No APQP, PPAP, PFMEA, SPC, MSA, capability index or control plan requirement was located in any Siemens Energy source; the only appearance of any of them is APQP and PPAP in a job advertisement's title. Establish whether supplier quality requirements documentation exists that names a method set. If it does, A3, A5, B1 and B3 are all understated and three NE ratings may be rateable.
6.5 Whether suppliers carry continuity obligations

C1 rests on risk identification. Establish whether critical suppliers are required to hold a contingency plan, whether its elements are specified, whether any exercise has ever been run and whether any recovery time has been measured. The cohort comparison is specific: Eaton specifies seven plan elements and a one-business-day reporting obligation; Honeywell requires 180 days' notice of a manufacturing location change with mandated buffer inventory and contractual tooling access during a disaster.
6.6 The size and reach of the supplier capability function

One role description in one business area is the whole of the located evidence. Establish the headcount, its distribution across business areas, how many suppliers each person covers and what proportion of critical suppliers receive any capability attention in a year. This number is calculable internally in an afternoon and is unavailable to any external reviewer.
6.7 What the disclosure gap costs

This chapter's substantive finding is not that Siemens Energy's supplier capability is weak. It is that an outside reviewer with full web access, reading English and German, could rate it on nine of sixteen criteria and could not find a single named supplier case. Customers, investors, analysts and prospective suppliers reach the same record. Several companies in this cohort publish supplier capability programmes with populations and outcomes; three of them — Toyota, TSMC and Schneider Electric — publish measured supplier capability results. That asymmetry is a strategic fact independent of the underlying practice, and it is correctable at the cost of publishing one case.
7 Research limitations and search gaps
7.1 Evidence scope

Cited primary sources were opened and the relevant sections read, in English and German, on 17 October 2026. Four of the five sources are company sustainability and supplier-portal publications; the fifth is a job advertisement. Company reporting establishes stated practice and published figures; it is not independent verification. Undated webpages are observations at access rather than proof that the described practices began or operated unchanged in that year.

Two figures are reported as found rather than reconciled. Purchasing volume appears as approximately €26 billion on the supplier portal and €23.5 billion in the fiscal 2024 Sustainability Report; the sources do not reconcile them and both are stated. The supplier sustainability risk coverage rate of 44.5% is published for fiscal 2024 with no fiscal 2023 comparative, so no trend can be computed.

The most important limitation is one of reach rather than interpretation. The fiscal 2024 Sustainability Report's dedicated sustainable supply chain management chapter could not be opened within this pass. It is the likeliest location for supplier audit counts, corrective-action figures, code-of-conduct detail and tier-2 data. If it contains them, B1, B2, C1 and C2 may be understated. This chapter should not be treated as final until that chapter has been read.
7.2 Unresolved and excluded claims

Third-party job-board compensation estimates attached to mirrored versions of the supplier quality manager posting are not employer-provided and are excluded. The TenneT saving of about 6,500 tons is an expectation rather than a realised result and is reported as such. The 44.5% coverage figure is retained with its denominator: it is coverage of a total sustainability risk score, not a proportion of suppliers made capable. Buyer-side localization, network diversification and own-operations climate targets are excluded as proof of supplier capability development.

Siemens Energy supplier capability building
Extended deep research for the Siemens Energy and Kearney Student Lab benchmark · Evidence reviewed 17 October 2026 · No maturity scores are assigned

The central question is what Siemens Energy does to change a supplier's ability to plan, manufacture, improve or recover. The sixteen-criterion framework guides discovery across the whole field. It is not used here to grade Siemens Energy or to calculate domain averages; the scored assessment is the companion chapter.

The evidence test is: business need → supplier gap → buyer and supplier contributions → implemented capability → verification → supplier-owned learning. A requirement establishes what Siemens Energy expects. An intervention must show what Siemens Energy helped change. Evidence of a completed change and evidence of lasting independent competence are recorded separately.

One structural caution applies throughout and does not apply to any other chapter in this benchmark. The subject of this report is also its reader. Everything below describes what a researcher could establish from public sources. Where this report finds nothing, the correct internal response is to check whether the record exists and is unpublished, or does not exist. Those are very different findings and no external pass can distinguish them.
1 Executive assessment

Siemens Energy publishes a coherent and reasonably sophisticated supplier due diligence system. It has a volume-triggered entry gate, a self-assessment with a renewal cycle, modular add-ons for contractor safety and cyber security, a named qualification end state, a commodity-and-country risk model incorporating statutory due-diligence categories, risk-selected third-party on-site audits, incident-driven inspections, binding corrective actions, a central warning system, an escalation path ending in global blocking, multi-tier minerals traceability to smelter level, and a decarbonization programme that engaged more than 3,400 suppliers in a single year. [1–3]

What it does not publish is any evidence of supplier manufacturing capability work. Across two research passes, in English and German, no named supplier case, no process intervention, no before-and-after production figure, no capability threshold, no method requirement and no supplier training beyond sustainability content was located. The one piece of evidence that a supplier quality function exists at all is a job advertisement and a passing reference to supplier quality audits carrying sustainability questions. [1, 5]

For the benchmark, the practical value is in separating decisions that are usually bundled: qualifying a source, diagnosing an operating gap, committing specialist help, accepting the changed process and deciding whether the supplier can now maintain it. Siemens Energy's published system covers the first comprehensively and is silent on the rest. An audit finding can initiate that sequence; it cannot substitute for its later stages.

2 Operating model and future business readiness
2.1 Qualification is a staged entry gate

The entry sequence is published and is more structured than a single threshold. Every new supplier commits to declaring products containing REACH and RoHS substances. A supplier expected to reach €10,000 of annual procurement volume completes a Sustainability Self-Assessment covering six areas, valid for three years, with corrective measures obligatory where answers fall short. Suppliers doing on-site service work add a contractor safety module; suppliers touching systems, data, software or firmware add a cyber security module. Above the volume threshold, additional modules may be needed to reach R4B status. [1]

For a benchmark interview the next distinction must be made at the individual part or production route. An R4B supplier may still lack a qualified welding procedure, a capable measuring system or the furnace time for the required mix; a fully qualified supplier may need development when the product or load changes. Supplier status is therefore treated throughout this report as context rather than as evidence of transferred capability.
2.2 Who owns support

Ownership is distributed and partly published. Business areas and Global Functions carry supply chain responsibility, with Global Functions managing expertise to secure critical components and minerals and monitoring risk exposure. A Human Rights Officer reports to the Executive Board on human rights compliance including supply chain measures. Central procurement decides whether a local supplier block becomes global. Appointed third-party auditors conduct External Sustainability Audits. A Gas Services supplier quality manager leads supplier improvement programmes within one business area. [1–3, 5]

This is identifiable governance for sustainability due diligence and a single visible role for supplier quality. It should not be read as a central manufacturing-engineering deployment capability. The reviewed evidence does not reveal who approves supplier-specific engineering effort, how competing requests are ranked, or what the supplier must commit before intensive work begins.

2.3 How suppliers are selected for different kinds of help

There is no single published selection formula, and the populations generated are genuinely different. Sustainability risk produces one population through commodity-and-country scoring; procurement volume produces another through the €10,000 threshold and the large-volume flag; carbon footprint share produces a third through the decarbonization programme; and a Code violation suspicion produces a fourth through incident inspection. [1, 2]

No published mechanism generates a population based on technical criticality, replaceability, qualification lead time or capability gap. For a company whose delivery risk concentrates in a small number of forging, casting and large-machining sources, that is the most significant structural observation in this report. A supplier can be commercially small, low-risk by country and low-carbon, and still be the single constraint on a turbine delivery.
2.4 A1 Future demand readiness

The published forward mechanisms are risk-facing rather than capability-facing. Annual risk assessments cover the entire supplier base. Physical climate risk is assessed at country level from NOAA or KNMI data, with suppliers ranked by risk level to guide selection and mitigation for high-risk segments. Supplier networks are being diversified and regionalized to reduce dependence on specific regions or raw materials, and long-term contracts secure material availability and price stability. [2, 3]

The missing evidence is a completed supplier readiness case: what future demand or mix a supplier could not support, how it changed its loading, staffing or investment decisions, and whether its later commitments became more reliable. Risk ranking tells a buyer where to worry. It does not tell a supplier what to build.
2.5 A2 Capacity confidence and A3 ramp-up readiness

This is the largest gap in the report and it is worth stating without hedging. No supplier capacity assessment, run-at-rate, capacity analysis obligation, demonstrated-capacity requirement or capacity roadmap was located in any Siemens Energy source. No enhanced launch control plan, production part approval, first-article requirement or equivalent industrialization gate was located either. The qualification architecture described in 2.1 is complete and is entirely sustainability-scoped. [1–4]

The development question begins where a supplier cannot pass a gate. For low-volume, high-complexity equipment, a conforming sample is weak evidence of sustainable capacity when furnaces, specialist labour and inspection resources are shared across orders. Whoever helps remove such a constraint, and how added capacity is accepted under representative conditions, is not established by any public source.

The best internal request is one completed capacity roadmap: the initial bottleneck, supplier investment, Siemens Energy contribution, representative output demonstration and the load assumptions that remain untested. If no such record exists, that is itself the finding.
2.6 A4 Localization readiness

Network diversification and regionalization are published as strategic levers, and supplier requirements vary by country, region or location through a document pool. This establishes buyer strategy and administrative variation. It does not identify a supplier whose production was transferred, workforce trained and output qualified with Siemens Energy assistance. [1, 3]

A localization case would need to name the receiving site and the process being established, and cover tooling transfer, local material equivalence, supplier-employee competence, first accepted output and performance after the support team leaves. Regionalized sourcing volume answers none of those questions.
2.7 A5 Technical complexity and new competence

Circular economy due diligence tracks recycled content for steel, copper, aluminium, plastics and critical raw materials, and the business areas describe supplier categories spanning specialised turbine parts, high-voltage components, electronics and castings. The supplier quality manager role requires the ability to read technical drawings and manufacturing processes. [1, 3, 5]

No joint development project, co-engineering case or technical collaboration record was located. This is the clearest point of contrast with the ABB chapter, whose year-long bearing development with SKF produced a supplier-owned design output and supports a scoped rating of 4. A company developing hydrogen electrolysers, large transformers and advanced turbine components is certainly doing comparable work; none of it is public.
3 Supplier production-system capability
3.1 A published remediation mechanism and its limits

The remediation loop is the strongest published process in this report. A short self-assessment answer obliges corrective measures. An external audit or incident inspection produces corrective actions that are binding. Serious findings produce repeat or follow-up audits. A central warning system lets procurement agree remedial steps quickly. Persistent failure or unwillingness removes the supplier from the approved list, with local blocks escalating to a central decision on a global block. Siemens Energy states that it aims to help suppliers improve. [1]

This is stronger than an unstructured demand to improve: it specifies the trigger, the obligation, the verification route and the escalation. It leaves open the content of the help. Whether personnel observe work on site, teach a method, redesign a process or only review corrective actions is not established. A published remediation process is retained as a supporting mechanism; it is not a substitute for an implemented supplier case.
3.2 The supplier quality audit programme

One sentence in the public record establishes that supplier quality audits exist: they are described as including sustainability questions. [1] That single reference is the whole of the public evidence for a supplier quality audit programme at a company with approximately 31,000 suppliers and approximately €23.5 to 26 billion of annual purchasing volume.

Everything that would make the programme assessable is unpublished: the audit standard, whether it is a process audit or a system audit, the scope, the criteria, the frequency, the auditor qualification, the population covered, the findings profile and the closure rate. If a process audit standard comparable with VDA 6.3 is in use — as it is at Siemens AG, which requires certified VDA 6.3 auditors — then the scored companion chapter understates B1.
3.3 The decarbonization due diligence programme

In fiscal 2024, more than 3,400 suppliers covering over 75% of the supply chain carbon footprint were encouraged to join a decarbonization due diligence assessment and report their measures. The programme runs with an external provider using an input-output economic model that estimates supplier CO2e from procurement volume and material-country combinations. [2]

The engagement scale is genuine and few companies in this cohort match it on any topic. Three qualifications bound what it shows. Suppliers are encouraged to join rather than required, and no participation rate is published against the 3,400. The model is spend-based rather than measured, so it estimates rather than observes supplier emissions. And the absolute upstream footprint rose 0.1% year on year while intensity fell 1.3%, so the published result is an intensity improvement against growth rather than an absolute reduction.

The useful discovery question is what a participating supplier actually did. Reporting a measure is an administrative act; changing a furnace cycle, a material route or an energy source is a capability. The programme's own data would distinguish them.
3.4 The TenneT partnership

Siemens Energy and TenneT committed in July 2024 to cutting emissions from shared supply chain activities by 30% by 2030, identifying ten actions over five years including recycled or greener copper, steel and aluminium, beginning with transformers made from 100% recycled copper expected to save about 6,500 tons. [2]

Two customers coordinating demand for lower-carbon materials is an unusual and effective lever, because it removes the first-mover problem that stops a single buyer from paying for a material transition. The capability implication sits upstream in the material supply chain. No supplier is named, no supplier process change is described and the saving is an expectation.
3.5 Contractor safety capability

Contractors and temporary workers are held to the same standards as employees, and contractor incidents are shared with Business Areas and Global Functions for lessons learned. Fiscal 2024 brought a Zero Harm engagement app for onboarding temporary labour, a Zero Harm building block for temporary labour and new general EHS requirements for contractors across all Business Areas. [2]

The lessons-learned loop across Business Areas and Global Functions is a structured horizontal knowledge transfer mechanism, and the onboarding instruments are deployed rather than planned. The scope is contractor and temporary-labour safety rather than supplying firms' manufacturing capability, and it is recorded here so that it is not mistaken for either.
3.6 Supplier training

A web-based supplier training on sustainability in the supply chain is offered, with specific training for third-party intermediaries, and all suppliers must know, accept and comply with the principles. Supplier days and workshops are named as engagement channels. [1, 3]

This is a delivered training route rather than a statement of intent, which is why the companion chapter rates B7 at 3 rather than NE. No enrolment, completion, competence verification or application evidence is published, and the content is sustainability rather than production method. Reach should be reported separately from application and from retained capability; none of the three is public here.

The practical boundary across these seven areas is attribution. A supplier can deliver better because the buyer clarified a drawing, changed order timing or added inventory. Those improvements matter and differ from a supplier learning to control variation, remove a bottleneck or maintain equipment. The evidence should identify the changed operation and its owner before the result is attributed to a manufacturing capability.
4 Resilience and continuity capability
4.1 C1 Prevention and preparedness

Critical supply chain is named among fiscal 2024 sustainability-related risks. Global Functions secure critical components and minerals and monitor risk exposure. Physical climate risk ranking guides mitigation for high-risk supplier segments. The contractor EHS programme builds prevention capability within its own scope. [2, 3]

No supplier business continuity requirement, contingency plan template, required-element list, risk platform obligation, exercise, drill, recovery time, incident case or post-event review was located. The distinction that matters is between prevention and recovery: risk ranking and exposure monitoring reduce the chance of an interruption, and neither demonstrates that a supplier could recover from one.

The next verification would ask which critical suppliers hold a continuity plan, what the plan must contain, whether any exercise has been run on an actual critical path and what recovery time was demonstrated under explicit assumptions.
4.2 C2 Dependency visibility and the limits of risk screening

Dependency visibility is the strongest published area. Annual risk assessments cover the entire supplier base. Risk is categorised by commodity and by country, incorporating the German Supply Chain Due Diligence Act categories and using indicators such as collective bargaining, worker safety and human rights. Physical climate risk is ranked from NOAA or KNMI data. Business partner due diligence runs risk-based screening with continuous monitoring through the Third Party Risk Management Tool and dashboards. Conflict minerals due diligence explicitly covers the entire supply chain rather than tier 1 alone, reaching raw minerals and including smelter assessments under the Responsible Minerals Initiative. Circular economy due diligence tracks resource inflows and recycled content by material. Risk coverage reached 44.5% against an 80% five-year goal. [1–3]

What a commodity-and-country screen cannot reveal is the operating dependency. For engineering supply chains the binding constraint is often a furnace, a qualified inspector, a single heat-treatment source or a special material shared by several apparently independent suppliers. None of the published instruments maps that. A useful development case would show a supplier constructing and maintaining its own dependency map, choosing mitigation and revising it after a test.
4.3 C3 Volatility management

Three deliberate levers are published: supplier network diversification and regionalization to reduce dependence on specific regions or raw materials; long-term contracts securing material availability and price stability; and a multi-bank supply chain finance programme letting selected suppliers convert receivables into non-recourse cash. Supply chain disruptions and raw material shortages are named among key industry challenges. [3, 4]

The supply chain finance instrument deserves particular note, because supplier financial fragility is a common and under-managed cause of delivery failure in long-lead-time equipment, and few companies in this cohort publish a liquidity instrument at all. What is unpublished is its population and whether any supplier's delivery performance changed as a result.

No completed case in the reviewed sources connects a demand or material shock to a supplier-owned revised plan and a verified delivery response. A convincing record would retain both the original and revised assumptions — mix, engineering release, qualified material, resource availability, committed dates — and would distinguish a genuinely feasible plan from expedites that protect one customer by displacing another.
4.4 C4 Structural adaptability

Network diversification and regionalization are buyer-side structural responses to tariff, geopolitical and raw-material exposure. The reviewed material does not trace a supplier through a site move, restructuring, technology change or ownership change with a documented Siemens Energy work package and verified continuity afterwards. [3]
The gap is not whether Siemens Energy manages these exposures; the published record shows that it does. The gap is how a supplier's own ability to adapt changed through the support.
4.5 How programme progress is checked

Progress reporting is genuine and dated. Supplier sustainability risk coverage is published at 44.5% for fiscal 2024 against a goal of 80% of the total sustainability risk score within five years. Scope 3 upstream intensity is published at 0.408 kg CO2e per euro against 0.414 the prior year and against a 30% reduction target for 2030, with 19.6% achieved against a partially extrapolated 2018 base. [2]

Four records should remain separate and only the first two are public: how many suppliers were reached; what actions were implemented; what operating result changed; and what competence remained with supplier employees. Coverage and closure are appropriate programme controls while leaving the fourth question unanswered. No assumption is made that a closed finding produces better yield, faster recovery or less dependence on the buyer.

5.1 Resource allocation and support intensity

The most important undisclosed details are intervention budgets, engineer caseloads, auditor capacity, supplier cost sharing, visit frequency, minimum supplier participation and approval authority. Neither a programme name nor a role title supplies a current delivery capacity. A published qualification threshold of €10,000 tells a reviewer how wide the net is; it says nothing about how deep the help goes for the suppliers that matter most.

A practical internal exercise is to take one recent closed supplier issue and reconstruct the decision from the original need through handover, then ask the supplier to describe the same sequence. Differences between the two accounts reveal whether the organisation delivered technical help, coordinated a recovery or mainly enforced a requirement.
5.2 Evidence of withdrawal and independent ownership

The public record is weaker on post-support learning than on assessment and corrective action, and this is the pattern in fourteen of the sixteen chapters in this benchmark. The missing documents are not additional policy statements. They are revised supplier standards, competence checks, recurrence records and evidence of an improvement made after external support reduced.

A second problem need not resemble the first. The relevant test is whether the supplier can use the underlying reasoning: define the issue, obtain reliable evidence, identify causes, test a change and maintain control. Supplier managers must also allocate time and protect the routine. An operator trained in a tool but unable to obtain resources cannot sustain the gain.
6 What this report cannot settle

The companion chapter carries the internal verification priorities. This section records only the boundary of what an external pass can establish, because that boundary is the most important finding for a reader inside the company.

This report can establish that Siemens Energy publishes a structured supplier due diligence system with a staged gate, a risk model, audit routes, binding remediation and multi-tier minerals traceability. It can establish that more than 3,400 suppliers were engaged on decarbonization in one year and that performance is reported annually against dated targets. It can establish that a supplier quality function exists in at least one business area and that supplier quality audits exist.

It cannot establish whether any supplier became better able to manufacture anything because of Siemens Energy, whether supplier capacity is assessed, whether a method set is required, whether suppliers hold continuity obligations, or how large the supplier capability function is. Those five questions are answerable internally and were not answerable externally in two passes.

The asymmetry itself is a finding. Several companies in this cohort publish supplier capability programmes with populations and outcomes; three — Toyota, TSMC and Schneider Electric — publish measured supplier capability results. Customers, investors, analysts and prospective suppliers reach the same public record this report reached.
7 Research method limitations

Research covered supplier entry and qualification, the Code of Conduct, sustainability risk detection, audit and inspection routes, remediation and escalation, supplier training, decarbonization programmes, minerals and circular-economy due diligence, contractor EHS, supply chain finance and continuity controls. Follow-up searches used supplier quality requirements, supplier development programmes, supplier awards and supplier days, LkSG due diligence reporting, and German-language equivalents. The Toyota attachment was read as the structural reference and the ABB chapter as the format reference. No existing benchmark content or company scores were changed by this report.

Two sources could not be fully reached and both matter. The fiscal 2024 Sustainability Report's dedicated sustainable supply chain management chapter was not opened within this pass; it is the likeliest location for supplier audit counts, corrective-action figures and tier-2 data. And the supplier quality manager posting was readable only through a third-party mirror, whose compensation estimates are not employer-provided and are excluded.

Sources, access dates and full bibliographic detail are given in the references section of the companion research chapter and are not repeated here. All web sources were accessed on 17 October 2026; undated webpages are observations at access, not proof that the described practices began or operated unchanged in that year.

Siemens AG | Supplier Capability Benchmark

Evidence reviewed: 17 October 2026. Ratings describe maturity visible in public evidence. Siemens publishes the largest quantified supplier remediation and supplier decarbonization figures in this cohort, and almost nothing about supplier manufacturing capability — a split that shapes every score below.
1. Summary and scope

Siemens AG's benchmark rests on a dedicated annual KPI disclosure for sustainable procurement, and the numbers in it are of a different order from the rest of this cohort. In fiscal 2025 Siemens ran 6,324 Corporate Responsibility Self-Assessments and 421 External Sustainability Audits, and agreed 7,453 and 6,559 corrective action measures respectively — broken out by topic. Its Carbon Reduction @ Suppliers programme involved about 7,300 participating suppliers covering 62% of upstream tier-1 emissions, with an average reduction of 9% among participants and a total reduction of 617 ktCO2e. Against that, supplier manufacturing capability appears only through role design, and four criteria cannot be rated.

Overall maturity: 3.54 / 5. Evidence coverage: 12/16 criteria. A Future business readiness: 3.50 (4/5); B Supplier production-system capability: 3.80 (5/7); C Resilience and continuity: 3.33 (3/4). Domains have equal weight; NE is excluded. These are evidence-bounded maturity ratings, not enterprise performance. B2 was raised from 3 in section 9 against two Siemens AG Smart Infrastructure supplier quality role descriptions located after sections 1-8 were written, superseding an overall figure of 3.48. That evidence is role-based and business-unit-scoped, and the stricter calibration used in the cohort overview would hold it at 3.
2. Supplier selection and support delivery

Supplier qualification, current performance status and selection for intensive capability-building are separate decisions. The evidence below distinguishes the signal for attention, the people involved, the intervention and its verification.

Resilience and continuity

Corporate Responsibility Self-Assessments target “suppliers based in higher-risk countries,” mainly non-OECD suppliers with purchasing volume above €50,000 a year; partners are monitored for the duration of the relationship with remediation depending on risk classification. [SI1, SI2]

Depending on risk classification, audits can be conducted on partners' premises by Siemens' own audit function or external service providers; digitalization and AI are presented as the route to transparency and predictive analytics. [SI2, SI5]

The self-assessment and audit machinery is the most quantified in this cohort, and Siemens publishes not only the activity but the remediation. In fiscal 2025 it recorded 6,324 Corporate Responsibility Self-Assessments — 4,113 in Asia and Australia, 1,388 in Europe, the CIS, Africa and the Middle East, and 823 in the Americas — and agreed 7,453 corrective action measures across them, broken out as 2,335 on health and safety, 1,595 on basic human rights, 1,558 on environmental protection, 1,361 on legal compliance and anti-corruption, 501 on supply chain and 103 on prohibition of child labour. [SI1]

External Sustainability Audits add a second, deeper layer: 421 audits in fiscal 2025 — 293 in Asia and Australia, 79 in Europe, the CIS, Africa and the Middle East, and 49 in the Americas — producing 6,559 agreed corrective action measures, of which 2,858 concerned basic human rights and 2,522 health and safety. The ratio is the striking part: an audit yields roughly 15.6 agreed corrective measures on average, against 1.2 for a self-assessment. Siemens defines the measures as relating to “actual deviations from the Supplier Code of Conduct, structural improvements in management systems, or missing specific processes and guidelines” — which places most of them in the structural-improvement category rather than simple non-compliance. [SI1]

Boundary: this is a sustainability and compliance system, and it is scored only where the criterion concerns cadence, remediation discipline or visibility. It is not evidence of production capability. What it does establish — unusually clearly — is that Siemens can define a target population by objective rule, reach it at scale, find structural gaps and agree measures to close them, in volumes an order of magnitude above most of this cohort.

The targeting rule itself is worth recording because it is published: self-assessments are completed mainly by non-OECD suppliers with a purchasing volume above €50,000 per year, in higher-risk countries, and counts cover questionnaires “initiated, completed, and concluded in the reporting period.” A stated monetary threshold and a stated completion definition are rare in this cohort, and they make the figures auditable rather than promotional. [SI1]
Resources, scale and measurement

The Carbon Reduction @ Suppliers programme is the one place where Siemens publishes a measured supplier-side outcome. In fiscal 2025 it reported about 7,300 participating suppliers, covering 62% of Scope 3 upstream tier-1 emissions, with an average reduction of 9% among participating suppliers and a total reduction of 617 ktCO2e. That is a population, a coverage figure, a per-supplier average and an absolute result — the four things most supplier programmes in this benchmark fail to publish together. [SI1]

Siemens also publishes the context that makes the number honest. Its target is a 20% reduction in Scope 3 upstream emissions by 2030 against a 2019 base of 8,107 ktCO2e, implying roughly 6,486 ktCO2e. Fiscal 2025 stood at 8,188 ktCO2e, 1% above the base year — while purchasing volume was 21% above it. The programme is therefore delivering measurable supplier-level reductions against a baseline that volume growth keeps pushing up, and Siemens publishes both halves rather than only the favourable one. The baseline itself was re-set to a new 2019 base “to align with material structural changes.” [SI1]

Boundary and domain fit: the capability built is carbon measurement and reduction. It is scored under capability building and sustainment, where the question is whether the company can take a defined supplier population and leave it able to do something it could not do before. It is not permitted to lift the production-specific rows, which rest on role evidence alone.

The technical function appears only through role design. A supplier quality engineer for mechanical components in Smart Infrastructure is accountable for component qualification and approval according to Siemens standards and procedures, for evaluating components through testing, validation, specification reviews and technical assessments, for driving “APQP and PPAP activities with suppliers” to ensure robust production readiness, for conducting audits and supporting supplier development initiatives, for applying design for manufacture and assembly and supporting early supplier involvement in development projects, and for reviewing tooling concepts and manufacturing process capabilities. ISO 9001 knowledge is required and VDA 6.3 experience is an advantage. [SI3]

Research implication: Siemens is the clearest case in this cohort of a company that has solved the measurement problem in one domain and not transferred it to another. The sustainable procurement KPI sheet shows exactly what a supplier programme looks like when a company decides to publish population, activity, remediation and outcome every year. No equivalent exists for supplier manufacturing capability, and the question for a benchmark is whether that reflects the absence of the work or only of the disclosure.

3. Future business readiness
Domain A: 3.50 / 5; 4/5 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

Readiness at Siemens is handled as component engineering rather than programme management. The supplier quality engineering role owns component qualification and approval to Siemens standards, drives APQP and PPAP with suppliers to ensure robust production readiness, reviews tooling concepts and manufacturing process capabilities, and applies design for manufacture and assembly with early supplier involvement in development projects. That last element matters: involving suppliers while the design is still movable is the cheapest form of readiness work and few companies in this cohort name it as a role accountability. [SI3]

Evidence limit: no supplier capacity verification, threshold or review cycle was found anywhere in public sources, so capacity confidence is unrated. On localization, the annual report notes a market shift “from globalization toward regionalization” linked to increasing supply chain resilience, and plans relocation of high-tech production facilities in Singapore, the United States and China — Siemens' own footprint, not a supplier transfer method. [SI4]
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Business need and capability: Siemens reports tariff and non-tariff trade measures as a significant source of uncertainty, temporary export restrictions affecting Digital Industries, and procurement problems during project execution in Mobility that “can result in significant costs for non-compliance.” The capability needed from suppliers is qualified output under shifting trade and project conditions. The published response is design-side and footprint-side: involve suppliers early, apply DFMA, regionalize production. [SI3, SI4]

What is missing is the capacity half. No company in this cohort with Siemens' industrial breadth publishes less about supplier capacity — no analysis requirement as at Eaton, no certification as at Cummins, no standing review as at Caterpillar. Whether that reflects a different operating model or only a different disclosure practice cannot be determined from public sources, and the criterion is left unrated rather than scored low.
Readiness and the limits of inference

Siemens' own manufacturing investments — automating and digitalizing its factories in Germany and China, a new technology campus in Erlangen, relocations in Singapore, the United States and China — are retained as Layer 1 context. They change where Siemens makes things; they are not evidence that any supplier became able to make something it previously could not. [SI4]
4. Supplier production-system capability
Domain B: 3.80 / 5; 5/7 criteria scored (B2 raised from 3 to 4 in section 9).
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

The production-side evidence is thin and the process-side evidence is enormous, and the two must be kept apart. On the production side: component qualification to Siemens standards, APQP and PPAP driven with suppliers, supplier audits against ISO 9001 with VDA 6.3 valued, manufacturing process capability and tooling concept review, and support for supplier development initiatives — all from one role description. On the process side: a self-assessment and audit programme running at 6,324 and 421 instances a year with 14,012 corrective measures agreed between them. [SI1, SI3]

Evidence limit: no capability thresholds, no corrective-action clocks for quality, no supplier production case and no outcome. Flow and constraint management and throughput and lead-time management are both unrated — nothing was found on either.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Situation and capability: a supplier in a higher-risk country lacks a management system, a process or a guideline that Siemens requires. Intervention as documented: a self-assessment or an on-premises audit identifies the gap, and corrective action measures are agreed — in fiscal 2025, 14,012 of them across both instruments, of which Siemens explicitly says many concern “structural improvements in management systems, or missing specific processes and guidelines” rather than straightforward deviations. Agreeing to install a management system a supplier did not have is capability building, within its subject matter. [SI1]

The limit is what happens next. Siemens publishes the measures agreed and not the measures completed, verified or sustained, and no graduation or re-audit statistic appears in the KPI sheet. Under the benchmarking standard, an assessment followed by structured gap closure counts and an assessment alone does not; Siemens publishes the agreement of closure, which sits between the two.
What the audit-to-measure ratio reveals

Siemens' two instruments produce very different yields: 421 external audits generated 6,559 agreed measures, about 15.6 per audit, while 6,324 self-assessments generated 7,453, about 1.2 each. The spread is a useful finding for anyone designing a supplier programme. Self-assessment reaches breadth cheaply and surfaces little; an auditor on the premises surfaces roughly thirteen times more per engagement. Siemens runs both deliberately and publishes both yields, which allows the trade-off to be reasoned about rather than assumed — and suggests that a programme relying on questionnaires alone is mostly measuring willingness to answer. [SI1]
5. Resilience and continuity
Domain C: 3.33 / 5; 3/4 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

Siemens' supplier-facing continuity evidence is compliance-shaped. Business partners are carefully selected and undergo risk-based compliance due diligence, are monitored for the duration of the relationship with remediation depending on risk classification, and — again depending on classification — may be audited on their own premises by Siemens' audit function or external service providers. Both business partners and suppliers are required to sign a code of conduct. [SI2]

The forward-looking position is technological rather than procedural. Siemens' chief procurement officer describes integrating “the unexpected into long-term strategic planning,” with digitalization and AI as the route to transparency and predictive analytics, supplier-network collaboration as a source of innovation, and sustainable sourcing as a lever for resilience, supported by tools including a product carbon footprint system and a green digital twin. The annual report adds the market direction: a shift from globalization toward regionalization to “increase supply chain resilience.” [SI4, SI5]
Evidence limit: no supplier business-continuity requirement, exercise, drill, recovery measure, dual-sourcing programme or multi-tier mapping was found. Structural adaptation support is unrated.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Situation: a portfolio spanning automation, electrification, mobility and healthcare, exposed to tariffs, export restrictions and long project execution cycles, with procurement problems in Mobility explicitly identified as a source of significant non-compliance cost. Capability that would need developing on the supplier side: continuity planning and recovery. The public record contains monitoring, due diligence, audits and a strategic intention to use AI for predictive transparency — all buyer-side. [SI2, SI4, SI5]

Under the benchmarking standard, risk maps, scoring, monitoring and visibility alone are flagged rather than counted. The reason dependency visibility still scores at the fourth level is that Siemens' monitoring is continuous for the life of the relationship, is tiered by risk classification with a defined escalation to on-premises audit, and is published with volumes — which is more than a map and more than an intention.

7. Case decisions, limitations and Siemens Energy hypotheses
Case decisions by domain (eligibility is separate from maturity)

A: KEEP early supplier involvement with DFMA and the APQP/PPAP readiness accountability; REJECT own-footprint regionalization as supplier evidence; INVESTIGATE the complete absence of published supplier capacity requirements.
B: KEEP the published targeting rule, counting definition and corrective-measure volumes; INVESTIGATE supplier development initiatives, which are named and undescribed.
C: KEEP continuous relationship-length monitoring with risk-tiered escalation; REJECT AI and analytics intent as standalone proof.
REJECT as standalone proof: EcoVadis ratings, code of conduct signature, audit counts taken alone, and digitalization intentions. Retain their useful Layer 1 evidence.

Next evidence: how many of the 14,012 agreed corrective measures were completed and verified; prior-year comparisons for self-assessments and audits; whether supplier capacity is managed and simply not published; what supplier development initiatives contain; any supplier continuity requirement. The published KPI sheet is the obvious vehicle for the first two and already has the structure to carry them.

Scoring note: all 16 criteria are first-time assessments and four are unrated. Siemens' figures are single-period in the retrieved sources, which caps several criteria that a two-year series would lift; this is a disclosure-format limitation rather than a judgement about the programmes.

Supplier Production-System Capability — Split. The cohort's largest remediation volumes in compliance, and role-level evidence only in manufacturing. [SI1, SI3]
Resilience and Continuity Capability — Medium. Continuous risk-tiered monitoring with real volumes; nothing supplier-side on continuity. [SI1, SI2]
Transferability hypothesis

Siemens adaptation to investigate: publish the targeting rule and the counting definition, not just the number. Siemens states that self-assessments go mainly to non-OECD suppliers above €50,000 annual purchasing volume in higher-risk countries, and that counts cover questionnaires initiated, completed and concluded in the period. Those two sentences turn an activity number into an auditable one, and they discipline the programme internally before anyone outside reads them.
Transferability hypothesis

Siemens adaptation and potential learning: use the audit-to-measure ratio to size the programme. Siemens' 421 on-premises audits produced about 15.6 agreed measures each, against about 1.2 per self-assessment across 6,324 questionnaires. For a small, critical, low-volume supply base the implication is uncomfortable but useful: questionnaires will find almost nothing, and the budget belongs in site visits. Test the ratio on one commodity before scaling either instrument.
Transferability hypothesis

Siemens adaptation to investigate: copy the honest denominator. Siemens reports a 9% average reduction among 7,300 participating suppliers and, in the same document, that its total upstream emissions are 1% above the 2019 base while purchasing volume is 21% above it. Publishing the programme result next to the figure that undercuts it is what makes the programme credible. Any Siemens Energy supplier capability programme should be designed with both numbers specified from the start — what the participants achieved, and what happened to the whole.
