9. Extended Deep Research - Siemens AG: Supplier Capability-Building Benchmark

This section re-examines Siemens AG at greater depth. Sections 1–8 rated Siemens AG 3.48 on twelve criteria and recorded in the search-gap log that four criteria — A3, A5, B2 and B3 — rested on a single role description, with the rationale for each marked “weak-moderate: single role.” That is the thinnest evidential basis for a score in the whole project, and the log asked for corroboration or correction.

The deeper pass located two further Siemens AG supplier quality roles, both in Smart Infrastructure: a Supplier Quality Manager position explicitly titled Lieferantenentwicklung — supplier development — in Berlin, and a Global Supplier Quality Manager position in Erlangen posted in September 2026. Together they corroborate the earlier role, add a named audit standard, add a verification step that sections 1–8 did not have, and reveal two mechanisms the first pass missed entirely: a universal Quality Assurance Agreement requirement and a global Supplier Quality Management community used to share lessons learned among suppliers. [SI9]

Scoring note: B2 moves from 3 to 4, taking Siemens AG from 3.48 to 3.54. Confidence rises on A3, A5, B1, B3, B6, B7 and C1. The evidence remains role-based and business-unit-scoped, and the cohort overview's stricter calibration would hold B2 at 3; that boundary is stated in the rationale and in 1.2.

One finding sits outside this chapter's scope and is recorded here because it bears on the project rather than on Siemens AG. The same search surfaced a Siemens Energy supplier quality manager posting whose title names audits, supplier development, APQP and PPAP. This benchmark treats Siemens Energy as the subject for whom implications are drawn and not as a benchmarked company, and every implications section in the project states that none of its content is observed Siemens Energy practice. That statement remains accurate as to the content of those sections, and the posting is noted as a lead for the project team rather than analysed here, since analysing the client inside the benchmark would confuse the two roles.
1. Executive Summary
Strongest evidence of actual supplier capability building

Siemens AG's strongest located evidence is a supplier development function with a named audit standard and an explicit effectiveness check. The Berlin role evaluates and develops suppliers' quality and process capability working closely with purchasing and engineering counterparts, coordinates the necessary improvement measures and verifies that they are effective, conducts supplier audits to VDA 6.3 on site and remotely, analyses data regularly to identify quality risks arising from components and suppliers, agrees actions with process partners, and reports on KPIs to quality and plant management. Its stated core goal is Lieferantenbefähigung — supplier enablement. [SI9]

Two elements of that are stronger than anything sections 1–8 had. VDA 6.3 is a demanding process-audit standard rather than a management-system audit, so a certified VDA 6.3 audit examines how a supplier's process actually runs. And “verifies that they are effective” is a closure step: the function does not stop at agreeing an improvement measure, which is where most of this cohort's published supplier quality work ends.
Two mechanisms the first pass missed

The global role adds both. First, every supplier must have a Quality Assurance Agreement; the role manages those agreements in its assigned areas and works with procurement to close gaps where they are missing. A universal contractual quality instrument, actively gap-closed, is a base-wide mechanism no other company in this cohort publishes. [SI9]

Second, the role leads the Supplier Quality Management community and shares knowledge and lessons learned among suppliers. Horizontal transfer — spreading what one supplier learned to the others — is rare in this benchmark outside the Japanese supplier associations, and it is the cheapest form of capability building available to a buyer because the content is already paid for.
Prevention orientation and qualification

The global role is mandated to ensure prevention-oriented supplier quality management and risk management methods are implemented and monitored, to plan supplier audits across the global network, to implement standardised supplier qualification processes together with procurement, and to develop SQM competencies and training. Named methods are FMEA, value stream mapping and VDA 6.3 auditor certification. [SI9]

Value stream mapping is worth flagging. It is a flow and lead-time instrument rather than a quality one, and its appearance as a core method expected of a Siemens AG supplier quality manager is the only flow content located for this company in either pass. It appears as a competence requirement rather than as a described supplier activity, so it does not support a rating, and it is recorded in 3.4 as the strongest B4 lead in the chapter.
Resilience and continuity

Unchanged. The prevention-orientation mandate covers risk management methods being implemented and monitored, and regular data analysis identifies quality risks from components and suppliers, which supports the existing C-domain ratings without moving them. No supplier continuity exercise, recovery measure or disruption case was located in either pass.
Overall assessment

Corrected score 3.54 on twelve criteria. Siemens AG reads as a company with a properly constituted, globally coordinated supplier quality function built on VDA 6.3 process auditing, universal quality agreements and a community for horizontal learning — and with no published supplier outcome of any kind. Its chapter remains the most role-dependent in the project, which is a disclosure characteristic rather than a capability one.

1.2 Why this chapter's evidence base is weaker than its score suggests

Siemens AG is scored almost entirely on role descriptions. Of its twelve rated criteria, five rest substantially on what Siemens AG says it wants its supplier quality people to do. That is real evidence — an organisation that recruits certified VDA 6.3 auditors with negotiation-level German and several years of supplier quality experience is staffing a genuine function, and role descriptions are reliable about intent and about the seniority a company will pay for — and it is not evidence of execution, coverage or result.

The honest comparison is with Toyota and TSMC, whose chapters rest on named suppliers, described interventions and before-and-after figures, and which score 4.05 and above. Siemens AG's 3.54 and Toyota's score are not measuring the same kind of thing: one rates a documented intent, the other a demonstrated outcome. The cohort overview's stricter calibration exists precisely to stop that difference from disappearing into a single number, and under that calibration B2 would hold at 3 and this chapter would sit lower. Both figures are reported in this project and the overview's is the more defensible for cross-company comparison.
2. Operating Model and Future Business Readiness
2.1 Reconstructed supplier quality operating model

The three roles now available permit a reconstruction at the level of function design. Strategy: the global role defines value-oriented supplier quality strategies across locations, aligned with sustainability goals and supply-chain ecosystem principles. Entry: standardised supplier qualification processes implemented with procurement, with a Quality Assurance Agreement required for every supplier and gaps actively closed. Assessment: supplier audits to VDA 6.3, on site and remotely, planned across the global network. Surveillance: regular data analysis to identify quality risks from components and suppliers, with findings shared with process partners and actions agreed jointly. Intervention: improvement measures coordinated with purchasing and engineering, then verified effective. Reporting: KPI-based reports to quality and plant management. Horizontal diffusion: the SQM community sharing knowledge and lessons learned among suppliers. Function capability: SQM competencies and training developed centrally. [SI9]

This is a coherent and fairly complete design. What it lacks at every stage is quantity — no supplier count, audit count, qualification volume, agreement coverage figure, community participation number or improvement result appears anywhere.

3. Supplier Production-System Capability
3.1 VDA 6.3 as the audit standard

The single most consequential detail in this chapter is that Siemens AG audits suppliers to VDA 6.3 and requires its global supplier quality manager to be a certified, experienced VDA 6.3 auditor or equivalent. VDA 6.3 is the German automotive industry's process audit standard; it assesses the supplier's actual production process — process inputs, process flow, personnel and material effectiveness, process outputs — rather than the documentation of a quality management system, and it produces a graded result with defined downgrading rules. [SI9]

Choosing a process audit standard over a management-system audit is a substantive decision. An ISO 9001 certificate establishes that a supplier has a system; a VDA 6.3 audit establishes how well a specific process performs. Siemens AG is the only company in this cohort whose supplier audit standard is named as VDA 6.3 in its own role requirements, and the fact that audits are conducted both on site and remotely indicates a working programme rather than an occasional exercise.
3.2 The effectiveness verification step

B2 moves from 3 to 4 and this is the element that carries it. The Berlin role does not merely coordinate improvement measures; it coordinates them and verifies that they are effective. Across this benchmark, the commonest failure mode in published supplier quality work is that the record ends when an action is agreed. A stated duty to verify effectiveness, combined with regular data analysis to identify risks and KPI-based reporting to plant management, is a closed loop. [SI9]

Why 4 and not 5: the loop is described as a duty rather than evidenced in operation. No closure rate, verification record, improvement population or supplier outcome is published, and the top band in this benchmark requires improvement demonstrated over time. Why not 3, which is where the cohort overview's calibration would leave it: the evidence is no longer a single role, it names a specific audit standard with certified auditors, it includes a verification step and a reporting cadence to management, and it is coordinated by a global function that leads a community of practice. That is practice defined and owned rather than merely stated.

5.2 What Siemens AG's public evidence still does not tell us
The deeper pass resolved section 8's principal gap-log entry: four criteria no longer rest on a single role description. It did not resolve the decisive one.

No supplier outcome of any kind has been located in two passes: no supplier named, no process changed, no before-and-after figure, no audit count, no qualification volume, no agreement coverage figure, no community participation number and no improvement result. Siemens AG publishes a function design and nothing about the function's work.

Three narrower gaps matter. Whether Siemens AG requires an APQP and PPAP equivalent is unknown — neither located role names either, which is unusual in this cohort and may reflect a documentation gap rather than a practice one. Nothing at all was located on supplier capacity, leaving A2 unrated for a company whose supply base supports large infrastructure programmes. And nothing addresses sub-tier suppliers, which several companies in this cohort cover explicitly.

A source-scope note that governs this whole chapter. Both new sources are role descriptions, both from Smart Infrastructure — one from Electrification and Automation specifically. Siemens AG is a large diversified group whose other businesses may operate differently, so this chapter describes supplier quality as Smart Infrastructure defines it. Role descriptions establish intent, staffing and method vocabulary, and do not establish execution. Of this chapter's twelve rated criteria, five rest substantially on such evidence, as 1.2 sets out.
6. Implications for Siemens Energy

Everything in this section is an analytical hypothesis for low-volume, high-complexity, long-lead-time supply. None of it is observed Siemens Energy practice, and none of it forms part of the maturity score.
6.1 Audit the process, not the system

VDA 6.3 is the most directly adoptable item in this chapter. An ISO 9001 certificate tells a buyer that a supplier has a quality management system; a VDA 6.3 process audit tells it how a specific production process performs, graded, with defined downgrading rules for the failures that matter. For engineer-to-order equipment where the risk sits in a particular weld, heat treatment or machining operation rather than in the supplier's paperwork, a process audit standard finds what a system audit cannot. It also has a trained auditor population and published criteria, so adopting it costs certification rather than development.

6.3 Add the verification step, and record it

The Berlin role's duty to verify that improvement measures are effective is a one-line addition to a job description with a disproportionate effect. Most supplier quality systems in this cohort close when an action is agreed, which means nobody finds out which actions worked. Requiring verification — and recording the verification result — produces the only data a supplier development function will ever have about its own effectiveness, and it is the data this entire benchmark could not find for any company except Toyota, TSMC and Schneider Electric.
6.4 Build the horizontal channel

A community that shares lessons learned among suppliers is the cheapest capability mechanism identified anywhere in this project, because the knowledge already exists and has already been paid for by whichever supplier learned it. The Japanese supplier associations have run on this principle for decades; Siemens AG names it; TSMC introduced a version in 2025. For a concentrated base of suppliers using similar fabrication processes, convening them to present solved problems to each other costs a room and a day, and the buyer captures improvement it did not have to engineer.
The obvious objection — that competing suppliers will not share — is weaker than it looks where suppliers specialise in different commodities, which is usually the case in heavy equipment supply.
6.5 Make every supplier have a quality agreement, then close the gaps

The Siemens AG provision is specifically that every supplier must have a Quality Assurance Agreement and that the function works with procurement to close gaps where they are missing. The second half is the part that matters: most organisations have a quality agreement template and an unknown number of suppliers operating without one, usually the ones onboarded quickly under schedule pressure, which correlates with the ones that later cause problems. Auditing the coverage of your own agreements is a week's work and tends to be revealing.
6.6 Name value stream mapping and then actually use it on a supplier

Siemens AG expects its supplier quality managers to know value stream mapping and publishes nothing about mapping a supplier's value stream. That gap is the single most common one in this benchmark: flow and lead-time capability at suppliers is almost entirely unaddressed across all sixteen companies, with four of them unrated on B4 and B5 entirely. For long-lead-time equipment, where the supplier's lead time is frequently the project's critical path, mapping one critical supplier's value stream jointly is both unusual and likely to find weeks rather than percentage points.

4. Interpretation

GE Aerospace leads on observed supplier intervention; EMI's trained employees applied FLIGHT DECK at their own plant, supporting a scoped B7=5, while Phoenix's 24-hour disruption response supports C1=4. Rolls-Royce's three-year supplier MBD/E study supports scoped A5=5 and B7=5 through measured digital-capability progress, knowledge transfer and recurring reviews; the HAL/IAMPL India partnership supports A4=4. Honeywell's bounded four-week kaizen supports B4=4, and RTX's external F135 additive-manufacturing collaboration supports A5=4. Airbus, Boeing and Safran retain their current scores.

Calibration remains criterion-specific: a documented standard, role duty, buyer-only metric or one planned event does not show routine supplier use. A 4 needs execution, ownership and recurring follow-up in the evidenced scope; a 5 needs improvement over time with learning built into operation. The three 5s are scoped to GE's EMI learning case and Rolls-Royce's longitudinal digital-capability program, not generalized to every supplier or criterion.

Coverage is 96/112. NE means insufficient public evidence of the specific criterion, not low capability; no 2 was assigned simply because evidence was missing. New material sometimes repeats an earlier case, which was counted once rather than as independent corroboration. Buyer diversification alone does not prove supplier preparedness, a global footprint does not prove localization transfer, and a training catalogue does not prove retained production skills.

Score
Maturity anchor
1 · Ad hoc
Mostly reactive or dependent on individual effort; no defined repeatable approach.
2 · Emerging
A practice or pilot exists in limited areas; ownership, cadence or follow-through is inconsistent.

Documented processes, roles or standards are used, but integration or follow-through remains uneven.

Calculation: criterion scores are averaged within each pillar using rated criteria only, so pillar mean = sum of its rated criterion scores ÷ number of rated criteria. NE is used when the specific supplier capability cannot be defensibly rated from public evidence; it is excluded rather than scored zero. B7 tests supplier skills, ownership and independent sustainment. A defined training route supports 3; recurring transfer with ownership and competence follow-up supports 4; retained learning and continued improvement support 5. Use the company chapters for all 16 scores, source identifiers and criterion-specific reasons, including changed NE coverage. Research method: business need → supplier gap → buyer/supplier contributions → implemented capability → verification → supplier-owned learning. Qualification, audit completion, training participation, planned capacity, scorecards, dashboards, buyer-only risk visibility, dual sourcing, inventory buffers and generic requirements without gap closure provide context; they do not alone establish a complete capability-building intervention. A complete capability-building case should explain:
1. What business need or exposure created the requirement?
2. What capability did the supplier need to build?
3. What did the buyer and supplier actually do?
4. What changed in the supplier's process, system, skills, or ownership?
5. How was improvement verified?
6. What evidence exists that the supplier can sustain or repeat the capability?

Rolls-Royce Aerospace Supplier Capability-Building: Deep Research Benchmark and Recommended Operating Model
Executive summary

Rolls-Royce has built a sophisticated supplier-management architecture around aerospace quality, industrialization, operational excellence, digital integration, risk management and sustainability. The core elements include its SABRe supplier requirements, Supplier Maturity Assessment, Drive for Zero Defects resources, Value Chain Competitiveness improvement framework, supplier training, Digital Minimum Standards, standards/specification portals, Nadcap-related controls, business-continuity requirements and sustainability due diligence. Rolls-Royce states that it spends more than £7 billion annually with suppliers and devotes resources to making that supply chain more resilient and efficient [4] [6] [17].

The central finding of this research is that Rolls-Royce is particularly well documented in defining what capable aerospace suppliers must do; the greater opportunity is to turn that architecture into a more visibly closed-loop supplier capability-building system. Public documentation is more complete on Rolls-Royce supplier assessment and feedback than on observed supplier-side learning and sustained changes.

That distinction matters because supplier assurance and supplier development are not the same activity. Qualification establishes that a supplier is acceptable; requirements specify expected behavior; scorecards identify gaps; corrective actions restore conformity. Capability building goes further: it changes the supplier's engineering, production, digital, managerial or resilience capability so that the supplier can perform reliably without repeated customer intervention. The Toyota report supplied as a structural guide articulates a useful evidence chain:
Business need → Supplier gap → Buyer/supplier contributions → Implemented capability → Verification → Supplier-owned learning.

Applied to Rolls-Royce, the most important public evidence of genuine capability transfer is emerging in digital engineering. A 2026 peer-reviewed study based on three years of engaged research with Rolls-Royce examined deployment of Model-Based Definition and Model-Based Enterprise practices across suppliers and two supply-chain tiers. It found that supplier-development activities, regular reviews and a Digital Minimum Standard helped suppliers develop the ability to absorb and use digital knowledge rather than merely receive digital requirements [8] [17].
This materially strengthens the case that Rolls-Royce already possesses ingredients for a broader capability-building model.

The strategic case for intensifying that model is strong. Rolls-Royce's 2025 results still described parts availability as constrained despite improvement; Civil Aerospace original-equipment deliveries were 483 engines in 2025, compared with 529 in 2024, while the company expected a further £150–200 million cash-flow impact from supply-chain constraints in 2026. At the same time, the large-engine order book reached 2,207 engines and aftermarket demand remained strong [9].

In other words, Rolls-Royce does not face merely a supplier-compliance problem. It faces the harder problem of raising qualified capacity, productivity, digital compatibility and resilience in a safety-critical supply system while demand grows.

The recommended response is not another generic supplier scorecard. Rolls-Royce should build a Supplier Capability Accelerator around its existing systems. It should use SABRe, Supplier Maturity Assessment, Integrated Supplier Scorecards/Supplier Engagement Plans, Zero Defects, Value Chain Competitiveness and Digital Minimum Standards as the diagnostic and governance backbone, then deploy small cross-functional capability teams into selected suppliers for time-bounded improvement missions. Each intervention should finish only when the supplier demonstrates ownership, not merely when a defect or delivery problem closes [6] [17].
The architecture recommended below has five distinctive features:
Design principle
Rolls-Royce-specific implication
Requirements become diagnostics, not the end state
SABRe, maturity assessments and scorecards identify capability gaps; they should trigger structured development where the business exposure warrants it.
The supplier's real bottleneck becomes the classroom

Use machining, casting, forging, heat treatment, coating, inspection, APQP/PPAP, engineering release or digital-data problems as practical learning environments rather than relying primarily on classroom instruction.
Quality, capacity, digital and resilience are treated together
An AS9100-compliant process that lacks throughput, digital-data capability or recovery capability is not fully ready for sustained ramp-up.
Capability transfer has an explicit exit test
The supplier should demonstrate the new method independently and apply it to a second problem before Rolls-Royce closes the development intervention.
Deeper-tier capability receives deliberate attention

Critical material, special-process, casting/forging, electronics and tooling dependencies should be mapped and developed through the Tier 1 where necessary, rather than being treated only as Tier-1 risks.

This recommendation borrows the hands-on learning and supplier ownership evident in Toyota's strongest cases and the closed-loop supplier sensing-to-kaizen logic documented for GE Aerospace, while retaining the much more demanding aerospace airworthiness, configuration-control, traceability and special-process environment within which Rolls-Royce operates.
Strategic context

The assessment uses future-readiness, production-system and resilience dimensions without assigning composite maturity scores. The aerospace framework organizes supplier capability around future-business readiness, production-system capability and resilience/continuity; its criteria distinguish demand, capacity, ramp-up, technical complexity, production stability, flow, throughput, operating routines, learning, disruption response and dependency management.
The Rolls-Royce capability framework also includes regulatory assurance, digital engineering, sustainability, contractual models and supplier capability transfer.

Toyota’s supplier-development practices illustrate the difference between supplier control and capability-building. Its strongest evidence does not come from a supplier rating; it comes from joint work at the supplier's operations, followed by demonstrated reuse of the learned methods. Toyota's Umemura example, for instance, combined direct observation, time measurement, process redesign, Kanban, repeated coaching and post-project application by the supplier.

The GE material offers a parallel aerospace reference: supplier health and readiness mechanisms identify problems, while FLIGHT DECK interventions bring sourcing, quality, engineering and operational specialists into supplier improvement work.

For Rolls-Royce, the appropriate question is therefore not simply, “Does the company have robust supplier requirements?” It clearly does. The more useful questions are: How are suppliers selected for development? What gap is being built out? Who works with the supplier? What changes? How is the result verified? And can the supplier sustain the capability independently?

Rolls-Royce describes suppliers as strategically important to its operations and reports annual supplier expenditure above £7 billion. Its public supplier resources emphasize a resilient and efficient supply chain, supplier improvement and collaboration rather than purchasing purely on piece price.

Its supplier-selection language combines manufacturing capability, financial stability, delivery reliability, price and compliance with the Global Supplier Code; the company also reports sanctions, watch-list and adverse-media screening for new and existing third parties.

The strategic context is unusually demanding because Rolls-Royce sits at the intersection of several constraints. Civil engine demand and aftermarket activity are rising, yet parts availability has remained a limiting factor. At the same time, aerospace components often have long raw-material and process lead times, controlled design definitions, qualification-intensive manufacturing routes and a relatively narrow base of approved special-process capability. Rolls-Royce's own 2025 results show both the improving economics of Civil Aerospace and the continuing operational drag from supply-chain constraints.
A useful way to characterize the current Rolls-Royce supplier model is therefore:
standards-led → assessment-enabled → increasingly digitally connected → selectively collaborative.
The opportunity is to make the final step more systematic:
standards → assessment → joint gap closure → verified operating capability → supplier-owned improvement.

This is not an argument for replacing SABRe or supplier assurance. In aerospace, the requirements layer is indispensable. The point is that requirements and audits protect the certified product; development mechanisms improve the supplier system that must repeatedly satisfy those requirements.
Supplier lifecycle, qualification and capability-building architecture

Rolls-Royce's public supplier documentation can be reconstructed into a lifecycle with several interacting gates. This is an analytical synthesis rather than a Rolls-Royce-issued universal process map, because the exact sequencing varies by business, product, regulatory scope and contract.

Strategic sourcing and initial screening. Rolls-Royce states that supplier selection should be fair, open and transparent and that prospective suppliers are considered against manufacturing capability, financial stability, on-time delivery capability, price and compliance requirements. Its procurement policy also makes clear that customer-specific, regulatory, ethical and sustainability obligations can flow into supplier requirements.

Technical and quality qualification. SABRe is the supplier-facing element of the Rolls-Royce Management System and applies, within its stated editions and contractual scope, to suppliers and partners providing products or services to Rolls-Royce. The Global Supplier Portal presently hosts the Civil & Defence Aerospace SABRe edition, Zero Defects material, training, standards/specifications and Nadcap-related information [2] [3].

Industrialization and product introduction. Rolls-Royce supplier training includes Product Introduction and PPAP-related material linked to SABRe, with role-oriented learning for APQP/PPAP, FMEA, measurement-system analysis, statistical process control and control plans. Rolls-Royce also offers a Supplier Needs Analysis Process to help identify training appropriate to a supplier's role and gap [5].

Operating assurance and development. The Supplier Maturity Assessment, Zero Defects materials and supplier scorecard/engagement-plan mechanisms provide ways to identify recurring weaknesses rather than treating each nonconformance as an isolated event. Supplier Maturity Assessment revisions combine industry standards, escape root causes and supplier feedback, with identified gaps feeding Zero Defects plans [4].

Digital capability. Rolls-Royce's Digital Supply Chain application includes Digital Minimum Standards. For suppliers covered by an Integrated Supplier Scorecard/Supplier Engagement Plan and an active Technology Engagement Plan, Digital Minimum Standards assessments can provide an explicit digital-capability baseline; Rolls-Royce encourages broader suppliers to use the application as a digital roadmap [6] [17].

Ongoing risk and sustainability management. Rolls-Royce reports requiring strategic suppliers to provide business-continuity plans and uses sustainability screening based on commodity/industry, country risk, spend and strategic significance. Higher-risk or significant suppliers can undergo deeper assessment, with identified gaps leading to improvement plans and available third-party support [10].

The central architectural strength is that Rolls-Royce does not need to invent most of the tools required for a supplier-development system. It already possesses the quality, Lean, digital, training, risk and sustainability instruments. What is less explicit publicly is an overarching intervention workflow that tells a supplier and a Rolls-Royce team: this is the diagnosed business need; these capabilities must change; these are the respective contributions; these are the operating outcomes; and this is the evidence required before support ends.

That gap is especially important for SMEs. Supplier requirements have accumulated as the industry has sought simultaneously to improve safety, prevent quality escapes, digitize engineering, raise cybersecurity, decarbonize and strengthen resilience. Harmonization therefore matters. Rolls-Royce's SABRe Edition 4 work explicitly sought greater alignment with AESQ AS13100 and AS9145 rather than proliferating unique customer requirements [2] [3].
AESQ likewise describes AS13100 as a mechanism intended to harmonize aero-engine quality requirements and reduce customer-specific variation.
This is an important capability-building principle: every hour a supplier spends reconciling unnecessarily different customer formats is an hour unavailable for improving the underlying process.
Quality, safety, certification, digitalization and operating capability

A Rolls-Royce supplier capability program must remain firmly inside the aerospace certification and product-safety system. Toyota-style operational coaching can inform the method, but aerospace cannot treat a faster production flow as successful unless it remains fully controlled, conforming, traceable and airworthy.
The assurance stack
Layer
Relevance to Rolls-Royce suppliers
Capability-building implication
EASA Part 21

A production-organization approval holder must maintain a quality system ensuring products, parts and appliances conform to approved design data and are in condition for safe operation. EASA rules explicitly contemplate assessment and surveillance of partners and suppliers; outsourcing does not remove the approval holder's responsibility.
Supplier development must preserve design/configuration control, conformity and surveillance evidence. A buyer cannot “Lean” away regulatory controls.
FAA Part 21 / production approval

FAA production approval includes review of the applicant's organization, facilities, quality system and design data. FAA Quality System Audits can extend to production-approval holders and selected supplier/delegated facilities.
Supplier quality systems need to produce reliable objective evidence, not simply good output during an isolated audit.
Safety Management Systems

FAA's 2024 SMS rule expanded SMS requirements to applicable Part 21 design and production approval holders. It is a proactive safety-management obligation rather than a supplier certification applied automatically to every sub-tier supplier.
Supplier escapes, process changes and emerging risks should feed the OEM's broader safety-risk system; capability programs need escalation routes for safety-significant issues.
IAQG 9100-series AQMS

IAQG 9100 establishes aviation, space and defense QMS requirements based on ISO 9001 plus aerospace-specific controls; the certification scheme and OASIS provide industry-recognized certification information.
Certification is a baseline assurance mechanism. Capability development should focus on whether the system is being used effectively to control and improve the real process.
AS9145 APQP/PPAP
IAQG 9145 formalizes APQP and PPAP concepts for aerospace and is aimed at improving on-time/on-quality execution across the value stream [20].
Provides a natural backbone for supplier industrialization, capacity readiness and preventive quality work.
AS13100A, revised in 2025, provides supplemental quality requirements for aero-engine design and production when contractually invoked [21].
Rolls-Royce can use industry-harmonized methods rather than adding unnecessary proprietary requirements.
Nadcap and special-process approvals

Nadcap provides industry-managed special-process accreditation; Rolls-Royce also tells users to verify relevant Rolls-Royce business-unit approval when applicable and controls work transfers under SABRe.
Capacity expansion and alternate sourcing can be constrained by accreditation and customer approval lead time; resilience plans must include qualification, not just an alternate company name.
The practical implication is that supplier qualification should be treated as a stack rather than a single pass/fail event:
organizational quality capability → product/process industrialization → special-process qualification → part conformity → capacity demonstration → stable serial execution → controlled change.

Different suppliers need different subsets of that stack. A machining supplier, a raw-material producer, an MRO provider and an engineering-services supplier should not be forced through a mechanically identical development pathway.

For MRO suppliers, Rolls-Royce makes the boundary particularly explicit: technical approval is tied to formally approved workscopes/products and appropriate regulatory approval, with self-assessment and surveillance used to maintain oversight.
Zero Defects as a development platform

Rolls-Royce's Zero Defects ecosystem is one of the most promising foundations for deeper supplier capability building. Public materials include PFMEA practitioner guidance, supplier self-help content, process-specific reference PFMEAs, maturity assessments and learning material spanning industrialization, process, human factors and supply chain [4].
The capability-building opportunity is to make the logic explicitly iterative:
escape / risk signal → process mechanism → PFMEA/control-plan revision → physical or managerial countermeasure → effectiveness verification → standard work → replication.

That is more valuable than measuring only whether a corrective-action report closed. Corrective-action closure establishes that an event was addressed; capability development asks whether the supplier has learned how to prevent the next analogous event.
Digitalization and Industry 4.0

Rolls-Royce's Model-Based Definition work is significant because it changes the supplier relationship from exchange of static drawings to exchange of reusable, machine-readable product definition. Rolls-Royce describes MBD as integrating information into 3D CAD so that semantic product data can flow from design into manufacturing and quality processes. It reports applications that include automated creation of AS9102 FAIR form information, automated nonconformance/inspection activities and direct use of design data in downstream manufacturing. The company's broader Digital “O” concept extends the digital thread across the product lifecycle and to suppliers, partners and customers [8] [17].

The 2026 scholarly study is particularly valuable because it examines the organizational problem behind digitalization. Hacker, Aitken, Handfield and Mirzabeiki studied Rolls-Royce's MBD/MBE deployment across suppliers over a multi-year period. Their conclusion was not simply that suppliers need software. Supplier digital absorptive capacity improves when the OEM combines digital requirements with development activity, a way to measure digital progress and recurring reviews; the Digital Minimum Standard served as an organizing mechanism for that development [8] [17].
That yields an important lesson for Industry 4.0 supplier programs:
A digital standard is useful only when the supplier can absorb, operationalize and continuously use the digital knowledge behind it.

For Rolls-Royce, this argues against treating Digital Minimum Standards as an IT compliance checklist. Digital development should connect directly to manufacturing outcomes: fewer manual drawing interpretations, fewer data transcription errors, faster FAIR preparation, more reliable inspection programming, better configuration control and shorter engineering-to-shop-floor feedback loops. Those are the outcomes through which digital capability earns its place in supplier development [6] [17].
Performance metrics without a maturity score

A supplier capability-building program needs metrics, but not necessarily a composite supplier-development score. Rolls-Royce already has mechanisms such as supplier scorecards, engagement plans, maturity assessments and digital standards; the exact internal weights and thresholds are not comprehensively public.
A capability program should therefore use descriptive operating measures tied to the problem being developed:

The final row is the most important addition. A capability program should measure whether the supplier learned, not only whether Rolls-Royce got a better KPI.
Resilience, sustainability and commercial architecture
Supply-chain resilience

Rolls-Royce's recent operating results show why resilience must be treated as an operating capability rather than only a risk-register exercise. Parts availability improved during 2025 but remained constrained, and the company expected another £150–200 million supply-chain cash impact during 2026. Civil original-equipment deliveries declined year over year despite strong market demand [9].

Rolls-Royce states that strategic suppliers are expected to share business-continuity plans so that the company can understand geographic, facility and people risks; it also describes investment of time and resources in identifying and mitigating weaknesses in the external supply chain [10].

SABRe's work-transfer controls are also directly relevant because transferring a process or changing a supplier in aerospace may require controlled qualification rather than a simple procurement switch.
Public evidence is less complete on three points:

Enterprise-wide dual sourcing. No publicly available Rolls-Royce source reviewed here establishes a universal requirement that every critical component be dual sourced, nor would that necessarily be economically or technically sensible. Aerospace forgings, castings, coatings and other special processes may have long qualification cycles and relatively few qualified producers.

Tested supplier recovery. Business-continuity planning is documented, but publicly disclosed supplier-level time-to-recover tests, alternate-tooling exercises and recovery performance trends are limited.

Inventory strategy. Secondary reporting has described strategic buffers in a specific Rolls-Royce business-aviation production context, but that should not be generalized into a company-wide buffer policy.

For a capability-building program, this means resilience should be built around criticality-specific options, not a simplistic “dual source everything” mandate. Depending on the process, the best resilience mechanism may be dual source, an approved alternate material, backup tooling, critical spares, reserved capacity, inventory at a decoupling point, trained alternate operators, a pre-qualified work-transfer package, or accelerated requalification instructions.

Supplier capability is particularly important because aerospace work cannot necessarily be moved at the instant a disruption occurs. The capability often must exist before the disruption: approved process route, tooling, drawings, gauges, special-process accreditation, competent personnel and quality evidence.
Sustainability and decarbonization

Rolls-Royce identifies purchased goods and services as a significant component of its broader emissions footprint outside product use, with raw materials forming an important part of supply-chain emissions. Its supply-chain sustainability work includes screening, environmental assessment, supplier engagement, circular-resource initiatives and industry collaboration.

The company encourages strategic suppliers to use environmental-management practices such as ISO 14001 and provides or references industry resources including IAEG greenhouse-gas guidance and CDP reporting.

Rolls-Royce also highlights circular-material practices such as metal “revert” recycling and states that more than 95% of a used aero engine by weight can be recycled; the company's closed-loop manufacturing activities are positioned as both environmental and material-efficiency measures.

Supplier decarbonization should therefore be integrated with operational improvement instead of placed in a separate ESG workstream. For many aerospace suppliers, the same intervention can improve both economics and emissions:
higher first-pass yield → less energy and material per conforming part;
less scrap → lower embodied-carbon loss, especially in nickel/titanium alloys;
shorter heat-treatment queues → lower energy and WIP exposure;
closed-loop revert → reduced dependence on virgin high-value materials;
better process capability → fewer repeat inspections, repairs and logistics moves.
That linkage makes sustainability more credible to suppliers because it is tied to operating performance rather than being only a reporting requirement.
Commercial models as capability enablers
Rolls-Royce's supplier relationships span very different commercial architectures. These should be deliberately connected to capability-development objectives.

Long-term supply contracts can create sufficient demand certainty for suppliers to invest. Rolls-Royce's 2024 agreement with Castle Precision, for example, was described as an £85 million multi-year contract for precision-machined critical rotating engine components, building on a roughly 40-year relationship. Castle described the agreement as providing growth and certainty [12].

Risk-and-Revenue Sharing Partnerships go substantially further. Rolls-Royce has long used such relationships with Japanese aerospace firms, and its 20-year relationship with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries Aero Engines began with a Risk and Revenue Sharing Partnership arrangement. Rolls-Royce has historically described these relationships as progressing from component supply toward major modules and broader technological capability [13].

Localization and licensed capability are another pathway. Rolls-Royce and Hindustan Aeronautics have expanded from longstanding engine relationships toward local maintenance and manufacturing capability, including initiatives involving Adour engines and Trent-related parts [14].

In 2026, Rolls-Royce and Reliance announced strategic intent around an Indian aerospace gas-turbine ecosystem, including joint design, development, manufacturing, testing and through-life support ambitions associated with the AMCA engine. That is a much deeper form of capability creation than conventional purchase-order sourcing [15].

Supplier finance addresses a different constraint: working capital. Rolls-Royce's disclosed supply-chain finance arrangement allows eligible suppliers on longer payment terms to obtain early payment from participating banks, with financing linked to Rolls-Royce's credit standing. At June 2024, £236 million had been drawn under the program, compared with £418 million at year-end 2023. Rolls-Royce also reported arrangements intended to pay certain smaller suppliers earlier than standard terms.

Commercial architecture therefore belongs inside supplier capability strategy. A supplier cannot make a credible equipment, tooling, workforce or digital investment if the commercial signal is too short-lived or unstable to justify it. Conversely, a long-term commitment should be paired with explicit productivity, capacity, quality and resilience obligations so that commercial certainty turns into operating capability.

An important inference follows from Rolls-Royce's downstream business model. Long-term service arrangements and TotalCare-type models place substantial time-on-wing, maintenance and availability consequences on Rolls-Royce. This makes upstream supplier reliability more strategically significant than the purchase price of an individual part alone.
A supplier-development business case should therefore consider the engine-lifecycle consequence of supply failure, not merely annual component spend.

The digital case is the most instructive for the recommended operating model. The 2026 academic research shows that Rolls-Royce did not merely tell suppliers to become digital. It coupled a defined minimum standard with supplier-development activities and recurring evaluation, recognizing that suppliers differ in their capacity to absorb new digital knowledge.
That is precisely the logic a broader supplier-capability system should use for industrial engineering, resilience and sustainability.

The older Rolls-Royce visibility case reaches a similar conclusion by a different route. Bartlett, Julien and Baines used a Rolls-Royce supply-chain case to show that performance problems could be addressed by jointly identifying visibility gaps and improving information exchange around areas such as capacity planning, material ordering and inventory. The resulting initiative was associated with significantly improved schedule adherence [18].
The lesson is that some apparent supplier execution problems originate not in shop-floor skill alone but in buyer-supplier information architecture.
Barriers and enablers
The principal supplier barriers are not all within supplier control.

Qualification complexity is unavoidable to a degree. AS9100-series systems, AS13100, APQP/PPAP, Nadcap, Rolls-Royce-specific approvals, configuration management and controlled work transfers can make expansion or alternate sourcing slow. Harmonization through AESQ and Rolls-Royce's SABRe alignment is therefore an important enabler.

Digital absorptive capacity differs materially among suppliers. The Rolls-Royce-sponsored academic work directly identifies this as an organizational development challenge; digital progress needs to be measured, reviewed and supported rather than assumed.

Capital and workforce constraints can make capacity expansion rationally unattractive to suppliers. Aerospace industry research has highlighted shortages of experienced labor and engineering capability, long investment paybacks and supplier reluctance to add capacity when OEM forecasts are perceived as uncertain after repeated cycles of expansion and contraction.
Long-term contracts and more stable forward commitments can therefore be capability enablers rather than merely commercial instruments.

Deep-tier opacity remains difficult. A Tier 1 may appear healthy while depending on a single qualified forge, casting source, coating facility, alloy feedstock or electronic component. Business-continuity plans are necessary but should be supplemented by process-level dependency mapping and exercised recovery. Rolls-Royce's existing requirement for strategic suppliers to share continuity plans provides a starting point [10].

Buyer-created volatility can degrade supplier performance. The broader supplier-development literature and the Toyota benchmark both suggest that forecast stability, engineering-change discipline and reliable information are part of the buyer's contribution to supplier capability.
Rolls-Royce's own historical supply-chain visibility research reinforces the importance of high-quality planning information.
Recommended Rolls-Royce supplier capability-building program
The recommended model is a Rolls-Royce Supplier Capability Accelerator, built on existing systems rather than created as an independent supplier-improvement bureaucracy.
Its objective should be:

Develop critical suppliers so they can independently deliver safe, conforming product at required rate and lead time, absorb new digital and technical requirements, recover from disruption and improve resource efficiency without persistent Rolls-Royce intervention.

Supplier-selection logic
The program should avoid a single weighted “maturity score.” Instead, intervention selection should begin with an exposure statement:
What happens to engine delivery, fleet availability, safety, cash or strategic technology if this supplier fails to improve?

A supplier should enter intensive capability development when several conditions coincide: the part or process is strategically important; an operating or future-readiness gap is real; normal corrective action has not been sufficient or is unlikely to be sufficient; Rolls-Royce can contribute relevant expertise or a commercial enabler; and there is a plausible path to supplier ownership.
High annual spend should not be required. A low-spend special-process supplier can be more critical than a much larger source of readily substitutable material.
Cross-functional capability cells

Rolls-Royce should create a small, deployable Supplier Capability Cell for each intensive intervention. The cell should not replace the buyer or Supplier Quality Engineer; it should add temporary depth.

The intervention cycle
A common intervention discipline should be used regardless of the technical topic:
Business exposure. Define the engine/program/customer consequence and the required future state.
Baseline. Establish current quality, delivery, capacity, lead-time, digital, resilience or sustainability behavior using real data.

Root capability gap. Separate symptoms from causes. A late part could result from inadequate capacity, poor process yield, unstable demand, drawing changes, inspection queues, supplier sub-tier shortages or all of these.

Joint work package. Identify what Rolls-Royce will provide and what the supplier will provide. The buyer contribution can include engineering clarification, training, commercial stability, data, coach time or qualification support; the supplier contribution may include people, equipment, maintenance, layout, standard work or management routines.

Implementation at the point of work. Change the process, not only the presentation. For a machining bottleneck this might involve setup reduction, tooling, maintenance, inspection sequencing and standard work. For digital capability it might involve direct MBD consumption and automatic inspection programming. For resilience it might involve actually running an alternate-work-transfer exercise.
Verification. Demonstrate that the capability performs under normal production conditions.
Handover. Supplier personnel run the routine without Rolls-Royce leading it.
Independent second application. The supplier applies the method to a different but comparable issue.
Sustainment. Review after withdrawal. A suggested cadence is approximately 30, 90 and 180 days, adjusted to the part's cycle time and production frequency.
Specific program modules

Production Constraint Lab. Intensive 8–12 week supplier interventions centered on one real constraint. Methods would include value-stream analysis, queue/WIP mapping, time studies, maintenance analysis, changeover reduction, quality-at-source, first-pass-yield analysis and daily management. It should draw from the existing VCC framework rather than introduce a competing Lean vocabulary.

Zero Defects Practitioner Pathway. Move selected supplier personnel from “training completed” to demonstrated practitioner status. The supplier would use Rolls-Royce's PFMEA/control-plan/Zero Defects material on a real process and then repeat the work independently.

Digital Supplier Accelerator. Institutionalize the process described in the 2026 MBD/E research: baseline using Digital Minimum Standards, jointly select operational digital use cases, review progress recurrently and verify that the supplier can sustain the capability [6] [17].

Industrialization War Room. For launch/ramp suppliers, integrate engineering maturity, tooling, raw material, qualified processes, APQP/PPAP, FAIR, staffing, inspection capacity and rate demonstration into one readiness review. This avoids quality, purchasing and capacity teams maintaining separate versions of supplier readiness. AS9145/APQP provides the natural industry structure.

Resilience Exercise. For each highly critical process, ask a practical question: If the identified machine/site/material/sub-tier disappeared tomorrow, what precisely happens next? The supplier should demonstrate people, tooling, process data, alternative capacity, special-process approval, quality requalification and decision rights rather than submit only a BCP document.

Supplier Coach Academy. Develop supplier employees who can teach the new methods internally. This is where Rolls-Royce can most directly apply Toyota's strongest lesson: the intervention should leave behind people who can solve the next problem.

Governance and descriptive success measures
The executive steering group should review capability-building as a portfolio of business exposures rather than as a league table of suppliers. Its key questions should be:

Are we solving the constraints that threaten engine delivery or service? Is the supplier's capability materially different after the intervention? Has the supplier taken ownership? Did Rolls-Royce behavior contribute to the problem? Can the improvement survive withdrawal of Rolls-Royce specialists?

At program level, Rolls-Royce should report descriptive measures such as the number of critical constraints eliminated; quality-escape recurrence; on-time delivery recovery; demonstrated rate increases; lead-time and WIP reductions; PPAP/FAIR right-first-time improvement; supplier-led second applications; tested recovery time; critical dependencies mitigated; digital-workflow adoption; material/energy savings; and the percentage of completed interventions still performing six months after handover.

The most revealing metric would be the proportion of later supplier improvements led by the supplier without Rolls-Royce personnel acting as the primary problem solver. That measure gets closer to actual capability transfer than attendance, audit closure or a composite maturity score.

Evidence limitations and open questions

Several important aspects of Rolls-Royce's internal supplier-management system are understandably not transparent in public sources. The research does not establish a public enterprise-wide formula for selecting suppliers for intensive hands-on development; the internal weighting of Integrated Supplier Scorecards; supplier-development staffing or budget; a universal dual-sourcing policy; common supplier time-to-recover thresholds; or a company-wide rule for declaring supplier capability development complete. Absence from public disclosure should not be interpreted as proof that these mechanisms do not exist.

Likewise, much of Rolls-Royce's public supplier documentation necessarily describes requirements. A requirement to conduct capacity planning, control special processes, maintain continuity plans or use APQP is evidence of governance, but by itself it does not demonstrate that supplier capability improved. The strongest future evidence would therefore consist of named cases showing the complete chain from diagnosed gap through buyer/supplier intervention, implemented change, verified operating result and supplier-led sustainment.

The 2026 scholarly work on digital supplier absorptive capacity is particularly significant because it supplies precisely that missing middle for one domain: it documents an actual Rolls-Royce supplier-development process rather than only a requirement.

A high-value next step for Rolls-Royce would be to make similarly rigorous, anonymized evidence available for production constraints, industrialization, resilience and decarbonization, creating a body of practice that suppliers can learn from without exposing commercially sensitive data.

The overall conclusion is therefore not that Rolls-Royce lacks supplier capability-building. Rather, the evidence indicates that it already has most of the necessary components—strong aerospace standards, supplier assessments, Zero Defects methods, Lean/VCC tools, digital-development mechanisms, APQP/PPAP training, strategic partnerships, continuity expectations and sustainability processes.
The highest-value evolution is to connect them through one explicit operating loop:
strategic need → supplier gap → cross-functional intervention → changed process/skill/system → verified operating performance → independent supplier application → sustained capability.

That would move Rolls-Royce's supplier system from an already substantial architecture of assurance and improvement requirements toward a more demonstrably scalable system for building the supplier's ability to solve the next problem itself.

GE Aerospace Supplier Capability-Building: Deep Research Report
Executive Summary
Supplier capability development extends beyond requirements, scorecards and corrective actions to changes in what a supplier can independently do. A complete development cycle follows:
Business need → Supplier gap → Buyer/supplier contributions → Implemented capability → Verification → Supplier-owned learning.

Supplier capability work spans future-business readiness, production-system capability and resilience/continuity. Audits, training attendance, dashboards, qualification and planned capacity are inputs, not proof of sustained operating capability.
Overall conclusion

GE Aerospace already has the essential components of a sophisticated supplier capability-building system. Its strongest distinctive feature is the combination of four mechanisms that many companies operate separately:
SEPM/SCORE provides structured supplier sensing, expectations, metrics, action planning, and recurring performance reviews.
FLIGHT DECK provides hands-on operating-system intervention at supplier sites rather than stopping at corrective-action requests.

GE deploys substantial cross-functional engineering and supply-chain resources into priority suppliers and directly co-invests in tooling, dies, fixtures, and equipment when physical capability is the constraint.

GE has begun transferring FLIGHT DECK problem-solving capability into supplier employees themselves, creating early evidence of the supplier-owned learning that the Toyota benchmark identifies as the highest-value end state. [1]

SEPM/SCORE identifies supplier risks and operating gaps; FLIGHT DECK addresses selected constraints; action plans, engineering support, capital investment and performance reviews support implementation and sustainment.

GE's strongest public operational evidence is unusually concrete. At the start of 2024, GE reported that roughly 80% of material shortages were concentrated at 15 priority supplier sites. It subsequently deployed more than 550 GE engineering and supply-chain resources into the supply base while working with suppliers using FLIGHT DECK methods. GE reported that material input from those priority suppliers increased 26% from the first half to the second half of 2024, while supplier volume commitments rose from approximately half early in 2024 to more than 90% by April 2025. [2]

In 2025, GE reported more than 40% year-over-year growth in material input from priority suppliers and seven consecutive quarters of improvement; total engine deliveries increased 26% that year. [3]  [67]
GE's 2026 quarterly disclosures indicated that supplier material-input improvement continued into the first half of 2026. [4]  [66]
Two supplier cases reveal different stages of maturity.

Steel Tool illustrates expert-led supplier recovery. GE and supplier personnel jointly mapped the value stream, identified constraints, changed flow and operating practices, and involved operators directly in experimentation. GE reported large gains in output and first-time yield, while a GE supplier-recovery leader remained engaged daily. This is strong evidence of joint capability intervention, but public evidence does not yet establish how much of the learning remained independently embedded after GE support was withdrawn. [5]

EMI is more important from a capability-transfer perspective. Fourteen EMI employees attended GE's FLIGHT DECK Foundations training at GE's Terre Haute facility and then returned to their own plant and applied the methods. GE reports that they redesigned a production flow that had required roughly 2.5 miles of movement and ten inter-building moves, shortening the travel distance by approximately a factor of ten. That sequence—training, return to supplier site, supplier-led application—is closer to the Toyota benchmark's desired transition from expert intervention to supplier ownership. [6]

The next step should therefore not be another supplier scorecard. GE already has strong scorecards, requirements, reviews, and interventions. The strategic opportunity is to make the supplier-development system more explicitly developmental and measurable:

SEPM should identify the gap; FLIGHT DECK should change the capability; supplier training should transfer ownership; investment should remove structural constraints; and SCORE should verify that the capability still exists after GE stops leading the intervention.
That last step—independent supplier replication and retained learning—is the clearest lesson from the Toyota reference model and the most important opportunity for GE to institutionalize.
Operating Model and Future Business Readiness
GE's emerging supplier-development architecture

GE Aerospace's public evidence points to a federated but increasingly integrated supplier-development model rather than a single centralized "supplier development department." In January 2025, GE combined safety, quality, engineering, manufacturing, and sourcing into a more cohesive organization intended to improve value-chain problem solving, and it indicated that the integrated approach would expand further across the commercial-engine lifecycle. [3]
A reasonable reconstruction of the current system is:

Supplier capability process (analytical reconstruction, not an official GE workflow): GE program and demand needs feed SEPM/SCORE supplier sensing, then identification of the supplier gap and its criticality. Readiness, quality and compliance actions lead to a FLIGHT DECK intervention; engineering, tooling and capital support may run alongside that work. GE and supplier teams implement process changes and workforce learning, then verify operating performance.

Sustainment decision: If the supplier cannot yet sustain or repeat the improvement, further FLIGHT DECK and technical assistance is proposed. If it can, supplier-owned daily management is the exit route, with learning captured in SCORE and future-readiness work. This is the report’s recommended loop, not a verified universal GE rule.

The first half of this architecture is already strongly evidenced. SEPM defines a holistic supplier-health model, while SCORE supports supplier performance information, action planning, and review. Suppliers and GE evaluate ratings, establish improvement goals, and monitor action plans; review frequency changes with supplier status and business need. [15]
The second half—especially the formal test that a supplier can independently repeat the improvement—is much less visible publicly and should become a deliberate design feature.
SEPM as the supplier "sensing layer"

GE's Supplier Expectations & Performance Management manual is more than a quality document. It combines six dimensions—Safety, Compliance, Quality, Delivery, Commercial, and Readiness—into an overall supplier-health construct. The composite color rating is driven by the lowest-performing dimension, which creates an intentionally conservative view of supplier health rather than allowing strong delivery, for example, to mask a compliance or readiness problem. [16]
The manual's content covers many of the exact capabilities relevant to an aerospace supplier-development system:

This is a sound architecture because supplier-development research consistently finds that assessment and certification can serve as precursors to deeper operational knowledge transfer, but supplier performance improves when those mechanisms are followed by active communication, site interaction and training rather than used alone. Modi and Mabert's empirical study of 215 supplier-development experiences found that evaluation/certification mechanisms can establish the basis for later operational knowledge transfer and that collaborative communication supports performance improvement. [21]
Future demand and capacity confidence

GE's strongest recent supply-chain lesson appears to have been that supplier capability cannot be managed effectively when the buyer's own demand signal is unstable. Its 2025 Annual Report states that GE began providing suppliers with more stable near-term forecasts and increased long-term visibility, allowing engineering and FLIGHT DECK resources to be deployed more effectively against actual constraints. [3]
That is significant because future readiness is not simply a supplier property. It is a joint system property:
[ \text{Supplier readiness} \approx f(\text{forecast stability},\ \text{capacity},\ \text{yield},\ \text{tooling},\ \text{skills},\ \text{sub-tier supply},\ \text{engineering maturity}) ]

SEPM's Readiness process explicitly allows GE to verify a supplier's operational, process and technical capability and current/future capacity through site visits, surveys, assessments and audits. Its S&OP approach compares capacity/capability at key constraints with demand and brings important gaps to senior GE leadership for collaborative review. [19]
That aligns directly with the benchmark's A1–A3 criteria—future demand, capacity confidence, and ramp-up readiness.

The development opportunity is to make the gap-closing mechanism just as standardized as the assessment itself. Public evidence establishes that GE measures readiness; it does not reveal one universal rate-readiness protocol specifying, for every critical supplier, a standard stress-test duration, yield assumption, maintenance allowance, labor-availability assumption, recovery buffer and formal exit threshold. That should not be interpreted as absence; it is a public-evidence gap.
Localization and strategic capacity creation

GE is also using supplier investment as a capability-building lever. Its 2025 U.S. manufacturing program included more than $100 million for the external supplier base, focused on tools and equipment intended to reduce constraints and defects; GE announced another supplier commitment above $100 million in its 2026 U.S. manufacturing investment program. [10]
In Europe, GE similarly described supplier tooling and custom dies as part of manufacturing investment intended to improve capability and reduce defects. [22]

Localization is becoming strategically important as well. In October 2026 GE said it had 17 major domestic supplier partners in India, approximately $200 million of in-country supplier spending in 2025, and an objective of doubling that spend by 2030. [23]

That provides evidence of regional supply-base expansion, although public information does not yet show a single GE-wide localization-capability-transfer methodology analogous to its clearer FLIGHT DECK production-system work.
The most effective model for localization should therefore link local-content targets to a capability work package:
Qualified process → workforce → tooling → special-process accreditation → measurement/test capability → export-control compliance → sub-tier material readiness → demonstrated production rate.
Without that chain, a local-source target measures purchasing localization but not whether the supplier has developed durable aerospace capability.
Supplier Production-System and Quality Capability
FLIGHT DECK changes the character of supplier development
The decisive difference between a conventional supplier-management program and GE's stronger cases is what happens after a supplier turns red or a constraint is identified.
Conventional supplier management often follows:
Metric miss → escalation → corrective-action request → supplier response → closure.
GE's FLIGHT DECK intervention evidence points toward a deeper model:
Constraint → joint observation → value-stream diagnosis → operator involvement → experiments → changed physical/process system → daily management → measured result.

This resembles Toyota’s hands-on approach: buyer specialists and supplier personnel change production processes together, teach the underlying problem-solving method and verify continued supplier use.
GE's Steel Tool and EMI cases indicate that GE is moving along the same capability-building continuum with its own operating system.
Steel Tool: strong evidence of applied supplier intervention

GE's Steel Tool case provides unusually rich public evidence of an actual supplier operating-system intervention. Approximately 40 GE and Steel Tool employees participated in a shingijutsu kaizen event. The teams used value-stream analysis, involved operators in diagnosing problems and trialing countermeasures, and focused on production constraints rather than simply demanding more output. A GE supplier-recovery leader was described as working with Steel Tool on a daily basis. [5]
GE reported 58 safety improvements, an increase of roughly 800 pieces per week, and first-time-yield gains of 45% and 68% on two processes, alongside less rework and waste. [5]

GE's Annual Report separately described a supplier honeycomb process that had been producing approximately 47 pieces per week before a joint kaizen involving about 40 participants identified four major constraints and increased output above 470 pieces per week. [3]

Because these disclosures describe the improvement using different production measures, they should be treated as complementary evidence of a large intervention rather than assumed to be the exact same denominator.
