Safran Group — Supplier Capability Building (Aerospace)
Executive Summary

Safran is a French aerospace and defense technology group active in aircraft propulsion, equipment and defense, and interiors. For 2025 it reported €31.329 billion of adjusted revenue (€31.189 billion consolidated) and approximately 110,000 employees. Its industrial network spans civil aerospace, military and helicopter propulsion, landing systems, nacelles, electrical and electronic equipment and cabin products. Its acquisition of Collins Aerospace’s flight-control and actuation businesses closed in July 2025, expanding those technical capabilities. [S1] [S2] [S3] [S4]

Safran’s supplier capability architecture rests on Group purchasing governance, a formal Responsible Purchasing Charter, SAFe requirements for external providers, supplier-specific quality and process approvals, operational-performance monitoring, training, APQP, industrialization control and risk management. Safran explicitly commits to developing suppliers through finance, innovation, international and human-resource support where appropriate, while managing mutual dependence. These are stronger documented mechanisms than a simple certification-and-scorecard approach. [S5] [S6] [S8] [S9] [S10]

The 2024 SAFe revision strengthened aerospace safety-management expectations, APQP, supplier capacity/load analysis through One Safran Baselines, supplier support through Aero Excellence and cybersecurity self-assessment. Safran also publishes a supplier e-learning catalogue and digital portals for procurement, technical exchange, quality exceptions and delivery-performance monitoring. Requirements and portal eligibility vary by provider category, business and contract; not every Safran vendor is subject to identical 9100/Nadcap rules. [S8] [S9] [S10] [S11]

Three published cases illustrate distinct forms of capability development: Safran’s in-house Additive Manufacturing Campus produced approximately 15,000 parts in 2025 with 18,000 expected in 2026; Safran and Log-hub reported logistics network reductions of up to 60% in vehicle mileage and about 30% in transport-related CO₂; and Safran is expanding selected manufacturing and engine-maintenance capacity in Texas and Hyderabad. The manufacturing campus is an internal Safran capability, whereas Log-hub is a logistics co-development case; neither is evidence of a universal supplier factory-improvement program. [S13] [S14] [S15] [S16]
Corporate Context

Safran’s FY2025 adjusted revenue was €15.668 billion in Propulsion, €12.302 billion in Equipment & Defense and €3.349 billion in Aircraft Interiors, plus €10 million in holding/other activities. These are adjusted reporting segments, not a claim that civil and military revenues are evenly split. Defense, civil original equipment and aftermarket activity each have different supplier requirements and demand profiles. [S2] [S3]

The July 2025 Collins Aerospace acquisition brought approximately 4,000 personnel in flight-control and actuation activities into Safran Electronics & Defense. It is a portfolio and industrial-capability acquisition, rather than an acquisition of a distressed supplier for remedial development. [S4]
Supplier Strategy & Governance

Safran’s centralized Purchasing division defines Group policy, procurement strategy and common controls. Purchasing departments in the individual businesses handle operational production purchasing. The Group’s stated mission includes identifying current/future suppliers, embedding CSR criteria, involving suppliers early, coordinating shared tools and supporting strategic suppliers. Safran’s supplier commitments call for balanced, sustainable relationships, transparent information, total-cost evaluation, management of mutual dependency and targeted development support. [S5] [S6]

Safran first received France’s Responsible Supplier Relations and Purchasing (RFAR) label in 2017, obtained its third three-year award in May 2024 and passed a continuation review in May 2025. The label provides evidence of a recognized responsible-purchasing framework, not a numeric audit score proving individual supplier capability. [S7]

Supplier coordination is supported by the SAFe document family: SAFe 1 (GRP-0087) details Safran requirements for external providers, SAFe 2 is the provider handbook, SAFe 3 the requirements compliance matrix, SAFe 5 covers fraud/falsification and SAFe 6 lists e-learning available to suppliers. SAFe revisions are used at supplier selection to assess commitment and applicability, including aviation safety, APQP, cyber, industrial capacity and CSR issues. [S8] [S9] [S10]
Supplier Selection & Onboarding

Potential suppliers are assessed according to the purchased product or service, applicable Safran sector/provider category and business-specific procurement and quality documents. The SAFe requirements compliance matrix determines which provisions apply; the registered supplier’s technical competence, process approvals, capacity, quality system and traceability should be assessed against the contract rather than against a one-size-fits-all checklist. Safran publishes PARAGON registration instructions and different authorized portals, including DigiBuy for purchasing collaboration; their presence does not establish that one portal alone confers technical production approval. [S8] [S9]

For aerospace built-to-print and built-to-spec providers, SAFe’s certification matrix identifies AS/EN/JISQ 9100. For distributors it lists 9120 or an industry-recognized alternative; for maintenance organizations, relevant 9100/9110 or civil/military repair authorization may apply; for nonproduction and interoperation services, ISO 9001 or other standards may be acceptable according to category and the Safran compliance matrix. Consequently, AS9100 is not an unconditional requirement for every supplier. [S9]

The actual authorization path also depends on first-article inspection, approved special processes, product/process qualification, technical data control, quality-management maturity, supplier risk and the specific Safran purchasing entity. Pilot manufacture, approved deviations, inspection records and qualification gates are prudent tools for higher-risk work, but no single mandatory group-wide sequence of demonstration parts, pilots and audit visits was established for all supplier types. [S9]
Supplier Development & Collaboration

Safran’s documented development model includes a Supplier Relationship Stakeholder (for example a buyer, Supplier Performance Manager, Supplier Quality Assurance Manager or external industrialization manager), who identifies the supplier’s needs and coordinates appropriate interventions. The SAFe e-learning catalogue requires supplier enrollment through such a Safran contact and limits concurrent courses to a manageable number. Courses include APQP, PPAP industrialization, PFMEA/FMECA, statistical process control, process capability, QRQC, 8D, foreign object damage prevention, safety management and SAFe requirements. Availability and registration are coordinated; this is not unrestricted public access or proof that each supplier attends every course. [S11]

Safran’s 2024 SAFe update also encourages Aero Excellence maturity work and One Safran Baselines for demand/capacity analysis. These create specific avenues for shared capacity discussions, gap identification and process stabilization. When technical problems persist, an appropriate work package can combine Safran’s supplier quality and purchasing personnel with supplier production, industrialization and engineering staff; objectives should be measured in actual good units, process stability, quality and independent supplier execution, rather than training attendance alone. [S10] [S11]
Quality Systems & Standards

Safran’s SAFe 1 GRP-0087 (issue 11, updated July 2024) includes a sector-and-provider QMS matrix rather than a single rule for all entities. It refers to 9100-series certification for applicable aerospace manufacturers and to alternative quality-system or regulatory standards for defined other categories. Supplier approval, contract applicability, configuration and regulatory requirements must all be checked before imposing a particular standard. [S9]

For special processes, SAFe requires Nadcap accreditation for processes listed in Safran’s GRM-0135; certain providers must identify Safran as a customer in eAuditNet. Laboratories can have specified alternatives through mutually recognized accreditation bodies. Safran also requires qualification of applicable special processes and sub-tier processes by the company that owns the product definition, with defined exceptions and applicability by activity. It is inaccurate to say that every heat-treatment, laboratory or nondestructive test provider must automatically have the same Nadcap scope. [S9]

Other requirements include APQP/PPAP according to applicability, first-article and process verification, traceability and configuration control, equipment maintenance and calibration, nonconformance management, corrective action and protection against suspected unapproved parts. Safran’s e-learning catalogue covers a number of these disciplines. Supplier process maturity is demonstrated by stable execution and validated corrective measures, not solely certificate possession. [S9] [S10] [S11]
Production Capability Building

Safran’s One Safran Baselines methodology and APQP reinforce engineering and production planning, while its supplier-facing courses build common understanding of process variation, capacity, rapid problem-solving and industrialization milestones. Lean flow, Kanban, statistical process control and controlled automation may be useful depending on the commodity, but the public SAFe documents do not impose one identical Lean/Six Sigma operating model or digital twin requirement on all suppliers. [S10] [S11]

Safran’s Additive Manufacturing Campus in Le Haillan has become a serial-production competence center serving ten of twelve Safran companies. A September 2026 company account states that approximately 15,000 additive parts were delivered in 2025 and anticipates 18,000 in 2026. Its specialist workforce grew from around 60 to more than 150; a UIMM-backed metallurgical professional qualification supports operators, and internal designer training has reached hundreds across Safran companies. These are internal Safran capability-building results; the published account does not establish that hundreds of external supplier engineers received the same training. [S13]

Safran also announced a new carbon-brake production facility near Lyon in 2025. Planned operation begins in 2030 and would support a gradual 25% increase in Safran carbon-brake volumes by 2037; that 25% figure is not a Group-wide aerospace production growth target. [S21]
Supply-Chain Resilience & Risk Management

Safran’s supplier commitments explicitly require management of mutual-dependence risks. The revised SAFe rules reinforce supply-chain resilience through supplier operational performance, One Safran Baselines capacity analysis, cybersecurity self-assessment and applicable risk controls. Choosing a second source, safety stock or transferred work package should depend on materiality, customer approvals, capacity and supplier criticality; public policy does not establish a universal mandate to dual-source every critical part. [S6] [S9] [S10]

Industrial geographic diversification is visible in Safran’s investment decisions. In September 2026, Safran Power Units announced plans to double Grand Prairie, Texas turbojet-engine capacity for missiles and drones, with incremental capacity expected online in 2028. Safran also inaugurated its largest LEAP-engine MRO facility in Hyderabad in 2025, designed to ramp to 300 annual engine shop visits. The investments strengthen Safran’s own network; they should not be counted as completed improvements at independent suppliers. [S15] [S16]

Operational resilience also depends on logistics-network design and data visibility. In its published 2025 account, logistics technology partner Log-hub described joint modeling with Safran of more than 2,000 supplier and customer locations and flows in Europe and the United States, identifying cross-docks that reduced modeled or observed vehicle mileage by up to 60% and transport CO₂ intensity by approximately 30%. Those results are partner-reported and pertain to the covered network scenarios, not Safran’s entire global supplier footprint. [S14]
Sustainability & ESG in Purchasing

Safran’s Responsible Purchasing Charter covers human rights, ethics, fair supplier treatment and environmental considerations. EcoVadis assessments have been progressively introduced since 2024 to identify and assess higher-risk suppliers. The 2024 RFAR award and 2025 review relate to responsible purchasing and supplier collaboration, not to automatic certification of every supplier as environmentally compliant. [S7] [S17]

Safran’s TOP400 supplier decarbonization initiative targets the roughly 400 suppliers contributing the most to purchased-goods/services emissions. As of 2024, Safran reported that more than 70% of those suppliers had disclosed Scope 1 and 2 reduction targets. The program requires assessment and engagement with these prioritized suppliers; it is not a published requirement for each small supplier to achieve net zero by 2050 or to hold ISO 14001 regardless of contractual scope. [S7] [S18]

Energy efficiency, scrap avoidance, lower transport intensity, responsible materials and process innovation can serve both industrial and climate aims. Progress should be measured with a clear emissions boundary (own operations, purchased materials or transported products) and tied to actual supplier operating changes, without counting an internal Safran plant decarbonization project as a verified supplier result.
Supplier Financing & Commercial Terms

Safran’s supplier-relations commitments include development support mechanisms involving finance, innovation and international growth, but the public purchasing documents examined do not establish a standardized, universally available Safran reverse-factoring or 100%-invoice early-payment scheme. Such access, if offered in an individual business unit, must be confirmed from the applicable agreement. Group purchasing conditions also differ by country, product and business. [S6] [S8]

For transactions governed by ordinary French commercial payment law, Code de commerce Article L441-10 sets a general default of 30 days absent agreement, with agreed terms generally capped at 60 days after invoice or, by explicit contractual derogation, 45 days end-of-month. These are legal maxima/structures subject to the law’s exceptions, not proof that Safran actually pays every supplier at one fixed 60-day or 45-day term. Warranty, development funding, tooling ownership, penalties and intellectual property obligations should be drawn from the signed purchasing conditions. [S19] [S8]
Case Studies: Supplier Improvement Initiatives

Case 1 — Safran and Log-hub logistics optimization. Log-hub reports that a co-construction exercise mapped more than 2,000 supplier and customer locations/flows, optimized cross-dock positions and reduced vehicle mileage by up to 60% and transport CO₂ metrics by approximately 30% in the project’s scope. The partnership received a 2025 Coup de Cœur co-construction award. This is a partner-described logistics systems improvement, not evidence that 2,000 separate suppliers achieved shop-floor productivity gains. [S14]

Case 2 — Safran Additive Manufacturing Campus. The Campus delivered 15,000 parts in 2025, projected 18,000 in 2026 and expanded internal production/operator competence. The described trainer and designer populations were Safran personnel; the cited publication does not substantiate a separate claim of hundreds of external supplier engineers trained or a particular supplier-produced safety-critical titanium helicopter bracket. [S13]

Case 3 — supplier-facing process learning. Safran’s SAFe 6 catalogue gives suppliers access, via Safran relationship sponsors, to specific e-learning on APQP, 8D, QRQC, SPC, FOD, PPAP, product safety, SAFe and counterfeits. This is a confirmed and directly relevant knowledge-transfer mechanism. A more conclusive outcome measure would be evidence that a supplier applied the technique to new production problems and retained better process performance over time. [S11]
Metrics & KPIs (Qualitative)

Safran publishes supplier-performance systems rather than one uniform numerical supplier maturity score. Its Perfo@Suppliers tools support on-time-delivery and parts-per-million (PPM) quality reporting in some businesses, including Landing Systems and Electrical & Power. The SAFe requirements and supplier relationship roles support review of quality defects, delivery adherence, industrialization and corrective actions. Frequencies, targets and maturity gates depend on the purchaser and contract; no single Group-wide quarterly scorecard or threshold was established by the cited documents. [S8] [S12]

Relevant operating indicators are: on-time delivery against agreed dates; part conformity and first-pass yield; defect PPM where meaningful; responsiveness to corrective actions; first-article/APQP qualification milestones; demonstrated good-unit output at the constrained process; capacity and supplier/sub-tier continuity; and the recurrence of previous problems. For capability development, changes in methods, qualified personnel and sustained output are stronger signals than simple audit closure.
Future Readiness: Digitalization, Electrification and SAF

Safran’s purchasing portals provide distinct functions. DigiBuy supports RFPs and contracts across Safran Group companies. Perfo@Suppliers reports delivery and quality metrics for specified businesses; e-Fournisseur supports supply/order and technical-document exchanges; e-Qualité supports deviation and nonconformity handling; supplier access and use vary by entity. PARAGON registration materials exist, but it is misleading to represent PARAGON or Ivalua as a single mandatory real-time ERP/MES system for every Safran supplier. [S8] [S12]

Safran and GE’s CFM RISE program is developing open-fan, compact-core and hybrid-electric technologies and exploring future compatibility with alternative energy. CFM reported further design and technology-testing milestones in July 2026. These are future propulsion industrialization and readiness demands, not existing certifications proving that current LEAP fleets are approved for 100% SAF in everyday service. [S20]

Safran’s future supplier capability needs therefore include design-for-manufacture skills, digital configuration management, qualified advanced materials and processes, capacity for new engine and aircraft platforms, and traceable climate and materials data. The exact implementation should be tailored to approved work scope rather than imposed as a universal Industry 4.0 or additive-manufacturing requirement.
Supplier Capability Development Lifecycle

Representative pathway, subject to applicable Safran supplier requirements: (1) Identify a sourcing need and register supplier contact through an authorized procurement channel. (2) Evaluate the product-specific technical scope, sector, supplier type and SAFe compliance matrix. (3) Confirm appropriate QMS, process, test and sub-tier qualifications. (4) Carry out any required industrialization, technical trials, first-article review or pilot production. (5) Begin authorized deliveries and monitor quality, rate, capacity and schedule. (6) Use joint root-cause problem solving, APQP, process improvement and training where gaps emerge. (7) Verify sustained operating performance under supplier ownership and review eligibility for expanded work. The precise gates vary by Safran business and purchasing agreement. [S8] [S9] [S10] [S11]

RTX (Raytheon Technologies) — Supplier Capability Building Practices
Executive Summary

RTX Corporation operates three principal aerospace and defense businesses: Pratt & Whitney, Collins Aerospace and Raytheon. Its supplier capability system combines business-specific quality requirements, purchasing and onboarding controls, shared expectations for ethical conduct, structured corrective action, technical education, advanced manufacturing partnerships and targeted capacity investments. The supplier website explicitly directs vendors to business-specific documentation; it does not describe one identical supplier-development program for all three businesses. [S1] [S3] [S5] [S6] [S7]

Pratt & Whitney’s current ASQR-01 Revision 15 (May 2025) and associated production part approval and process-control requirements provide a detailed assurance framework. Collins Aerospace’s supplier quality standard is separate, and Raytheon quality notes and customer contract clauses apply to Raytheon scope. Raytheon UK publishes a particularly clear three-stage supplier assessment and Approved Vendor List (AVL) process, but its JOSCAR and RESA steps are specific to that operation. [S2] [S3] [S4]

The clearest supplier capability-building evidence goes beyond compliance requirements: Pratt & Whitney has offered technical courses on APQP/PPAP, PFMEA, statistical process control, 8D and related tools; Raytheon UK’s SpaRk program offers SMEs financing, mentorship and engineering access; and Pratt & Whitney co-developed an additive-manufacturing solution for an F135 turbine-exhaust-case component with a supplier. RTX’s CORE and connected-factory initiatives demonstrate internal operational improvement, not proof of universal adoption by outside suppliers. [S2] [S8] [S11] [S12] [S13] [S14]

RTX also uses long-term government demand commitments, capacity expansion, business-specific supplier management and defense cybersecurity to manage risk. The 2026 Raytheon missile-production framework agreements, some extending up to seven years, are agreements with the U.S. government and must not be confused with evidence that every sub-tier supplier has itself received a seven-year contract. A separate DARPA-funded Raytheon BBN resilience-modeling project concerns development of a research simulator rather than a fully deployed RTX-wide supplier early-warning system. [S15] [S16] [S17] [S18]
Supplier Development Programs

Small-business and innovation support. Raytheon UK’s SpaRk (Small to medium-sized enterprise Partnerships Advancing Raytheon Knowledge) was established in 2015 to support technology ideas from UK SMEs and academic institutions. The program offers financial assistance, mentoring, engineering expertise and access to partners, customers and markets. Raytheon UK also uses supplier outreach, trade-association events and targeted identification of new small firms. SpaRk is a documented UK program, not an RTX global supplier funding entitlement. [S2] [S23]

Operating-system improvement. RTX defines CORE (Customer Oriented Results and Excellence) as its operating system for execution, continuous improvement and product quality. Published company manufacturing cases describe CORE events to reduce process waste and improve cycle times and defects. Supplier capability projects can draw on the same structured problem-solving concepts, but RTX does not publicly establish a uniform requirement for every supplier to install CORE, obtain Lean/Six Sigma certification or participate in a centrally organized supplier academy. [S11] [S13]

Technical collaboration. Pratt & Whitney uses its Additive Manufacturing Process and Capability Center to mature additive techniques for production and sustainment, and has worked with an external supplier to print and finish an F135 turbine-exhaust-case trailing-edge component. Separately, it redesigned the TJ150 engine using unitization, reducing more than 50 components to a handful. These are distinct engineering examples. Potential cost savings from the F135 approach are not booked, verified realized savings across the supply network. [S14]

Industrial diversification. Pratt & Whitney’s September 2026 production-license agreement with Hermeus creates an additional authorized source for the F100-PW-229 engine under Pratt & Whitney quality and site-activation standards. This is evidence of controlled manufacturing-capability expansion, with future production dependent on industrialization and approved readiness; it is not a completed, quantified supplier-yield improvement. [S25]
Supplier Selection and Onboarding

RTX offers enterprise potential-supplier registration and directs candidates to the relevant business for assessment, purchase terms and qualification. Pratt & Whitney’s supplier pages explain that portals vary across strategic business units, legacy companies, transaction types and purchased products. Vendor registration, secure portal access and demonstrated technical/quality approval therefore represent different stages rather than interchangeable statuses. [S1] [S6] [S23]

Raytheon UK’s published AVL process has three stages. Stage 1 covers product/service fit, need identification, financial/reputational/capability due diligence, JOSCAR assessment, site visit where appropriate and an NDA. Stage 2 proceeds when a potential award becomes likely and includes a supplier questionnaire, enhanced due diligence, JOSCAR checks, site assessment and RESA when applicable. Stage 3 consists of ongoing due diligence, specified JOSCAR registration within 60 days for selected suppliers, repeat RESA or site visits by program and quarterly scorecards where required. The 60-day timing applies to selected Raytheon UK suppliers; it is not an RTX-wide onboarding SLA. [S2]

Quality qualification is governed by the purchase order, business-specific supplier documents and nature of the work. ASQR-01 Rev 15 applies to Pratt & Whitney supplier quality systems, while Collins Aerospace uses COL-ASQR-PRO-0003 Rev 06. The RTX requirements hub also identifies ASQR-02 for relevant maintenance organizations, production-part approval requirements, sampling controls, qualified-distributor lists and Raytheon’s separate quality notes. Industry AS9100/AS9110/AS9120 and Nadcap obligations must be determined for each production, distribution, maintenance and special-process scope, rather than assumed for every RTX vendor. [S3] [S4] [S5] [S6] [S7]

The path to repeatable production capability may involve document and configuration control, sub-tier identification, acceptance authorities, source inspections, product-process qualification, first-article inspection, approved special processes, PPAP and timely corrective action. The required sequence and approvals must follow the relevant RTX buyer and contract, not a generalized description of Raytheon UK or Pratt & Whitney alone. [S3] [S4] [S10]
Technical Capability Building

Advanced quality planning. Pratt & Whitney ASQR-01 and ASQR-09.2 specify supplier quality and production-part approval requirements. Its published PPAP toolbox includes FMEA, gage repeatability/reproducibility, capability calculations and risk/control templates. The application and latest revision of these tools are defined by contract and supplier classification, but they create a concrete basis for technical improvement in process flow, prevention controls, process capability and acceptance evidence. [S3] [S4] [S10]

Defect prevention and root-cause problem solving. ASQR-01 Rev 15 defines a Quality Clinic System integrating trained personnel, standard work, measurement, visual management, metrics and management support to address customer escapes, supplier escapes and internal process defects. RTX supplier-quality roles reference root-cause support, corrective-action verification and supplier visits. These indicate a real operating mechanism; no published source proves that all underperforming suppliers are enrolled in clinics at a fixed threshold or frequency. [S4] [S22]

Manufacturing and materials. Pratt & Whitney’s additive activities can simplify process routes and reduce lead-time exposure when the approved design and quality plan permit. HMI Metal Powders, an RTX-owned business, supplies engineered metal powders for aerospace uses; this exemplifies industrial integration, not merely coaching of an independent outside supplier. Technical readiness of advanced composites, metal components, electronics and special processes should be established through qualification and validated production controls. [S14] [S24]

Digital and Industry 4.0. RTX describes a corporate program to connect machinery at selected internal factories, consolidate operating data and use AI/analytics to diagnose constraints, improve yield and reduce rework. A 2026 company report described prioritizing about 60 RTX factories representing more than three quarters of production. This supports a strong internal digital-manufacturing capability, but not a conclusion that suppliers universally transmit live machine data to RTX or receive predictive maintenance alerts from a common supplier platform. [S12] [S13]
Training and Knowledge Transfer

Supplier-facing learning is publicly documented at Pratt & Whitney. Its Supplier Quality Communications offered online instruction in 8D root-cause analysis, PFMEA, process flow/control plans, process control including SPC, measurement-system analysis and PPAP-related techniques to Pratt & Whitney suppliers in the specified 2023–2024 sessions. The notices describe enrollment by invitation or supplier-quality contacts, with online session links and supporting AESQ materials. They establish actual course availability at those dates rather than permanent, unlimited free access for all RTX suppliers. [S8] [S9]

Continued implementation support is also documented. A January 2026 Pratt & Whitney communication addressed the transition to ASQR-01 Rev 15 and AS13100A, announced a general compliance deadline of March 31, 2026 and directed suppliers to AESQ training and gap-assessment resources. Pratt & Whitney Poland’s supplier bulletins also provide training notices, first-article guidance, escape alerts and part-marking instruction. These materials show a sustained technical communication channel, while exact business applicability follows the notice. [S9] [S26]

Training becomes supplier capability when the supplier independently applies the learning. A suitable intervention would select an actual repeat defect or bottleneck, document baseline yield/delivery conditions, train the supplier’s process owners, implement controlled PFMEA/control-plan changes and verify production performance over time. Supplier-led use of the method on a second problem would provide stronger evidence than participation in one webcast. This is a recommended closure test, not a disclosed RTX-wide corporate requirement.
Supplier Performance Management and Continuous Improvement

RTX publicly emphasizes supplier quality, delivery, cost and customer satisfaction. Pratt & Whitney states that supplier performance is integral to building a reliable supply chain, while Collins Aerospace describes its high standards for quality, delivery and cost. The Raytheon UK process provides a concrete, business-specific example of quarterly supplier scorecards when required; no common enterprise-wide cadence or public numeric RTX supplier-development maturity score was established from these sources. [S2] [S5] [S22]

Relevant performance measures include on-time delivery against agreed dates, purchase-order commitment stability, escape incidence, defects/PPM where appropriate, first-pass yield at the critical operation, first-article/PPAP readiness, corrective-action timeliness, and demonstrated output at the constraining process. ASQR and Quality Clinic methods support evidence-based root cause and corrective action. Benchmarks, red/amber/green thresholds and review intervals are program specific; they should not be presented as published companywide thresholds. [S3] [S4] [S10]

The supplier-development loop should connect: operating problem → verified root cause → qualified corrective action → trained supplier ownership → repeatable production improvement → observation of sustainment. This complements RTX’s internal CORE methodology without conflating internal factory metrics with supplier performance. [S11] [S22]
Supply-Chain Resilience and Risk Management

Long-term production signals. Raytheon and the U.S. government entered five framework agreements in February 2026 to expand production of Tomahawk, AMRAAM and Standard Missile variants, with terms extending up to seven years. Subsequent announced awards included a seven-year Tomahawk production contract in August 2026. Longer government demand visibility supports planning and investment in the industrial base and can benefit small suppliers, but it does not mean every RTX sub-tier receives an equivalent fixed-volume purchase guarantee. [S15] [S16]

Diversification and local industrial capability. Raytheon UK encourages buyers to look for alternative sources outside its existing AVL, including SMEs offering specialized engineering and electronics. Pratt & Whitney’s F100 licensing arrangement with Hermeus is another instance of creating a qualified production source. Regionalization and multi-sourcing can reduce exposure only when the alternate producer meets configuration, export-control, quality and rate requirements. [S2] [S25]

Supply-chain stress modeling. RTX’s Raytheon BBN won an $8 million DARPA Resilient Supply-and-Demand Networks contract in December 2023. The announced research would use historical, survey, economic and behavioral data to simulate shocks and possible countermeasures for military supply networks, including essential materials. This confirms a funded R&D effort, not that the tool was already operational across RTX’s commercial and defense purchasing functions or had generated quantified avoidance of disruptions. [S17]

Cybersecurity. RTX’s supplier cybersecurity website addresses covered defense information, controlled unclassified information and supplier obligations under NIST SP 800-171 and DFARS clauses where invoked. It also reported the July 2026 temporary suspension of CMMC Phase II implementation while Phase I Level 1/2 self-assessment obligations continued. The precise requirements depend on contract clauses and subsequent amendments; an RTX supplier outside covered defense activities does not automatically inherit all CMMC obligations. [S18]
Sustainability and Compliance

RTX’s supplier code of conduct, ethics program and standard purchase terms emphasize lawful conduct, anti-corruption, environmental stewardship, labor and human-rights expectations, training and timely reporting of misconduct. RTX’s 2025 supplier purchasing terms state that a supplier must adopt policies meeting the company’s minimum code-of-conduct principles. The applicability of any specific labor, environmental, materials, security or reporting provision follows the relevant purchase order, jurisdiction and flowdown. [S1] [S20] [S21]

Trade and cybersecurity risk. ITAR, EAR, FAR/DFARS, export-data access restrictions, cybersecurity rules and foreign ownership/control assessments apply according to contract, controlled technology and defense program. RTX’s June 2026 notice described a proposed DFARS rule addressing foreign ownership information, not a final blanket requirement for every global supplier. Raytheon UK lists potential readiness items such as JOSCAR, Cyber Essentials, customer terms and net-zero strategies, with expectations determined by sector and individual requirements. [S2] [S18] [S19]

RTX publishes supplier energy- and water-management resources and corporate responsibility information, including its conflict-minerals due diligence and supplier expectations. These demonstrate governance and supplier guidance but do not, by themselves, confirm a compulsory ISO 14001 certificate or one shared carbon-reduction deadline for every RTX supplier. [S1] [S21]
Case Studies and Documented Outcomes

Case 1 — Pratt & Whitney F135 additive-manufacturing supplier collaboration. Pratt & Whitney reports working with an outside supplier since 2018 to 3D-print the trailing-edge (TE) box for the F135 turbine exhaust case. By printing and finishing a more integrated component in-house, the supplier can reduce outsourced casting/machining steps and lead-time complexity. RTX described potential savings on casting and molds approaching $1 billion; the article does not claim $1 billion of realized, audited savings or a single conversion of more than 50 F135 parts into one. [S14]

Case 2 — TJ150 engine design simplification. Pratt & Whitney’s GATORWORKS team used additive unitization in its TJ150 engine to reduce a design that previously had over 50 parts to a handful and completed design-to-test in roughly eight months. This is primarily an internal engine development example and should not be counted as a separate measured achievement of independent supplier learning. [S14]

Case 3 — Raytheon UK SpaRk. The SME partnership program has provided financial support, mentoring and access to expertise and customer networks since 2015. Raytheon UK documents real technology partnerships, including work with academic institutions. The information demonstrates an access-and-capability support mechanism; it does not provide one consistent public denominator of participating firms or a validated average productivity benefit. [S2]

Case 4 — Raytheon BBN resilience research. An $8 million DARPA-funded simulator initiative seeks to quantify supply-network vulnerabilities and stress responses through economic and decision models. The announced scope is documented, but an expected future software capability should not be written up as a successful deployed early-warning platform without subsequent results. [S17]

Case 5 — New F100 production source. RTX and Hermeus entered a September 2026 engine-production licensing agreement that authorizes Hermeus to manufacture the F100-PW-229 to Pratt & Whitney standards. The new license broadens potential U.S. production capability; it is not an already demonstrated rate increase at a mature supplier. [S25]
Gaps and Recommendations

Broaden supplier skills beyond compliance. Extend quality-focused instruction in 8D, APQP, SPC, measurement systems and PPAP with practical courses on constraint removal, equipment reliability, workforce cross-training and digital industrialization; prioritize suppliers whose performance limitations materially affect rate or safety.

Make capability transfer visible. Require major interventions to record initial performance, applied process changes, quality/configuration approvals, supplier process-owner training, 30/90/180-day sustainment and a second supplier-led improvement. These are proposed criteria, not disclosed enterprise-wide RTX mandatory gates.

Develop a consistent supplier-risk view. Combine contractual delivery and quality data with sub-tier dependencies, sole-source exposure, alternate qualification, financial stability, cybersecurity, and time-to-recover. Use the results to guide sourcing and engineering interventions, not a single universal maturity ranking.

Scale targeted SME and technical partnerships. Draw on Raytheon UK SpaRk and Pratt & Whitney co-development cases to design commodity- and geography-specific partnership packages. Maintain export and aerospace qualification rigor before expanding new-source production.

Link demand commitments to qualified capacity. Government long-term missile demand supports investment in tools, workforce and supply chains, but suppliers should demonstrate approved equipment, process yields and rate-readiness before additional contracted output is treated as secured.
Supplier Capability Development Lifecycle

Representative pathway: (1) Register the potential supplier and confirm the relevant RTX business and work scope. (2) Assess commercial, technical, ethical, regulatory and quality readiness using applicable business requirements; Raytheon UK may use JOSCAR and RESA. (3) Establish authorized procurement, portal access and controlled technical-data exchange. (4) Verify required QMS, process, first-article and PPAP/qualification evidence. (5) Begin authorized production and monitor delivery, quality and capacity. (6) When an issue arises, verify its root cause and apply corrective action or a joint technical development intervention. (7) Confirm reliable production under supplier ownership, sustainment of process controls and any need for expanded sourcing. The sequence is a recommended synthesis; actual approval and monitoring rules depend on business unit, part and contract. [S1] [S2] [S3] [S4] [S6]

Maturity anchor
1 — Ad hoc
Mostly reactive or dependent on individual effort; no defined, repeatable approach.
2 — Emerging
A practice or pilot exists, but only in limited areas; ownership, cadence, or follow-through is inconsistent.
3 — Defined
Documented processes, roles, or standards exist, and there’s evidence they’re used; integration or follow-through remains uneven.
4 — Routine
The practice is used regularly in the relevant scope, with clear ownership and recurring follow-up. It need not be deployed company-wide.
5 — Leading and sustained

Evidence shows the practice improves outcomes over time and that learning is built into how it operates. Replication strengthens the case but isn’t required; evidence can be qualitative when that fits the criterion.
NE — Not enough evidence
Public evidence is insufficient for a defensible rating. Exclude from averages and show coverage; NE does not mean the capability is absent.

Calculation: average rated criteria within each pillar, excluding NE; overall = (A + B + C) ÷ 3 using unrounded pillar means. Do not calculate overall if a pillar is entirely NE. B does not receive extra weight because it has seven criteria. A 4 does not require published outcome metrics; a 5 needs improvement over time and embedded learning, not company-wide replication or proof that buyer support ended.
The shared 16-criterion framework

Domain descriptions preserve the problem-statement wording. Assess the supplier-facing process relevant to each criterion; internal fab performance, training counts and awards alone are not evidence of all capabilities.
A · Future Business Readiness
B · Supplier Production-System Capability
C · Resilience and Continuity Capability
Preparing suppliers for future business needs such as ramp-up, localization, future demand, capacity confidence, or increased product and process complexity.
A1 Future demand readiness: Anticipates future changes in volume, product mix, and demand.
A2 Capacity confidence: Demonstrates sufficient and reliable capacity to meet future requirements.
A3 Ramp-up readiness: Increases production without compromising quality, cost, or delivery.
A4 Localization readiness: Establishes or transfers supply and production capabilities to required regions.
A5 Product and process complexity readiness: Manages increasingly complex products, technologies, and production processes.

Strengthening the supplier’s ability to deliver stable, scalable, and repeatable operational performance. This may include production-system maturity, operational excellence, process stability, yield, flow, constraints, throughput, lead time, and operating routines.
B1 Production-system maturity: Uses a structured, standardized, and repeatable system to manage production.
B2 Operational excellence: Continuously improves quality, cost, delivery, and productivity.
B3 Process stability and yield: Maintains consistent processes while reducing variation, defects, rework, and waste.
B4 Flow and constraint management: Improves material and production flow while identifying and resolving bottlenecks.
B5 Throughput and lead-time management: Increases sustainable output and reduces end-to-end production time.
B6 Operating routines: Uses standard work, daily management, performance reviews, and clear escalation processes.
B7 Capability building and sustainment: Uses coaching, structured problem-solving, verification, and closed-loop learning to build and sustain supplier improvements.
Improving the supplier’s ability to sustain supply under disruption, dependency exposure, volatility, or changing business conditions.
C1 Disruption preparedness and response: Anticipates disruptions and responds quickly to protect supply.
C2 Dependency visibility and exposure management: Identifies critical suppliers, materials, sites, and concentration risks.
C3 Demand and supply volatility management: Adjusts capacity and supply plans as demand or availability changes.
C4 Adaptability to changing business conditions: Sustains supply through tariffs, M&A, downsizing, and other structural changes.

Evidence approach: retain documented management practices, then separately examine stronger development cases through need → supplier gap → contribution → implemented change → verification → retained learning. Confidence and case scope remain separate from the numeric maturity score.

Semiconductor Benchmark: TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company)

Scoring calibration note — 16 October 2026: the shared 1–5 anchors govern this assessment. A 4 requires routine use, ownership and follow-up; a 5 requires improvement over time with embedded learning. Earlier suggestions below for independent performance after coaching ends are stronger follow-up tests, not additional mandatory scoring rules. The linked overview contains the current comparative scorecard.

Evidence reviewed: 15 October 2026. Scope: TSMC’s development and management of materials, parts, chemical and facility suppliers, mainly in Taiwan. Scores describe the evidenced supplier practice and its date/scope, not TSMC’s own fab performance. [R1–R9]
1. Executive assessment

TSMC has stronger supplier capability-building evidence than the previous draft showed. Its best cases identify a supplier gap, buyer engineering or expert support, implemented supplier changes, and measured outcomes. The most transferable mechanisms are technical localization, factory maintenance routines, and targeted hazard prevention. No reviewed case proves a 5 across the full supplier base.

Domain A · Future business readiness: 3.40 (5/5 rated). A1–A3 = 3; A4–A5 = 4. Strongest evidence is completed local materials/parts development, while future-demand translation, reliable capacity and sustained ramp performance are less visible.

Domain B · Supplier production-system capability: 4.14 (7/7 rated). B2/B3 = 5; B1/B5/B6/B7 = 4; B4 = 3. The leading scores reflect improvement over time and learning embedded in the supported suppliers' maintenance and anomaly-resolution processes.

Domain C · Resilience and continuity: 3.25 (4/4 rated). C1 = 4; C2–C4 = 3. Supplier hazard-prevention development is well evidenced. Buyer risk visibility, multi-source design and material-life extension need supplier-owned decisions or tested adaptation to reach a higher level.

Directional overall = 3.60/5, the equal-weight mean of unrounded domain means: A 3.40, B 4.14, C 3.25. Coverage is 16/16. Evidence reviewed through 17 October 2026. See Semiconductor Overview for the ranked comparison and criterion rationale; ratings retain their stated supplier and programme scope.
2. How TSMC selects suppliers and delivers support

S.H.A.R.P. began in 2020 for key/high-risk suppliers. TSMC’s internal experts and a third party inspect supply risk, quality, safety and management issues, meet supplier management to define solutions, and follow improvement requests monthly. By January 2021, 36 key suppliers had been assessed and 1,213 requests were being tracked. Those are requests, not verified completed improvements. Later reports describe ongoing audits, plans and guidance. This is a recurring selection and follow-up mechanism; an audit by itself is not evidence of a changed supplier capability. [R5]

The 2024 Parts Localization and Innovation Program uses a committee, supplier proposals, equipment support and TSMC engineering guidance across five technical areas. TSMC also has earlier raw-material guidance and a new-factory design program. Support intensity therefore varies by technical need: design/simulation, factory-process coaching, production validation, or expert safety counseling. Published sources do not show a universal rule converting supplier criticality into engineer hours or graduation criteria. [R1, R2, R4, R6]
3. Domain A | Future business readiness
A.1 Local parts technology and development capacity

Need and supplier gap. Advanced processes require domestic parts with tighter materials, geometry and durability specifications. In 2024 TSMC launched a localization program covering metal machining, brittle materials, ceramic sintering, coatings and O-rings. Supplier proposals go to a Parts Localization Committee. [R1]

Intervention and result. TSMC contributes equipment subsidies, materials analysis, design simulation, parameter specifications, machining-path optimization and production validation. As of February 2026, 12 suppliers had produced 22 improvement solutions. TSMC reports a 50% reduction in parts validation/development lead time and more than NT$2 billion in annual output benefit. The benefit is a program-level figure, not a per-supplier profit or capacity result. [R1]
A.2 Lithography-material localization

A 2019 supplier raw-material technology guidance program combined TSMC materials-management and nano-patterning specialists. They supported technology development, quality analysis, calibration, sample verification, factory layout, tank optimization and expansion planning. TSMC reports a local production line, a 50% reduction in line setup and verification time, and over NT$1.5 billion annual output value. The source does not identify a specific supplier or post-support independent learning. [R2]
A.3 Electroplating-additive line and phased validation

TSMC guided a Japanese supplier establishing a Taiwan production line for advanced-packaging additives through line design, equipment optimization, quality inspection and sample verification. Locally produced additives entered Advanced Backend Fab 2 in January 2026. TSMC reports cycle time falling from 60 to 20 days and a phased path from small to larger production volumes. Further deployment was a stated plan at publication, so it is not counted as achieved ramp capacity. [R3]

Interpretation. These are unusually concrete A4/A5 examples of buyer-supported supplier technology and localization. A1–A3 are defined, used practices or scoped validation, but the public record does not show recurring joint demand planning, measured future-volume attainment or completed ramp stabilization across cases. Neither overseas foundry investment nor TSMC’s own technology roadmap is counted as supplier capability building.
4. Domain B | Supplier production-system capability
B.1 Five-supplier maintenance and factory-management improvement

TSMC selected suppliers from on-site audits of maintenance quality, repair processes and abnormalities. It helped establish maintenance/repair procedures, regular improvement tracking and a management process from anomaly to resolution. Across five suppliers, reported production-line anomalies fell from 513 in 2022 to 82 by August 2024 (84%); mean repair time fell from 12.3 to 5 hours. The source does not disclose denominators, attribution method or performance after TSMC steps away. [R4]

A related New Factory Construction Plan applied best-known methods, questionnaires, site interviews and audits to supplier factory designs. By August 2024, 16 supplier factories had design optimizations; examples include distributed control systems for three suppliers, filter-plan changes for seven and separated power circuits at one. These are scoped examples of supplier operating-system design, not proof that every participating factory achieved production gains. [R4]
B.2 Technical process and quality interventions

The parts program uses material analysis, simulation, critical specifications, machining route and tool selection, plus machine validation to guide suppliers through more complex work. The electroplating case adds supplier factory setup, equipment tuning, third-party testing and phased sample validation. The reported 50% development/validation lead-time reduction and 60-to-20-day cycle-time change apply to their stated case scopes; neither proves an across-network throughput trend. [R1, R3]

S.H.A.R.P. gives structured diagnosis and monthly follow-up, while the factory project demonstrates implemented procedures and lower anomaly counts. The prior draft’s claims of 145 suppliers already receiving direct consultation and 100% rectification closure are removed: 145 was a future target in a 2024 report; the accessible S.H.A.R.P. account reports 1,213 tracked requests, not their completed closure. [R4, R5]
5. Domain C | Resilience and continuity
C.1 Supplier-owned prevention skills and site improvements

A 2024 hazardous-materials site program targeted small, critical, high-risk suppliers. TSMC screened sites, investigated stored materials, assessed gaps with an external fire-protection expert and supported physical fixes. Ten suppliers had completed counseling and hardware improvements by June 2025, including fire zoning, exhaust and protective construction. This supports prevention capability in a defined scope; avoided outages and tested recovery times are not reported. [R6]

Earlier small-group fire/EHS workshops used practical exercises and tests before/after class; TSMC also increased supplier participation in emergency drills. These support learning and exercise, but the public case does not connect each trained supplier to a later site-level recovery outcome. [R7]
C.2 Exposure and volatility management

S.H.A.R.P. examines supply risk and upstream-supplier management, while Supply Online 360 records risk assessments and improvement measures and provides supplier learning resources. Its documented function is sustainability/risk management; the launch account does not establish complete raw-material-origin mapping or supplier-owned dependency maps. [R5, R9]

TSMC and 18 suppliers analyzed shorter-life raw materials through measurement, simulated use, quality checks and fab validation. TSMC reports 15 materials with usable life extended 30–50%. This is a concrete response to longer shipping times and increased usage, but it does not show how individual suppliers adapt capacity or material plans to recurring demand swings. [R8]

The Taiwan electroplating line also responds to import dependence and longer transport. Its operating introduction is a real structural adaptation, but the source describes one line and leaves later planned rollout unverified. Dual-source development is a buyer network mechanism; without a traced supplier capability gain, it should not carry a 4 or 5 under Swaroop’s elevated lens. [R3]
6. Criterion scorecard | practice first, elevated evidence second

Anchors: 1 ad hoc; 2 emerging; 3 defined and used; 4 routine with clear ownership and recurring follow-up in the stated scope; 5 sustained improvement with embedded supplier learning. NE means insufficient evidence and is excluded from a domain mean. Ratings assess reviewed evidence, not TSMC’s entire hidden capability.
A | Future business readiness — 3.40, 5/5

A1 Future demand readiness — 3. Local parts and additive projects respond to stated advanced-process/packaging needs. Supplier-specific recurring forecast-to-action review is not shown. A 4 needs owned demand/mix reviews and follow-up. [R1, R3]

A2 Capacity confidence — 3. New supplier lines and factory plans establish production preparation. Validated reliable output at required future volume is not disclosed. A 4 needs capacity tests tied to demand and repeated gap closure. [R2–R4]

A3 Ramp-up readiness — 3. Additives undergo third-party testing and phased small-to-large fab validation; wider deployment was planned. A 4 needs verified supplier ramp milestones, controlled output and recurring bottleneck review. [R3]

A4 Localization readiness — 4. Multi-year local-material work, the 12-supplier parts program and an operating additive line show buyer engineering, supplier implementation and measured benefits. A 5 needs retained local supplier learning across later projects and independently sustained results. [R1–R3]

A5 Product/process complexity readiness — 4. Materials analysis, simulation, specifications and real-machine testing convert advanced-process requirements into supplier work. A 5 needs repeated supplier-led resolution of later complexity challenges. [R1, R2]
B | Supplier production-system capability — 4.14, 7/7

B1 Production-system maturity — 4. Maintenance standards, anomaly-resolution procedures and new-factory design guidance were implemented in scoped supplier groups. A 5 needs connected routines sustained across later cycles without buyer coaching. [R4]

B2 Operational excellence — 5. Multi-year improvement and learning embedded in operating/design standards meet the agreed anchor within the supported scope. Buyer withdrawal and broader replication are not prerequisites. [R4]

B3 Process stability and yield — 5 — Leading and sustained. The five-supplier maintenance programme connects diagnosis, implemented repair procedures and recurring progress reviews with fewer production-line abnormalities between 2022 and August 2024. Supplier procedures cover an abnormality from occurrence to resolution, while audit experience informs design standards. This supports improvement over time with learning embedded in process-stability management. Scope: supplier facility reliability; reported counts have no published exposure denominator. [R4]

B4 Flow and constraint management — 3. Machining-path and tool-selection guidance is defined and used; a supplier bottleneck baseline and repeated end-to-end flow review are not shown. A 4 needs owned constraint removal and follow-up. [R1]

B5 Throughput and lead-time management — 4. Scoped additive cycle time fell 60 to 20 days; the parts program reports 50% shorter validation/development time. These are different measures. A 5 needs sustained supplier output/lead-time improvements across later cycles. [R1, R3]

B6 Operating routines — 4. The five-supplier case establishes maintenance/repair processes and recurring improvement tracking, supported by S.H.A.R.P.’s monthly follow-up. A 5 needs later supplier-owned routine effectiveness. [R4, R5]

B7 Capability building and sustainment — 4. Technical coaching, supplier process designs and self-management routines yielded implemented gains. A 5 needs evidence supplier staff maintain gains and independently solve new problems after support ends. [R1, R4]
C | Resilience and continuity — 3.25, 4/4

C1 Disruption preparedness and response — 4. Targeted fire-risk counseling produced site fixes at ten suppliers, with practical training and drills in the wider program. A 5 needs supplier-owned lessons and demonstrated prevention/recovery improvement over time. [R6, R7]

C2 Dependency visibility and exposure management — 3. Risk audits and the portal collect/track supplier risk information; supplier-owned sub-tier mapping and mitigation follow-through are not established. A 4 needs suppliers using maintained maps to close dependencies. [R5, R9]

C3 Demand/supply volatility management — 3. Material-life extension and local line establishment provide defined responses to longer shipping and demand growth. A 4 needs recurring supplier planning scenarios and verified flexibility. [R3, R8]

C4 Adaptability to changing business conditions — 3. The additive line and local parts program demonstrate responses to import reliance and changing technical needs. A 4 needs a recurring supplier-owned transition process and verified results across changes. [R1, R3]
7. Transferability and evidence limits

For Siemens Energy, the most relevant design ideas are a supplier proposal and engineering-support pathway for complex parts; standard maintenance and anomaly-resolution routines at selected suppliers; and expert-supported prevention at hazardous sites. These are analogies for testing, not disclosed Siemens practices. Selection rules, technical work packages, outcome measures and handover should be specified before adaptation.

Do not equate TSMC’s own fab quality, automotive qualifications, overseas joint ventures or a digital portal with improvement inside a supplier. The same case can inform distinct criteria but does not become independent replication. Public reporting is mainly TSMC-authored, so confidence in reported outcomes is moderate; post-support independence and measurement methods are the most material gaps.
