Long-lived energy assets require reliable service parts, repair, and continuity of supply

ASML's 2025 strategy discussion also highlights the role of supplier proximity in accelerating engineering collaboration and the increasing use of regional sourcing and repair for mature products and service operations. [3]

Benchmarking implication: The most useful question is not simply whether ASML has good suppliers. It is how ASML makes technically specialized suppliers ready for future demand, detects emerging constraints, coordinates improvement, and verifies that the resulting capabilities are sustainable.
3. Supplier Development Organization and Operating Model
3.1 Strategic Sourcing & Procurement
ASML's Strategic Sourcing & Procurement organization is central to supplier management.
The 2025 Annual Report identifies several recurring channels for supplier engagement:
Annual Suppliers' Day.
Annual Supplier Collaboration Day.
Direct interactions through supplier account teams.
Supplier audits.
Supplier collaboration engagements.
Site visits.
Supplier newsletters.
Responsible Business Alliance self-assessment questionnaires.
Sustainability knowledge sessions.
Conflict-minerals due diligence and follow-up. [1]

A published ASML sourcing account-leader role describes responsibility for strategic, tactical, and operational goals at suppliers, including global QLTCS accountability and coordination among commercial, quality, logistics, and new-product-introduction stakeholders. This supports the interpretation that supplier performance is managed through cross-functional account ownership rather than purchasing alone. [11]
3.2 Supplier Collaboration Program
ASML introduced its Supplier Collaboration Program in 2022.

Under this program, experienced ASML personnel work at supplier locations, typically for four to six months. The stated objectives include understanding suppliers' operating practices, aligning technology and production roadmaps, identifying dependencies, and determining which suppliers have the capacity to grow alongside ASML. [2]
This is more substantial than a periodic audit because it creates prolonged contact between OEM personnel and supplier operations.

Nevertheless, the published description does not establish that every engagement includes production-line redesign, lean coaching, statistical process-control implementation, or measurable yield improvement. The documented mechanism is embedded collaboration and capability alignment; the exact shop-floor interventions remain largely undisclosed.
3.3 Supplier onboarding and transfer teams
ASML has established transfer teams to manage the integration of new suppliers.

The company explains that new suppliers must understand its ways of working, rapid engineering iterations, quality expectations, and delivery requirements. Transfer teams support cross-functional onboarding, while briefings and training materials communicate ASML's requirements. [2]
This mechanism is particularly relevant when introducing additional capacity, moving production between sites, or transferring complex assemblies to a new manufacturing partner.
3.4 Supplier assessments and QLTCS governance
ASML evaluates supplier performance and risk across:
Q — QualityL — LogisticsT — TechnologyC — CostS — Sustainability
Its SupplierNet portal explicitly identifies these five dimensions as expectations for suppliers. [4]

The 2025 Annual Report states that sustainability aspects are assessed through on-site QLTCS assessments and that ASML follows up on identified gaps and risks. It reports 114 audits in 2025, versus 107 in 2024. [1]
This provides strong evidence for a structured assess → identify gaps → agree actions → follow up process.
It does not, however, disclose the complete internal audit methodology, every corrective-action deadline, or the supplier-level improvements achieved after closure.
3.5 Supplier engagement and recognition
ASML uses annual supplier events to communicate priorities, reinforce long-term relationships, and recognize achievement.

Its 2025 supplier awards covered six categories: collaboration, quality, logistics, technology, cost, and sustainability. The recipients were Gigaphoton, Zollner Elektronik, Anvil Industries, TRUMPF, NTS, and Benchmark Electronics. [6]
These examples are useful indicators of the outcomes ASML values. They are not substitutes for verified supplier-development case studies.
4. Domain A — Future Business Readiness
A1. Future demand and technology planning

ASML's suppliers operate in a market characterized by substantial long-term growth potential and short-term volatility. The company expects them to prepare for steep growth while remaining flexible enough to accommodate periods of lower demand.

ASML addresses this challenge through long-term supplier relationships, communication of its business outlook, supplier account management, technology-roadmap alignment, and direct engagement with strategic partners. [1][2]

The 2025 Annual Report confirms that ASML shares its outlook and customer expectations with suppliers while encouraging them to communicate their constraints and concerns. Its annual supplier events provide additional opportunities for strategic alignment.
Supplier capability-building mechanism: Early visibility of future requirements allows suppliers to assess equipment, staffing, engineering, and investment needs before demand materializes.

Evidence limitations: The public record does not disclose detailed supplier forecasting protocols, forecast accuracy, planning horizons, capacity-commitment mechanisms, or the extent to which forecasts are integrated into suppliers' production-planning systems.
TO582 relevance: A1 — Future demand readiness.
A2. Capacity confidence and production-risk management
ASML recognizes that its growth depends on suppliers' ability to expand production capacity without undermining quality or delivery.

Its approach includes supplier selection and qualification, ongoing performance assessment, risk-based audits, supplier collaboration engagements, and direct discussion of production constraints. [1][2]

The Supplier Collaboration Program is particularly relevant because ASML personnel spend extended periods at supplier facilities. This helps ASML understand suppliers' actual production capabilities and assess whether growth would create excessive operational or commercial dependencies. [2]
Supplier capability-building mechanism: Joint identification of future capacity constraints, coupled with sustained supplier engagement and production-roadmap alignment.

Evidence limitations: Public sources do not provide supplier-specific capacity utilization, output commitments, run-at-rate results, capital-expenditure support, or quantified capacity improvements attributable to ASML intervention.
TO582 relevance: A2 — Capacity confidence.
A3. Ramp-up readiness and industrialization
ASML's production environment creates unusually demanding industrialization requirements.

Its suppliers may need to accommodate repeated design iterations, complex technical specifications, small production volumes, and stringent quality requirements. ASML explains that it often performs engineering activities in parallel that other organizations might execute sequentially. [2]
The company uses transfer teams to help new suppliers understand its operating requirements and become integrated into its supply chain.
Its Supplier Collaboration Program can also support ramp-up readiness through closer coordination of technology and production roadmaps.
Supplier capability-building mechanism: Cross-functional onboarding, knowledge transfer, engineering coordination, and prolonged supplier-site collaboration.
Evidence limitations: Public sources do not provide a complete industrialization-gate framework, standardized production-readiness assessment, or supplier-level ramp-up curves.
TO582 relevance: A3 — Ramp-up readiness.
A4. Localization and regional capability development
ASML has developed regional repair capabilities to support its globally distributed customer base.

Its 2023 supply-chain article identified repair centers in the Netherlands, United States, Taiwan, South Korea, and China. The company explained that these facilities work with local material suppliers and specialized repair partners. [2]
This approach reduces the need to send every component back to the Netherlands, potentially shortening repair turnaround times and reducing transportation requirements.
ASML's 2025 strategy discussion also identifies localized sourcing for service operations and increased sourcing from lower-cost geographies for mature product lines. [3]
The NTS supplier example provides a named illustration of cross-regional manufacturing transfer involving operations in the Netherlands and Singapore. [7]
Supplier capability-building mechanism: Development of regional production and repair ecosystems, supplier onboarding, and transfer of complex manufacturing activities between locations.

Evidence limitations: The 2023 target for 10% of field repairs to be performed locally by 2025 was a stated ambition; the source does not establish that the target was achieved. Public documentation also does not identify every supplier involved or quantify the impact on regional delivery performance.
TO582 relevance: A4 — Localization readiness.
A5. Product and process complexity readiness
ASML depends on external partners capable of developing and manufacturing components at the limits of precision engineering.

ZEISS supplies critical optical systems, while TRUMPF is a key technology partner for EUV laser systems. ASML's public materials describe close collaboration with such partners and the use of parallel engineering to accelerate development. [2][3][8][15]
The relationship is not simply transactional. Supplier technology development and ASML system architecture must advance together.
ASML's 2025 strategy discussion describes joint research and development, advanced quality-management approaches, and data-driven process improvements across its ecosystem. [3]

Supplier capability-building mechanism: Early engineering involvement, joint technology development, integration of design and manufacturing requirements, and long-term technology-roadmap coordination.

Evidence limitations: Co-development is not automatically equivalent to supplier production-system development. Public evidence rarely identifies the precise manufacturing competencies transferred from ASML to a supplier or quantifies improvements in the supplier's factory performance.
TO582 relevance: A5 — Product and process complexity readiness.
5. Domain B — Supplier Production-System Capability
B1. Structured supplier assessments and production-system evaluation
ASML maintains formal supplier-assessment processes spanning quality, logistics, technology, cost, and sustainability.
Its 2025 Annual Report confirms the use of supplier audits, on-site assessments, supplier engagement projects, and follow-up on identified gaps. [1]
The report discloses 114 audits during 2025, compared with 107 during 2024, in its responsible-supply-chain discussion.
This is strong evidence that assessments are a recurring management process rather than an occasional reaction to supplier problems.
ASML also evaluates suppliers against the Responsible Business Alliance Code of Conduct and uses self-assessment questionnaires to identify sustainability and human-rights risks. [1][5]
Supplier capability-building mechanism: Structured assessment identifies weaknesses that can be addressed through supplier improvement plans and collaboration.

Evidence limitations: An audit establishes visibility and accountability, but not necessarily capability transfer. Public sources do not disclose a complete production-system maturity model or the proportion of audits resulting in verified operational improvement.
TO582 relevance: B1 — Production-system maturity.
B2. Operational excellence and gap closure
ASML's supplier-management model includes follow-up on identified performance gaps.

The annual report explicitly states that gaps and risks identified through QLTCS assessments are followed up. For suppliers with high-risk RBA findings, ASML seeks clarification, evaluates the risks, and agrees action plans when needed. [1]

The company reports that 100% of suppliers identified as having overall high risk under its defined RBA process were evaluated and had follow-up actions agreed in 2025. This is a meaningful measure of process execution, although it concerns the defined responsible-supply-chain population rather than all supplier production problems. [5]
Supplier capability-building mechanism: Assessment findings are translated into agreed actions and reviewed rather than left as standalone audit observations.
Evidence limitations: The report does not publish closure rates for manufacturing-related findings, average closure times, or before-and-after productivity and quality results.
TO582 relevance: B2 — Operational excellence.
B3. Process stability, yield, and quality improvement
ASML's technical requirements create strong incentives for suppliers to maintain highly stable processes.
Quality is an explicit component of QLTCS. Supplier account teams coordinate with quality stakeholders, and supplier awards recognize exceptional quality performance. [4][6][11]

A notable example is Zollner Elektronik, which received ASML's 2025 Quality Supplier Award. ASML's award announcement credited the company with zero customer notifications, while Zollner described standardized quality processes, data-based analysis, and continuous improvement at its Neukirchen facility. [6][9]
Supplier capability-building mechanism: Quality assessment, cross-functional engagement, problem escalation, and continuous improvement expectations.

Evidence limitations: The Zollner example does not disclose its starting defect rate, the period covered by the zero-notification result, or a specific ASML-led intervention that caused the performance.
TO582 relevance: B3 — Process stability and yield.
B4. Material flow and constraint management
Logistics is a core component of ASML's supplier-performance framework.

The company monitors supplier delivery performance and recognizes improvements in logistics reliability. Anvil Industries received ASML's 2025 Logistics Supplier Award for sustained improvement leading to strong on-time delivery performance. [6]
ASML also addresses material constraints through engineering and sourcing alternatives.
For example, its engineers identified an alternative composition for rare-earth magnets used in its equipment, reducing dependence on one specific material combination. [2]
Regional repair centers further illustrate an effort to redesign parts flows and reduce unnecessary transportation between customers and the Netherlands.
Supplier capability-building mechanism: Supplier logistics performance management, collaborative identification of constraints, and redesign of sourcing or repair flows.

Evidence limitations: Public sources do not describe supplier-level value-stream mapping, inventory-control systems, work-in-process reduction, bottleneck-elimination projects, or measured flow improvements resulting from ASML coaching.
TO582 relevance: B4 — Flow and constraint management.
B5. Throughput and lead-time management
ASML's ability to deliver equipment depends on timely supply of complex modules and components.
Supplier capacity, delivery reliability, and production planning are therefore closely linked to ASML's manufacturing performance.
The Supplier Collaboration Program helps ASML understand supplier production capabilities and identify whether suppliers can scale to meet future requirements. [2]

The Anvil Industries award provides an example of strong delivery performance, while NTS's cross-regional production transfer demonstrates an effort to increase manufacturing flexibility and competitiveness. [6][7]
Supplier capability-building mechanism: Capacity and production-roadmap alignment, supplier logistics management, and cross-regional manufacturing capability development.

Evidence limitations: The public record does not provide supplier-level cycle-time reductions, throughput increases, constraint-capacity improvements, or lead-time reductions directly attributable to ASML interventions.
TO582 relevance: B5 — Throughput and lead-time management.
B6. Operating routines, governance, and escalation
ASML uses recurring supplier interactions rather than relying exclusively on annual assessments.
Its documented engagement channels include supplier account teams, audits, site visits, collaboration projects, newsletters, supplier events, and sustainability knowledge sessions. [1]
Published sourcing roles indicate that supplier account leaders coordinate cross-functional stakeholders and are accountable for supplier objectives across QLTCS dimensions. [11]
For responsible-supply-chain risks, the 2025 Annual Report describes regular review meetings used to track self-assessment completion and agreed follow-up actions. [1]
Supplier capability-building mechanism: Defined ownership, recurring reviews, documented action tracking, and cross-functional escalation.

Evidence limitations: Public materials do not reveal the standard daily or weekly management routines used inside supplier factories, the structure of joint performance boards, or the escalation cadence for manufacturing problems.
TO582 relevance: B6 — Operating routines.
B7. Capability building and sustainment
ASML's strongest publicly documented supplier-development mechanism is prolonged, direct engagement.

Its four-to-six-month Supplier Collaboration Program creates an opportunity for employees from both organizations to develop a shared understanding of processes, technology needs, production constraints, and future investment requirements. [2]
The company also supports supplier capability indirectly through onboarding materials, engineering collaboration, talent-sharing initiatives, and sustainability training.

Its 2025 Annual Report documents training for internal supplier account teams and auditors on emissions-related topics, alongside work with suppliers to improve emissions-data quality and reporting capabilities. [1]
Supplier capability-building mechanism: Embedded collaboration, knowledge transfer, supplier training, and recurring engagement.

Evidence limitations: The published record does not show whether specific suppliers independently sustained improvements after ASML personnel left their sites. Nor does it provide supplier employee skill assessments, documented problem-solving routines, or longitudinal manufacturing KPIs.
TO582 relevance: B7 — Capability building and sustainment.
6. Domain C — Resilience and Continuity
C1. Disruption preparedness and supplier financial stability
ASML operates in a supply chain exposed to cyclical demand, geopolitical uncertainty, specialist-capacity shortages, and long development lead times.
Its stated approach emphasizes supplier transparency, early identification of dependencies, and close collaboration with critical partners. [1][2]
The original research also considered whether ASML provides direct financial assistance to suppliers.
Public evidence is insufficient to establish a general supplier-financing program, such as supplier loans, payment guarantees, or structured supply-chain finance intended to prevent supplier failure.

The company's talent-sharing initiative is a clearer example of nonfinancial support: with applicants' consent, ASML may share suitable recruitment leads with suppliers that need similar technical skills. [2]
Supplier capability-building mechanism: Early visibility of business risks, relationship-based planning, and selective ecosystem support.

Evidence limitations: The original report suggested possible commercial or financial interventions but did not substantiate them. These should not be treated as established ASML practices without additional evidence.
TO582 relevance: C1 — Disruption preparedness and response.
C2. Dependency visibility and exposure management
ASML explicitly recognizes the danger of excessive dependence on individual suppliers or scarce materials.
The Supplier Collaboration Program helps ASML understand suppliers' growth capacity and identify business dependencies. [2]
The rare-earth magnet example demonstrates a concrete engineering response to a materials dependency: ASML developed a second material composition capable of performing the same function. [2]

ASML's conflict-minerals due diligence also extends beyond direct suppliers toward smelters and refiners. However, the 2025 Annual Report acknowledges incomplete information about some mineral origins and processing facilities. [1]
Supplier capability-building mechanism: Dependency identification, supplier engagement, technical substitution, and targeted upstream due diligence.
Evidence limitations: Public sources do not establish comprehensive mapping of all Tier-2 and Tier-3 production dependencies or disclose contingency plans for every critical component.
TO582 relevance: C2 — Dependency visibility and exposure management.
C3. Demand and supply volatility management
ASML expects suppliers to balance long-term capacity expansion with the ability to withstand short-term market fluctuations.
Its response includes business-outlook sharing, supplier collaboration, capacity discussions, and regional supply-chain development. [1][2]
Local repair centers reduce reliance on a single central repair flow. The NTS manufacturing-transfer example also demonstrates how production capabilities can be distributed across regions. [2][7]
Supplier capability-building mechanism: Long-term capacity alignment, flexible production networks, regional sourcing, and repair-network diversification.

Evidence limitations: Public sources do not disclose supplier-specific demand-volatility buffers, contractual capacity-flexibility arrangements, inventory policies, or quantitative resilience outcomes.
TO582 relevance: C3 — Demand and supply volatility management.
C4. Adaptability to changing business conditions
ASML's supplier ecosystem must adapt to changing technology requirements, regional sourcing opportunities, cost pressures, environmental expectations, and geopolitical constraints.
The company's 2025 strategy discussion describes increased use of regional sourcing and lower-cost manufacturing locations for mature product lines. [3]
Its sustainability program also requires suppliers to develop new capabilities in emissions measurement, reporting, materials management, and environmental risk assessment. [1][5]

In 2025, 32% of the suppliers representing the top 80% of supplier-related emissions had committed to reducing their carbon footprint by 2030, compared with 17% under ASML's restated 2024 methodology. However, ASML missed its interim 2025 ambition of 45%, illustrating that the program is still developing and faces practical barriers. [1][5]
Supplier capability-building mechanism: Adaptation of supplier processes and capabilities to new commercial, geographical, technical, and sustainability requirements.
Evidence limitations: Sustainability commitments are not equivalent to verified emissions reductions, and geographic sourcing changes do not necessarily demonstrate improved factory capability.
TO582 relevance: C4 — Adaptability to changing business conditions.
7. Detailed Supplier Case Studies
The following cases expand the named examples in the supplied research using identifiable public sources.
They are classified according to what the evidence actually establishes:
Direct operational supplier development: ASML demonstrably intervened in a supplier's production processes or operating capability.
Joint industrialization or technology development: ASML and the supplier developed or transferred a technology or production capability.
Supplier performance improvement: A supplier achieved an operational result, but ASML's direct contribution is not established.
Strategic ecosystem development: ASML helped establish regional, technical, or organizational capabilities across its supply base.
Case Study 1 — NTS: Cross-Regional Manufacturing Transfer and Cost Competitiveness
Supplier and context
NTS is a high-technology manufacturing partner supplying complex mechatronic systems and precision components to ASML.
ASML identifies NTS as one of its important suppliers of mechatronic systems serving multiple lithography-related product lines. [12]
Business challenge
ASML's mature and expanding product portfolio requires suppliers capable of maintaining precision and quality while improving cost competitiveness and supporting production in different regions.
Transferring complex manufacturing activities between facilities creates risks involving process reproducibility, workforce capability, supplier qualification, and delivery continuity.
Documented actions
NTS received ASML's 2025 Supplier Award for Cost.

According to NTS, the award recognized successful transfers of high-technology production across Europe and Asia. NTS specifically highlighted collaboration between its Hengelo and Singapore teams. [7]
ASML's supplier-award announcement described NTS's contribution to its Asia expansion through internal transfers and local sourcing. [6]
Documented outcomes
The public evidence establishes:
Successful cross-regional transfer of high-technology production.
Recognition by ASML for cost performance.
Support for ASML's expansion in Asia.
Supplier-reported maintenance of quality and precision requirements.
The award announcement refers to substantial cost benefits but does not disclose a verified savings figure.
Evidence limitations
No public source identifies:
The exact manufacturing processes transferred.
The starting and final process capability.
Ramp-up duration.
First-pass yield before and after transfer.
Labor productivity or throughput improvement.
Specific ASML engineers who coached the transfer.
Whether ASML directly redesigned NTS's production system.
Assessment
Classification: Joint industrialization and regional capability transfer.
Strength of evidence: High for the transfer and supplier recognition; limited for direct ASML-led factory capability development.
Siemens Energy implication
This is a relevant model for transferring qualified manufacturing processes between suppliers or regions while maintaining engineering requirements.

Siemens Energy could apply a similar approach to critical machining, fabricated structures, electrical assemblies, or other specialized components, but should explicitly measure transfer readiness, process capability, yield, and ramp-up performance.
Case Study 2 — TRUMPF: Next-Generation EUV Laser Co-Development
Supplier and context
TRUMPF is a strategic technology supplier involved in the laser systems used for EUV lithography.
The relationship illustrates the interdependence between an equipment OEM and a supplier whose technology is central to the performance of the finished machine.
Business challenge
Future EUV systems require increasingly powerful and reliable laser technology while reducing energy consumption and supporting higher equipment productivity.
The development challenge extends beyond manufacturing a part to advancing a complex subsystem.
Documented actions
TRUMPF and ASML collaborated on a new high-energy EUV laser.
In October 2025, TRUMPF announced that the laser had achieved its first successful light-generation test. ASML recognized TRUMPF with its 2025 Supplier Award for Technology. [8]
TRUMPF described the new laser as comprising more than 450,000 individual parts and weighing more than 20 tonnes.

At the time of the announcement, series production was scheduled to begin in 2026. This was a forward-looking production plan, not confirmation that full-scale production had already been achieved. [8]
Documented outcomes
Successful initial technology demonstration.
Completion of a significant joint development milestone.
A redesigned laser intended to improve reliability, availability, and energy efficiency.
Recognition of TRUMPF's technological contribution by ASML.
Evidence limitations
The public record does not disclose:
Manufacturing yield improvements at TRUMPF.
Reduction in laser assembly hours.
Production-cycle-time changes.
Ramp-up performance against plan.
ASML-led changes to TRUMPF's shop-floor routines.
Verified performance of the new laser after series-production ramp-up.
Assessment
Classification: Strategic technology co-development.
Strength of evidence: High for the technology milestone; insufficient for a claim of ASML-led operational supplier transformation.
Siemens Energy implication
The transferable lesson is the need to align the OEM's future product architecture with a supplier's technology and manufacturing roadmap.

For Siemens Energy, this could apply to specialized power electronics, high-performance materials, insulation systems, turbine components, or other technologies where supplier capability must develop alongside product design.
Sources: [6][8]
Case Study 3 — Zollner Elektronik: Stable Quality Performance
Supplier and context
Zollner Elektronik is an electronics manufacturing supplier.
Its relationship with ASML illustrates the importance of reliable electronics production in complex capital equipment.
Business challenge
High-complexity equipment requires stable electronic assemblies and disciplined control of defects, variation, and manufacturing processes.
A small number of defects can create disproportionate disruption when components are integrated into sophisticated systems.
Documented actions
Zollner received ASML's 2025 Supplier Award for Quality.
ASML recognized the supplier for achieving zero customer notifications. [6]
Zollner's own public statement identified its Neukirchen site and attributed its performance to:
A stable, established quality-management system.
Data-driven analysis.
Continuous process improvement.
Standardized quality processes.
Modern software tools.
Close collaboration with ASML. [9]
Documented outcomes
The strongest published outcome is the zero-customer-notification result associated with ASML's award.
Zollner also reported reliable delivery and effective implementation of its quality-management practices.
Evidence limitations
“Zero customer notifications” should not be interpreted as proof of zero defects across all products and processes.
The public record does not define the measurement period, initial defect level, volume of components supplied, or scope of the metric.
Nor does it identify an ASML-led root-cause workshop, process redesign, statistical process-control intervention, or employee training program responsible for the result.
Assessment
Classification: Supplier operational performance improvement, with evidence of collaboration.
Strength of evidence: High for recognition and the reported outcome; limited for attribution to ASML's supplier-development intervention.
Siemens Energy implication
The case reinforces the value of measuring supplier quality through customer-impact indicators rather than audit compliance alone.

A Siemens Energy supplier-development program should connect such outcomes to documented improvement actions, including root-cause analysis, process-control changes, and sustained performance after intervention.
Sources: [6][9]
Case Study 4 — Anvil Industries: Logistics Reliability
Supplier and context
Anvil Industries was recognized by ASML for logistics performance.
The case represents the delivery-reliability dimension of ASML's QLTCS model.
Business challenge
Complex-equipment manufacturing depends on the synchronized arrival of many specialized components.
Late delivery from a critical supplier can disrupt assembly, testing, and customer commitments even when the supplied component meets all technical requirements.
Documented actions
Anvil Industries received ASML's 2025 Supplier Award for Logistics.
ASML's supplier-award announcement credited the company with continued improvements that produced strong on-time delivery performance. [6]
Documented outcomes
The public evidence supports a qualitative finding of improved logistics reliability.
However, no exact on-time-delivery percentage, baseline, improvement period, or lead-time reduction is disclosed.
Evidence limitations
There is no public description of the methods behind the improvement.
It is therefore not possible to determine whether the result came from:
Better production planning.
Inventory changes.
Supplier capacity expansion.
Transport optimization.
Material-flow redesign.
ASML-led coaching.
Supplier-initiated operational improvements.
Assessment
Classification: Recognized supplier logistics improvement.
Strength of evidence: Moderate for the achievement; insufficient for a detailed intervention case.
Siemens Energy implication
Delivery improvement should be assessed at the level of the underlying production system.
For critical suppliers, Siemens Energy should investigate whether on-time delivery is sustained through stable processes and realistic capacity rather than overtime, expediting, or excess inventory.
Source: [6]
Case Study 5 — Gigaphoton: Long-Term Collaboration and Flexibility
Supplier and context
Gigaphoton is a specialist semiconductor-industry technology supplier.
Its ASML relationship demonstrates the importance of sustained partnerships in technically demanding supply chains.
Business challenge
Long-term suppliers must accommodate changing technical requirements, market fluctuations, and delivery expectations without undermining reliability.
Documented actions
Gigaphoton received ASML's 2025 Supplier Award for Collaboration.
ASML's announcement highlighted approximately 25 years of partnership, strong delivery performance, and improved flexibility. [6]
Documented outcomes
The public record establishes recognition for long-term collaboration and delivery flexibility.
It does not quantify improvements in output, lead time, cost, or quality.
Evidence limitations
No specific ASML supplier-development engagement, on-site intervention, production-system redesign, or capability-transfer project is disclosed.
Assessment
Classification: Strategic supplier relationship and performance recognition.
Strength of evidence: High for the long-term relationship and award; low for demonstrable operational capability transfer.
Siemens Energy implication
Long-term partnerships can support mutual planning and knowledge accumulation, but relationship duration should not be used as a proxy for supplier capability maturity.
Source: [6]
Case Study 6 — Benchmark Electronics: Supplier Sustainability Capability Development
Supplier and context
Benchmark Electronics is an advanced manufacturing and engineering-services supplier.
Its collaboration with ASML provides a more detailed example of supplier-side capability development in sustainability.
Business challenge
ASML seeks to reduce emissions across its supply chain, but much of the relevant energy consumption and manufacturing activity occurs at external suppliers.
Suppliers therefore need their own measurement capabilities, improvement programs, employee engagement, and infrastructure investments.
Documented actions
Benchmark describes a collaboration with ASML focused on reducing emissions associated with ASML's supply chain.
Its initiatives included:
An employee-led Environmental Challenge competition.
Energy-efficiency projects.
Waste-reduction initiatives.
On-site renewable-energy projects.
Investment in solar generation and renewable-energy credits.
Employee participation in identifying environmental improvements. [10]
Benchmark received ASML's 2025 Supplier Award for Sustainability. [6]
Documented outcomes
Benchmark reports an approximately 22% absolute reduction in its Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions relative to a 2021 baseline. [10]
This is a meaningful before-and-after supplier-side outcome.
However, it is a Benchmark-wide emissions result, not an ASML-specific manufacturing productivity measure.
Evidence limitations
The published case does not quantify the portion of the reduction attributable specifically to ASML's intervention.
It also does not establish that ASML directly managed Benchmark's employee-improvement competition or implemented its infrastructure projects.
Assessment
Classification: Supplier sustainability capability development and strategic alignment.
Strength of evidence: High for Benchmark's reported emissions improvement; moderate for the collaborative relationship; limited for direct causal attribution to ASML.
Siemens Energy implication
This example is useful because it connects an OEM's strategic requirements with a supplier's internal employee-led improvement program.

For Siemens Energy, the transferable principle is to help suppliers establish their own improvement capabilities and measure outcomes over time, rather than relying solely on declarations of compliance.
Sources: [6][10]
Case Study 7 — ZEISS: Deep Technology Integration and Supplier Interdependence
Supplier and context
ZEISS is a critical optical technology partner for ASML.
ASML's published materials identify ZEISS as the supplier of optical lenses for its lithography systems and describe close cooperation in developing advanced EUV optics. [2][3]
Business challenge
Lithography optics require exceptional precision, complex materials, and highly specialized manufacturing capabilities.
These technologies cannot be readily substituted with conventional components from a broad supplier market.
Documented actions
ASML and ZEISS collaborate closely on optical technology and system development.
ASML's 2025 technology account describes joint work on EUV optical systems involving multilayer mirrors and extremely demanding engineering requirements. [3]
Documented outcomes
The public record establishes a long-standing, strategically important technology partnership supporting advanced lithography equipment.
Evidence limitations
This is not a documented factory-level supplier-development case.
The sources do not identify a specific ASML-led improvement at a ZEISS production facility, nor do they provide supplier-level yield, throughput, or productivity results.
Assessment
Classification: Strategic technology co-development and critical-supplier integration.
Strength of evidence: High for technical collaboration; insufficient for direct operational supplier-development outcomes.
Siemens Energy implication
The case demonstrates that some supplier relationships must be managed as long-term technology dependencies.
For critical single-source technologies, Siemens Energy should integrate technical-roadmap governance with capacity, continuity, and supplier operating-capability assessments.
Case Study 8 — Regional Repair Centers: Building Local Supplier Ecosystems
Context
ASML supports semiconductor manufacturers operating in multiple global regions.
Shipping every repairable component to the Netherlands would create unnecessary transportation, cost, and turnaround time.
Documented actions
ASML established regional repair capabilities in the Netherlands, United States, Taiwan, South Korea, and China.
Its public description states that these centers work with local materials suppliers and specialist repair partners. [2]
The company also set a 2025 ambition for 10% of field parts requiring service to be repaired locally.

Faster access to repair services.
Reduced transportation distances.
Lower logistics costs.
Reduced transportation-related emissions.
Development of regional repair capabilities.

Strength of evidence: High for the operating concept; limited for quantified supplier-level outcomes.

The model is relevant to regional repair and refurbishment capabilities for long-life energy equipment.
Siemens Energy could use similar principles to develop qualified regional repair partners, provided that process capability, technical authorization, and repair quality are measured and controlled.

11. Evidence Limitations and Critical Assessment
11.1 Program documentation is stronger than outcome documentation
ASML's 2025 Annual Report provides strong evidence that the company has an established supplier-engagement system.
It identifies recurring activities, responsible organizational functions, on-site assessments, and mechanisms for follow-up.
However, the existence of these mechanisms does not establish the effectiveness of every supplier-development intervention.
A mature audit process may identify problems without necessarily transferring the skills needed for suppliers to solve them independently.
11.2 Supplier awards are not equivalent to supplier-development cases
ASML's 2025 awards identify suppliers that achieved strong results in collaboration, quality, logistics, technology, cost, and sustainability.
They do not ordinarily establish:
The supplier's initial operational weakness.
The specific ASML intervention.
The employees or teams involved.
The tools used to change the supplier's production system.
The supplier's measured before-and-after performance.
The durability of the improvement.
This is particularly important when comparing ASML with Toyota-style supplier-development cases that document hands-on production-system interventions.
11.3 Technology co-development must be separated from operational capability building
TRUMPF and ZEISS illustrate sophisticated technical collaboration.
Such partnerships can develop new manufacturing capabilities and may require major investments in engineering and production infrastructure.

Nevertheless, public evidence of a successful new technology does not automatically prove that ASML improved the supplier's existing factory management, flow, yield, or workforce problem-solving system.
Both are important, but they are analytically different.
11.4 ASML's own operational results are not supplier results
ASML reports numerous technology, sustainability, and business-performance indicators.
These should not be substituted for supplier-level KPIs.
For example, improved lithography-system productivity is not evidence of improved supplier factory throughput unless the causal link is established.
Similarly, reductions in ASML's emissions do not demonstrate that a particular supplier's manufacturing processes improved.
11.5 Supplier sustainability evidence is comparatively detailed
ASML's responsible-supply-chain disclosures are stronger in several respects than its public factory-development disclosures.
The 2025 Annual Report identifies audit activity, risk follow-up, supplier emissions commitments, training initiatives, and obstacles to supplier progress.
It also acknowledges shortcomings, including missed interim emissions-commitment ambitions and limitations in supplier data quality. [1][5]
This transparency is useful, but sustainability performance should remain distinct from manufacturing-operational maturity.
11.6 Multi-tier visibility remains an open question
ASML undertakes upstream due diligence for conflict minerals and recognizes supplier dependencies.
However, its annual report also acknowledges incomplete information concerning some upstream mineral sources. [1]
The public record does not establish comprehensive operational visibility across every critical sub-tier manufacturing process.
11.7 Financial support is insufficiently documented
The supplied research raised the possibility of supplier financial assistance, guarantees, or favorable commercial arrangements.
These possibilities should be treated as unverified.
The public evidence reviewed here does not establish a general ASML program for financing external suppliers' production-capacity expansion or preventing supplier insolvency.
11.8 The strongest remaining research question
The most important unresolved question is:
What happens inside a supplier's factory during an ASML Supplier Collaboration Program engagement, and what operational capabilities remain after ASML's personnel leave?
Answering that question would require supplier interviews, internal project records, or published case studies containing actual operational results.
12. Siemens Energy Implications
12.1 Adopt multidimensional supplier capability ownership
ASML's QLTCS model demonstrates the value of managing suppliers across multiple interconnected performance dimensions.
For Siemens Energy, the equivalent approach should integrate:
Quality and process capability.
Delivery and logistics.
Technology and industrialization readiness.
Cost and productivity.
Sustainability and regulatory requirements.
Capacity and business-continuity risks.

The critical design choice is to make one accountable supplier leader responsible for coordinating these dimensions rather than allowing disconnected functions to manage the same supplier independently.
12.2 Establish targeted embedded supplier-development engagements
The Supplier Collaboration Program is one of ASML's most transferable practices.
Siemens Energy could establish time-limited, cross-functional engagements at selected critical suppliers.
These should be reserved for suppliers where an identified operating-capability gap materially threatens future business.
An engagement could combine supplier quality, manufacturing engineering, industrialization, planning, and logistics expertise.
Unlike a conventional audit, the team should work jointly with supplier personnel to improve the underlying process.

Recommended distinction: The engagement should not be considered complete merely because actions were closed. It should demonstrate improved operating performance and the supplier's ability to sustain that performance independently.
12.3 Connect future demand to supplier investment readiness
ASML emphasizes the need for suppliers to prepare for long-term growth while managing cyclical demand.
Siemens Energy faces a comparable challenge when supplier investment must precede future equipment orders.
A practical approach would combine:
Forward-looking demand scenarios.
Critical-process capacity assessments.
Identification of long-lead equipment and specialist skills.
Supplier capital-investment requirements.
Ramp-up readiness milestones.
Contingency plans for delays or underperformance.
This would convert demand communication into a more rigorous supplier capability-development process.
12.4 Treat industrialization as a supplier capability-building activity
ASML's transfer-team approach is relevant whenever suppliers must introduce new technologies, products, sites, or production processes.
Siemens Energy should ensure that supplier transfers and launches include explicit assessments of:
Process capability.
Operator and engineering competence.
Equipment qualification.
Material and tooling readiness.
Production planning.
Quality-control routines.
Delivery stability.
The goal should be a demonstrably capable production system, not simply completion of technical documentation.
12.5 Develop regional capability without weakening process control
ASML's regional repair strategy illustrates how local capabilities can reduce dependence on centralized logistics.
For Siemens Energy, regional supplier development could improve repair turnaround, spare-parts availability, and resilience.
However, localization should include a disciplined transfer of technical requirements, qualified processes, workforce skills, and quality-management routines.
Regional sourcing should not be treated as a resilience improvement unless the new capability can reliably deliver.
12.6 Combine supplier development with dependency management
ASML's rare-earth magnet example demonstrates that supplier risk can sometimes be reduced through engineering rather than purchasing action alone.
Siemens Energy should consider technical substitution, alternative manufacturing routes, and design simplification as part of supplier-resilience planning.
These actions should complement—not replace—development of the capabilities of existing strategic suppliers.
13. Recommended Siemens Energy Implementation Roadmap
The following roadmap is a proposed application of the benchmark findings, not a description of an existing ASML program.
First 90 days — Define priorities and establish visibility
Objective: Identify the suppliers where capability development will create the greatest business value.
Recommended actions:
Segment critical suppliers by future demand exposure, process complexity, capacity constraints, delivery risk, and substitutability.
Define a common assessment framework covering future readiness, production-system capability, and resilience.
Identify the highest-risk manufacturing processes rather than assessing suppliers only at company level.
Assign cross-functional supplier account ownership.
Establish baseline KPIs for quality, throughput, lead time, delivery, and capacity.
Select a limited number of suppliers for initial development engagements.
Expected deliverable: A prioritized supplier-development portfolio with documented starting conditions and accountable owners.
Days 90–180 — Execute supplier-site development pilots
Objective: Demonstrate measurable operational improvement through direct collaboration.
Recommended actions:
Deploy small cross-functional teams to selected supplier sites.
Agree a joint problem statement with each supplier.
Map the critical manufacturing process and identify its constraints.
Establish a measurable improvement plan.
Implement changes jointly with supplier personnel.
Introduce supplier-owned management routines and escalation processes.
Track results against the original baseline.
Potential KPIs include:
First-pass yield.
Scrap and rework.
Constraint throughput.
Production lead time.
On-time delivery.
Work in process.
Equipment availability.
Operator qualification and problem-solving competence.
Expected deliverable: A documented set of supplier improvement cases with before-and-after evidence.
Days 180–365 — Verify sustainment and scale
Objective: Convert isolated improvement projects into a repeatable supplier-development system.
Recommended actions:
Verify that improvements remain stable after Siemens Energy reduces its on-site involvement.
Assess whether supplier teams can independently identify and solve new problems.
Standardize successful development methods.
Integrate capability findings into future sourcing and industrialization decisions.
Link supplier roadmaps to expected business demand.
Expand the program to additional critical suppliers.
Establish periodic management reviews of both supplier outcomes and development-program effectiveness.
Expected deliverable: A scalable supplier-development model supported by verified operational results and evidence of sustainment.
14. Overall Conclusions
ASML demonstrates a sophisticated approach to managing an external supplier ecosystem in an exceptionally demanding complex-equipment industry.
Its publicly documented practices show that supplier management extends beyond purchasing, qualification, and compliance.
The company has established mechanisms for long-term supplier engagement, technical collaboration, on-site assessments, gap follow-up, supplier onboarding, and future capacity alignment.

The Supplier Collaboration Program, which places experienced ASML personnel at supplier sites for four to six months, is particularly relevant to Siemens Energy because it provides a structured opportunity to understand and address supplier capability constraints directly.
The QLTCS framework is another important lesson. It recognizes that supplier performance must be managed across technical, operational, commercial, logistical, and sustainability dimensions.
Named supplier examples demonstrate meaningful achievements:
NTS: Cross-regional manufacturing transfer and cost competitiveness.
TRUMPF: Joint development of next-generation EUV laser technology.
Zollner: Recognized quality performance.
Anvil Industries: Improved logistics reliability.
Gigaphoton: Long-term collaboration and flexibility.
Benchmark Electronics: Documented emissions reduction and employee-led sustainability initiatives.
ZEISS: Deep technology integration.
Regional repair partners: Development of local service capabilities.
However, the available public evidence does not establish a comprehensive set of ASML-led, factory-level supplier transformations with quantified before-and-after operational outcomes.
The central benchmarking conclusion is therefore precise:

ASML is a strong model for the strategic governance, technical integration, and structured engagement of complex-equipment suppliers. It is a less fully documented model for hands-on production-system improvement and long-term supplier capability sustainment.
For Siemens Energy, the strongest opportunity is to combine ASML's disciplined supplier ecosystem management with a more explicit, measurable approach to factory-level capability development.
That combination would connect future business readiness, production-system improvement, and resilience in a single supplier-development operating model.

Infineon Technologies | Supplier capability-building research dossier

Research cut: 17 October 2026 • Current benchmark score: 3.25/5 (A 3.50, 4/5; B 3.00, 3/7; C 3.25, 4/4). See the five-company overview for criterion-level ratings. The dossier below preserves its original research-only framing.
Scope and evidence rule

Infineon is an integrated semiconductor company: it manufactures differentiated power, sensor and analog products internally, while using foundries and outsourced assembly/test partners where external production offers advantage. This benchmark examines Infineon as a BUYER developing wafer, foundry, packaging/test and other upstream suppliers. Its own fab expansions and its support to downstream customers are context, not supplier-development evidence. [S1]

Apply the guide’s causal test: what new capability can the supplier perform, what did Infineon do to build it, who did the work, and what changed? Capacity reservation, multisourcing, assessment, certification, inventory and continuity plans alone are weaker than engineering support, asset/skills transfer, joint industrialization or verified corrective action. “Keep” means the intervention is documented, not that a maturity score or sustained performance gain has been proved. “Investigate” marks missing buyer intervention or result.
Executive synthesis

Infineon’s most distinctive public practice is partnering with manufacturers through embedded engineering and transfer of production assets. In Porto, its Amkor agreement specifies a dedicated packaging/test center: Amkor expands space and operates the line while Infineon provides on-site engineering and development support. The public 2024 announcement stated an expected start in first-half 2025, but this research did not find a later primary-source operating or yield report; treat the outcome as unverified. [S2]

Three executed fab/backend transfers show another capacity-building model: Infineon transferred two backend sites to ASE in August 2024, its Austin 200 mm fab to SkyWater in June 2025, and its Bangkok/Nonthaburi backend site to MPI in February 2026. In each, a former Infineon production asset and personnel moved to an external manufacturing partner, while Infineon secured a multi-year supply relationship. This demonstrably expands the partner’s asset base; public evidence does not show improved supplier yield, throughput, or resilience after transfer. [S3–S8]

Infineon also has a broad silicon-carbide substrate sourcing network (Wolfspeed, Resonac, TanKeBlue and SK Siltron CSS). Agreements articulate 150-to-200 mm wafer transition and geographic diversity; the latest Wolfspeed 200 mm agreement was announced 15 October 2026. These are excellent future-readiness and dependence-management leads but mainly commercial commitments. None of the public announcements specifies Infineon-funded supplier tooling, training or process improvement, so they should not automatically be called capability-building. [S9–S12]

Across Domain B, Infineon publicly describes Total Supplier Management, per-use qualification, supplier statistical process control expectations, audits aligned to its fabs and cooperation on sustainable quality improvements. Those establish the operating framework but no named supplier-level before/after case. Supplier continuity requirements likewise show assessment and planning, not tested supplier recovery. [S13, S14]
Case portfolio — buyer action, supplier capability, evidence boundary
Case 1 | Amkor Porto: dedicated packaging/test line with Infineon engineers — KEEP for documented intervention; operating outcome open

Situation and capability: Infineon wanted more European backend packaging/test capacity, especially for automotive and industrial applications. A 2024 multi-year agreement specified a dedicated center at Amkor’s Porto facility. Amkor would expand the site, provide cleanroom space and operate the production line; Infineon would supply an on-site team with engineering and development support. This is a concrete division of labor for process transfer, ramp and supplier production capability. [S2]

Evidence boundary: the 2024 release forecast operations in first-half 2025, but the source itself does not verify commissioning, yields, qualifications, actual volume or the impact of Infineon’s embedded team. A 2024 sustainability report later expected production in calendar 2026; timing is therefore not reliable without a newer operating disclosure. Do not present the center as a proven production success. [S2, S15]

Transferability: strong model for low-volume, high-spec packaging or module suppliers: buyer engineers embedded during line design, qualification and ramp; supplier owns facility and production; joint exit gates document capability transfer. For Siemens Energy, adapt to castings, electronics, complex assemblies or test stations with supplier-owned process controls.
Case 2 | ASE: two backend sites and workforce transferred to an OSAT partner — KEEP for executed capacity transfer

Situation and capability: Infineon agreed in February 2024 to sell Cavite (Philippines) and Cheonan (South Korea) backend sites to ASE, with production personnel, continued services and future-product support. The FY2024 annual report confirms both site sales closed 1 August 2024 and five-year supply contracts were signed. ASE gained operating assets, experienced teams and a route to serve more customers. [S3, S4]

Intervention and roles: Infineon transferred established plants and secured demand; ASE took over operations and planned to develop the sites. This is a supplier-capacity and skills-base transfer rather than an audit or extra order. The sources do not identify a specific new process, buyer-led coaching, before/after productivity or independently verified recovery performance. Do not equate additional ASE ownership with improved process maturity. [S3, S4]

Transferability: useful where a buyer’s non-core production line could become a supplier platform with retained specialists and a long-term offtake contract. Less portable if Siemens has no suitable asset to transfer; the core principle is preserving tacit production knowledge during outsourcing.
Case 3 | SkyWater Fab 25: US foundry capability via asset and personnel transfer — KEEP for executed capacity transfer

Situation and capability: Infineon sold its Austin, Texas 200 mm Fab 25 to SkyWater; closing was 30 June 2025. The facility brought 65 nm infrastructure, copper processing scale and high-voltage BCD technology, together with nearly 1,000 manufacturing employees. A long-term supply agreement retained US production for Infineon. SkyWater’s 2025 results independently confirm acquisition completion and Fab 25 contribution. [S5, S6]

Intervention and roles: Infineon conveyed a running fab, process assets and workforce to a foundry partner; SkyWater operates it, serves Infineon and can broaden use to other customers. This is a substantial supplier capability addition, though it is acquisition-based rather than process coaching. Expansion and dual-source benefits were stated ambitions; public sources do not establish post-transfer yield, capacity increase or successful second-site qualification. [S5, S6]

Transferability: strategic foundry or component-capacity creation through asset transfer plus guaranteed demand. Explicitly separate transferred installed capability from new capability learned by the partner.
Case 4 | MPI/Carsem Bangkok: backend site transfer with long-term supply — KEEP for executed capacity transfer; co-development open

Situation and capability: Infineon announced in September 2025 that it would transfer its Bangkok/Nonthaburi backend site to Malaysian Pacific Industries (MPI), an existing OSAT supplier, with a long-term supply agreement and intention to co-develop new packaging solutions. The transaction closed on 4 February 2026; MPI assumed operations and production employees. This adds an established manufacturing site and team to the supplier. [S7, S8]

Evidence boundary: the completed transfer and continuing supply are documented. The new packaging co-development was an agreement/intention in the 2025 announcement, not a documented completed product or improved process. Infineon’s separate new Thai backend fab is its OWN capacity, not MPI supplier development. [S7, S8]

Transferability: combines supplier asset transfer, staff continuity and contractual demand. Ask how technical documentation, quality system ownership, change control and process knowledge were transferred; these mechanisms are not detailed publicly.
Case 5 | European Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (ESMC): equity-backed regional foundry capacity — INVESTIGATE as supplier development

Situation and capability: TSMC, Infineon, Bosch and NXP formed the ESMC joint venture for a Dresden fab operated by TSMC; Infineon’s equity share is 10%. Groundbreaking occurred in August 2024. Planned output is 40,000 300 mm wafers/month when fully operational on 28/22 nm planar and 16/12 nm FinFET processes, with production originally targeted by end-2027. Infineon’s participation supports a future European foundry capability and geographic resilience. [S16, S17]

Evidence boundary: this is funded capacity creation in a partner ecosystem, but construction and forecast output are not delivered capability as of this research cut. The public record does not show Infineon-specific process engineering, supplier workforce development or qualified production. Treat as a strategic investment lead, not a realized supplier ramp. [S16, S17]
Case 6 | SiC wafer supplier network and 200 mm transition — INVESTIGATE for buyer-led capability building

Infineon reserved multi-year capacity with Wolfspeed for 150 mm SiC wafers in 2024 and signed a separate 200 mm agreement on 15 October 2026. Resonac’s agreement covers a double-digit share of forecast demand and later 8-inch transition; SK Siltron CSS and TanKeBlue agreements similarly anticipate 200 mm supply. This is a coherent A2/A4/C4 sourcing roadmap across regions and suppliers. It does not disclose buyer-funded supplier equipment, shared process experiments, 200 mm supplier qualifications or verified capacity added because of Infineon intervention. Infineon’s own 200 mm SiC production in Villach/Kulim must be kept separate. [S9–S12, S1]
Case 7 | Total Supplier Management and quality improvement — INVESTIGATE for supplier-level results

Infineon assesses supplier expertise, sustained manufacturing capability, security and quality systems; it qualifies materials/equipment/services for each use. For raw-material, foundry and OSAT suppliers it cites ISO/IATF requirements; it expects SPC/data analysis and zero-defect programs, monitors performance and uses audits/inspections aligned with internal fabs. Infineon says it works with suppliers on sustainable improvements. This describes a structured buyer system, but no named defect, intervention, supplier-owned corrective process or measured yield/escape reduction is disclosed. [S13]
Case 8 | Supplier Engagement Program for climate targets — KEEP as adjacent capability model; do not map directly into A/B/C

Infineon’s FY2025 sustainability report describes supplier-specific plans tailored to maturity and commitment, training, annual reduction-plan reviews, a carbon scorecard and collaborative projects. Its annual report says procurement works with over 100 suppliers on emissions solutions; 54% of supplier-related emissions were from suppliers with validated science-based targets in FY2025. This shows an actual supplier education/measurement loop, but target adoption is not proof of supplier production, capacity or continuity capability. Include only as a transferable program-design analogue, not a scored core example. [S1, S18]
Criterion evidence map — research notes only, no scores
DOMAIN A | Future business readiness

A1 Strategic planning / sourcing master plan — Infineon’s 2025 report distinguishes in-house production from long-term foundry/OSAT partnerships. The SiC substrate network and ESMC equity show multi-year technology and geographic planning. Missing: supplier-specific development roadmaps and performance gates. [S1, S9–S12, S16]

A2 Capacity planning and contracting — Multi-year wafer agreements, Amkor’s dedicated line and long-term supply contracts tied to ASE/SkyWater/MPI transfers. Evidence is strongest for contracted capacity and asset transfers, weakest for measured added output. [S2–S12]

A3 Supplier ramp-up and launch — Amkor’s planned on-site Infineon engineering and MPI’s proposed packaging co-development could support NPI/ramp. No public supplier-specific first-article, qualification, yield or ramp-time result found. [S2, S7, S13]

A4 Product/design complexity and localization — SiC 150-to-200 mm transition, localized European ESMC/Amkor capacity and US SkyWater site are relevant. Infineon’s own Villach/Kulim/Dresden technology should not be attributed to suppliers. [S1, S2, S5, S9–S12, S16]

A5 Concurrent engineering with suppliers — Amkor agreement explicitly names Infineon’s on-site engineering/development support; MPI agreement names future joint package work. Evidence of completed product/process co-development remains open. [S2, S7]
DOMAIN B | Supplier production-system capability

B1 Structured production assessment — Total Supplier Management assesses expertise, sustained manufacturing capability and supplier QMS; material/service qualification is per use. These are diagnostics and entry requirements, not demonstrated improvement. [S13]

B2 Structured gap closure — Infineon states it works with suppliers on sustainable improvements and expects self-driven zero-defect programs. No public example traces a supplier gap from root cause through action and validation. [S13]

B3 On-site intervention — The Amkor model assigns an Infineon engineering/development team at the supplier’s Porto line. Public evidence is prospective and lacks staffing duration or line result. [S2]

B4 Logistics and material flow — Multi-year supply contracts and network redesign show planning; the press releases do not document supplier WIP, lead-time, bottleneck or throughput improvement. Avoid treating Infineon’s own fab efficiency as supplier progress. [S1–S8]

B5 Quality problem-solving — SPC, data analysis, audit/inspection alignment and zero-defect expectations are explicit. Missing a named supplier 8D/containment case, process-control change and sustained defect/yield trend. [S13]

B6 Technology/process transformation — SkyWater gained 65 nm, copper and high-voltage BCD assets; ASE/MPI gained backend assets; Amkor’s dedicated line may add packaging/test capability. Asset transfer is verifiable; learned new process capability and productivity outcomes are not. [S2–S8]

B7 Sustaining improvements — Long-term supply contracts and Infineon’s supplier quality framework suggest continuity, but no public supplier control-plan, repeat audit, replication or multi-year yield trajectory demonstrates sustainment. [S3–S8, S13]
DOMAIN C | Resilience and continuity capability

C1 Financial stability and risk financing — Long-term offtake and ownership transfers can support partner economics; ESMC equity supports new regional capacity. No case found of Infineon lending to or recapitalizing a distressed supplier, nor evidence of a supplier financial-health improvement. [S3–S8, S16]

C2 Risk identification and contingency planning — Infineon evaluates supplier risk and requires key suppliers to prove continuity plans, controls and mitigation. The 2025 annual report identifies supplier concentration and Taiwan exposure. These are risk-identification practices; no supplier-specific coached risk-closure example found. [S1, S14]

C3 Business continuity — Geographical diversification via SiC supplier network and ESMC, plus outsourced footprint in Europe/US/Asia, is visible. Infineon says its OWN sites undergo stress tests; do not transfer that claim to suppliers. No public supplier recovery drill, restoration time or qualified emergency switch is documented. [S1, S14, S16]

C4 Strategic supply dependence — Multi-source SiC procurement and fab/OSAT partnerships reduce some concentration. The annual report explicitly says alternatives are not always available and flags Taiwanese-partner exposure. Diversification is a sourcing result, not automatic proof of supplier capability building. [S1, S9–S12]
Key evidence boundaries and interview questions

Do not count the 2026 Wolfspeed supply announcement as already-delivered 200 mm capacity. Do not count Amkor’s forecast opening as observed operation. Do not count the three fab transfers as proof of process yield improvement. Do not count Infineon’s internal One Virtual Fab, Kulim, Villach, Dresden or new Samut Prakan site as upstream supplier development. Do not count supplier certification or BCP possession as a developed or tested capability. [S1, S2, S9, S13, S14]

Priority follow-ups: (1) Did the Amkor Porto line enter production, with what Infineon engineering tasks, qualifications and 6/12-month yield/throughput? (2) Which specific new packaging process has MPI co-developed since February 2026? (3) Did ASE/SkyWater/MPI improve output, yield, unit cost or recovery speed after transfer, beyond inheriting assets? (4) For one 200 mm SiC supplier, what process/tooling/qualification support did Infineon provide and what supplier-owned capability resulted? (5) Can Infineon show a supplier quality gap-to-closure case and a tested supplier continuity scenario?
