Limitation: The evidence does not establish whether suppliers receive structured engineering or manufacturing-process training during these changes.
B5. Capability retention and continuous improvement
This is one of the largest gaps in the public record.
There is credible evidence that Volvo Cars:
Assesses supplier processes.
Identifies nonconformities.
Provides direct support in particular situations.
Uses structured improvement and escalation tools.
Monitors whether suppliers meet operational requirements.
However, the reviewed sources do not establish a company-wide method for measuring whether suppliers become independently capable of maintaining improvements after Volvo personnel withdraw.
For example, no sufficiently documented public case was found showing all of the following:
Initial supplier performance → Volvo intervention → production-process changes → measured improvement → sustained performance after intervention.
This distinction matters for Siemens Energy because correcting a delivery problem is not necessarily equivalent to building the supplier's long-term production-system capability.
Domain B findings
Volvo Cars has demonstrable supplier coaching, manufacturing assessment, production approval, material-flow coordination, and operational recovery mechanisms.
The evidence supports describing these as active supplier-management and development capabilities.
It does not yet justify describing Volvo Cars as operating a fully documented, enterprise-wide supplier manufacturing-excellence or supplier-kaizen program.
4. Domain C: Resilience and Continuity Capability
This domain concerns the ability to identify supplier risks, prevent disruption, develop alternatives, and recover from problems.
C1. Operational disruption prevention
At plant level, Volvo Cars uses direct supplier communication, delivery monitoring, inventory parameters, and early escalation.

The Ridgeville supply-chain function is expected to detect material-flow abnormalities and prevent production interruptions through supplier follow-up and corrective or recovery actions. Volvo Cars Careers
Capability identified: Operational supplier continuity management embedded in daily material planning.
Limitation: No publicly established company-wide supplier time-to-recover or recovery-effectiveness metric was identified.
C2. Regionalization and supplier alternatives
Volvo Cars' 2026 procurement strategy connects supplier scale to supply resilience.
The company reported that approximately 80% of relevant spending, representing around SEK 120 billion, was with suppliers shared across Volvo Cars and Geely, with an ambition to exceed 90%.
Parts commonality was approximately 10%, with a longer-term ambition of around 30%. Volvo Cars Investor Relations

Gamboni explained that greater procurement scale can make dual sourcing more economically feasible because sufficient volume can support multiple suppliers and duplicate tooling. Volvo Cars Investor Relations
Capability identified: Strategic supplier-network design intended to support alternative sourcing and reduce concentration risk.
Limitation: Management's explanation demonstrates a sourcing mechanism and strategic rationale. It does not reveal how many components currently have qualified alternate suppliers.
C3. Battery supply-chain risk: The NOVO Energy example
The Northvolt–Volvo Cars battery partnership provides an instructive example of the limits of supplier-development ambitions.

Volvo Cars initially planned joint battery R&D and manufacturing development with Northvolt. However, following difficulties with the partnership, Volvo Cars began the process of taking full ownership of NOVO Energy.
In January 2026, NOVO Energy announced an operational pause, explaining that battery production could not proceed as previously planned without a new technology partner. Volvo Cars
This case is particularly relevant to supplier resilience because it illustrates the dependence of strategic localization projects on partners' financing, technology, and execution capabilities.
Capability implication: Volvo Cars has experience pursuing deep strategic supplier partnerships, but these arrangements can introduce development and continuity risks of their own.
The planned battery manufacturing capability should not be presented as successfully deployed.
C4. Responsible sourcing and upstream supply-chain visibility
Volvo Cars' most thoroughly documented corrective-action system concerns responsible sourcing.
SLR Consulting describes working directly with Volvo Cars on battery-mineral supplier audits, corrective-action follow-up, training, and supplier improvement interventions.
The program included:
41 audits from 2019–2022.
20 additional audits in 2023.
Coverage of cobalt, lithium, nickel, mica, and later graphite.
Agreed corrective-action plans.
Follow-up when suppliers failed to implement corrective actions.
Discussions of root causes and support needed to close identified gaps.
Supplier training on responsible-sourcing requirements.
SLR also describes the Better Mining program, where local monitoring agents gather risk information and follow the implementation of corrective actions. SLR Consulting

Volvo Cars' 2025 Annual and Sustainability Report provides broader evidence of recurring activity. The company reported 88 audits and People Policy Assessments at high-risk sites and stated that 85% of corrective-action plans from preceding RBA Validated Assessment Program audits had been addressed. Cision
These are meaningful indicators of a functioning intervention and follow-up process.
However, responsible-sourcing improvements should remain separate from improvements in manufacturing productivity.
Domain C findings
Volvo Cars has evidence-backed capabilities in operational disruption management, supplier-network regionalization, alternative-sourcing strategy, and responsible-sourcing risk mitigation.
The responsible-sourcing program provides a particularly clear example of supplier assessment followed by training, corrective action, and verification.
The public evidence is less complete concerning supplier business-continuity testing, recovery capability development, and supplier-specific resilience improvements.

6. Implications for Siemens Energy
For the TO582 supplier capability-building project, Volvo Cars is most useful as a benchmark for how different organizational functions contribute to supplier capability development.
Three mechanisms are particularly transferable.

First, connect supplier assessments to a defined industrialization process. Volvo Cars' documented process links supplier evaluation, manufacturing assessment, capacity verification, and production approval. Siemens Energy could use a similar sequence to connect supplier capability findings to qualification and ramp-up decisions.

Second, integrate supplier development with operational performance management. The Ridgeville example shows supplier coaching embedded directly in material-flow and production-continuity responsibilities. This is relevant for Siemens Energy's complex industrial suppliers, where delivery reliability often depends on detailed capacity, scheduling, and process coordination.

Third, treat corrective-action closure as a structured capability-building activity. The SLR example shows the value of identifying a gap, agreeing on corrective action, following up, providing support, and checking implementation. Siemens Energy could extend this logic beyond compliance to production-system performance.
What Siemens Energy should not assume

The public evidence does not establish that Volvo Cars has a universally standardized supplier-development curriculum, a formal supplier capability maturity ladder, or proven supplier-wide productivity gains.
Consequently, a Siemens Energy model should not copy assumed practices that cannot be demonstrated.

A useful next research step would be to investigate Volvo Cars' VSIM methodology, including its intervention triggers, standard work, problem-solving procedures, engineering resources, closure criteria, and follow-up process.
These are the operational details most likely to distinguish a genuinely developmental supplier program from a supplier performance-management system.
7. Overall conclusion

Volvo Cars demonstrates a supplier-development approach built around technical qualification, manufacturing readiness, plant-level operational engagement, localization support, and risk-based corrective action.

The strongest available evidence shows that Volvo Cars does more than evaluate suppliers. Its personnel and partners can provide training, coaching, process-related assistance, and structured follow-up when supplier gaps are identified.
Nevertheless, the public record supports a more qualified conclusion than claiming a comprehensive supplier manufacturing-excellence program.
The most important unanswered question is how Volvo Cars measures and sustains improvements in the supplier's own operating capabilities after an intervention.
That question should be resolved, where possible, before applying the 16-criterion scoring framework.

Volvo Group | Supplier Capability Benchmark
Evidence reviewed: 14 October 2026. Ratings describe maturity visible in public evidence; historical, regional, role-based and pilot observations retain their stated scope.
1. Summary and scope

Volvo Group combines formal supplier qualification, launch gates and low-performing-supplier escalation with documented Volvo CE production-development cases. The strongest operating and learning evidence is historical and divisional; it does not establish uniform Group-wide deployment or tested supplier recovery.

Overall maturity: 3.57 / 5. Evidence coverage: 12/16 criteria. A Future business readiness: 3.00 (3/5); B Supplier production-system capability: 4.71 (7/7); C Resilience and continuity: 3.00 (2/4). Domains have equal weight; NE is excluded. These are evidence-bounded maturity ratings, not enterprise performance. Audit completed 17 October 2026.
2. Supplier selection and support delivery

Supplier qualification, current performance status and selection for intensive capability-building are separate decisions. The evidence below distinguishes the signal for attention, the people involved, the intervention and its verification.

Before award. Purchasing screens prospective suppliers, then Short SEM gathers company capability and quality history. RFQ responses include preliminary APQP, technical-specification review, capacity assessment, special characteristics and potential Tier 2 suppliers; gaps can require an action plan. On-site SEM is required per manufacturing location shipping to a Volvo Group site. Its 11 dimensions make capability assessment broader than size or spend alone. Trucks and other divisions use different pass scores. [VG1][VG5]

Critical processes. Index Audits focus on production technologies critical to vehicle/product function and apply to supply partners, sub-suppliers and subcontractors. They are required before award and can also support process improvement or investigation. This is an explicit complexity/criticality-based route; it is separate from the general SEM score. [VG1]

suppliers. The portal scorecard tracks PPM, QPM, delivery precision and service level, as well as prior audit/incident signals. Volvo reviews indicators monthly. Negative trends or significant abnormalities can move a supplier into LPS; the issue can be scoped to one part, multiple parts or the supplier organization. The public manual does not provide a universal formula combining strategic importance, spend, geography and performance into one priority rank. [VG1][VG2]

Sustainability risk is a separate route. The 2025 annual report reports 254 on-site audits of prospective and existing supply partners. Direct-material partners in high-risk countries receive additional risk analysis; indirect-material partners in high-risk countries are audited above a contract-value threshold. These results inform sourcing and development, but the audit count measures due diligence, not production-system improvement. [VG3]
How support is prioritized: a less uniform historical picture

The Chalmers Purchasing Management compilation contains a Volvo 3P business-unit interview describing support concentrated on suppliers with declining or poor quality, especially when their components were important. It contrasts that intervention logic with lower-intensity management of satisfactory suppliers. The interview also describes QPM and SEM feedback and early supplier participation in product/process development. This is a course-based case chapter drawing on a single business professional, so it carries less weight than a peer-reviewed multi-site study. It is useful evidence of one historical targeting logic, not a current Group-wide resource-allocation rule. [P11]

Interpretation: this adds a qualification to the report’s strong Volvo CE findings. Supplier development can be selective and problem-driven even when a formal supplier system exists. A group-level manual tells the analyst what can trigger action; the case evidence explains how assistance worked in a particular setting. The chapter should preserve both observations rather than generalize intensive coaching to all suppliers or infer that a premium supplier category is itself a capability-development programme.
Resources, scale and measurement

Identify → A shared SEM, Index Audit and monthly scorecard flag a pre-award, launch or in-production gap. The thresholds are clearest for admission: ≥80% for trucks, ≥70% for other divisions, and no stopping-parameter failure. For existing suppliers, negative trends or abnormality bring case-based LPS consideration. [VG1]

Engage → The buyer, SQE/SDE, quality manager and supplier management participate according to the issue. In APQP, the supplier names a project leader and cross-functional team; Volvo names an SQE/SDE. In LPS, the warning letter goes to supplier quality leaders, with higher management joining as escalation rises. [VG1]

Improve → For launch, use APQP reviews, technical specification checks, process audits, significant production runs, control plans and Run at Rate. For production incidents, contain, apply 8D root-cause work, update controls and audit the process. Current European Volvo CE supplier-development roles also describe tailored mentoring and Lean/VPS productivity projects. This evidence supports hands-on development in that business unit, but does not prove identical staffing in every Volvo Group company. [VG1][VG4]

Measure and sustain → The supplier scorecard reports PPM, QPM, delivery precision and service level. LPS exit requires improved performance and implemented process improvements; failure to meet a stage’s deadline moves the supplier upward, while success moves it to monitoring. The manual asks suppliers to target their largest problem areas and show positive trends in incidents and recurrence. 8D effectiveness is checked by 20 working days unless separately agreed, and lessons are extended to similar products/processes. [VG1][VG2]

Scale → Common supplier portal, manual, RFQ/SEM/Index Audit templates, phased PPAP and scorecards provide a shared operating system. Regional business units then provide different levels of direct development; the Volvo CE Europe role is a concrete example. Public sources do not reveal engineer-to-supplier ratios, intervention cost or global outcome distribution. [VG1][VG4]

3. Future business readiness
Domain A: 3.00 / 5; 3/5 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

Future demand and launch needs are translated into APQP and phased PPAP gates. The supplier RFQ includes a Capacity Assessment Sheet and potential Tier 2 list. A Significant Production Run validates process stability, cycle and throughput with real production conditions; Run at Rate then checks the required capacity across lines, machines and tooling. Volvo’s SQE and the supplier agree the production-run quantity and timing. This is a useful capacity-confidence benchmark for high-complexity components, although its rate-based automotive thresholds need adaptation to low-volume production. [VG1]

The Group’s purchasing roadmap explicitly names cross-functional planning, readiness at launch, supply-network development and risk/crisis management. Its 2025 annual report warns that electrification increases dependence on new suppliers/materials while declining conventional components can threaten incumbent supplier viability. These are strategic context for readiness rather than supplier-level pass/fail metrics. [VG6][VG3]
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

SEM and phased PPAP/capacity gates identify gaps but are insufficient alone under the guide. A Volvo CE Bangalore development-engineer role describes liaison across supplier, purchasing, engineering and operations, new-part development and supplier improvements in quality, efficiency and cost, including hydraulics/powertrain manufacturing processes. These are intended practical contributions, not reported project results. [RV1]

Capability target: a supplier learns to industrialize a complex process and meet requirements, not merely submit approval evidence. Investigate the actual technical intervention, supplier staffing, qualification trial and later repeatability. The role page was indexed in this pass but direct retrieval was unavailable; it must not be used as proof of deployed coverage.
Equipment procurement research: a diagnosis and proposal, not proven implementation

Kloos and Käkelä’s 2016 Volvo Powertrain thesis studies production-equipment procurement delays using focus groups with Volvo personnel and supplier interviews. It links the findings to supplier-development theory and proposes an updated Volvo Equipment Procurement Model. The accessible abstract does not demonstrate implementation of the proposed model or verified reductions in procurement delay. Equipment suppliers are also a different population from recurring vehicle-component suppliers. [P10]

Interpretation: the thesis makes a useful connection to long-lead industrial production. Capability gaps can sit in the design, communication and coordination of a production system before it is installed. For the report, however, this remains an investigative lead: inspect the actual project phases, responsibility handoffs and validation results before claiming a new readiness capability. A proposal produced for a company is not evidence that the company operates it. The prescriptive evidence supports A2/A3/A5 at 3 pending executed supplier-readiness evidence; A1 and A4 are NE because the relevant supplier-level processes are insufficiently evidenced.
4. Supplier production-system capability
Domain B: 4.71 / 5; 7/7 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

Volvo Group provides an unusually explicit workflow: capability screen (Short SEM and on-site SEM) → technology/process audit → APQP and phased PPAP → monthly operational scorecard → corrective action or three-stage LPS → effectiveness verification and monitoring. The manual connects shop-floor evidence to escalation rather than treating certification as the outcome. [VG1]

Key measures and gates: SEM score and stopping parameters; process audit findings; product/process/capacity PPAP approval; OEE, cycle and throughput evidence in the Significant Production Run; PPM and QPM; delivery precision/service level; 8D response deadlines; LPS stage exit based on improved results and implemented process changes. Volvo CE Europe additionally describes Lean/VPS mentoring, while the historical CE/SIAP case below reports scoped production improvements; current Group-wide post-program gains remain unverified. [VG1][VG2][VG4]
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Case evidence: Volvo Group’s 2016 magazine describes Volvo CE’s joint diagnosis, education, kaizen and action plans, with suppliers owning the process. At SIAP, support beginning in 2011 included root-cause methods, SMED, kanban and layout changes. By 2016, methods were spreading beyond the pilot; reported WIP fell 54%, lead time 69% and space 25%. A second cooling-system supplier reduced lead time from about 11 days to 5–6. [D1]
What the supplier VPS case actually explains

The documented Volvo CE evidence should be read as a development sequence rather than only as three improvement percentages. SIAP’s case links joint diagnosis and practical methods to supplier ownership and extension beyond an initial line; the second cooling-system supplier provides an additional application. That sequence is what makes the historical programme useful for capability benchmarking. It separates an assessment of a bottleneck from technical work on the production system and subsequent supplier use of the method. [D1]

Interpretation: the intervention has both an operating dimension and a learning dimension. Smaller batches, layout changes and replenishment methods affect the system; repeated employee participation and ownership affect the supplier’s ability to keep improving it. The same case therefore can inform B2, B4, B5 and B7, but should not be counted as four independent demonstrations. Its results do not establish equivalent practice across all Volvo Group divisions.
5. Resilience and continuity
Domain C: 3.00 / 5; 2/4 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

The same system protects continuity: supplier capacity checks and Tier 2 disclosure before launch; monthly scorecards and early negative-trend detection; 24-hour plant protection when nonconforming material appears; third-party firewalls and backup-sourcing cases at higher LPS levels. Volvo Group’s purchasing roadmap adds supply-network mapping, risk/crisis management and lessons learned. The 2025 annual report highlights material scarcity and transition risk in both new and declining technologies. Public sources do not show common recovery-time targets or avoided-disruption results. [VG1][VG3][VG6]
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Volvo’s non-automotive WebEDI page offers an accessible connection route for suppliers lacking EDI capability or with low delivery volumes. The buyer initiates connection with the EDI team; suppliers nominate users and receive access details. E-learning and online training support use of schedules, dispatch advice and invoices. This demonstrates buyer-supported information-exchange capability, not a risk map alone. [RV3]

Decision boundary: keep as a supporting digital-enablement mechanism relevant to small/low-volume suppliers, not a complete continuity benchmark. Tested fallback, disruption recovery and maintained delivery gains are not published on the page. The LPS firewall/backup-source controls in existing research likewise require a retained-capability case before being called resilience development.
What a leading production score does not imply

A capable production-improvement programme does not establish tested recovery capability. WebEDI onboarding can improve information exchange, and LPS actions can verify an immediate correction, but neither alone shows that a supplier can reconfigure production after a severe disruption. C-domain ratings reflect these evidence limits. Likewise, a missing publicly disclosed leading indicator is not a reason to erase the historical supplier outcomes: an advance-warning measure, an intervention and retained learning are different parts of the evidence chain.

8. Implications for Siemens Energy
Volvo Group offers several practical lessons for designing a supplier-development operating model.
8.1 Separate supplier assurance from supplier development
Volvo's SEM, audits, APQP, and PPAP provide a structured way to identify supplier capability gaps.
Its Supplier VPS activities demonstrate how those gaps can then be addressed through practical improvement interventions.
For Siemens Energy, this suggests maintaining two complementary functions.
Supplier assurance: Determines whether the supplier meets required standards and manufacturing readiness.
Supplier development: Helps the supplier build the capability needed to meet those standards consistently and independently.
The two functions should be connected, but their outputs should not be confused.
8.2 Use phased manufacturing-readiness verification
Volvo's phased PPAP provides a useful model for industrial equipment supply chains.
Siemens Energy could adapt the underlying logic:
Stage
Key question
Product conformity
Can the supplier manufacture the required component?
Process capability
Can the supplier manufacture it consistently?
Capacity readiness
Can the supplier manufacture the required volume within the necessary lead time?
This would be particularly relevant for complex components involving long manufacturing cycles and specialized equipment.
The automotive-specific test quantities and production rates would need to be adapted to Siemens Energy's manufacturing context.
8.3 Develop technology-specific supplier assessment methods
Volvo's Index Audit approach demonstrates the value of evaluating critical manufacturing technologies individually.
For Siemens Energy, supplier capability assessments could be tailored to particular technologies rather than relying only on general quality-management certifications.
Examples include heavy forgings, welding, castings, machining, coatings, and special processes.
The assessment should identify technical weaknesses that can then be addressed through engineering support.
8.4 Establish an intensive supplier-development track
Volvo CE's Supplier VPS Programme targeted important suppliers and provided hands-on production-system assistance.
Siemens Energy could use a similar approach for selected strategic suppliers.
Potential selection factors include:
Strategic importance.
Critical manufacturing constraints.
Single-source exposure.
Future demand requirements.
Operational performance gaps.
Supplier willingness to participate.
The objective should be to develop lasting supplier capabilities, not simply resolve immediate delivery problems.
8.5 Develop supplier problem-solving capability
Volvo's corrective-action framework emphasizes containment, root-cause analysis, permanent correction, and effectiveness verification.
For Siemens Energy, this suggests that supplier-development interventions should not end when an immediate problem disappears.
The supplier should demonstrate that it understands the root cause and can prevent recurrence.
This is particularly important for recurring quality problems and constrained manufacturing processes.
8.6 Measure sustained capability improvement
The most important evidence gap in Volvo's public reporting is the limited availability of long-term supplier-development results.
Siemens Energy could address this by requiring every development project to document:
Evidence stage
Required information
Business need
Why the supplier capability matters
Initial capability gap
What the supplier cannot currently achieve
Baseline performance
Quality, capacity, lead time, yield, or other relevant measures
Intervention
What Siemens Energy and the supplier actually changed
Implementation
Evidence that the change was introduced
Verified result
Measured improvement
Sustainment
Evidence that the improvement remained effective
Supplier ownership
Evidence that the supplier can maintain the capability independently

For example, a capacity-development project should document the initial bottleneck, actual demonstrated capacity, equipment or process changes, repeat capacity testing, and subsequent sustained performance.
A production-system project should document baseline work in progress, lead time, throughput, or quality performance, followed by measured results after implementation.
This would allow Siemens Energy to distinguish between:
Assessing a supplier, helping a supplier improve, and developing a lasting supplier capability.
9. Overall Conclusion

Volvo Group demonstrates a supplier-development system built around technical qualification, supplier industrialization, production-capacity verification, supplier quality management, operational improvement, and supply-network resilience.
Its strongest public evidence concerns three capabilities.
1. Supplier industrialization and manufacturing readiness
Volvo uses APQP, phased PPAP, Significant Production Runs, Run at Rate, and capacity assessments to verify that suppliers can manufacture products consistently and at the required volume.
These mechanisms are supported by designated supplier quality and development engineering roles.
2. Hands-on supplier manufacturing improvement
Volvo Construction Equipment's Supplier VPS Programme demonstrates direct supplier capability-building through Lean methods, workforce education, process redesign, and continuous improvement.
The SIAP case provides measurable evidence of reduced work in progress, shorter production lead time, and lower production-floor space requirements.
3. Structured supplier performance recovery
Volvo's Low Performing Supplier process connects performance monitoring to corrective actions, management escalation, and evidence-based recovery.
The process provides a repeatable framework for responding to persistent supplier problems.
Principal evidence gaps
Despite these strengths, public sources do not establish:
The current scale of intensive supplier-development coaching.
Aggregate improvements in supplier productivity or manufacturing capacity.
The percentage of underperforming suppliers successfully recovered.
Long-term sustainment of supplier improvements.
Quantified resilience outcomes.
A systematic supplier financial-turnaround program.
Final assessment
Volvo Group provides credible evidence of genuine supplier capability-building, especially in production-system improvement and manufacturing readiness.
The Supplier VPS Programme is particularly relevant for Siemens Energy because it demonstrates how an industrial manufacturer can work directly with suppliers to improve their production systems.
However, the strongest quantitative cases are historical, and their results should not be generalized to every Volvo Group supplier.
For Siemens Energy, the most transferable principle is:
Structured supplier assessment → Engineering-led intervention → Implemented manufacturing change → Verified operational improvement → Supplier-owned capability.
No benchmark scores have been assigned.

Supply-chain tier describes a supplier’s position in the chain. Quality classifications describe capability. Sustainability categories describe a different risk domain. The benchmark should keep these fields separate, even when one supplier appears in all three. Volkswagen’s Formel Q document assigns Tier 1 responsibility for communicating requirements and managing risks in its sub-supply chain. [2]

The Responsible Supply Chain system assigns low, medium, or high sustainability risk using business-model and risk data. Country exposure raises some initially low-risk sites to medium risk. The classification guides the package of actions. This is evidence of risk-based targeting for sustainability, rather than a universal rule for operational coaching. [6]

Research implication: qualify suppliers for business first, then determine the support need. A supplier’s strategic role alone does not reveal whether the need concerns technology, throughput, quality, or continuity. Public sources reviewed do not publish one formula combining spend, criticality, size, and assessed gaps into a support-priority score.

The 2025 S-Rating process begins with supplier self-assessment and external validation. Risk-based audits add scrutiny where needed. Suppliers address findings through action plans, followed by desktop reviews or further audits. Volkswagen also offers workshops and online learning in eight languages. These activities build sustainability-related skills. [6]

The 2025 report also makes the sustainability feedback loop clearer: risk analysis is updated regularly; high-risk suppliers may receive targeted actions; audits, grievances, and media monitoring can trigger supplier-specific remediation. Action effectiveness is checked through desktop reviews or follow-up audits, and the ReSC System evaluates standard actions using an Input–Output–Outcome–Impact approach. This is closed-loop evidence for sustainability due diligence, not production-system performance. [6]

Volkswagen reported 87% coverage of total procurement volume by relevant direct suppliers with a positive S-Rating in 2025, against an 85% target. This measure reflects procurement coverage, rather than 87% of supplier locations or an operational maturity score. [7]

Keep the S-Rating separate from Formel Q quality classifications. A sustainability result does not establish production capacity, defect performance, or recovery readiness. The benchmark should record the assessment topic beside every rating to prevent false comparisons.

Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.
Launch and capacity preparation

Volkswagen’s 2025 procurement report describes audits early in new projects, purchased-part support through project milestones, and on-site attention for complex components. A production-capacity acceptance test closes this launch sequence. During series production, Volkswagen compares demand with capacity and reviews adjustments, including when existing components enter new projects. [1]

The 2025 risk report also flags local-content requirements and constraints on local supplier pools. This establishes a localization-related risk context, but does not show a defined supplier localization-readiness or capability-building process. [10]

This approach places readiness checks before demand reaches full production. For benchmarking, the useful feature is the connection between the project schedule and physical production evidence. The reviewed report does not publish common acceptance thresholds, test duration, or supplier-level pass rates.
Strategic collaboration through FAST

FAST, launched in 2015, provides a historical example of future-oriented supplier engagement. Volkswagen’s 2019 report describes regular exchanges, shared assessments of the previous year, and discussions about innovation and globalization. Selected partners presented innovations to senior procurement and technical-development representatives. Named partners included Infineon, Microsoft, Cree/Wolfspeed, and AVL List. [8]

Volkswagen reported strategic discussions with 55 suppliers across 61 competencies in 2016. Those counts describe the program at the time, rather than current participation or the full supplier base. [9]

Evidence assessment: strong evidence for a launch-readiness process and a documented historical partnership model. The sources reviewed do not confirm the present membership or operating rules of FAST. A strategic meeting or program membership alone does not prove successful capability transfer.

4. Supplier production-system capability
Domain B: 3.43 / 5; 7/7 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.

Formel Q Capability, ninth edition dated December 2022, combines quality-system expectations with process and product assessment. Delivery or quality failures, site relocations, and significant process changes trigger further attention. Its problem-analysis method investigates causes at the relevant production location, assigns corrective and containment actions with dates and responsibilities, and requires proof of effectiveness. [2]

A public CARIAD nomination agreement offers a concrete contractual example. A facility with a B or C quality-capability rating must implement measures toward an A rating. The supplier must submit an action plan within the specified period, no later than two weeks after the audit, and confirm effectiveness after implementation. These terms apply to the disclosed agreement. They do not establish one current deadline for every Group supplier. [3]

Evidence assessment: strong evidence for diagnosis, accountability, and follow-up. The evidence supports a structured improvement requirement. Public material reviewed provides less detail on the amount of hands-on coaching, supplier staff development, or measured reductions in defects and production losses.

The PowerCo/QuantumScape case establishes a production-specific joint engineering route and implemented pilot milestones. That case supports B2=4, B4/B5=3 and a defined B7 learning route. The PowerCo–QuantumScape case remains a different development mechanism. It addresses a frontier manufacturing technology through joint engineering, equipment and pilot milestones. Ntinga addresses the readiness and operating methods of existing manufacturing businesses entering an automotive supply relationship. Both can be useful benchmarks, but the analysis should not merge them into one standardized Volkswagen programme. [Existing D10–D13; R1–R2]

Interpretation: the comparison suggests two intervention pathways to investigate with an industrial sponsor. One develops a supplier’s organizational and operating methods; the other develops a specific technical production capability. The appropriate pathway depends on the gap. This is an analytical implication of the cases, not a claim that Volkswagen publicly uses this two-path classification. PowerCo’s licensing rights still do not establish realized commercial output, and Ntinga’s commercial participation still does not establish sustained throughput gains. B2/B4/B5 are assessed separately.
5. Resilience and continuity
Domain C: 3.50 / 5; 4/4 criteria scored.
Layer 1 — documented practices. Prescriptive requirements and intended roles are identified separately from demonstrated use.
Financial exposure and supply intervention

Volkswagen’s 2025 risk report describes financial reviews before project commitments and continuing monitoring by procurement specialists in restructuring and supply reliability. The report also discusses early warnings, task forces, strategic supplier relationships, and longer-term commodity arrangements. These measures address risks from insolvency, constrained investment, and material shortages. [4]

The disclosures identify concrete exposures: supplier financial distress, rising material and financing costs, geopolitical and shipping interruptions, climate events, and concentration in critical battery materials. Volkswagen describes ongoing financial monitoring, early-warning systems, task forces, and mitigation structures. It also reports analyzing demand and raw-material trends and adjusting regional capacity when demand falls. These support risk sensing and response; public evidence does not quantify supplier recovery outcomes or demonstrate a standard supplier-localization program. [4,10]

The practical research question is how an identified exposure changes the intervention. Monitoring detects a risk. Capability building requires a supplier to improve a process, resource, or recovery routine. The reviewed disclosure does not provide a standard supplier recovery-time target or quantified results for continuity training.
Semiconductor coordination across supplier tiers

Volkswagen’s August 2023 announcement describes a shift toward specifying electronic parts with Tier 1 partners and buying strategically important semiconductors directly. Its Semiconductor Sourcing Committee brings together procurement and development representatives from brands, Group Components, and CARIAD. Volkswagen linked improved parts visibility to identifying alternatives faster and reducing hardware variants. COMPASS began in 2022 in response to the chip crisis. [5]

This example shows how a dependency below the direct supplier changes the engagement model. The transferable lesson is to involve technical decision makers in continuity planning. Faster substitution still depends on engineering approval and product requirements. The announcement describes the intended mechanism without proving a specific reduction in outage time.
Layer 2 — capability-building interventions and evidence gaps

Current procurement material describes supply-risk work and continuous demand/capacity matching. Those are useful sensing and response elements; they do not establish a supplier learning to recover a disrupted critical process. Catena-X visibility, task forces and alternative sourcing must not be collapsed into a single proven capability-building intervention. [RW1]

Next evidence: ask for a supplier crisis case where Volkswagen engineers changed recovery arrangements, qualified an alternate process or transferred skills, then tested or observed maintained capability. Separate temporary financial support from a viable, independently sustained operating change.

9. Extended Deep Research - Volkswagen Group: Supplier Capability-Building Benchmark
Research scope: Volkswagen Group, including Group-wide procurement and supplier-management systems. Brand-specific examples are identified separately rather than treated as universal Group practices.

Evidence cutoff: October 15, 2026.Approach: Identify actual supplier-development capabilities, implementation mechanisms, organizational ownership, examples, and outcomes. Use the Siemens Energy 16-criterion framework for coverage, but do not score or rank capabilities yet.
1. Executive summary

Volkswagen Group has a particularly well-documented supplier-development system spanning supplier industrialization, manufacturing readiness, quality management, strategic supplier collaboration, and supply continuity.
Its strongest differentiator is the connection between supplier assessments and direct operational intervention.

Volkswagen's 2025 Annual Report explicitly describes providing support during supplier industrialization, deploying supplier-management personnel on-site for complex components, checking production capacity before launch, and continuing demand-versus-capacity monitoring during series production. These activities go beyond purchasing requirements and supplier audits. They demonstrate a supplier-management function that participates in production readiness and operational problem resolution. Volkswagen Group Annual Report 2025

Volkswagen reported that 6,470 suppliers received sustainability training in 2025 and that 7,050 direct suppliers improved their sustainability self-assessment scores. Central finding
Volkswagen provides unusually clear public evidence that its own personnel actively support suppliers' manufacturing readiness and industrialization.

The principal remaining evidence gap is the outcome of those interventions at individual supplier plants. Volkswagen documents what its teams do more clearly than it discloses before-and-after changes in supplier throughput, first-pass yield, downtime, or long-term operational independence.
That distinction is important for Siemens Energy's benchmarking project.
2. Supplier-development operating model
Volkswagen's supplier-development activities are distributed across procurement, supplier management, quality assurance, engineering, production, logistics, and risk management.
The company does not publicly describe these activities as one consolidated supplier-development department. Instead, the evidence points to several interconnected operating functions.

Its risk report separately identifies procurement personnel specializing in supplier restructuring and supply reliability. Volkswagen Group Annual Report 2025
How Volkswagen develops suppliers operationally
The company's documented approach can be reconstructed into five stages:
Stage 1: Supplier assessment and selection
Before awarding business, Volkswagen evaluates whether suppliers can meet technical, quality, production, and commercial requirements.
Stage 2: Industrialization planning
During new vehicle projects, supplier-management teams follow the maturity of purchased parts and their production processes against project milestones.
Stage 3: On-site technical support
Complex components can require Volkswagen supplier-management specialists to work at supplier sites, helping address industrialization issues before production begins.
Stage 4: Production-capacity verification
Volkswagen conducts capacity acceptance tests to confirm that suppliers can meet required production volumes.
Stage 5: Series-production monitoring and intervention
Once production begins, Volkswagen monitors supplier capacity and delivery capability, coordinates necessary capacity adjustments, and responds to emerging supply problems.

This sequence is directly supported by Volkswagen's 2025 procurement disclosures. Earlier reports provide additional operational detail on tooling experts, simulated production runs, and milestone-based performance testing. geschaeftsbericht2016.volkswagenag.com
Why this matters: Volkswagen's supplier-development model is integrated into the product lifecycle. It does not end when the supplier receives a contract.
3. Domain A: Future Business Readiness
This domain examines how Volkswagen prepares suppliers for new technologies, product launches, capacity requirements, and geographic expansion.
A1. Supplier technical capability assessment
Volkswagen uses a structured system of technical and quality requirements to evaluate suppliers.
One central element is Formel Q, Volkswagen's supplier quality-management framework.
The Group's March 2022 customer-specific requirements reference several associated systems:
Formel Q Capability for evaluating supplier manufacturing and quality capabilities.
Formel Q Konkret for contractual quality-management requirements.
Formel Q New Parts Integral for production-part approval and maturity-related requirements.
Formel Q Capability Software for software supplier assessment.
QPN-I for maturity-level assurance during development.
The requirements also establish the use of certified auditors for supplier process assessments. IATF Global Oversight
Capability identified: A common assessment architecture covering product, process, and increasingly software-development capabilities.
This standardization allows Volkswagen to evaluate suppliers against consistent expectations across complex programs.

Limitation: Formel Q is primarily evidence of a supplier qualification and assurance system. Its existence does not establish that Volkswagen provides extensive hands-on coaching to every supplier that fails an assessment.
A2. Supplier industrialization and launch readiness
This is one of Volkswagen's most clearly documented operational capabilities.
Its 2016 Annual Report described a global network of tooling and industrialization specialists supporting purchased-parts management.
These experts were involved in:
Monitoring tooling development.
Supporting selected components before the start of series production.
Responding to component problems during series production.
Exchanging technical experience across global projects.
Conducting supplier performance tests at product-development milestones.
The specialists worked closely with plant quality-assurance teams to confirm that suppliers possessed sufficient production capacity for vehicle launches. geschaeftsbericht2016.volkswagenag.com
Volkswagen's 2025 Annual Report confirms that the broader industrialization-support model remains part of its procurement activities. Volkswagen Group Annual Report 2025
Capability identified: Technical supplier industrialization support through specialized personnel, milestone reviews, tooling oversight, and launch capacity verification.
Why it matters for Siemens Energy: This is directly relevant to suppliers producing technically complex, low-volume, or long-lead-time components.

The transferable practice is not necessarily Volkswagen's specific approval procedure. It is the use of specialists to identify manufacturing constraints before those constraints become delivery failures.
A3. Production-capacity verification
Volkswagen does not rely exclusively on a supplier's promised capacity.
Its procurement documentation describes formal acceptance testing of supplier production capacity before the beginning of vehicle production.
An earlier 2018 report provides additional detail: Volkswagen conducted simulated series production at supplier facilities during pre-series development to detect potential disruptions.
The process included multistage performance testing and cooperation between purchased-parts management and plant quality assurance. Volkswagen Annual Report 2018
A typical application would examine whether a supplier's equipment, staffing, material flow, and production processes can sustain the required output.
That last sentence describes the operational implication of a production-capacity test, rather than a published list of Volkswagen's specific test parameters.
Capability identified: Supplier-site production validation before launch.
Limitation: Volkswagen does not publicly disclose detailed acceptance thresholds, test duration, or the proportion of suppliers requiring subsequent capacity-improvement intervention.
A4. Strategic supplier technology development
Volkswagen also develops future supply capabilities through early collaboration with strategically important suppliers.
Case: FAST — Future Automotive Supply Tracks
Volkswagen introduced the FAST initiative in 2015 to strengthen cooperation with key suppliers.
The initiative focused on identifying suppliers with specialized technological capabilities and involving them earlier in product development.
By October 2016, Volkswagen reported:
55 strategic supplier partners.
61 fields of competence.
Earlier supplier participation in innovation cycles.
Closer integration of supplier production networks.
Volkswagen stated that early supplier involvement had already enabled supplier ideas to be incorporated into product-development processes. Volkswagen Group
A named example was LG Electronics, which became a strategic electronics partner within FAST and entered a joint agreement with Volkswagen to develop connected-car technologies. Volkswagen Group
Capability identified: Strategic supplier identification, early technical collaboration, and integration of external innovation.

Limitation: The participation figures are historical. The reviewed sources do not establish that FAST continues today in its original format or report systematic before-and-after improvements in supplier capabilities.
A5. Local supplier development and regionalization
Volkswagen has also pursued supplier development by combining local engineering resources with procurement functions.
In 2023, Volkswagen announced the creation of Volkswagen Group China Technology Company, also known as 100%TechCo.
The company's purpose was to integrate local development and procurement capabilities more closely and involve Chinese suppliers earlier in product development.
Volkswagen expected the unit to involve more than 2,000 employees from R&D and procurement and to help shorten product-development timelines by approximately 30%. Volkswagen Group

In 2024, Volkswagen and XPENG formalized a joint development and sourcing agreement for vehicles intended for the Chinese market. The agreement included sourcing cooperation for common vehicle and platform components. Volkswagen Group
Capability identified: Localized technical sourcing and supplier integration as part of faster product development.

Limitation: The 30% development-time improvement was a strategic objective, not verified supplier-level productivity improvement. XPENG's role is a technology-development partnership, not a conventional supplier coaching case.
Domain A findings
Volkswagen has documented capabilities in supplier qualification, industrialization, production-capacity validation, technology partnerships, and local supplier integration.
The most directly transferable mechanisms for Siemens Energy are supplier-site industrialization support and production-capacity validation.
These mechanisms connect technical assessments to the supplier's actual ability to manufacture and deliver.

B2. Supplier manufacturing-process stabilization
Volkswagen's purchased-parts management function has historically monitored supplier manufacturing processes to identify problems before they threaten production.
Its 2020 Annual Report describes a sequence beginning with supplier audits before nomination, followed by industrialization maturity monitoring and final confirmation of production capacity.

This is more substantial than final-product inspection because the focus includes the supplier's production system.
Limitation: Public sources do not consistently disclose whether countermeasures are designed by Volkswagen specialists, supplier engineers, or jointly.
B3. On-site supplier intervention
Volkswagen's 2025 Annual Report confirms that complex components frequently require supplier-management personnel to provide on-site support.
This is the most direct evidence that Volkswagen deploys personnel to suppliers rather than relying entirely on remote performance monitoring. Volkswagen Group Annual Report 2025
However, the published description does not specify the standard on-site intervention toolkit.
For example, the available disclosures do not establish whether these visits systematically include:
Value-stream mapping.
Standardized-work redesign.
Bottleneck analysis and line balancing.
Statistical process-control implementation.
Equipment-maintenance improvement.
Operator training.
Formal knowledge transfer and exit criteria.
Capability identified: Direct supplier-site technical support.
Evidence gap: The detailed content, intervention intensity, and measurable effects of that support remain largely undisclosed.
B4. Supplier logistics performance improvement
A particularly valuable source is a peer-reviewed research paper involving Volkswagen Group Logistics employees and academic researchers.
Case: Volkswagen Group Logistics supplier-development optimization
In 2023, researchers published Volkswagen Group Logistics Applies Operations Research to Optimize Supplier Development in the INFORMS Journal on Applied Analytics.
The paper describes an existing collaborative supplier-development approach intended to identify suppliers disrupting logistics operations and apply improvement measures.
Volkswagen Group Logistics sought to improve how it selected and allocated those measures.
The research team developed a three-stage approach:
Prepare supplier and logistics-performance data.
Evaluate possible supplier-development measures.
Allocate improvement measures using optimization methods.
The analytical framework combined Monte Carlo simulation with a knapsack optimization model.
The approach was validated using 18 existing less-than-truckload logistics networks.
The researchers found that the approach could achieve average cost savings of 31% compared with the previous allocation procedure. PubsOnLine
This is among the strongest supplier-development examples identified because it documents an actual decision problem, analytical method, implementation context, and quantified potential benefit.

Important qualification: The 31% figure is a modeled or validated potential cost improvement reported by the researchers. It should not be represented as a verified 31% reduction in Volkswagen's realized logistics spending.
Capability identified: Data-driven supplier development that allocates improvement resources to suppliers according to expected system-wide operational benefits.

Potential application to Siemens Energy: Supplier-development resources are scarce. Volkswagen's approach suggests that intervention selection should consider both individual supplier weaknesses and the consequences of those weaknesses for the broader production network.
B5. Quality problem-solving and corrective action
Volkswagen's quality requirements include supplier defect reporting, recurring product and process verification, and coordination of necessary corrective action.
A key element is the ability to connect supplier manufacturing-process issues to measurable quality incidents.
The official customer-specific requirements also identify the Supplier Cockpit Quality Status (ONE-SCQ) platform for quality incident and parts-per-million defect information. IATF Global Oversight
Capability identified: Digital quality-performance visibility connected to a formal corrective-action and escalation process.
Limitation: The reviewed evidence does not establish the frequency with which Volkswagen personnel directly facilitate root-cause workshops or train suppliers in specific problem-solving methods.
B6. Supplier technical transformation
Volkswagen's supplier collaboration includes helping its industrial ecosystem transition toward electrification and new manufacturing technologies.
Its 2025 Group Supplier Awards provide examples.
Magna International received recognition for the rapid joint development and industrialization of a complex battery-cover solution.
Astemo was recognized for transitioning from internal-combustion-related supply toward electromobility.
Texas Instruments received recognition for resilient semiconductor supply strategies and investments in manufacturing capabilities. Volkswagen Group
These examples demonstrate the kinds of capability transformations Volkswagen values in its supply base.
However, they require careful interpretation.

The Magna case explicitly references joint development and industrialization. The Astemo and Texas Instruments examples demonstrate supplier achievements, but the awards alone do not prove that Volkswagen directly developed those capabilities.
B7. Sustaining improvements
Volkswagen's recurring audits, production monitoring, capacity checks, and quality reporting create mechanisms for identifying when supplier performance deteriorates.
Its supplier-development research also demonstrates interest in embedding improvement decisions within a repeatable workflow.

Nevertheless, there is insufficient public evidence to establish that Volkswagen systematically measures whether suppliers retain independent problem-solving capabilities after direct assistance ends.
For Siemens Energy, this is an important distinction.
A supplier might satisfy its immediate delivery commitments after Volkswagen intervenes without necessarily having improved its underlying ability to prevent future problems.
Domain B findings
Volkswagen provides credible evidence of supplier production-system assessment, on-site intervention, quality management, logistics improvement, and technical industrialization.
The Volkswagen Group Logistics research case is particularly valuable because it provides an analytical framework for prioritizing supplier-development interventions.
The primary gap is supplier-level evidence connecting specific interventions to sustained manufacturing-performance gains.
5. Domain C: Resilience and Continuity Capability
This domain evaluates how Volkswagen identifies supplier risks, maintains delivery continuity, develops alternatives, and supports recovery.
C1. Supplier financial risk management
Volkswagen's 2025 Annual Report explicitly identifies a dedicated supplier risk-management function within Procurement.
Its responsibilities include evaluating supplier financial conditions before assigning new projects.
Volkswagen also employs procurement personnel specializing in restructuring and supply reliability who continuously monitor supplier financial health.
The company identifies rising input costs, financing constraints, and supplier insolvency as potential causes of production disruption. Volkswagen Group Annual Report 2025
Capability identified: A dedicated organizational mechanism for assessing financial viability and identifying suppliers that may be unable to maintain or expand production.

Limitation: Volkswagen does not publicly disclose standardized supplier financial-rescue measures, intervention budgets, or successful restructuring cases in sufficient detail to benchmark their effectiveness.
C2. Early warning and supplier risk identification
Volkswagen states that Procurement uses early-warning systems to identify supply risks and task-force structures to reduce them.
The broader risk-management approach includes monitoring the supply network for emerging geopolitical, financial, operational, and environmental threats.
Its procurement strategy also emphasizes expanding digital supply-chain transparency and improving the ability to identify risks and develop alternatives. Volkswagen Group Annual Report 2025
Capability identified: Integrated supplier risk monitoring and escalation.
The important distinction is between a system that identifies risk and a system that builds supplier resilience.
Volkswagen clearly demonstrates the former. The latter is supported by its intervention and contingency-management activities, but supplier-specific improvement results are less visible.
C3. Supply disruption response
Volkswagen's 2025 procurement report describes an established crisis-management structure involving Procurement, Quality Assurance, Development, Production, and Logistics.
The function is intended to coordinate action when supplier problems threaten vehicle production. Volkswagen Group Annual Report 2025
The operational mechanisms include:
Identifying potential supply disruption.
Coordinating across responsible business functions.
Reviewing supplier capacity and material availability.
Initiating mitigation or recovery measures.
Using the global supply network to identify alternative technologies or locations where feasible.
Capability identified: Cross-functional supply-crisis management integrated with ongoing procurement and production operations.

Limitation: Public disclosures do not consistently provide supplier-specific recovery timelines, cost of intervention, or evidence that an intervention improved the supplier's ability to withstand subsequent disruptions.
C4. Semiconductor supply resilience
In 2024, Volkswagen introduced a strategic semiconductor management system.
The company moved toward direct relationships with strategically important semiconductor manufacturers and greater influence over component selection within its electronic architecture.
The goal was to protect the availability of critical semiconductor components and improve long-term competitiveness. Volkswagen Group Annual Report 2025
This represents a strategic change in how Volkswagen manages the supply of technically critical components.
Capability identified: Direct engagement with critical upstream manufacturers rather than relying exclusively on immediate Tier 1 suppliers.

Limitation: The available evidence demonstrates a revised sourcing and relationship-management model. It does not establish that Volkswagen directly improved semiconductor manufacturers' operational capabilities.
C5. Supply-chain sustainability and upstream corrective action
Volkswagen also operates a substantially documented supplier-improvement system focused on environmental and social risks.
This is relevant to supplier capability building but should be distinguished from operational resilience and manufacturing productivity.
Responsible Supply Chain System
Volkswagen's Responsible Supply Chain System (ReSC) combines supplier risk classification, self-assessment, audits, corrective-action plans, supplier training, and follow-up verification.
The S-Rating mechanism has been used Group-wide since 2019.
The 2025 reporting process distinguishes suppliers meeting sustainability requirements from those lacking evidence or violating those requirements.
Suppliers requiring corrective action must implement a defined action plan, with effectiveness reviewed through documentation checks or repeat audits. Volkswagen Group Annual Report 2025

Domain C findings

Volkswagen demonstrates an established supplier risk-management system, direct attention to financially vulnerable suppliers, cross-functional crisis response, and strategic management of critical upstream supply chains.
Its sustainability system provides the clearest publicly quantified example of recurring supplier training and corrective-action follow-up.

The principal evidence gap is whether similar capability-building mechanisms are systematically applied to suppliers' operational resilience, including recovery time, inventory flexibility, production redundancy, and continuity testing.

7. Implications for Siemens Energy
Volkswagen's experience suggests that supplier capability building should not be designed as a standalone assessment exercise.
It should connect supplier diagnostics to technical support, improvement activities, and operational follow-up.

This lifecycle orientation is potentially more useful for Siemens Energy than a uniform intervention approach.
7.2 Develop a supplier intervention portfolio
Volkswagen's practices suggest several types of interventions that Siemens Energy could consider:
Technical interventions: Tooling reviews, manufacturing engineering support, capacity validation, industrialization assistance.
Operational interventions: Process-stability improvement, scheduling and material-flow support, quality problem-solving, bottleneck assessment.
Strategic interventions: Technology partnerships, supplier localization, investment-readiness discussions, alternative-source development.
Resilience interventions: Financial risk reviews, contingency planning, recovery preparation, and targeted supply assurance.
These categories are proposed applications to Siemens Energy, not a claim that Volkswagen formally organizes its programs in this manner.
7.3 Prioritize supplier interventions according to system-wide value
The Volkswagen Group Logistics example is particularly instructive.
Rather than selecting suppliers solely because their individual performance is poor, Siemens Energy could prioritize suppliers based on a combination of capability gaps and operational consequences.

For example, a supplier with moderate quality problems but a critical role in a constrained production system might deserve more immediate attention than a supplier with worse performance but ample alternatives.
Volkswagen's operations-research study provides evidence for applying analytical methods to that allocation problem. PubsOnLine
7.4 Build a stronger improvement verification process
Volkswagen's sustainability system demonstrates a structured approach to corrective-action tracking.
Siemens Energy could translate this into a manufacturing-focused sequence:
Assessment → Root-cause diagnosis → Intervention → Implementation → Performance verification → Sustained capability review
The final step is particularly important.
Supplier development should ideally demonstrate that the supplier can independently maintain improved performance, rather than merely complying with an OEM's immediate request.

8. Overall conclusion

Volkswagen Group demonstrates a supplier-development system built around technical qualification, supplier industrialization, manufacturing-process assurance, operational intervention, strategic collaboration, and supply continuity management.
Its public evidence is particularly strong in three areas.
First, Volkswagen explicitly documents supplier-site technical support and pre-production capacity verification.
Second, the Group has a structured production-quality framework covering audits, maturity assurance, approval processes, and corrective-action coordination.

Third, Volkswagen Group Logistics has published an analytical approach to prioritizing supplier-development interventions, providing a useful example of how development resources can be allocated systematically.
However, the evidence does not support an unqualified claim that Volkswagen consistently delivers manufacturing productivity coaching across its entire supplier network.

The most important distinction is between Volkswagen's ability to identify and resolve supplier problems and its ability to create lasting improvements in the supplier's independent operating capabilities.
The former is well documented. The latter requires more detailed supplier-level evidence.

For the Siemens Energy project, Volkswagen is therefore a particularly useful benchmark for connecting supplier assessments, technical intervention, and production readiness into one operating process.

B: How are improvement opportunities converted into gains?
Diagnosis, owned countermeasures, verification and learning over time.
Retain. Improvement process; do not duplicate every operating metric.
B3 Process stability and yield
B: Does the process perform consistently with less loss?
Variation/defect mechanism, process change, control and verified yield/stability.
Retain. Separate stable quality from flow and output.
B4 Flow and constraint management
B: How does the supplier diagnose and remove flow constraints?
VSM, bottleneck/queue/setup analysis, implemented countermeasure and follow-up.
Retain. Tool availability or a capacity test alone is insufficient.
B5 Throughput and lead-time management
B: Does sustainable output/time improve?
Output, cycle or end-to-end lead-time baseline; change and continuing verification.
Retain. A local speed gain is not automatically end-to-end lead-time improvement.
B6 Operating routines
B: How are problems managed in daily operation?
Standard work, daily reviews, named owners, escalation and recurring follow-up.
Retain. Cadence does not prove skills transferred.
B7 Capability building and sustainment
B: Can supplier employees maintain gains and solve future problems?
Teaching, practice, competence verification, supplier ownership and later independent use.
Keep definition as is: Builds supplier employees’ skills and ownership so they can maintain improvements and solve future production problems independently.
C1 Disruption preparedness and response
C: Has supplier recovery capability been developed and tested?
Buyer-assisted recovery design, supplier exercise, corrective learning and response verification.
Retain. A BCP requirement or emergency expedite alone is not development.
C2 Dependency visibility and exposure management
C: Can the supplier identify, maintain and act on critical dependencies?
Mapping training, supplier-owned data/use, identified dependency and mitigation follow-through.
Retain. Buyer-only dashboards are context; mapping enablement is a partial mechanism.
C3 Demand/supply volatility management
C: Can the supplier adapt plans and operations under volatility?
Scenario work, planning skill, implemented capacity/material response and review.
Retain. Buffers/multisourcing alone do not establish improved supplier capability.
C4 Adaptability to changing business conditions
C: Can supplier capability adapt to structural change?
Buyer-supported process/technology/location/skills transition under tariffs, M&A or downsizing; verification.
Retain. A risk description or sourcing switch alone is insufficient.
4. Interpretation and evidence boundaries

One case may inform several distinct criteria, but does not count as independent replication. A scoped historical case can demonstrate a mature process while leaving present coverage unverified. A deployed mechanism can be retained without claiming proven long-term success. A company's current scores and rank are stated in the overview and its criterion assessment.

The evidence chain is business need → supplier gap → buyer contribution → implemented supplier capability → verification → retained supplier learning. Source type, access limits, dates and scope determine confidence. No score increase follows solely from adding more references.
